(a) Each applicant must provide evidence of— (1) At least 90 days of service as a deck officer or an engineering officer on one or more tankships or self-propelled tank vessels certified to carry DL or LG appropriate to the endorsement applied for; (2) At least 90 days of rating or cadet service on deck or in the engine department on one or more tankships or self-propelled tank vessels certified to carry DL or LG appropriate to the endorsement applied for; or (3) A combination of the service in paragraphs (a) (1) and (2) of this section. (b) Each applicant must provide evidence of participation, under the supervision of a Tank Vessel-PIC, in at least 10 transfers of liquid cargo in bulk of the classification desired on tankships or self-propelled tank vessels, including at least— (1) Five loadings and five discharges; (2) Two commencements of loading and two completions of loading; and (3) Two commencements of discharge and two completions of discharge. (c) Each applicant already holding an MMC endorsed as Tank Vessel-PIC for DL and seeking an endorsement for LG, or the converse, must— (1) Provide evidence of at least half the service required by paragraph (a) of this section; and (2) Comply with paragraph (b) of this section, except that they need provide evidence of only three loadings and three discharges along with evidence of compliance with paragraphs (b)(2) and (3) of this section.

§ 13.405 Proof of service for Tank Vessel-Assistant endorsement.
text:
§ 13.405 Proof of service for Tank Vessel-Assistant endorsement. Service must be proved by either— (a) Evidence in a method prescribed by the Coast Guard from the owner, operator, or Master of a tankship or self-propelled tank vessel. The evidence must specify— (1) The name of the vessel(s), the applicable dates, and the port(s) or terminal(s); (2) The classification of cargo (DL or LG) carried while the applicant accumulated the service; (3) The number of days of deck service the applicant accumulated on the tankship or self-propelled tank vessel; and (4) That the applicant has demonstrated an understanding of cargo transfer and a sense of responsibility that, in the opinion of the signer, will allow the applicant to safely carry out duties respecting cargo transfer and transfer equipment assigned by the PIC of the transfer without direct supervision by the PIC; or (b) Certificates of Discharge from tankships with the appropriate classification of cargo (DL, LG, or both); and a letter on company letterhead from the owner, operator, or Master of one of the tankships or self-propelled tank vessels stating that they have demonstrated— (1) An understanding of cargo transfers; and (2) A sense of responsibility that, in the opinion of the signer, will allow them to safely carry out duties respecting cargo and its equipment assigned by the PIC of the transfer without direct supervision by the PIC.

section_titles: § 13.603 Requirements to qualify for an STCW endorsement for Advanced Oil Tanker Cargo Operations.
text:
(a) When all tank vessel endorsements are issued, renewed, or otherwise modified, the Coast Guard will determine, upon request, whether the applicant meets the requirements for an STCW tank vessel endorsement for service on seagoing vessels. If the applicant is qualified, the Coast Guard will issue the appropriate endorsement. An applicant for any STCW endorsement must hold the appropriate national endorsement unless otherwise specified. (b) Applicants for an STCW tank vessel endorsement must— (1) Meet the training and service requirements for the endorsement sought; and (2) Meet the appropriate standard of competence identified in the STCW Code (incorporated by reference, see § 13.103). (c) The Coast Guard will accept the following as proof of meeting the standards of competence: (1) In-service experience: Documentation of successful completion of assessments, approved or accepted by the Coast Guard, and signed by a qualified assessor, deck or engineering, as appropriate. (2) Training ship experience: Documentation of successful completion of an approved training program involving formal training and assessment onboard a school ship. (3) Simulator training: Documentation of successful completion of training and assessment from a Coast Guard-approved course involving maritime simulation. (4) Training program: Documentation of successful completion of an approved training program involving formal training and assessments.

[SECTION BREAK]

(d) The Coast Guard will publish guidelines that should be used to document successful demonstrations of competence. Organizations may develop alternative assessment documentation for demonstrations of competence; however, such documentation must be approved by the Coast Guard prior to its use and submittal with an application.

[SECTION BREAK]

§ 13.603 Requirements to qualify for an STCW endorsement for Advanced Oil Tanker Cargo Operations. (a) Every applicant for an endorsement in Advanced Oil Tanker Cargo Operations must— (1) Qualify for a national endorsement as Tank Vessel-PIC Dangerous Liquids (DL); (2) Meet the standards of competence identified in Table A-V/1-1-2 of the STCW Code (incorporated by reference, see § 13.103); and (3) Provide evidence of 90 days of sea service onboard oil tankers. The Coast Guard will accept service submitted to qualify for a national endorsement as required in § 13.203, provided that the service was on oil tankers.

section_titles: Only to be used in the event of grave and imminent danger and assistance is requ
text: Only to be used in the event of grave and imminent danger and assistance is required. Send a distress alert using digital selective calling (DSC), (press and hold the button until the alert is sent). On receipt of a DSC acknowledgement or after about 15 seconds, transmit the distress call and message on Channel 16: “Mayday, mayday, mayday “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]. “Call sign or other identification “Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) of own vessel “Mayday “This is [name, call sign and MMSI]. “Position [preferably as latitude and longitude]. “Nature of distress “Assistance required “Number of persons on board “Other information “Over”

section_titles: When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm
text: When a DSC radio receives a distress alert it will sound an audible alarm. Immediately cease any transmission that may interfere with distress traffic and continue a listening watch on Channel 16. If there is no DSC acknowledgement after a short interval (5 minutes) then, if you are able to offer assistance, acknowledge by voice on Channel 16: “Mayday “Name of vessel sending the distress message, followed by their call sign or MMSI “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times]; Call sign or MMSI of your vessel “Received mayday “State what assistance you can give [including estimated time of arrival (ETA) if proceeding to the casualty] “Over” You should use any available means to relay the distress message to an appropriate coast station. Urgency If you are concerned about the safety of a person or vessel, you can send an urgency announcement using a DSC All Ships Urgency Call, nominating a working channel. Tune to Channel 16 to make the urgency call: “Pan pan, pan pan, pan pan “All stations – say 3 times. “This is [name of own vessel – say 3 times] “Call sign or other identification “MMSI of own vessel “Please go to Channel [nominated working channel] “Out” Tune to the working channel and send your urgency message. Safety To pass safety information to HM Coastguard (HMCG) use an Individual DSC call with safety priority if available on your radio, entering the appropriate MMSI number. Transmit the DSC call and wait for the Coastguard acknowledgement. Accept the acknowledgement and ensure your radio is on the working channel indicated in the response. You should wait for the Coastguard to contact you on that channel. If your radio does not support the call, then you should make a voice call on Channel 16.

text: Use an Individual DSC call with routine priority. Enter the MMSI or select from the directory and indicate the inter‑ship channel that will be used for radiotelephony (R/T) communication. When the called radio ‘rings’ the called vessel should acknowledge the DSC call. The conversation can then start on the selected inter‑ship channel.

Foreword You are holding the yearbook of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2016. In this annual overview, you will read about how the navy was deployed in major international operations and exercises, and what happened on shore to make all of this possible. Prominent in 2016 was the provision of emergency assistance. After the devastating force of Hurricane Matthew, particularly Haiti lay in ruins and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected country to provide aid and deliver supplies. Marines were also deployed to ensure that the assistance could be distributed safely among the population. Additionally, the navy also showcased its best side in the Mediterranean by rescuing migrants in perilous situations at sea.

[SECTION BREAK]

The maintenance program for the Walrus-class submarines is well underway, and the maintenance of Zr.Ms. Van Speijk was successfully completed.

[SECTION BREAK]

Personnel underwent many new trainings, courses, and participated in (international) exercises. During the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and several ships to introduce visitors to our work.

[SECTION BREAK]

We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy. Maritime Interdiction Operations training in Den Helder. text:
The expenditures by C-ZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher than budgeted last year. This increase was largely caused by personnel expenditures and additional costs for readiness and maintenance. Furthermore, C-ZSK deployment, partly as a result of the involvement with the European Border and Coast Guard Agency Frontex and the European Union Naval Force Mediterranean, better known as EU Operation Sophia, accounted for a larger share of the BIV budget (Article 1, defense budget) this year. In response to the increasing pressure on the defense budget, an Interdepartmental Policy Investigation (IBO) was conducted this year into the readiness process. This particularly mapped and analyzed the costs of deployment and readiness of the amphibious transport ships (LPDs). It became clear that the extensive deployment was displacing the available resources for readiness for basic warfare tasks. Additionally, a significant portion of the costs incurred for deployment was not reimbursed through the BIV. The financial challenges this year were further exacerbated by a rising necessity to replace outdated systems or repair them more frequently due to delays in replacement investments. Furthermore, the available budget limited the possibilities to maintain logistical supplies, resulting in an increasing so-called logistical debt.

[SECTION BREAK]

This year, the study 'Policy Review Marine Study' was also published. The starting point for this was the namesake study from 2005, based on which the composition of the fleet changed drastically. The study revealed that despite the fact that not all investment plans had been realized, all financial expenditures and the subsequent decision-making proceeded in a controlled manner. Thus, there was no need for additional measures. Zr.Ms.

The expenditures by C-ZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher than budgeted last year. This increase was largely caused by personnel expenditures and additional costs for readiness and maintenance. Furthermore, C-ZSK deployment, partly as a result of the involvement with the European Border and Coast Guard Agency Frontex and the European Union Naval Force Mediterranean, better known as EU Operation Sophia, accounted for a larger share of the BIV budget (Article 1, defense budget) this year. In response to the increasing pressure on the defense budget, an Interdepartmental Policy Investigation (IBO) was conducted this year into the readiness process. This particularly mapped and analyzed the costs of deployment and readiness of the amphibious transport ships (LPDs). It became clear that the extensive deployment was displacing the available resources for readiness for basic warfare tasks. Additionally, a significant portion of the costs incurred for deployment was not reimbursed through the BIV. The financial challenges this year were further exacerbated by a rising necessity to replace outdated systems or repair them more frequently due to delays in replacement investments. Furthermore, the available budget limited the possibilities to maintain logistical supplies, resulting in an increasing so-called logistical debt.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.11) — narrative]
This year, the study 'Policy Review Marine Study' was also published. The starting point for this was the namesake study from 2005, based on which the composition of the fleet changed drastically. The study revealed that despite the fact that not all investment plans had been realized, all financial expenditures and the subsequent decision-making proceeded in a controlled manner. Thus, there was no need for additional measures. Zr.Ms.

text: Further developing the adaptability of the CZSK organization to changing circumstances, both within Defense and in society. This was particularly relevant for the supporting and administrative processes. In practice, this proved to be considerably more challenging, but the organization must be sufficiently prepared for the future, and therefore it is deemed necessary for this process to continue. Personnel and Organization The further elaboration of the first partial agreement was still pending in 2016, which hindered the job allocation process due to uncertainty about when a new service end system would be implemented. At the end of November, an interim arrangement was put into effect, allowing personnel with a retirement date in 2017 to choose to work longer for a period of up to two years, until the new system is implemented. Due to increasing personnel shortages and a high ambition level of the organization, it became increasingly difficult in 2016 to find suitable solutions for personnel issues and vacancies. By clearly prioritizing and, where necessary, holding even more intensive consultations with the relevant departments and units, suitable solutions were found. The task assignment of the respective unit was also regularly adjusted. Following the vision document prepared by the Defense Personnel & Organization Division (DPOD) regarding the further development of the HR functions within the organization, a Cougar helicopter conducts fast rope training with marines.

text: 24 25 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Defense, a number of advisors from HR together with colleagues from other branches of the armed forces have considered the challenges faced by HR professionals in 2020. Based on their proposals, this will continue in 2017, focusing on strategic HR themes such as talent management, strategic workforce planning, further development of the HRM system (E-HRM), sustainable employability, the change agent, and the driver of social innovation. Career Guidance Career guidance involves aligning the wishes of personnel with the opportunities provided by the organization. This alignment takes place in the form of a career conversation, which is held during each position or once every three years. This conversation focuses on personal developments in the near future and in the (medium) long term. The personal development of the employee is necessary to remain valuable to the organization. In addition to this internal mobility, the career counselor also pays attention to external mobility for employees who will not advance in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section consists of four military offices for the operational service groups, marines, technical service, logistics service, and one office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of 2016, this section had 37 military positions and 1 civilian position, of which a total of two were temporary positions. During the past year, one temporary position at the Marine Career Guidance Office and Technical Service was made permanent in the formation. Additionally, during the course of this year, a second civilian career counselor for civilian personnel was appointed.

Various groups of personnel, such as junior officers and the middle management among non-commissioned officers, experienced shortages. Unlike the previous year, a decision was made to implement more differentiation in compensation. In 2016, the 'Technical Allowance' was introduced for the next three years, which means that technical personnel in the rank of corporal up to and including warrant officer will receive a retention bonus under certain conditions. The idea behind this is that a retention bonus over multiple years will have more effect than the usual one or two years. Furthermore, an excessive number of first lieutenants of marines and corporals of technical service should eventually fill the shortages in the next higher ranks. Another sub-project within P-continuity that took shape is the establishment of Subject Matter Experts for various career paths. Questionnaires were also compiled to collect data on irregular departures and dropouts in initial training.

26 27 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Policy acts as the first point of contact (mailbox) for the Defense Staff and the Executive Staff (Main Directorates) regarding policy documents, studies, parliamentary matters, and the so-called Hague consultations. Important activities this year included efforts within the framework of the 'Development of the Armed Forces' (DOKM) concerning the strengthening and renewal of the armed forces. The Knowledge team delved into the 'new' domains of Hybrid Warfare, Cyber, and Space in 2016 and contributed to various follow-up assignments under DOKM, such as 'Information as a Weapon' and 'Information as an Enabler'. This team was also actively involved in the network of the foundation 'Netherlands Maritime Country' and the analysis of the inspection reports from the Inspector General of the Armed Forces regarding visits to CZSK units. The IMS team supports CZSK in its international contacts and collaborations in cooperation with the Defense Staff (IMS). In addition to preparations for regular meetings within the framework of Belgian-Dutch cooperation (BeNeSaM) and the Naval Steering Group (NSG) with Germany, a highlight in 2016 was the organization of the Channel Command (CHANCOM) meeting. The Policy Planning & Budgeting Office (BPB) The Planning Coordination & Integration section (PLINT) is responsible for the integral planning process within CZSK. Over the past year, PLINT, in close cooperation with Finance & Control (F&C), proposed integral measures to Consumer Products and Retail (CP&R) and All Risks (AR) to keep the realization in 2016 within the budgetary framework. Mid-year discussions were also held with the Executive Staff regarding this. As a result, the execution this year was managed. In drafting the business plan for 2017, the integral planning was further improved. The Group Leaders and CP&R were explicitly involved for the first time in determining the key multi-year objectives to be achieved and the necessary activities for that. The increased focus on the groups contributes to more product-oriented thinking and working within CZSK operations.

The desk note was replaced this year as input from the DOs in the Bureau Policy, Planning & Budgeting (BPB) process by the execution note.

[SECTION BREAK]

As a result of the internal planning process, issues such as logistical debt, obsolescence problems, and currency issues were raised. The additional funds for enhancing operational readiness in the 2017 budget will be used to address issues from the 2016 desk note. As part of the BPB office, the Programming section is responsible for the establishment of the Readiness Plan (GSP). This GSP forms the long-term plan of the CZSK and looks about ten years ahead. It serves as the basis for various sub-plans within the CZSK, including the Maintenance Plan of the DMI, the Operational Annual Plan of the DOPS, the filling plan of P&O, and the training plan of Royal Netherlands Navy Training (OKM). This year, the establishment proved to be a dynamic process, where all parties involved had to regularly adapt flexibly to rapidly changing environmental factors affecting both the GSP and the various sub-plans. Changes in the Maintenance Program for the Walrus class (IPW) are an example of this.

[SECTION BREAK]

Furthermore, 2016 was focused on creating 'contingency plans' in preparation for expected financial shortfalls. For the Mine (Counter Measures Vessels) Operational Sea Training (M(CMV)OST) section, 2016 was marked by the responsibility for planning and monitoring material exploitation, particularly in the context of further implementing the demand and supply management (VAM) organization and processes. Additionally, under the leadership of CDS/DAOG, work was done on drafting the Defense Exploitation Plan – Weapon Systems (DEP-W). Of course, there were also several material processes that required the 'magic oil' of the section. As a result of MvdS, the section was expanded at the end of the year with a new component that must coordinate the introduction of new or renewed equipment within CZSK. The Investment Bureau (INV) is responsible within CZSK for the planning and realization of the bandwidth budget allocated to the defense components from the Defense Investment Plan (DIP). The Bandwidth Investment Plan (BIP) used for this includes all bandwidth projects of the CZSK, with a five-year outlook.

By December 31, 2016, the EC3 was ready and was eighty percent staffed.

[SECTION BREAK]

The department also began taking over activities from the Sea Chain program (responsible for the CZSK migration to SAP), which ended on July 1. The program started with the takeover of the U2SAP project, which is responsible for the migration of material logistics operations from ULTIMO to SAP. U2SAP proved to be a complex project in 2016 that required significant attention from both BVIV and the users. Part of the project was completed this year, while the remaining portion is to be completed in 2017. The projects Migration Mercuur and Karel Doorman also took place under the auspices of BVIV in 2016 and were completed. Additionally, BVIV took over the documentation and temporary personnel, including contracted staff, from the Sea Chain program.

[SECTION BREAK]

The management that the department exercises over the phasing out of legacy IT systems, whose functionalities are being taken over by ERP M&F, remains essential. By the end of the year, the dismantling of a cluster of these legacy IT systems, which have influenced the material logistics operations of the Royal Netherlands Navy for many years (such as VAS, SGA, VPA, BUVA, BBSKM, FIDOKM, MATRACS, POS), was completed. This allows the department to gain further experience with the challenges surrounding the phasing out of applications. This is necessary as the phasing out or rationalization of applications is receiving increasing attention within Defense. The impetus for this is the intended transition of Defense to a new IT that is better able to support future IT-supported operations and command management. Not only is the migration to the new IT facilitated when there are fewer applications; where possible, savings on operating costs also follow. This phasing out certainly impacts the CZSK.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.16) — narrative]
The management that the department exercises over the phasing out of legacy IT systems, whose functionalities are being taken over by ERP M&F, remains essential. By the end of the year, the dismantling of a cluster of these legacy IT systems, which have influenced the material logistics operations of the Royal Netherlands Navy for many years (such as VAS, SGA, VPA, BUVA, BBSKM, FIDOKM, MATRACS, POS), was completed. This allows the department to gain further experience with the challenges surrounding the phasing out of applications. This is necessary as the phasing out or rationalization of applications is receiving increasing attention within Defense. The impetus for this is the intended transition of Defense to a new IT that is better able to support future IT-supported operations and command management. Not only is the migration to the new IT facilitated when there are fewer applications; where possible, savings on operating costs also follow. This phasing out certainly impacts the CZSK.

30 31 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations detachment present on the Greek island of Chios as part of FRONTEX. In preparation for this, considerations were made regarding the provision of good personnel care, including aftercare. Additionally, the FRISC (Fast Response Intervention Ship Command) operators received a brief supplementary medical training on dealing with drowning victims and hypothermia. In March, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel departed for the Aegean Sea as part of Standing NATO Maritime Group 2 (SNMG2). At that time, there were still significant migrant flows between Turkey and Greece, and there was a possibility of having to rescue drowning victims in the event of a SOLAS case, so a plan was developed in preparation for how to accommodate the migrants. This took into account medical aspects such as extra oxygen, medication, and a reception plan. There was considerable attention to the aspects of Hygiene Preventive Medicine (HPG). Infectious diseases, such as scabies and lice, are present among migrants, and good HPG measures could prevent this from being transmitted to the crew.

[SECTION BREAK]

An additional AMV (Medical Assistant) was also added to increase medical capacity.

[SECTION BREAK]

During its deployment in the Aegean Sea, the Van Amstel did not have to rescue any drowning victims. At the beginning of May, it became clear that the Van Amstel would also be deployed as part of FRONTEX in the Mediterranean Sea between Italy and Libya. Experiences from other ships in this area indicated that migrants often needed to be rescued from unseaworthy vessels. Reports from allied nations showed that there were many minors and pregnant women among the migrants. In preparation for FRONTEX, the reception plan for migrants was reviewed in detail regarding HPG and medical aspects. Given the potentially large number of migrants to be accommodated over 24 to 48 hours, the medical team was expanded to a total of two AMA (Medical Officers) and three AMV (Medical Assistants). Additional courses and internships in pediatrics and obstetrics were undertaken in preparation.

Diving Medical Center 2016 is the special year in which the Diving Medical Center (DMC) celebrated its fiftieth anniversary. To commemorate this, a symposium was organized in building Albatros, in the presence of the Commander of the Royal Netherlands Navy (C-ZSK). The guest speaker was Mr. Jean-Jacques Suurmond, who led the audience reflectively through the function and utility of the DMC. The DMC introduced a new emblem to celebrate its 50th anniversary and to define its own identity. The accompanying motto further underscored this: ‘Bene Emergas’. The theme of ‘safely coming back up’ is intended to guide all the work of the DMC. Among others, NLMARSOF participates in the anti-terrorism exercise Port Defender in Rotterdam. Emblem Diving Medical Center.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations In 2016, a definitive separation became possible in the examination floor of the DMC and the physician floor. This was to optimally utilize both scarce, yet equally necessary, qualities. Additionally, the reorganization of all examination processes of the DMC began. These had been in a status quo for years in execution and with much dynamism in the staffing and organization of Defense, and were due for renewal. Follow-up steps were taken for the creation of new diving tables. Research for operational deployment was continued. An example of this was the promotion trajectory of Drs.

[SECTION BREAK]

T.T. Wingelaar under Prof. Dr. R.A. van Hulst (Hyperbaric and Diving Medicine) at the AMC (former HDMC). Drs. Wingelaar was the latest addition to the series of diving physicians (still in training that year) of the DMC. Support for escape activities further expanded due to the increased safety awareness within both the ranks and visitors from outside. Furthermore, the content of this support was reviewed, and preparations were made to have it evaluated in the following year. In 2016, much energy was invested in the further development of deep diving tables.

In 2016, the Social Medical Service (SMD) provided occupational health care and personnel guidance to approximately 300 outpatient and about 50 inpatient patients, as part of the reintegration policy C-ZSK. The clinical patients almost always have an injury or damage to the musculoskeletal system and are internally guided to achieve the high fitness level of their operational unit. Over the past year, the physical profile of marines was improved, and the sports guidance was adjusted accordingly. Patients who worked internally at the SMD could, after completing their sports guidance, take both the tests for the required fitness level and the required strength level corresponding to the physical profile of marines at their own unit.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Primary Health Care Company (EGB) started on April 4.

[SECTION BREAK]

The SMD was not part of this. The SMD provided, among other things, primary occupational health care to soldiers of CZSK who were absent for more than six weeks and were seconded to the SMD. Since occupational health care also formally falls under the responsibility of the EGB, this was realized for the medical personnel of SMD through a delegation. The SMD also followed the quality requirements of the EGB regarding occupational health care. Over the past year, contacts with the Reintegration Services Center (DCR) were intensified to establish clearer agreements between SMD and DCR. The SMD carried out the reintegration in the first track for the first 12 months itself on behalf of CZSK, while the other military branches transferred reintegration to DCR after six months of absence. Meetings were held at set times with DCR: during the bi-monthly Social Medical Consultation and at 6 and 12 months of absence. With the relocation in 2016, the SMD made further progress. The intended location and the buildings on site Aardenburg in Doorn were examined, including the identification of bottlenecks and shortcomings. In the last quarter of 2016, discussions were intensified to establish a program of requirements. The SMD also provided input for the new reintegration policy document for Defense. The new document clearly described the obligations under the 'Improvement of Gatekeeper Act' and the medical examination for fitness for service, as well as the procedures to be followed in cases of social employability limitations, dropout during initial training, and service-related conditions. The new reintegration policy document will be evaluated by the unions in 2017.

text:
In het kader van de personeelsontwikkeling is er een focus op het verbeteren van de loopbaanmogelijkheden voor medewerkers binnen de Koninklijke Marine. Dit omvat het aanbieden van gerichte trainingen en opleidingen die aansluiten bij de behoeften van de organisatie en de persoonlijke ambities van de medewerkers. Het afgelopen jaar zijn er verschillende initiatieven genomen om de betrokkenheid van personeel te vergroten en een cultuur van continue verbetering te bevorderen. Dit omvat onder andere het organiseren van feedbacksessies en het stimuleren van open communicatie binnen teams. De Directie Personeel en Bedrijfsvoering blijft zich inzetten voor een professionele en gemotiveerde organisatie, waarbij de ontwikkeling van personeel centraal staat. De evaluatie van opleidingen en de implementatie van nieuwe onderwijsmethoden zijn belangrijke stappen in het realiseren van deze doelstellingen.

An important driving force for this was that the allocated budget to OKM was significantly lower than estimated, based on the training needs of the various departments within CZSK. In this context, for the first time in 2016, a portion of the budget was allocated to the different department heads within CZSK. HOKM remained ultimately responsible for the expenditure of the budget. In the case of prioritization, the question arose as to which training programs the available funds should be spent on, which was submitted to the Competent Authority.

text: Bureau Practical Learning An important task of the Bureau Practical Learning is to create internship positions for students who register for an internship at CZSK via the Defense internship bank. The bureau processes the applications, searches for internship positions within the CZSK organization, and coordinates the administrative handling. The table below indicates how many internship positions of which type have been realized: Number of CO internships 30 WO/HBO 52 MBO students 149 Sniffing internship 448 Learning agreement 22 DMI (Tetrix) 80 The Belgian-Dutch catering school (CCSp Dept Catering BENL) Commander: Major R. Dejaghere Commander NL-DET: Lieutenant Commander (SD) H.C.M. Feitsma This year partially marked 20 years of cooperation between Belgium and the Netherlands in the field of training for defense catering. Where in 1996 kitchens were equipped with mobile stoves, 20 years later we have grown into a school where various kitchens and restaurants are used as simulations of our professional practice. Although there is still much to gain in terms of infrastructure, we increasingly recognize the value of context-rich learning activities. Thus, we not only look at the ship's galley, but also pay attention to barbecues and field lunches, using various kitchen materials. It broadens the horizon of our students and helps them think solution-oriented when facing the different challenges they may encounter in their workplace. In 2016, we paid special attention to the ship's baker training. In a binational composition, research was conducted on both Belgian and Dutch ships regarding the tasks, responsibilities, and authorities of a baker on board. A new qualification profile was developed for this, resulting in a new design of the training program. In addition to the school part, there is a standard curriculum. Number of realized internship positions at CZSK in 2016.

46 47 Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Directorate of Personnel and Operations has accomplished a lot on board. It helps the bakers in training to get to know the workplace in a structured manner and to further discover the 'tricks of the trade'. This year, the school participated in a pilot program surrounding Gamified Peer to Peer Adaptive Learning (GPAL). The bakers were able to create instructional videos of their own creations and share them with other bakers for the exchange of ideas. Many experiences were gained through this pilot on board Zr.Ms. Van Amstel and Zr.Ms. Groningen. The highlight of the year was the celebration of the 20th anniversary of the training program. This was marked on two occasions. The anniversary was celebrated with the concept 'Kookeet', a reference to the annual culinary festival in the city of Bruges, Belgium. Guests could visit all the kitchens to taste small bites, thereby experiencing the content program of our training courses up close. During the first occasion, the guest list consisted of the 'hierarchical line' and various business relations, while the second occasion was open to the crew and former colleagues of the school. The second occasion was entirely organized by students of the Advanced Vocational Training. They proved to be exceptionally capable in this, which provides confidence in the successful 'delivery' of a class of young leaders who are able to maintain the Logistics Service Provision at an excellent level.

In 2016, the new LMV modules (Management Development Course) started, which were developed in accordance with the O&T methodology prescribed by the ECOD, including quality profiles, O&T proposals, and scripts. The LMV consists of six modules, with content better linked to the career and rank of the personnel. Additionally, the modules are now also open to civilian personnel of CZSK, and the practical part of the practical instructor (PLM) is anchored in the new LMV1. Besides the many LMV modules, the department also offers more and more customized training courses, such as individual modules for 1st/2nd assessors and Personnel Assessment Advisors (PBA). Defense Diving Group & Defense Diving School (DDG) Commander: kltz B.A. Visser The DDG has undergone a significant transformation over the past decades. From a relatively small department within the Mine Service, the DDG became an independent unit, including its own training institution. In terms of diving, the DDG has become the knowledge advisor to the Commander of the Armed Forces, as well as the Single Service Manager, the Expertise Center, and supplier of both training products and operational teams. Teams that are quickly and reliably deployable nationally and globally to combat threats in and from (under)water. The arrival of advanced and costly search equipment, changes in the Occupational Health and Safety regulations regarding diving, and a fourfold increase in well-trained, professional, and certified diving personnel accompanied the aforementioned changes. Overall, these are changes that placed high demands on operations. The necessary changes in operations were addressed independently. Various methods have been worked on and fine-tuned to establish a sound quality management system. Several private standards were passed, not... A training exercise for repair work underwater.

[SECTION BREAK]

52 53 Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Directorate of Personnel and Operations is unprofitable, the review. In the current situation, our training meets the private standard ISO 9001 and personnel is ISO 17024 certified at the direction of the Minister of Defence. The DDG is positioned under two separate directorates within CZSK, delivers defense-wide products, and also has customers from both non-military public organizations and private organizations. The task of the DDG includes translating objectives from the individual directorates. Commanders Intent The Commanders Intent of the DDG carries the title "guaranteed combat power." The DDG is quickly, globally, and guaranteed deployable for military diving tasks including Very Shallow Water (VSW), port protection, and salvage to serve the security interests of the Netherlands.

[SECTION BREAK]

It is the supplier of the toolboxes for the Mine Countermeasures (MCM) diving teams, maritime disaster response, and 'blue' maritime advanced search for Defence. As a specialist in high-end Mine Warfare, combined with a focus on integration with the MCM community, it demonstrates within three years to be the logical supplier for the to-be-formed MCM toolbox.

text:
The DDG is a streamlined organization that collaborates intensively with components of the four Operational Commands, the Belgian armed forces, the German Sea Battalion, the police, customs, fire department, and various ministries. It acts as the senior function group Diving for CZSK and as a knowledge advisor to the Ministry of Defence. Realization in 2016 It was an operationally interesting year for the diving company of the DDG. The diving teams participated in major international exercises such as IMCMEX in the Persian Gulf, RIMPAC in the Pacific Ocean, and Northern Coasts in the Baltic Sea. One Very Shallow Water diving team was ready for the NATO Response Force, and the various teams were deployed nineteen times, sometimes for longer durations, in support of the police and justice. There was also regular collaboration with the naval divers of the Maritime EOD company. With the signing on February 4 of a 'Letter of Intent' by Defence Minister Hennis-Plasschaert and her German colleague Ursula von der Leyen regarding cooperation with the German Sea Battalion, a more intensive collaboration between the naval diver and the 'Minentaucher' became a reality. Divers from the DDG went, among other places, to the Norwegian Eckernfjörde in May for joint training with their German colleagues. Training Institution Defence Diving School The Training Institution Defence Diving School consists of the training units Diving, Underwater Weapons and Explosives, Specialist Operations, and Medical, as well as the Office of Training & Education. In addition to executing the regular training calendar, where divers, dive leaders, and diving medical personnel were trained or retrained for the four Operational Commands (CZSK, CLAS, CLSK, and KMar), external partners, including the police, customs, the Ministry of Education, Culture & Science (OCW), and the civil sector, were also able to make use of the available residual capacity in the training programs. The second half of 2016 was also marked by the re-operationalization of the ISMix diving system (specially designed for safe diving in mine countermeasures). Therefore, the training units and the Office of Training & Education began once again to provide retraining courses.

[SECTION BREAK]

Following a tragic accident with the diving system in November 2015, a diving ban was temporarily imposed on the use of this system due to the ongoing investigation within CZSK.

Meijer EMSD The Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) stands for 'inspiring education & training in the technical military maritime domain.' The Dutch Certification Institute has ISO-certified the KMTO (ISO9001:2008). The school provides vocational and functional education for the personnel of the Technical Service (TD), but also for the (technical) personnel of other services and defense components. Furthermore, the school plays an important role in the training and development of crews of operational units, both above and underwater. For both training and development purposes, the KMTO has representative practical resources and simulators. Students All new incoming sailors of the TD of the navy begin their careers at the KMTO. In 2016, over 80 sailors, divided into eight classes, started the First Vocational Training. Additionally, four classes of aspiring corporals began the First Adjustment Module.

[SECTION BREAK]

Part of the vocational education is outsourced to the Regional Training Center (ROC) Kop van Noord-Holland.

text:
Here, every year, 48 aspiring corporals, who already gained operational experience as sailors, follow their technical MBO3 training in Mechatronics. In addition to the 'regular' entrants, there are also VeVa (Safety and Craftsmanship) students. The KMTO collaborates with Regional Training Centers (ROC) spread across the country, which provide the VeVa training, specializing in Mechatronics levels 2 and 3. The VeVa students follow their vocational education at the ROCs and receive their Practical Vocational Training (BPV) at the KMTO. In 2016, 110 VeVa students joined the KMTO. The instructors of the KMTO link the learning objectives of these students to tasks in the naval practice. For example, they sail with naval ships and/or assist with technical tasks. In addition to the new entrants, the KMTO provides education for the already serving technical personnel. Various employees follow various technical vocational and/or functional training courses at different times in their careers, both in groups and individually, ranging from one-day to long-term courses. Through international cooperation, the KMTO also trains foreign naval colleagues. For instance, twenty Italian colleagues attended the Submarine Escape Training at the KMTO, five Chilean naval personnel completed the Module Training M-Frigates MK emergency measures, six German students finished the MIRADOR training, and the Peruvian Navy was visited to undergo the mechanical lessons 'Maintenance Gun.' All in all, the KMTO provided education for about sixty foreign students in 2016. To continue achieving this, the KMTO maintains international contacts to initiate new forms of cooperation or further develop existing agreements. Instructors and students during the technical training at the KMTO at naval base Erfprins.

[SECTION BREAK]

56 57 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Directorate of Personnel and Operations Development, Innovation, and Projects In addition to the 'core business' of the KMTO, which is training students in technology, the school is working on its own development. For instance, KMTO personnel are being certified. Instructors and educational development teams are undergoing training at the Expertise Center for Defense Training (ECOD). Furthermore, the school is working on the development of training equipment and environments. In 2016, for example, a new practical training room was opened, where the KMTO provides practical training for handling submarine batteries. By conducting training in this practical room, students gain a realistic view of the practical work environment aboard a submarine.

text:
In 2016, the KMTO was also active in innovative projects and pilots, such as GPAL, the development of the VeVa learning pathway, and MBO4 'Distance Learning'.

[SECTION BREAK]

It is a simple app that facilitates 'learning in the workplace' using videos. The VeVa learning pathway being developed is intended to offer students a challenging program during their BPV (Vocational Practical Training). The assignments in the learning pathway are related to tasks aboard the ships. In this learning pathway, the KMTO can implement this in a structured, safe, long-term planable manner, fully linked to the qualification dossier and learning activities at school (ROC). The MBO4 'Distance Learning' pilot for the maintenance technician is an outsourced training program from ROC Kop van Noord-Holland, where students (corporals TD) can obtain their MBO4 Service Technician diploma from the workplace within a year. The new form of technical education, the Continuous Technical Learning Lines (DTL), was also a major project that occupied the staff of the school in 2016. The DTL are becoming increasingly known within the TD of the navy, and the changes in technical education are gradually becoming noticeable and felt within the organization. To effectively guide and support these changes, the KMTO launched the communication campaign 'DTL, Tell-Tell-Tell!'. In 2016, the school communicated intensively with all involved target groups, organizing information sessions and conducting (ship) visits. To support this, the Glossy DTL, 'Tell-Tell-Tell', was developed, which outlines all the facts about the new learning pathways. The implementation of the DTL is a long-term process, and the total transition will take considerable time.

Training This year, the NLBEOPS provided 578 training courses, ranging from the 'Commando Central Officer' (CCO) training to the 'Military Navigation Certificate' training. Students Total number of trainees: 2732 Foreign trainees: 12 First Vocational Training (EVO): 180 started, of which 155 passed (dropout 14%) Advanced Vocational Training (VVO): 92 started, of which 88 passed (dropout 5%) On January 4, the CCO training started with 24 students, including 2 from Germany, 4 from Belgium, and 18 from the Netherlands. During the basic training, 3 students dropped out: 1 Belgian (medical) and 2 Dutch students. The subsequent type training commenced with 16 students in GBW (type LCF and MFF) and 3 students in the Submarine Service type. Furthermore, 1 Belgian student continued with the MIJBO specialization and 1 Dutch student began the TACCO training. Ultimately, 15 students passed the GBW Type Training and 2 passed the Submarine Service Type Training. On December 16, the diploma ceremony took place, presided over by the Commander of the Netherlands Maritime Force, Commander Boelema Robertus, and Corvette Captain Staff Officer Colonval. The German Defense Attaché FKP S. Helbig KTZ and the Belgian representative KTZ J. de Beurme presented the diplomas to the German and Belgian students. During this ceremony, the corresponding CCO insignia was also awarded.

[SECTION BREAK]

Netherlands Submarine Command Course (NLSMCC) 2016 In January, the NLSMCC started again. This time with 6 participants: one Dutch, 3 Australians, one Canadian, and one American. Four of the participants passed, while 2 trainees did not successfully complete the course. This involved the Canadian and one of the Australian trainees. The NLSMCC has been working closely with the SMCC of Great Britain and Norway for several years with the aim of efficient deployment of available resources and the exchange of acquired knowledge and experiences. Training This year, the NLBEOPS provided 578 training courses, ranging from the 'Commando Central Officer' (CCO) training to the 'Military Navigation Certificate' training. Students Total number of trainees: 2732 Foreign trainees: 12 First Vocational Training (EVO): 180 started, of which 155 passed (dropout 14%) Advanced Vocational Training (VVO): 92 started, of which 88 passed (dropout 5%) On January 4, the CCO training started with 24 students, including 2 from Germany, 4 from Belgium, and 18 from the Netherlands. The German Defense Attaché FKP S. Helbig KTZ and the Belgian representative KTZ J. de Beurme presented the diplomas to the German and Belgian students. Four of the participants passed, while 2 trainees did not successfully complete the course. This involved the Canadian and one of the Australian trainees. This collaboration has proven to be of great value for the three countries time and again.

Lenssen 

The Maritime Battle Staff (MBS) is the deployable C2 element of NLMARFOR. The MBS has various forms of appearance. In order of complexity, these are Commander Amphibious Task Group (CATG), Commander Task Group/Commander Task Force (CTG/CTF), and specific staff elements such as Mine Counter Measures – Tasking Authority (MCM-TA). As CATG, the MBS must be deployable within a readiness period of seven to – depending on the chosen organization – twenty days. In some cases, the MBS must be supplemented for deployment as CATG with pre-identified and (partially) trained personnel from the CZSK and other operational commands (OPCOs) (augmentees). The main task of the MBS is to plan, coordinate, prepare, and execute (inter)national joint exercises and operations in which single deployed units (operationally ready naval and/or marine units) operate together to maintain operational readiness. In 2016, the MBS was active in various forms, during which the following diverse exercises were conducted:

COLD RESPONSE (February 18 to March 16) 
Participation in Cold Response was for NLMARFOR focused on maintaining the amphibious capabilities of MBS during the NRF year. Exercises were conducted in the highest spectrum of violence under the most extreme winter conditions.

[SECTION BREAK]

COMNLMARFOR led an amphibious task group consisting of Dutch, British, and American marines, Zr.Ms.

ADELBORSTEN CRUISE DURING BALTOPS (May 23 to July 1) The annual Adelborsten Cruise coincided with the Baltic Operations exercise (BALTOPS) and had a binational character this year. The task group consisted, in addition to Zr.Ms. Luymes, Schiedam, and Zierikzee, of the Belgian supply ship BNS Godetia, which served as the flagship. The main objectives of the deployment were to train and motivate the adelborsten. Zr.Ms. Urania was additionally involved in the cruise to provide the cadets with sufficient practical experience in the form of sailing hours. A challenging program was created that included at-sea replenishment, man overboard drills, navigation exercises, and hoisting exercises using the Alouette III embarked on BNS Godetia. Port visits took place in the following order: Berga, Stockholm, Kiel, and Aalborg. These visits were a good opportunity for the training naval officers to become acquainted with the representative tasks that belong to the responsibilities of an officer. JOINT VENTURE 16 (June 27 to July 11) MBS participated together with participants from the United Kingdom, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Norway in the Joint Venture 2016 exercise of the Joint Expeditionary Forces Headquarters (JEF HQ) in Cornwall, United Kingdom. Joint Venture is the annual joint exercise of the UK at the operational level. The objective of JV16 was to declare the Standing Joint Forces Headquarters (SJFHQ) Initial Operating Capable (IOC) for the JEF 2018. JV16 is part of a series of joint exercises that ultimately lead to the Full Operating Capability (FOC) status of the JEF in 2018.

BOLD ALLIGATOR (August 15 to 27) The amphibious exercise Bold Alligator (BA) took place in Norfolk.

[SECTION BREAK]

This large-scale exercise served as a rehearsal for the actual execution in 2017. Eleven members of MBS, consisting of marines and fleet personnel, participated in this exercise. BA is a large-scale amphibious maneuver in an artificial (Gulf region) scenario on the east coast of the United States. In addition to a complete amphibious task group, consisting of three large amphibious platforms with a full brigade of marines (up to 18,000 personnel), a carrier strike group (7,500 personnel) also played a prominent role to emphasize the importance of the air component. The exercise included various spectrums of violence and was primarily intended to strengthen the integration between the American marines and fleet along with international coalition partners. The participation of CZSK was valuable for knowledge exchange, such as in conducting river operations. The US Navy is partially capable of clearing a large area of mines in a relatively short time; however, they lack the capacity to do this in shallow water. The Netherlands does have this capacity and knowledge in the form of Very Shallow Water (VSW) teams, which proved to be of great added value.

[SECTION BREAK]

NLMARFOR MCM Work Up 2016 (September 5 to October 7) The triennial Binational work-up program MCM Work Up 2016 was conducted by Zr.Ms. Snellius, Vlaardingen, Schiedam, Zierikzee, BNS Primula, and a NL REMUS/VSW team. The units were supported by EGUERMIN, MOST, and the Naval Mine Warfare Mission Support Center. The deployment began with MCM training in the Firth of Forth near Leith/Edinburgh, United Kingdom. After that, there were percentage clearance and detection trials near Den Helder. The primary objectives were to improve MCM proficiency and increase operational readiness. Zr.Ms. Zierikzee practiced the detection and destruction of mines during an MCM exercise.

BA is a large-scale amphibious maneuver in an artificial (Gulf region) scenario on the east coast of the United States. In addition to a complete amphibious task group, consisting of three large amphibious platforms with a full brigade of marines (up to 18,000 personnel), a carrier strike group (7,500 personnel) also played a prominent role to emphasize the importance of the air component. The exercise included various spectrums of violence and was primarily intended to strengthen the integration between the American marines and fleet along with international coalition partners. The participation of CZSK was valuable for knowledge exchange, such as in conducting river operations. The US Navy is partially capable of clearing a large area of mines in a relatively short time; however, they lack the capacity to do this in shallow water. The Netherlands does have this capacity and knowledge in the form of Very Shallow Water (VSW) teams, which proved to be of great added value.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.36) — narrative]
NLMARFOR MCM Work Up 2016 (September 5 to October 7) The triennial Binational work-up program MCM Work Up 2016 was conducted by Zr.Ms. Snellius, Vlaardingen, Schiedam, Zierikzee, BNS Primula, and a NL REMUS/VSW team. The units were supported by EGUERMIN, MOST, and the Naval Mine Warfare Mission Support Center. The deployment began with MCM training in the Firth of Forth near Leith/Edinburgh, United Kingdom. After that, there were percentage clearance and detection trials near Den Helder. The primary objectives were to improve MCM proficiency and increase operational readiness. Zr.Ms. Zierikzee practiced the detection and destruction of mines during an MCM exercise.

70 71 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations EMERALD MOVE (September 21 to October 14) Near the Italian island of Sardinia, MBS participated in the exercise Emerald Move. A total of ten European countries, including France, Spain, and Great Britain, practiced for the European Amphibious Initiative. The aim of this initiative is to create a multinational amphibious unit that can be deployed anywhere, both in EU and NATO operations. This year, the exercise was led by Italy and focused on testing and improving cooperation between the different nationalities. The Dutch participation consisted of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, which had 117 marines on board for this purpose.

[SECTION BREAK]

The program included many different exercises and a so-called freeplay phase in which air strikes, submarine threats, and amphibious landings were practiced. ULTIMATE SWORD 16 (December 7 to 20) The Command Post Exercise (CPX) Ultimate Sword was, after Truthful Sword, the second building block for the development of 1 German/Netherlands Corps (1GNC) into a supported Joint Task Force Headquarters (Land) (JTF HQ(L)). A small team from MBS participated in the planning and execution of this exercise. This included the deployment phase in the early stage of a small joint land-heavy operation for the subsequent certification exercise Trident Jaguar 17. For 1GNC, NLMARFOR is the natural partner in the maritime domain to operate (bi-) nationally at Joint Task Force level. During the execution of the exercise at the NATO Joint Forces Training Centre (JFTC) in Bydgoszcz, Poland, the MBS team acted as Maritime Component Command (MCC) and as a maritime advisor within the Initial Command Element (ICE). The team demonstrated the potential of maritime and amphibious capabilities to support a land operation and also emphasized the importance of cooperation with commercial shipping through the Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) organization. NATO Response Force (NRF) COMNLMARFOR was responsible as Commander Amphibious Task Group (CATG) for forming and preparing the Dutch Amphibious Task Group (ATG) as part of the CZSK contribution to the NRF for 2016.

Throughout the year, the ATG was on 20 days notice-to-move. This year was designated as the standby year. The composition of the ATG varied each month. The maritime contribution consisted of one or more amphibious transport ships, a submarine, a mine countermeasure vessel, a LCF, an M-frigate, and a hydrographic survey vessel. text:
The Operations Director of CZSK established the Guideline for the Operational Readiness of Marine Units in July, under the citation title VCZSK DOPS ALG 254. This formally described the systematics of preparing and maintaining the operational readiness of marine units, thereby ensuring quality. The participation around the project 'Michiel Adriaanszoon De Ruyter Barracks (MARKAZ)' was formally organized. The staffing of the involved participation committees of the (marine) units first needed to be arranged. The Temporary Reorganization Participation Committee "Moving MARKAZ" has C MTC/GO MARNS as Head of the Unit and meeting chair. To support the information provision and involvement of the home front during missions and the future move from Doorn to Vlissingen, the Home Front Committee of the Marine Corps was established. There was significant interest from the home front to contribute to this committee. Under the supervision of the Operational Personnel Care department, various activities were initiated and executed. Under the chairmanship of the GO MARNS, the working group 'Preparing for the Introduction of Female Marines' examined what preparations needed to be made to allow female candidate-marines to enter the recruitment, selection, and ultimately the training process as of January 1, 2017. The premise was that the term marine is gender-free and remains so, and therefore the same requirements are imposed on every marine.

[SECTION BREAK]

The limited necessary adjustments were initiated at the end of 2016.

Sea Training Command (STC) Commander, also Senior Officer of Large Surface Units: Captain (ktz) A.S. Warnaar The STC is primarily responsible for the singular preparation of Dutch and Belgian naval units and the Coast Guard Cutters in the Caribbean. It also provides support to the fleet and NATO allies. The STC consists of 6 departments: Large Surface Units, Submarine Service, MOST, Force Protection and Boarding Operations (FPBO), Weapon System Management (WSM GBW), and STC-Shore. The Shore department consists of the Ship Operations Bureau (SBV), the Bureau for Consolidation, Preparation, and Maintenance (CG&B), and the Safety and Environment Bureau (V&M). Sea Training Command: Shore In 2016, the preparation trajectory for seven larger naval units was initiated. After successfully completing their SARC-1 and SARC-2, these units were further prepared at sea by the Large Surface Units department. Twenty smaller units, ranging from tugboats to training vessels, diving vessels, and landing craft, started their preparation trajectory this year. Sixteen of them were ultimately declared operationally ready. During the operational cycles of the units, they were also monitored and corrected where necessary. A total of thirty readiness checks were conducted. During such a check, it was assessed whether the units still met the high standard established during their preparation trajectory. At three units, an assessment was made at the end of their operational term on how they were preparing for maintenance. The V&M bureau supported three ships in updating their risk inventory and evaluation. Sea Training Command: Submarine Service For both operational and training missions, a total of fourteen towed array coupling actions and recovery operations were carried out. Sea Training Command: Large Surface Units (GBW) In 2016, STC GBW prepared eleven ships to various levels over twenty sailing weeks. At the beginning of the year, the next step was taken in the preparation trajectory of Zr.Ms. De Ruyter (January 25 to February 5).

Operations Directorate 

During the intervening weekend, a port visit was made to Plymouth. A successful completion led to the status of "exercise ready" and made the subsequent process at FOST in Plymouth, United Kingdom, possible. After successfully completing the Netherlands Operational Sea Training (NOST), Zr.Ms. De Ruyter was declared organically operationally ready on April 8 and was prepared for her role as flagship of SNMG2. There was also a continuation and completion of the training process for Zr.Ms. Rotterdam this year. Although it is customary for the SARC-5 and SARC-6 to be conducted by FOST, this was not feasible for Rotterdam.

[SECTION BREAK]

Therefore, it was decided to have the final part of the training process conducted by STC-GBW. This took place during the exercise Cold Response 2016. In the Norwegian fjords, under the leadership of COMNL-MARFOR and together with Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, an intensive training program was executed, after which Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was declared organically operationally ready. After the first regular training process of Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was disrupted in the previous period by the first deployment during the Ebola mission off the coast of Africa, the training process could be continued this year. Since there was a high percentage of new personnel among the crew, it was decided to restart the training process entirely. From March 29 to April 4, the SARC-3 was successfully executed, and the sailing readiness status was confirmed.

[SECTION BREAK]

Unfortunately, propulsion problems then arose, causing the continuation of the training process to be canceled once again. After the necessary repairs and modifications, the training process will restart next year.

After the ceremony, it was time for summer leave and the last weeks at home before the ship would set off again for five months. After three weeks of absence, the entire crew was present again for two days of preparations, after which the ship departed on Wednesday, July 20, towards Somalia to participate in the EU mission Atalanta. text:
Tromp checked many EU-sponsored buoys designed to attract fish. The mission commander, Commander (cdr) Luyckx, was also taken to various other units for visits regarding the approach to piracy in the Gulf of Aden. After two port visits to Oman, the next two visits were to two southern countries. First, Tanzania, where the ship spent six days in Dar es Salaam, and then Port Victoria in the Seychelles. As part of the anti-piracy mission Atalanta, Zr.Ms. Tromp provided training to the local coast guard during its port visit to Port Victoria. This training focused on local maritime capacity building, where local authorities were trained in various skills necessary for maritime law enforcement. The training was specifically tailored for the coast guard personnel of the African country, who participated with a team of nine on the helicopter deck of the Air Defense and Command Frigate. The training was conducted by the Enhanced Boarding Element (EBE) of the Marine Corps, which has been added to the frigate's crew for the current mission. The training included apprehending and searching a suspicious person, entering a space, and moving around a ship. The participants demonstrated a high level of performance and showed great enthusiasm and eagerness to learn. This combination ensured that the training was a success. The new skills contribute to enhancing the capabilities of the Seychelles coast guard to better ensure maritime safety in the future.

Jansen In the period from January 10 to June 20, 2016, Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën was deployed as the Station Ship Caribbean Area (SSCG). text: Rotterdam, and the American USS Fort McHenry. Both small vessels, manned by American, British, and Dutch marines, as well as various helicopters filled with sea soldiers, took off from the warships to participate in this exercise. From both the air and the water, about 350 marines, equipped with mortars among other things, landed. They advanced towards the nearby Namsos to secure two strategically important bridges so that ground troops could push through. There was some enemy resistance, but the marines, with the help of air support from four Norwegian F-16s, maintained control and drove the opponent away. Thus, the mission of the amphibious task group was successful. During the BALTOPS exercise (June 6 to 16), the amphibious training opportunities in a multinational setting were extensively utilized. Johan de Witt had a Swedish-Finnish task group on board for the occasion, the Swedish-Finnish Amphibious Task Unit (SFATU). The Swedish battalion staff was supplemented with Finnish staff officers and a complete Finnish company. Additionally, a German platoon was accommodated in this company, which was a guest on board Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, as part of the cooperation between the Marine Corps and the German Seebataillon. From Sweden, five Combat Boats (CB90) were also embarked that were part of the SFATU. Furthermore, several Finnish vessels (Jurmo and Jehu) joined this boat group in the theater. Finally, the Netherlands added two Cougar helicopters from the Defense Helicopter Command to the exercise. May 24, Girls' Day on Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt.

Operations Directorate

The first days of the exercise were marked by the so-called Combat Enhancement Training and Force Integration Training (CET/FIT) phase off the coast of Finland. This consisted of platoon and company actions in the Finnish archipelago. The CET/FIT was supported by Swedish Saab fighter aircraft and British Apaches from HMS Ocean. Subsequently, a tactical phase was conducted off the Swedish coast. Ultimately, the SFATU executed a joint advance with a company from the United States Marine Corps (USMC). The exercise concluded with an amphibious demonstration off the Polish coast near Ustka. After the handover of command and a well-deserved port visit in Kiel, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt prepared for the four-year maintenance (BO-2). On June 24 and June 29, the ship went to sea for the sailing family day and to support the relationship sailing day. On Sunday, July 17, the ship entered dry dock at the Keppel Verolme shipyard in Rotterdam Botlek.

From that moment, EO Lieutenant Commander (kltz) Veken took command in an acting capacity.

On February 15, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam departed for Norway for the exercise Cold Response. This trip was not only for the exercise but also for the Safety And Readiness Checks (SARC) 5 and 6. Normally, these SARCs are conducted in Great Britain under the leadership of the Flag Officer Sea Training. Due to various reasons, this was not possible, and it was now conducted under the leadership of the Dutch training authority Seatraining Command. After these training activities were successfully completed, the ship was declared operationally ready. During Cold Response, several assaults were carried out in the fjords near Namsos together with Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt and USS Fort McHenry. Onboard our ship, a British-Dutch Marine unit was deployed with British landing craft Offshore Raiding Crafts (ORC) for various amphibious tasks. [SECTION BREAK]

On April 22, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam returned to the port of Den Helder. As a ready duty ship, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam went to sea again on May 8 to escort a Russian frigate sailing through the North Sea.

[SECTION BREAK]

The planned exercise Wetfeet for the First Military Training of Marines that followed was therefore slightly shortened. [SECTION BREAK]

Rotterdam participated in the World Port Days (WHD) in Rotterdam from September 1 to 4. The short sailing trip from Den Helder to Rotterdam was in celebration of the 25th anniversary of the Central Military Hospital. The official opening of the World Port Days took place on Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. During the WHD, the ship was opened to many thousands of satisfied visitors. Onboard was a beautiful exhibition of various historical military vehicles from World War II from the Foundation '39-'45. Additionally, several members of Vessel Protection Detachments were decorated during a medal parade onboard. On September 21, a longer journey began, consisting of the exercise Emerald Move, followed by the EU training mission Sophia. Emerald Move is a large-scale international exercise for the European Amphibious Initiative (EAI), during which units are trained in amphibious operations in a European context. The exercise was led by Italy and was conducted on land and in the waters around Sardinia. Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was equipped for this with the staff of the second Marine battalion, 45-commando Z-coy, 21st Raiding Squadron, a unit of the Belgian light infantry Brigade, LCTU-1 of the SATG, and two Cougar helicopters from 300 SQN. During the exercise, the port of Cagliari was visited twice for 'rest and recreation'.

text: Operations Directorate After the completion of the exercise Emerald Move, the EUNAVFORMED mission Sophia commenced, during which Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, together with ITS San Georgio, was tasked with providing a platform for training the Libyan Coast Guard. The training for 37 Libyan trainees was conducted on board by ten British marines, five German naval technicians, two Greek boarding specialists, and an English teacher. Additionally, we also had a Cultural Advisor from CLAS, a Defense imam, and two interpreters on board to assist and support the Libyan military personnel. During the mission, 300 SQN with a Cougar, the boat company, and several marines were present for support. On October 31, the Minister of Defense, Jeanine Hennis-Plasschaert, along with the Chief of Defence, General T.A. Middendorp, visited Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. The Italian Force Commander also made regular visits on board. During the mission, the ports of Catania (Sicily), Valletta (Malta), Augusta (Sicily), and Palma (Mallorca) were visited. In Augusta, an ‘EU medal parade’ took place on board at the conclusion of the mission. On December 14, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam was welcomed back by the home front in its home port of Den Helder. Shortly thereafter, the winter leave began. Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman Commander: ktz P.F.M. Reesink, from February 10 ktz S.L. Schot The first half of 2016 was focused on preparations. After the leave, the ship was to become part of a NATO formation, with a trip to East Asia planned for 2018. However, 2016 turned out to be the year in which everything went differently than expected. On January 7, the preparation process began with SARC-1, the first step in the ‘sea acceptance and readiness check process’.

On June 3, the ship transitioned from SNMG2 to FRONTEX. For this, the ship moved to the sea area between Italy and North Africa via a short stop in Catania. The deployment for FRONTEX lasted until July 4. During this period, more than 1000 migrants were rescued from unseaworthy vessels and taken on board. At one point, there were more than 440 migrants on board. During this period, a baby was also born on board. The girl was named Gelila. The migrants were disembarked in Trapani, Valletta, or Augusta.

With the end of the Designated Maintenance in sight, she handed over command on September 2, 2016, to Lieutenant Commander (kltz) R. van Twuijver, under whose leadership the ship began its work-up process. On November 15, 2016, the maintenance period was concluded with the first Safety and Readiness Check (SARC-1). This marked the start of the work-up process, which will be completed in July 2017.

From that moment, the ship will be fully operationally deployable: "Ready for any mission." Zr.Ms. Friesland Commander: Captain (ktz) H. Suurveld MSc EMSD, from August 25 Lieutenant (ltz) 1 H. van den Berg Since September 2015, Zr.Ms. Friesland has been a station ship. On January 3, two children of naval colleagues stationed in Aruba were traditionally baptized on board. After a final visit to Curaçao on January 7 for a debriefing and loading and unloading, the ship set course for Havana, Cuba. In support of the trade mission to Cuba, Zr.Ms. Friesland docked in Havana on January 10, as the first Dutch naval ship in 66 years. After her departure on January 14, the rather stormy crossing to the Netherlands began. On January 26, the Deputy Commander of the Royal Netherlands Navy (C-ZSK) and the Chief of the Royal Netherlands Navy crew welcomed Zr.Ms. Friesland upon her return to Den Helder. After reuniting with loved ones, several weeks of being in port followed, with opportunities for leave and maintenance. The sailing program consisted until summer of alternating day trips with guests from the Marine Information Department, interested parties in a position with the navy, and sailing weeks for the qualification of pilots, flight deck, and helicopter direction officers. During the Easter weekend, a Russian task group consisting of four ships was escorted by Zr.Ms. Van Speijk in maintenance in Den Helder.

text:
Groningen would be the first major surface unit of the Dutch Navy to participate in FRONTEX. The ship's task was to patrol south of Italy to monitor migrant flows and, where necessary, to bring migrants to safety when they were in distress. However, the mission changed due to a new prioritization, into a counter-drug operation of four months in the Caribbean from June to September. In a short period, the ship and crew were prepared for their West deployment. Groningen departed on June 5 from Den Helder to sail towards the Caribbean via the Azores. For its mission, the ship was equipped with an NH-90 onboard helicopter with an accompanying flight crew. Additionally, a team of marines came on board, as well as team members from the Caribbean Coast Guard and the U.S. Coast Guard. Even before the ship entered its first Caribbean port, it intercepted four hundred kilograms of drugs. A day earlier, the naval ship inspected a distressed sailing boat, whose crew had already been brought to safety shortly before. It turned out to be a successful deployment, during which nearly three thousand kilograms of drugs were intercepted and two search and rescue operations were conducted. Upon returning to Den Helder, one of the two main propulsion engines of the ship exhibited a technical failure. This led to additional maintenance being required in the autumn.

[SECTION BREAK]

Operations Directorate Operations Directorate was scheduled to repair the propulsion system. A planned sailing period to train navigation officers was canceled. However, a training week was conducted in November focusing on helicopter operations. In the last month of the year, the ship undertook various activities to strengthen ties with the province of Groningen. On Thursday, December 8, the traditional Christmas tree was hoisted in the mast by a delegation from the aforementioned province. A day later, a cheque worth €2,500 was donated to the children's hotel Stichting de Burcht Wedde by the commander and a delegation from the crew.

text:
Pelikaan, the ship transported 450 tons of aid supplies to the coastal areas of Haiti. During this deployment, the naval ship primarily focused on alleviating human suffering and laying a solid foundation for other aid organizations to build upon. After the deployment in Haiti, the patrol ship conducted over a month of coast guard operations in cooperation with the Coast Guard Caribbean Area. During this period, the naval ship intercepted a Venezuelan drug transport. Additionally, it played an important role in the ceremonial celebration of the 240th anniversary of the first international recognition of American independence by the Netherlands on Sint Eustatius. A fishing vessel in distress was also rescued and brought to safety, and Zr.Ms. Holland docked in Aruba. Marines stationed there embarked aid supplies, such as water and tents for Haiti.

98 99 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations conducted numerous shipping inspections. Halfway through the voyage, the crew celebrated their midterm in Curaçao, where members of a helicopter squadron from the U.S. Coast Guard and members of a U.S. law enforcement team embarked. The following period was therefore focused on drug enforcement operations in collaboration with U.S. authorities. Over a span of more than a month, several drug transports were successfully disrupted, and six crew members from a sinking ship were rescued and brought to safety.

After the summer leave, the next exercise was already on the horizon: the MCM Work-up trip of NLMARFOR.
