Schiedam also went into maintenance in Zeebrugge for six weeks. During this period, the crew was distributed across various units and departments, while the maintenance was carried out by the Binationaal Support Team. In week nineteen, the ship conducted the Control Operations of Sailing Units, which was completed satisfactorily. From the end of May, the ship participated in the Adelborsten Cruise. During the cruise, three groups of four to five cadets were able to sail along for two weeks. The journey began with a port visit to Ostend to participate in 'Oostende voor Anker', a large maritime event. The ship then sailed through the Nord-Ostseekanaal to Berga, where the start of the international exercise BALTOPS took place. In these two weeks, in addition to mine hunting, various maneuver exercises were conducted with a large naval formation. BALTOPS concluded in Kiel, where the large maritime event Kieler Woche was taking place at that time. After departing from Kiel, the cadets navigated via the Little Belt, the Great Belt, and along Copenhagen to Aalborg. This was also the last foreign port, after which the group returned to Den Helder.

104 105 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations of Eguermin and MOST conducted a mine countermeasures (MCM) work-up program. The MCM WORK UP started with the participating ABNL ships gathering in the North Sea, after which they proceeded together towards the Firth of Forth. There, a brief visit was made to Leith, and the 'Pre-Sail Conference' took place. The NLMCMFOR staff, EGUERMIN, and the Mission Support Center (MSC) presented their plans for the planned MCM exercises. In the Firth of Forth, the focus was primarily on the correct deployment of mine hunting systems under various environmental conditions and procedural training. This phase concluded with a port visit to Sunderland, United Kingdom. Subsequently, the connection began with various trials off the Dutch coast, examining how effectively and efficiently these systems operate. Unfortunately, the trials were hampered by poor weather conditions, but the initial results were interesting. In early November, Zr.Ms. Schiedam carried out several weeks of Beneficial Cooperation in conjunction with the duties of the Ready Duty Ship. Among other tasks, an aircraft bomb was cleared off the Belgian coast. The ship then conducted Continuation Training (CT) under the guidance of MOST, successfully completing it. After the CT, the ship remained in Den Helder until the winter leave for modifications to the radio central.

During two short sailing periods near Den Helder, where the home port was visited every day to embark and disembark personnel for the VMBs, the first steps were taken regarding familiarization with the new IPW systems. The first overseas trip, in which Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw would go underwater for the first time after the BO south of Norway, was scheduled only after the summer leave.

text:
Zeeleeuw departed for Norway to conduct VMBs and Sea Acceptance Trials (SATs).

[SECTION BREAK]

The next milestone in the training program of Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw was the achievement of SARC 4A. As a result of the IPW, the training trajectory of Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw was more extensive and spread over a longer period than in a typical training trajectory. In Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw shortly after modernization off the Norwegian coast. Modernized submarine Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw during dry exercises.

[SECTION BREAK]

110 111 Operations Directorate Operations Directorate in practice meant that SARC 4 was divided into several blocks. In this context, Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw departed on October 6 to set course for Ulsnes, near Stavanger in Norway. At this location, from October 12 to 14, the Zeeleeuw was assessed by the SARC team and was awarded the status SARC 4A. Subsequently, a visit was made to the port of Stavanger, after which the S803 visited the Sognefjord. Among other activities, the Maintenance Trials (BNO) of the GTHW, sensor calibrations, a deep dive, displacement and stability tests were on the agenda, with support from Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Vlaardingen. The journey took the crew via Bergen further along the acoustic measurement track, where the acoustic signature of the vessel was mapped, to the Swedish Göteborg and back towards the Norwegian Fjords for the final measurements. During this phase of the journey, the crew had the opportunity to further familiarize themselves with the operation of the IPW systems. Additionally, necessary new methods and procedures were further developed. Besides the permanent crew, personnel from JIVC/SATS were often on board to further test and develop the IPW systems. More than seven weeks after departing from the Netherlands, Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw arrived back in Den Helder on November 25.

text: 1st Marine Combat Group (1MCG) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) I.D.L. Moerman MMS 2016 was largely focused on preparation and readiness for the 1st Marine Combat Group (1MCG). The MCG staff prepared in the first half of the year and was declared operationally ready during the Storm Tide exercise in Belgium by the MTC. 11 Raiding Squadron completed their preparation year in the first half of the year and was certified MARC-4 from June. 13 Raiding Squadron and 15 Reconnaissance Surveillance & Target Acquisition Squadron both began their preparation programs in August. Command Changes Regarding the subunits, the appointments were as follows: C-10 CSS SQN: Major (majmarns) S. Baan C-11 RSQN: Major (majmarns) A.T. Broersma C-12 RSQN: Major (majmarns) G.C. Roosjen MA C-15 RSTA SQN: Captain (kaptmarns) F.A. Achttien until April; thereafter Captain (kaptmarns) T.G. de Smidt BBA took over command. text:
Operations Directorate Marine Spearhead Task Unit (MSTU) The MSTU is a rapidly deployable unit of the Marine Corps, which can be deployed within 48 hours. The core of the unit is a Raiding Squadron, supplemented by enablers from 10 Combat Service Support Squadron, 14 Combat Support Squadron, and 15 Reconnaissance Target Acquisition Squadron. Command & control is provided by a staff element from the MCG staff. In the first half of 2016, this task was assigned to 12 Raiding Squadron. From August, 11 Raiding Squadron took over this task.

[SECTION BREAK]

VPD As in previous years, VPD teams were also deployed in 2016 for the protection of Dutch ships. This year, 2 MCG provided the six primary VPD teams and 1 MCG was required to provide five secondary VPD teams. During the first half of the year, 13 RSQN fulfilled this task. From August 2016, 12 RSQN took over this task again. Detachment Sint Maarten Personnel from 13 RSQN completed two rotations in Sint Maarten during the first half of the year. The marines provided support to the civil authorities where necessary. National Assistance Personnel from 1 MCG was also deployed in the national domain in 2016. For example, in March, a Maritime Advanced Search Team (MAST) provided support to an operation by the Ministry of Security and Justice in Weststellingwerf.

[SECTION BREAK]

Training and Exercises 2016 was largely focused on training and preparation for 1 MCG, and the annual program was well filled. The larger exercises of 2016 included shooting training in the United States (Black Alligator) and mountain training in Garelochhead, Great Britain. 11 RSQN completed the preparation cycle in the first half of 2016. Training during this period included winter training in Norway, SOUT in Germany, BHT and Fast Rope in the Netherlands, and concluding with the MIO and Marsoc Certifex.

[SECTION BREAK]

With the completion of the preparation cycle, 11 RSQN was MARC-4 certified and ready for operational deployment. This meant that 11 RSQN was on standby as Marine Spearhead during the second half of the year. Members of the VPD in the Red Sea aboard the Red Zed II. Three-day mountain exercise including survival night, 13 RSQN and 22 RSQN.

As part of the preparation for the VJTF(L), 11 RSQN participated in the exercise Black Alligator with the aim of conducting a Live Tactical Firing Exercise up to level 4. Subsequently, 11 RSQN, including the enablers from the supporting units, participated in the integration exercise Silver Arrow in Latvia. During this exercise, the unit operated as part of the Grenadier Guards Battle Group. 12 RSQN participated in the exercise Cold Response in Norway in February. Throughout the rest of the year, 12 RSQN provided extensive support to training and events.

[SECTION BREAK]

As a result, it had little opportunity to conduct its own training. The squadron also had the task of providing the secondary VPD capacity during this period.

[SECTION BREAK]

In October, a Troop from 12 RSQN participated in a Live Fire Tactical Training of the SATG in Sweden. A shooting team from 12 RSQN took part in shooting competitions with our British and American colleagues. In March, this was the USMC Long Shot Competition in Quantico and Camp Lejeune, and in September, the Royal Marines Operational Shooting Challenge near Lympstone. The mountain training took place in 2016 from October 17 to November 18 in the vicinity of Garelochhead, Great Britain. Both 13 and 22 RSQN, along with approximately 30 novices from other operational units (SATG, SSG, NLMARSOF, 2 MCG), completed the Mountain Movement and Survival Course (MMSC), Mountain Warfare Training (MWT), and a final exercise during this training. Additionally, the MTC provided a Cadre Conti training for the non-commissioned officers and officers, thereby ensuring a good implementation of differentiated training, allowing for a professional deepening. Besides the larger exercises, many unit trainings took place at the squadron level or lower. 14 CS SQN conducted its own training in the Netherlands, such as a 'Last Animal Course', shooting training at the ISKH, and an exercise in the Marnewaard.

116 117 Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate contributed to Atalanta and various Vessel Protection Detachments (VPD) for the protection of Dutch merchant shipping. In the Caribbean, 2MCG provided various Guard Teams (GT) for counter-drug operations and detachments were supplied to support local authorities in Sint Maarten. 2MCG also contributed to FRONTEX in the Mediterranean and provided a security team for the training of the Libyan Coast Guard during Operation Sophia. Throughout the year, 2MCG was on standby as the core of the ‘Landing Force’ for the NATO Response Force under the command of COMNLMARFOR. For the staff of 2MCG, two major exercises were scheduled. The first was the Joint Arctic Training (JAT), organized for the training of units from 1- and 2MCG, as part of the first training year. This was an exercise in which more than eight hundred military personnel participated, as large parts of 24 Combat Support Squadron (CS SQN) and 25 Reconnaissance Surveillance & Target Acquisition Squadron (RSTA SQN) were also involved. The JAT concluded with a final exercise at MCG level. Another major maneuver was the European Amphibious Initiative (EAI) exercise Emerald Move in Sardinia (Italy), where the MCG staff commanded a multinational squadron and utilized various landing craft and Cougar helicopters.

[SECTION BREAK]

20 Combat Support Squadron (CSS SQN) began supporting the JAT in 2016. From two fixed locations and several field locations, the 20th enabled the achievement of 2MCG's objectives. Subsequently, the MARSOC CERTIFEX was supported. The chain was also supported again during the Close Quarter Battle Instructors-course (CQBI) and the Live Fire Special Operations Urban Terrain module. 20 CSS SQN also participated in Emerald Move and supported the Sniper Concentration of 25 RSTA SQN. Despite limited space in the program, the 20th was able to conduct its own training during Emerald Move. The 21 RSQN successfully completed its training year and was MARSOC-certified at the end of the first quarter. Subsequently, they, in combination with 23 RSQN, were deployed extensively. Both units provided various rotations for CBMI and the Marine detachment in Sint Maarten. Additionally, they also supplied the VPDs and an EBE on board Zr.Ms.

A FST participated in the Joint Fires Exercise Jasco Blue, together with units from the USMC and Royal Marines. The Recce Sniper Troop conducted a Sniper Concentration Exercise in Curaçao. Additionally, a Mortar Troop participated as part of the Very High Readiness Joint Task Force (VJTF) in the international exercise Noble Mariner and in the VJTF exercise Silver Arrow. Members of the VPD take anti-piracy measures to defend the ship, such as placing concertinas.

[SECTION BREAK]

118 119 Directorate of Operations Directorate of Operations Netherlands Maritime Special Operation Force (NLMARSOF) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J. van Nee 2016 showed a high operational tempo for NLMARSOF. Many exercises and frequent deployments took place at the team level, but despite this small scale, the workload was high. For the staff and logistical support of NLMARSOF, the preparation, guidance, and processing of these small-scale deployments differed little from large-scale deployments. For the majority of activities, the focus this year was primarily on one of the three main tasks of NLMARSOF, namely Military Assistance (MA).

[SECTION BREAK]

During the annual multinational exercise Flintlock, led by the US Special Operations Command Africa (SOCAFRICA), the Joint Special Operations Taskforce - Trans Sahara (JSOTF-TS) contributed to the Trans Sahara Counter Terrorism Partnership (TSCTP). The Netherlands has been participating in this initiative since 2017.

text:
This year, a combined team from NLMARSOF, MARSOC, and ATG was involved in training and educating Senegalese NAVYSOF and COFUMACO, the equivalent of MARSOC and ATG. This training for special units took place in the maritime border region of northern Senegal and Mauritania. In 2016, NLMARSOF also provided Military Assistance elsewhere on the African continent. Among other things, to African partner units during the multinational maritime exercise Cutlass Express, led by Naval Forces Africa (NAVAF), where the focus was again on providing training in and around East Mauritius. Additionally, NLMARSOF trained alongside Danish SOF colleagues sister units from Cameroon and Nigeria in Cameroon, as part of the also multinational exercise Obangame Express. Serious deployment for NLMARSOF took shape in 2016 by deploying operators and staff on a small scale together with the Korps Commando Troepen within the Combined Joint Special Operations Task Force Iraq (CJSOTF-I), at and from Baghdad International Airport. In this mission, the focus was also on Military Assistance. Iraqi sister units and staff were trained and prepared for the fight against Islamic State (IS). NLMARSOF also trained and tested its basic and specialized skills again this year. For practicing SOF skills in ‘mountain and arctic’ conditions, one team and staff participated in Cold Response 2016. This time, integrated cooperation took place with American colleagues from Seal Team 2 and Norwegian colleagues from MJK within SOTG-40.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Snipers of NLMARSOF were able to sharpen and practice their skills in Denmark during Falcon Eye in 2016. This year again showed that the connections with Denmark, particularly the Fromandskorpet (FMK), are strong and have been of great value to NLMARSOF for years. The training opportunities in Denmark have also increased over the years, in line with the further professionalization of the Danish SOF component. An example of this was exercise Nighthawk, which was led by a Danish SOCC and where NLMARSOF participated with a team within SOTG 1.1. Seabased Support Group Commander: Major (majmarns) S.

text:
Peters In the past year, various logistically complex matters took place. Because the other operational units had a more than full Operational Year Plan (OJP), combined with various 'serious deployments', this placed a corresponding strain on the necessary logistical support. Although smaller units often went out, more smaller exercises meant significantly more work for logistical support and command. Also, the essential NLMARSOF during the counter-terrorism exercise Port Defender.

[SECTION BREAK]

120 121 Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate faced regular pressure in the execution of an exercise or the necessary maintenance of used materials. For some already scarce operational pool resources, this meant that they were less available for certain units. Additionally, progress was made in further optimizing operations supported by SAP. To apply SAP optimally, several adjustments were made in the setup. However, working with SAP remains specialist work, which places increasingly higher demands on the training level of the personnel. In terms of training, there were also various challenges regarding IATA, ADR, and munitions. Regulations require that certain tasks be performed by qualified personnel.

[SECTION BREAK]

This year, the Material Management Quality Monitor (MKM) was also conducted. The unit passed this assessment with flying colors and sees the MKM as an excellent supplementary tool for further optimizing operations, thereby providing even better support to the operational units. From the unit, several specialists were again deployed with other units for exercises and 'real operations' to support them worldwide in their specific specialties. This includes logistics and munitions management, armaments technicians, communications service, and automotive mechanics. Expert groups have been established for the potential new barracks in Vlissingen. All specialist knowledge has been consolidated in this project with the aim of creating a logistics operational complex that is maximally designed to support the units of the Corps of Marines operationally in the future.

[SECTION BREAK]

Surface Assault and Training Group (SATG) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J.W.

text:
Scheltema This year was marked by the development of the unit. It was the first time that the intended development methodology was applied at SATG to an operational subunit. Before the summer leave, LCTU-1 was officially certified as operationally ready. The second half of 2016 was characterized for LCTU-1 by the international exercise Emerald Move and operation Sophia. Operational Deployment Just before the summer leave of 2016, it became known that Zr.Ms. Rotterdam might be deployed for the EU mission Sophia in the Mediterranean Sea. The focus of this mission would be on training the Libyan Coast Guard so that they could better control and limit the migration flows to Europe. After the summer leave, it was still unclear whether the mission would proceed and what the exact tasks of LCTU-1 would be.

[SECTION BREAK]

During the exercise Emerald Move 2016, it was announced that Sophia would take place, and from the exercise near Sardinia, Zr.Ms. Rotterdam sailed on to Sicily for the 'swop' to Sophia.

[SECTION BREAK]

The task of LCTU-1 was to provide the 'guard teams' together with personnel from 21 Rsqn and to act as hosts for the Libyan trainees. Additionally, LCTU-1 supported the British trainers in providing various vessels during the 'boarding' training. Sophia was a special mission for LCTU-1, as the task package did not consist of assignments for which marines are initially trained. Nevertheless, Sophia was an interesting and educational period for LCTU-1, during which the camaraderie within the unit was significantly strengthened. For the European exercise Emerald Move, the action was prepared on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam during a briefing with a model.

Operations Directorate Operations Directorate Training and Exercises In the first period of 2016, LCTU-1 had not yet been formed and consisted of a staff with ABU (LCCT-Heavy). In addition to individual training, personnel from LCCT-Heavy participated in the Joint Arctic training. The reconnaissance element of the unit also supported the NLMARSOF exercise Flintlock in Senegal. From early April, all units were available again, and the assigned vessels were also prepared to SARC-3, so they could be handed over to LCCT-Heavy. From this HOTO, the combined unit was named LCTU-1 and worked together to SARC-4 and MARC-3. After training its own TTPs during various support tasks such as Practical Training for Officer of the Marines (POTOM) and Amphibious Dagger, support was provided from Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Rotterdam in May and June to the exercise Stormtide, initiated by the Belgians. Due to poor weather conditions, not all amphibious aspects were addressed.

[SECTION BREAK]

After supporting the FINEX of the POTOM in Rotterdam, LCTU-1 embarked on Zr.Ms. Rotterdam to support the MARSOC CERTIFEX of 11 Rsqn and to certify LCTU-1 to MARC-3.

[SECTION BREAK]

Also during this exercise, the weather conditions were not favorable, and improvisation was necessary to certify the amphibious ship-to-shore capability. Ultimately, this was successful on Bankert Boulevard in Vlissingen, and LCTU-1 was declared operationally ready by MTC. After the summer leave, LCTU-1 prepared for the exercise Emerald Move. This amphibious exercise at brigade level, held near Sardinia, was initiated by the European Amphibious Initiative (IAE/EAI). The emphasis during this exercise was on demonstrating European amphibious capability. Through various sub-exercises and a high degree of integration exercises with various international partners, Emerald Move proved to be of great value for the operational deployability of the unit. Both the staff, the vessels, the beach element, and the reconnaissance element received more than sufficient training in Emerald Move to be well-prepared for the EU mission Sophia. Second Landing Craft Task Unit (LCTU-2) In January, part of the personnel from LCTU-2 participated in winter training in Norway. Thirteen personnel members were awarded a cold weather badge. Subsequently, amphibious support was provided to the exercise Cold Response in the Norwegian coastal waters.

text:
The months of May, June, and July were filled with participation in various exercises such as Safeguard, EMMV, and MIO training for 11 RSQN. After the summer leave, the World Port Days in Rotterdam began, where support was provided with 2x LCVP and 3x FRISC. After this, LCTU-2 supported the 22 RSQN with MIO training.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the end of November, the staff and 2x LCVP and 3x FRISC went to Brown Alligator in Sweden. Here, a shooting training for SATG was completed. FRISC Squadron Operational Deployment After a short preparation, in January 2016, a unit of five personnel was added to the Border Security Team (BST). This is an interdepartmental team that assists the Greek Coast Guard in processing the flow of migrants from Turkey. This support was part of FRONTEX, the European agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders. The BST was a new Dutch concept, consisting of personnel from the Royal Marechaussee, port police, customs, and the Royal Netherlands Navy. In this successful concept, a FRISC was chosen to patrol the territorial border between Turkey and Greece. This enabled early detection of migrants. Ultimately, hundreds of boat migrants were rescued, and arrests were made of individuals suspected of human smuggling. During the exercise Brown Alligator, amphibious and infantry operations with live firing by marines were practiced.

[SECTION BREAK]

124 125 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations The coordination between the caregiver and the enforcer proved to be a challenging task for the crews of the FRISCs. Ultimately, the contribution lasted until December 2016. After that, due to the decrease in the flow of migrants, it was decided to end the contribution at sea. Training and Exercises One of the other primary tasks of the FRISC Squadron was to provide vessels for FRISC training and to supply personnel and vessels for the various missions of the LCTUs. In addition, the FRISC Squadron trained intensively throughout the year with NLMARSOF units for the national task in the area of maritime counter-terrorism. Attention was also paid to intensifying cooperation with NLMARSOF in the training of conventional support for operations on and over water.

text:
Franken from August 31, 2016 In 2016, the CZSK had the following 'large' KBW units: six mine countermeasure vessels: Zr.Ms. Makkum, Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Urk, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, Zr.Ms. Willemstad, and Zr.Ms. Zierikzee, as well as two hydrographic survey vessels: Zr.Ms. Luymes and Zr.Ms. Snellius and the torpedo vessel: Zr.Ms. Mercuur.

[SECTION BREAK]

The 'small' KBW fleet consists of diving vessels, tugboats, LCVPs (Landing Craft Vehicle Personnel), LCU (Landing Craft Utility), FRISCs, the Marine Training Vessel (MOV) Van Kinsbergen, and Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Urania. Assembly and Commissioning The minehunter Makkum has started the commissioning process under the leadership of MOST in Zeebrugge after major maintenance. Operational Activities Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen and Willemstad were part of NATO's permanent mine countermeasures squadron in 2016: the Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 1 (SNMCMG1). In addition, participation in various exercises took place and contributions were made to operation Beneficial Cooperation. Equipment In 2016, Zr.Ms. Makkum and Urk underwent Named Maintenance in Zeebrugge, coordinated by the new Binational Support Team (BST). The BST was also evaluated in its first year of existence by both the Belgian Navy and the Royal Netherlands Navy. This team is responsible for the Named Maintenance of Dutch and Belgian minehunters, which makes a crew available and reduces the costs of Dutch personnel in Belgium. The effectiveness and efficiency of the BST exceeded expectations, and this team continues its work with the support of the Belgian Navy. Personnel On August 31, Captain (ktz) J. Franken took over the position of Group Leader Mine Service and Klein Bovenwater from Captain (ktz) J. van Zanten. He had a staff of three people (Chief of the Crew, Weapon System Management Officer, and NLMARSOF Ship Manager during the counter-terrorism exercise Port Defender.

As in every previous year, the first major commitment of 2016 was facilitating the NLSMCC.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.65) — narrative]
During this period, a multitude of exercises were conducted in Norwegian and British waters by a large number of units in support of this training. Once again, a Dutch student succeeded this year. He was added as a commander to the Submarine Service. The next milestone in the IPW has now been achieved; namely, the continuation of the SARC trajectory of Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.65) — narrative]
This brought many new challenges for this first IP unit. Operational deployment also formed an important part of the Submarine Service's tasks this year. Additionally, participation in necessary international exercises took place throughout the year, including Joint Warrior 161 and Cold Response. Furthermore, support was provided to Flag Officer Sea Training (FOST), and Zr.Ms. Bruinvis was present at the Belgian Navy Days in Zeebrugge. Naval Aviation Service (MLD) Group Leader: Commander (cdr) G.A. Polet.

text:
For the Naval Aviation Service, 2016 proved to be another dynamic year. The introduction of the NH90 helicopter was still in full swing for a long period. The availability of helicopters showed an upward trend, and user experience with the NH90 helicopter also increased as a result. Corrosion negatively affected the deployment of helicopters, but improvement programs showed increasing returns. The multitude of configurations of the helicopter also had a negative impact on availability, as the number of spare parts in the supply chain was insufficient. Retrofit programs were underway to standardize the helicopter fleet. The material exploitation budget for the NH90 helicopter was significantly increased during the year.

[SECTION BREAK]

The first effects are expected in 2017.

Operational Data In 2016, the MWC provided operational data to operational units and staffs nearly ninety times.

[SECTION BREAK]

Furthermore, seven pre- and post-deployment briefings were conducted. Analysts were again active as seariders on board; primarily for data collection but also, upon request, for training. Additionally, analysts also functioned as instructors this year. The MWC conducted the Acoustic Consolidation Course and Radar Techniques and Operations training in 2016.

[SECTION BREAK]

Military Operations in Extreme Conditions (MOX) In 2016, the role of Single Service Manager for MOX for the entire Dutch armed forces was further developed. For this, the Joint Knowledge Center MOX (JKCMOX) participated in national and international consultation structures in the Mountain & Arctic domain, such as the International Snow Safety Workshop in the USA and the Mountain Training Initiative in Austria and the Netherlands. The JKCMOX also supported (inter)national exercises. Examples include the Joint Arctic training in Norway, the Cold Response exercise with CLAS 43rd BE in Norway, the advanced module Avalanche Safety in Switzerland, and the retraining of UK Mountain Leader to Mountain Leader Teacher. In the jungle domain, a Military Tracker Instructors (MTI) course and a Military Tracker training were conducted, as well as two Jungle Warfare Instructors courses. In the last course, three students from CLAS and three from the CZSK were trained. Additionally, under the supervision of the JKCMOX, a Ground Sign Awareness Instructors course was conducted. Through contributions to the various trainings, the JKCMOX achieved a better structure in the Instructor, Teacher, and Supervisor system and facilitated the exchange of more experience within the jungle domain among the armed forces components. This will enable military components in the future to conduct their own trainings and courses, while the JKCMOX will continue to ensure quality.

text:
Manaslu Expedition In 2016, a unit from the Marine Corps climbed one of the world's highest mountains, Manaslu (8,163 m) in Nepal. As climbing high mountains falls within the expertise of the JKCMOX, Mountain Leaders from the JKCMOX supported the expedition. In preparation, several mandatory risk-mitigating activities were established for all participants, such as mandatory participation in the Alpine project in 2015, a medical examination, avalanche cases, a week of team building, and a simulated altitude activity in the pressure chamber of the Center for Humans and Aviation (CML). The expedition was also meteorologically prepared in close collaboration with the Joint Meteorology Group. By reaching the summit on May 9, 2016, the Mountain Leaders of the Marine Corps made Dutch history 60 years after the first ascent: the first military expedition to a mountain higher than 8,000 meters.

[SECTION BREAK]

132 133 Operations Directorate Hydrographic Service Chief Hydrographer: Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck In January, Chief Hydrographer Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck and Director of Data Acquisition and Analysis of Rijkswaterstaat V.N. Zeijlemaker signed the management statement of the Dutch Hydrographic Institute (NHI). This provided a new impetus for the collaboration between both organizations. In June, the biennial North Sea Hydrographic Conference (NSHC) took place in Dublin, Ireland. The Dutch Chief Hydrographer chaired this conference. Important themes included participation in European projects, establishing a common reference level for depths, and coordinating hydrographic survey activities. In September, the Steering Committee of the International Centre for ENC’s, which distributes ENCs on behalf of more than forty hydrographic services worldwide, met in Amsterdam. During this meeting, the Chief Hydrographer was elected as the chair of the Steering Committee. In December, the IHO Meso American & Caribbean Sea Hydrographic Conference (MACHC) took place in Belem, Brazil. Again, the Dutch Chief Hydrographer chaired the conference. Important topics discussed included the international alignment of nautical charts, promoting the 'blue economy' by making hydrographic data and products more accessible, Capacity Building, and Satellite Derived Bathymetry (SDB). The MACHC elected the Chief Hydrographer as the representative of the region in the new IHO Council, alongside Brazil.

The recording campaign was interrupted to support the Human Disaster Relief Operation Haiti after Hurricane Matthew.

[SECTION BREAK]

The hydrographic team and recording system were embarked on Zr.Ms. Holland to conduct hydrographic REA operations along the Haitian coast. The ports of Port-au-Prince, Miragoane, Jeremy, and Les Cayes were mapped with the new MHP2 survey package. The MEIC not only provided searider support. Many operations and exercises were supported with specific products, such as Environmental Briefing Dockets (EBD) and Additional Military Layers (AML). Additionally, several missions were supported with very specific information deliveries, including for the Harpoon Trials, the MCM Work-Up, the LFAPS trials, and Torpedo Firing eXercises (TFX) southwest of Great Britain. These missions required custom-made products that integrated as much information as possible to provide a complete picture of the prevailing conditions.

[SECTION BREAK]

Support and Capacity Building The Hydrographic Service was also able to provide support for hydrographic education in 2016, for example, by allowing students from the Ocean Technology (Hydrography) program at the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz to sail with HOVs. The REMUS course held in Ostend for the Defense Diving Group and the Mine Service also received support from a hydrographer this year. Equipment Just like in 2015, the management of hydrographic quality standards remained a continuous source of concern in 2016. Throughout 2016, the service continuously assisted the DMO and DMI organization in efforts to maintain the material condition of hydrographic and METOC equipment within CZSK according to the prevailing qualitative standards. In 2016, a new hydrographic network was established aboard the HOVs, including a data server with greater capacity, faster network connections, and new recording and processing PCs. With this modernization, fast data transfer and good data storage are guaranteed for the near future.

For the first time in 2016, Ellipsoid Referenced Surveying (ERS) was used on the HOVs. With ERS, it is possible to reference the measured GPS antenna height to a Zr.Ms. Snellius.

text:
Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate has accurately established an ellipsoidal reference surface. With the availability of the Ellipsoid-LAT difference surface, a result of research from Delft University of Technology, a direct link between GPS height and the LAT reduction surface is now possible. In this way, measured depths can be directly referenced to LAT, without the need for tide measurements. To enable the ERS technique, the latest GNSS techniques have also been utilized. With the use of new GNSS receivers and a correction signal, the Hydrographic Surveyors (HOV) now have a very precise positioning capability at the decimeter level. In 2016, the need to replace the current Side Scan Sonars with a new system was approved. This means that in 2017, the replacement of the current systems can begin. This replacement ensures object detection during hydrographic surveys for the near future and allows the ships to continue meeting the requirements of the International Hydrographic Organization. Military Personnel Despite a tight personnel situation, the hydrographic and METOC personnel have been deployed multiple times for missions, training, and large exercises, see deployment MEIC (2.4). Their specialization and expertise are highly valuable and contribute significantly to the success of missions and exercises. Retaining this knowledge and expertise requires continuous attention, given the tight personnel situation combined with the limited training budget.

Civil Production In addition to regular production work, significant efforts were made in 2016 to complete the SHIP2 project. The topics Bathymetry and Spatial Data Infrastructures have been finalized.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, the Civil Production section was closely involved in the preparations for ISO certification. Personnel were trained as internal auditors or contributed to the creation of process descriptions. Work was also done on a quality workbook, which describes work instructions. A total of 53 new ENC cells were published, along with 9 paper nautical charts for the corresponding area. Furthermore, a new edition of HP1 The Netherlands Coast Pilot was released, along with the annual editions of HP7, HP1D, HP33, and HP33D. In total, 462 "Notices to Mariners" were published.

Operations Directorate The Operations Directorate has accurately established an ellipsoidal reference surface. With the availability of the Ellipsoid-LAT difference surface, a result of research from Delft University of Technology, a direct link between GPS height and the LAT reduction surface is now possible. In this way, measured depths can be directly referenced to LAT, without the need for tide measurements. To enable the ERS technique, the latest GNSS techniques have also been utilized. With the use of new GNSS receivers and a correction signal, the Hydrographic Surveyors (HOV) now have a very precise positioning capability at the decimeter level. In 2016, the need to replace the current Side Scan Sonars with a new system was approved. This means that in 2017, the replacement of the current systems can begin. After reaching an agreement with Belgian colleagues on a more logical map layout of the joint surveying area around the Western Scheldt, these new products were prepared in 2016. Publication of these will follow in January 2017.

[SECTION BREAK]

In the context of IHO, participation occurred in the Hydrographic Standards and Services Committee (HSSC) and various related working groups: Nautical Cartography Working Group, Nautical Information Provision WG, Electronic Navigational Charts WG, and the S100 WG. A major focus is the development of standards for data exchange based on S100 (the Universal Hydrographic Data Model). Furthermore, the section was represented at the IC-ENC Technical Working Group in Taunton and held working meetings with colleagues from neighboring countries. One colleague also attended the CARIS world tour in Bologna, Italy.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the request of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, a staff member from the Service (the head of Data Management) participated in a working group under the Sub-Committee on Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue (NCSR) of the International Maritime Organization (IMO). This working group assessed proposals for routing measures submitted by IMO member states. The service participates as a subject matter expert. Geodesy and Tides The Knowledge Center for Geodesy & Tides (KCG&G) provides expertise for the measurement processes and publications of the Hydrographic Service, as well as for other branches of Defense and the government. The geodetic expertise is applied at sea, where water levels are of great importance. Tide knowledge is linked to marine geodesy. An important application is determining the correct coordinate systems and enabling conversions between them. This concerns both horizontal and vertical references. The choice of a system affects the calculation of points, lines, and areas. Another application is providing geodetic and tide data for general use, such as calculating boundaries at sea and publishing tide predictions.

text:
Hydrographic Information Provision and Management The Hydrographic IV & Management section also focused this year on maintaining the current hydrographic production system and activities related to the SHIP2 project. Following the recalibration of the SHIP2 project in early 2015, further development of several increments took place in 2016, namely: • Nautical Publications: Replacement of the largely manual process. • Bathymetry: Replacement of the current bathymetric database with Workflow support. • SDI: Adequate integration of HYD systems with supplying data sources and provision of own data (in the context of ‘compliance’ with INSPIRE (new European legislation and regulations)). The increments Bathymetry and SDI were ultimately completed and put into production in 2016. The increment Nautical Publications will be phased out under regular management. Since the SDI increment ultimately took less time than planned, an additional increment was initiated: Management Information. This increment has been completed as far as possible and offered for testing.

[SECTION BREAK]

Personnel from the Hydrographic Service aboard Zr.Ms. Holland are conducting a test off the coast of Aruba.

[SECTION BREAK]

140 141 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations With the completion of the SHIP2 project on December 31, 2016, a clear milestone was reached in the further professionalization of the supporting IT for the Hydrographic Service. Subsequently, the further development and professionalization of its functional management within the Hydrographic Service began. In particular, supporting tools play an important role in this. In 2016, the section also contributed to the broad implementation of quality management across HYD in the context of ISO 9001. Certification for this is scheduled for early 2017. Furthermore, cooperation with JIVC was intensified, particularly regarding standard (office) automation.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, the Hydrographic Service partially transitioned to Windows 7 and preparations began to transition to Windows 10. Finally, the section made significant efforts, with the help of the released operational funds for 2015 and 2016, to address the IT backlog within the Service. Clear progress has been made in this regard. Staff Group/Account Management Operational Units In December 2016, the Sales and Distribution module of SAP was added to the inventory management system. This simplified the invoicing process.

Risks and opportunities were identified and elaborated on per section and at the level of the Hydrographic Service. 142 143 Directorate Operations Directorate Operations areas therefore have earlier issues with unfavorable loading conditions, such as high seas. Poor weather conditions caused the ship to return. On February 7, the ship entered Den Helder again. On February 9, the A-crew departed to sea for loading operations, and then on February 13 sailed to Zeebrugge, Belgium. In Zeebrugge, it conducted a Continuation Training (CT) for a week to enhance the level and competence of the crew. The Belgian-Dutch MOST led and provided the training. During this period, maneuvering, navigation, and fire drills were conducted, among others. The training period lasted until Friday, February 19, and resulted in a Satisfactory rating. The ship was to continue its way to the operational area for the execution of loading operations; however, these could not proceed again due to poor weather conditions. Therefore, the ship docked again in Den Helder on Monday, February 22. The B-crew set sail that same Monday for two weeks of loading operations. During this period, an ash scattering at sea was conducted.

[SECTION BREAK]

A select group carried out the ceremony with attention and respect, and a minute of silence was observed. Photos of the ceremony were taken for the home front. After the period of loading operations, the B-crew returned to the port of Den Helder on March 7. On the same day, the A-crew departed for a week of loading operations. A week later, they briefly returned to Den Helder to pick up a new navtex, before resuming loading operations at sea. A navtex provides the ship with necessary navigational and meteorological information and is required to be present on the bridge. Due to the bad weather, not much loading was done, but they mainly waited in the area for better conditions.

[SECTION BREAK]

On Monday, March 21, the A-crew returned. With this, they also completed their last voyage on Zr.Ms.

text:
Luymes for 2016.

[SECTION BREAK]

That same Monday, the B-crew set sail to conduct loading and wreck contact research. During this, the found wrecks in the area were further and accurately examined to determine the least water depth. On March 26, a tide gauge buoy that had been laid the previous year was picked up. This buoy with a sensor on the bottom measures water levels. By measuring this for a period of months, an accurate tide measurement and prediction can be made.

[SECTION BREAK]

On Sunday, March 27, they docked again in Den Helder. Between Monday, April 4, and Wednesday, May 11, the B-crew conducted loading operations, during which a few days were planned to be in Den Helder. This period went quite efficiently as the weather was good and the ship performed well technically and hydrographically. During this period, a tide gauge buoy was also streamed, and wreck contact research was again on the agenda. On Tuesday, May 17, the ship departed to load until May 19. The short duration of this period was due to the fact that the ship unexpectedly had to participate in the Adelborsten Cruise. For this, the ship was prepared in a very short time for an intensive six-week voyage. This posed a considerable challenge that was taken on with much enthusiasm by the crew. On Monday, May 23, a large group of cadets embarked for the Adelborsten Cruise, and Zr.Ms. Luymes, with the B-crew, set course for Ostend.

[SECTION BREAK]

Throughout the entire cruise, a Weekly Practice Program (WPP) was maintained.

text:
Together with the Belgian ship BNS Godetia, they anchored on May 24 at Vlissingen. A day after anchoring, the ships advanced towards Ostend. Along the way, various exercises were conducted, including helicopter operations with the Allouette from BNS Godetia and towing and RAS approaches with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and the aforementioned Belgian ship. On Friday, May 27, they docked alongside BNS Godetia in Ostend, where a festive weekend, 'Oostende voor Anker', was taking place. The crew and the cadets were able to enjoy themselves here after an intensive first week of the cruise. Early on Sunday, May 29, the weekend came to an end, and they departed for Berga, Sweden. Along the way, the lock in Brunsbüttel had to be passed. The ship then sailed through the Nord-Ostsee Canal to the Holtenau lock near Kiel and then further into the Baltic Sea towards Berga. Along the way, various exercises were regularly conducted together with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and BNS Godetia, including a Force Protection exercise and an NBCD carousel on board the ships themselves. On Friday, June 3, they docked in Berga, a naval base in Sweden. This port was filled with ships participating in the large exercise BALTOPS. After a short port visit, they set sail again on Sunday, June 5, towards Stockholm.

[SECTION BREAK]

However, Zr.Ms. Luymes fell outside the BALTOPS program due to the sudden involvement in the cruise. Therefore, the ship organized its own program with various exercises.

At the end of the week, there was participation in a large photex where Zr.Ms. Luymes was positioned directly behind the command ship USS Mount Whitney. After a beautiful approach through thousands of islands, on Saturday, June 11, it docked alongside BNS Godetia in Stockholm. On Monday, June 13, it was time to depart towards Kiel to merge with Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Zierikzee, and EML Tasuja, a ship from Estonia. This week also had many exercises planned, including a hoisting exercise with the Alouette from BNS Godetia, RAS approaches, and a maneuvering exercise with small vessels. On Thursday, June 16, it docked for Kieler Woche in the Tirpzhaven in Kiel with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and Zr.Ms. Zierikzee alongside. During the open days that weekend, the line for other ships turned out to be just a bit longer than for Zr.Ms. Luymes; apparently, a hydrographic ship is less interesting than the Chinese or Spanish frigate that was positioned in front of and behind the Dutch ship.

[SECTION BREAK]

On Monday, June 20, the ship departed from Kiel with new cadets on board. It immediately set course for the Little Belt to conduct navigation exercises. This area was perfect for this purpose due to the many visual entry and exit marks.

[SECTION BREAK]

On the way, a hoisting exercise was conducted with an NH90 from the Danish Coast Guard. At night, the Great Belt was crossed to then continue the route around the north through the Oresund towards Copenhagen. On Wednesday, a large shooting exercise was held with moving targets at a Danish shooting range.

144 145 Operations Directorate Operations Directorate including small caliber weapons firing, anchoring, and finally a barbecue. At the end of the week, there was participation in a large photex where Zr.Ms. Luymes was positioned directly behind the command ship USS Mount Whitney. After a beautiful approach through thousands of islands, on Saturday, June 11, it docked alongside BNS Godetia in Stockholm. On Monday, June 13, it was time to depart towards Kiel to merge with Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms. Zierikzee, and EML Tasuja, a ship from Estonia. This week also had many exercises planned, including a hoisting exercise with the Alouette from BNS Godetia, RAS approaches, and a maneuvering exercise with small vessels. On Thursday, June 16, it docked for Kieler Woche in the Tirpzhaven in Kiel with Zr.Ms. Schiedam and Zr.Ms. Zierikzee alongside. During the open days that weekend, the line for other ships turned out to be just a bit longer than for Zr.Ms. Luymes; apparently, a hydrographic ship is less interesting than the Chinese or Spanish frigate that was positioned in front of and behind the Dutch ship.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.74) — narrative]
On Monday, June 20, the ship departed from Kiel with new cadets on board. It immediately set course for the Little Belt to conduct navigation exercises. This area was perfect for this purpose due to the many visual entry and exit marks.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.74) — narrative]
On the way, a hoisting exercise was conducted with an NH90 from the Danish Coast Guard. At night, the Great Belt was crossed to then continue the route around the north through the Oresund towards Copenhagen. On Wednesday, a large shooting exercise was held with moving targets at a Danish shooting range.

The following morning, Friday, June 24, it docked in Aalborg. After yet another last port of the cruise, the ship departed on Monday, June 27, for the final week with Den Helder as the end destination. On the way, Tromøysundet was visited for the photex. This beautiful area is located in a kind of fjord. After a rough journey across the North Sea characterized by bad weather and high waves, Den Helder was entered on Thursday, June 30. The sailing family day planned for the next day unfortunately had to be canceled due to the circumstances. This marked an early end to the Cadet Cruise. On July 15, the C crew departed for the first time with Zr.Ms. Luymes to sea for loading operations and wreck contact investigation. Halfway through the journey, from Friday, July 22, to Monday, July 25, Stavanger was visited for a routine port visit, after which it docked again in Den Helder on July 28. On Monday, August 1, the B crew departed for loading operations with a port visit to Aberdeen. On the way, a Russian vessel was escorted for a short period. Luymes was in Aberdeen from Thursday, August 11, to Sunday, August 14, for a routine port visit. After this port visit, the rest of the week was spent loading until the day of entry. On Monday, August 22, the C crew went to sea for loading operations until September 5. On September 5, the B crew departed for loading operations.

Commander (ltz1) S.M. Duineveld The first months of the year were focused on maintenance for Zr.Ms. Snellius. Nevertheless, the C crew had the opportunity to conduct the first hydrographic days of 2016 from January 8 to 12. After that, the ship was under maintenance until March 18. The diesel-electric engines received their necessary 10,000-hour maintenance during this time. Immediately after this maintenance, the C crew headed to Vlissingen for navigation exercises. These exercises lasted until March 24. From Tuesday, March 29, the ship resumed loading operations. During this period, the A crew and C crew switched.

147 Directorate of Material Maintenance 146 Directorate of Operations manned each other. The A crew visited Portsmouth from April 8 to April 11 for a routine visit. The C crew had a routine visit to Harlingen scheduled from April 23 to April 28. The A and C crews alternated loading operations until August 24. The A crew participated in the exercise Northern Archer from September 7 to September 27. They primarily served as a flag and hotel ship during this exercise. More than fifty boat transfers were carried out during this exercise. The ports of Leith and Sunderland, Great Britain, were also visited.

[SECTION BREAK]

After this exercise, the B crew took over the ship for two weeks, after which they exchanged again with the A crew. They maintained this arrangement until the end of the year.

[SECTION BREAK]

On November 17, the A crew had to cease their loading operations due to meteorological conditions. The ship then diverted to Rotterdam to wait for better weather.

148 149 Directorate of Materiel Maintenance Directorate of Materiel Maintenance Maritime Logistics (ML) Head: P.W. Ridley Following the migration to SAP in 2014, this year was also characterized by further organization and making processes workable. At the same time, learning to work with and manage SAP required a lot of attention. This consumed significant capacity throughout the entire logistics chain.

[SECTION BREAK]

As we transitioned to 2016, the focus shifted to chain performance and structural improvement through an integral action plan with critical performance indicators (KPI). Significant progress was made, especially regarding the focus areas of data, organization, planning, prioritization, and production. Maritime Logistics also set clear performance goals for improving Materiel Readiness (MG). Examples of this include delivery performance and inventory availability, which have been made not only visible but also measurable. ML held roadshows within Defense on improving performance in the logistics chain. This simultaneously resulted in support for the Supply Chain Monitor developed within ML. This monitor could be used as a tool to gain insight into the Defense-wide logistics chain performance. Significant efforts were made towards the further implementation of the Defense-wide assortment investment (Assortiments Gewijs Werken, AGW).

[SECTION BREAK]

However, it is noticeable that a lot of capacity is still consumed by the incomplete allocation of assortments. This has not yet been fully realized.

In 2016, charging stations for electric cars were installed and put into operation by the EDB in various parking areas throughout the MBDH. These can be used for a fee by both employees and visitors. Shooting Range (SSB) Various infrastructural improvements have taken place at the shooting range. The paving has been renewed, and the inner courtyard is now also paved. Additionally, almost every building has received new roofing, reducing the chance of leaks. A fire-resistant storage container has also been placed at the SSB. Finally, a new access gate has been installed, and cameras have been set up. Almost all buildings have been painted and maintained on the outside. In addition to all regular and irregular requests for the shooting range (schools, MBV shooting, boarding teams, NLMARSOF), the International Shooting Competition for the Shooting Trophy took place at the end of the year. Besides the Dutch participation, many foreign teams also took part in this competition, and it was a great success again this year. FT&S At the beginning of each year, the first event on the agenda of the Sports Office is the New Year’s Run/Dive. Subsequently, events followed in rapid succession. MK indoor football, NMK indoor football, 45+ Ron. v.d. Ham Memorial Badminton tournament, MK Duathlon, the Triathlon in Biddinghuizen, the Harbor Run, Veterans indoor football, and MK field football. For all these events, the MBDH Sports Office provides organization and/or support. Also, military personnel who wanted to stay fit could return to the gym, where they could participate in lessons/training in boxing, circuit training, Cross Fit, Navy Fit, running training, spinning, and training for obtaining the NOC/NSF medal under the guidance of professional sports instructors.

[SECTION BREAK]

Transport Despite the ever-increasing demand, the Transport department also tried to support the operational activities as much as possible in 2016.

text:
Events in 2016 In the first half of 2016, only smaller events could take place due to support for the EU presidency. Although the event center was closed in the first half of the year, visitor numbers decreased, but less than expected. This was mainly due to more intensive use of other facilities. However, from the summer period, operations could resume at full capacity. The last four months of the year saw visitor numbers nearly the same as in previous years. The total number of visitors this year was 17,639, during 776 events.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Marine Etablissement Amsterdam is still one of the few defense locations with flexible large hall capacity. Its central location in the Netherlands, the city center of Amsterdam within walking distance, and proximity to international entry and exit points make the barracks an extremely suitable and unique location for discussion forums, symposia, and presentations within the international defense community. In addition to the Golf World Cup, we were responsible for various large NATO conferences and symposia, including the CHANCOM: the meeting of all NATO naval commanders from the area around the Channel and the North Sea. Furthermore, the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam was once again the host location for BeNeSaM discussions between the Belgian Command Council and the Dutch Admiralty Council. New this year was the shared use of the conference facilities by civil partners, introduced by the Project Bureau Marine Terrein Amsterdam. Accommodation This year, 15,845 reservations for Short-Term Accommodation were processed for activities on and around the Marine Etablissement Amsterdam. Port Visits The number of port visits remained nearly the same this year. The largest applicants continue to be the port and towing service Den Helder and DDG. In many cases, a port visit was made to Amsterdam as part of a transit, but also to a greater extent for deployment in support of national authorities. This year, several foreign visits also occurred. Entrance Europagebouw. The building is beautifully illuminated in colors.

text: After Zr.Ms. Evertsen in 2015, there were no CZSK units for maintenance in Vlissingen, which caused the accommodation of ship crews to stagnate. As a result, the two core tasks for Naval Base Vlissingen consisted of logistical support for a large number of exercises for CZSK units and other military components, and collaborating and networking with government agencies and the business sector for the new barracks to be built in 2021. The closing date of Naval Base Vlissingen has been moved from July 1, 2017, to April 1, 2018. This year, various units were accommodated at the base for battlefield tours. Among others, the MAROST (Maritime Support) staff, the Middle Defense Education (MDV), various CLAS units, and the Royal Marines (UK) were guests. The VeVa training program set up its camp at MKVLIS for a week in mid-2016, and the Certifex of the Marine Corps took place here in June. Additionally, MKVLIS provided space for the CLAS exercise Falcon Autumn this fall, as well as various other brigades. For a DBBO training this fall, accommodation was offered at MKVLIS due to a shortage of lodging at airbase Woensdrecht. Besides providing accommodation and food, the base was frequently visited throughout the year for theme days from the Zeeland Safety Region and consortia Michiel Adriaanszoon de Ruyterkazerne (MARKAZ), DSI, meetings, reunions (former crew members, COM, AVOM, BNMO, BOSS), and receptions. It also provided logistical support for festivities for the anniversary year, such as the tenth edition of ‘Rescue Vlissingen’ held in the summer. Permanent office and other facilities were provided to the staff of Defense Suppliers Oversight from DMO, 30 National Reserve (NATRES) battalion A-company, and a support team from CLSK. Furthermore, there has been a good relationship with the police and fire department for many years. The latter trains our emergency response organization biannually as standard. Week 19 was characterized by peak activity, as various components and agencies made use of the facilities. For instance, two defense components, the German/Dutch specialist organization in ground-based air and missile defense, and the Belgian Defence College, organized a battlefield tour.

Nearly three hundred cyclists participated in this tour of approximately ninety kilometers. Additionally, the crew of MKVLIS held the annual barbecue, a team-building outing to the shipping museum with a boat tour from the MEA in Amsterdam, and concluded the year with a Christmas dinner.

After an intensive onboarding period, the foundation was laid for the continuation of the path that had been set. There were many personnel changes, partly due to the expiration of regular placement periods. Crucial in this was the change of the Head of Logistics, a position that was not filled again for several months. Maintaining behavior (in the broadest sense) remained a challenge throughout the year. Measures were taken with unit-wise barracks, allowing for direct supervision by the user cadre. This did not always have the desired effect. Notably, there were regular acts of vandalism in the barracks accommodation. The organization recognized that the barracks accommodation in particular had been in need of improvement over the years. A budget was made available for this, which, supplemented by a planned maintenance budget, was expected to lead to extensive renovation.

Furthermore, the kitchens that had already been tendered in the barracks were completed just before the summer. The tendering of the second series also started, which was ultimately delivered in December.

This led to a significant improvement in the barracks facilities. A long-running project, the armory, was brought back to the required security level after the summer. This had some impact on operations. Due to the increase in personnel, there was an additional need for storage, as well as for office and workspaces. With minor adjustments, this need could be met. However, for the storage issue, it was necessary to resort to Maartensdijk. In terms of maintenance, the outdated condition of the barracks continued to take its toll. The KKW shooting range also experienced significant wear problems, making it unavailable for shooting training for several months. Due to the increase in equipment and personnel in the barracks, certain operational activities were more or less forced to relocate to Maartensdijk. With this relocation and expansion, the last location increasingly became a stronghold of storage and transshipment activities and maintenance, leading to operational risks. During an IL&T inspection in August, covering both the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks and Maartensdijk, several minor deficiencies were identified. Fortunately, these could be quickly remedied.

Nevertheless, due to the results of the inspection in Den Helder, all of CZSK was placed under intensified supervision. Main building of the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks, Doorn.

To prevent unauthorized individuals from gaining access to the public side of the sports hall, a smartcard reader was installed at the entrance. Regarding the overall security of personnel, stricter checks were conducted at the gate and on protected interests.

text:
Due to the deterioration in relations with Russia, a Very High Readiness Joint Task Force (VJTF) unit was prepared within the framework of NATO for the entirety of 2017. In December, an alert exercise was held for this purpose, which will be further rolled out throughout 2017. In terms of support provision, both internally and to third parties, many activities were organized that aligned with previous years. This year also featured a family day, during which future relocation was also considered. For this purpose, the province of Zeeland and the municipality of Vlissingen were willing to contribute by providing information to the military personnel and their family members. In the context of the repurposing of the barracks area, in addition to many tours, other activities were also developed. A cultural-historical study of the area has since taken place, and wildlife counts have also been conducted. Furthermore, the ongoing development of the needs for the new barracks in Vlissingen has once again required significant attention from several staff members of the barracks. A considerable amount of time and capacity has been devoted to the elaboration of the Output Specification, which received a follow-up in a second phase (December 2016).

[SECTION BREAK]

This year also featured a family day, during which future relocation was also considered. For this purpose, the province of Zeeland and the municipality of Vlissingen were willing to contribute by providing information to the military personnel and their family members. In the context of the repurposing of the barracks area, in addition to many tours, other activities were also developed. A cultural-historical study of the area has since taken place, and wildlife counts have also been conducted. Furthermore, the ongoing development of the needs for the new barracks in Vlissingen has once again required significant attention from several staff members of the barracks. A considerable amount of time and capacity has been devoted to the elaboration of the Output Specification, which received a follow-up in a second phase (December 2016).

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.84) — narrative]
Corps Marine Fire Brigade Commander: Deputy Chief Commander A.F.M. Langenhuizen BBA In mid-2016, the equipment replacement plan for the Corps Marine Fire Brigade was initiated. With this plan, the KMB outlined the necessary replacements for the coming five years.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.84) — narrative]
Several expansion projects were also launched, such as the acquisition of a rescue vehicle and a Cobra Cold Cut system. By the end of 2016, the first expansion had been delivered: an environmental incident response container.

Schuitmaker Three themes were central this year for the product group port facilities: the replacement of four Lingeklasse tugboats with three Noordzeeklasse tugboats, the optimization of internal operations, and the best possible continuation of the management of smaller vessels. The product group port facilities, with its own crews, retrieved a new Azimuthing Stern Drive (ASD) tugboat from Romania three times in January, April, and June 2016. This was the result of a longer period of preparations that were undertaken together with DMO. The crews experienced the journey as unforgettable, gaining many new experiences with the new tugboats. On July 11, 2016, after the arrival of the third and final tugboat, the Noordzeeklasse was officially... The family day of marines at the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks in Doorn. Display of Medical Material.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance was officially transferred from DMO to CZSK with the unveiling of the nameplates Noordzee, Waddenzee, and Zuiderzee. Three captains (ktz) were fully trained and authorized to deploy the Noordzee-class for towing operations by mid-2016. The plan is for the two remaining captains to be fully trained by early 2017, resulting in five operational crews for the Noordzee-class from that point onward. In the months following the transfer, four tugboats of the Lingeklasse: Regge, Linge, Hunze, and Rotte, were decommissioned. The Gouwe is then the only remaining Lingeklasse tugboat that is part of the fleet. In addition to the fact that the operation of the Noordzee-class is very different compared to the Lingeklasse, the maintenance system was also significantly changed. This maintenance was structurally carried out at a civilian shipyard. The warranty period of the three boats has shown that civilian outsourcing of maintenance has so far yielded positive experiences.

The second major theme within the product group was the optimization of operations. The goal was to facilitate the operational fleet as effectively as possible with the available resources. There was a continuous tension between the available personnel from the towing service and harbor watchmen (Steiger 19), various tasks, and a continuously fluctuating workload that is visible in the short term. The many ship-related activities such as dock planning, oil loading and unloading planning, ammunition loading and unloading planning, tours, practical lesson planning, responding to extreme weather conditions, and the deployment of tugboat crews posed a constant challenge for the Harbor Operations and Coordination Center (HOCC) and resulted in a dynamic planning process. The aim is to continue improving this process. In addition to coordinating and planning, active support was provided multiple times to the National Police, and civil-military cooperation with Port of Den Helder was continued. The Traffic Center (VTS) Den Helder registered more than 50,000 ship movements in 2016. The traffic management, which makes traffic decisions on behalf of the Rijkswaterstaat to ensure safe and smooth shipping movements, underwent several personnel changes, including the promotion of one of the former traffic managers to the position of Deputy Head of Traffic Service. Additionally, two candidates completed the training to become traffic managers; one of them is already a traffic manager, while the other will be ready early next year.

[SECTION BREAK]

The harbor watchmen (Steiger 19) played an essential role in the (un)mooring of ships. The small team, consisting of three employees in 2016, experienced a personnel change with the departure of a permanent staff member.

[SECTION BREAK]

Despite the highly fluctuating workload, the harbor watchmen made it possible for many vessels to enter the Waddenzee, the second tugboat of the new Noordzee-class, from Romania. Bridge of the Waddenzee.

text:
Directorate of Material Maintenance The Directorate of Material Maintenance carried out facilitating activities, allowing operations to continue uninterrupted. The bridge operators also experienced a personnel change and continue to operate the Vice Admiral Moorman Bridge with great enthusiasm. At the Central Quay Surveillance (CWB), the trend of recent years continued, with units being connected for longer periods of time. For more than two-thirds of the year, units made use of the CWB, significantly relieving ship crews from watch duties. Optimizing the operations of the CWB was an important point of focus. At the end of 2016, various control rounds were conducted under the leadership of the Seatrain department of ship operations for this reason. The last major theme of the product group port facilities was the management of smaller vessels and pontoons. The work boats of the Schelde class, the multifunctional port vessels Nieuwediep, Marsdiep, and Landtdiep, the sailing/rowing boats (WR-1), and a variety of pontoons made it particularly challenging for the Kabelgat. Over the past year, the management of the DBBO vessels, the Noorderhaaks and Zuiderhaaks, was added here. In consultation with other parts of DMI, much effort was made to keep the availability of the vessels as high as possible. Despite many temporary personnel changes, where the formation of multiple shifts could proceed unhindered, the Kabelgat made a significant contribution to this.

[SECTION BREAK]

Product group energy distribution company Head: Ms. Drs. A.M. Valent-Groot The Energy Distribution Company has been the energy supplier and network manager for defense locations in Den Helder since 1957. With its own power plant, the Combined Heat and Power Station, electricity is generated, and the heat released is used to provide approximately half of the buildings at the Nieuwe Haven with warmth. Across the defense sector, the Energy Distribution Company manages contracts and invoice control for electricity, gas, and water. It also addresses demand requests and reports consumption figures, which are used to provide advice on reducing energy use.

In 2016, it was 100 years since shore power was first supplied to a ship of the Royal Netherlands Navy in Den Helder. This means the Navy is far ahead of civil shipping, which has only recently begun to adopt shore power.

[SECTION BREAK]

With funds from the Van der Staaij Motion, a new employee for Integrated Safety and Quality was appointed at the EDB in April. This allowed for better compliance with safety, security, and environmental requirements within the EDB. In the same month, the assortment management of Energy and Water was formally transferred from the CDC to the EDB. The work had been carried out by the EDB since 2005. May 12 was a special day for the EDB. For the first time in 100 years of shore power, a ship returned power to the shore. Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Karel Doorman had, in parallel with the KWS, supplied electricity to the EDB electricity grid. If necessary, the Karel Doorman can supply electricity to ships or to the shore, for example during maintenance of the generators on board or in exceptional circumstances, such as in aid to areas affected by a natural disaster. In June, the site lighting along the Koegraszeedijk was replaced with LED lighting. After the closing time of the Zuidpoort, the lighting is dimmed. Particularly, dimming contributes to energy savings compared to traditional site lighting.

Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) P.J. Baijards and project leader P.W. Terpstra took the first charging stations for electric cars into use.

[SECTION BREAK]

170 171 Directorate of Material Maintenance Directorate of Material Maintenance This contributed to the environmental objective of defense to save 1.5% electricity per year. It also resulted in financial savings. On July 11, the new hybrid tugboats were officially put into service. The EDB had constructed a new shore facility for this purpose because the new ships require more power. On July 14, the charging stations for electric cars at the Helder defense locations were officially put into use by Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) P.J. Baijards and project leader P.W. Terpstra.

[SECTION BREAK]

Employees and visitors can use these charging stations for a fee. This makes Defense the first within the central government to have such a facility. For service vehicles, there had already been several charging stations on the premises of the Marinebedrijf for a number of years. A new transformer station was installed at pier 21 that can provide both low and high voltage. Delivering the corresponding reel for the high-voltage cable presents some challenges, but nevertheless, on August 17, Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman was connected for the first time to the fixed high-voltage supply. Until August 17, a temporary mobile facility was used there.

Bongaerts The performances of the Marine Band in 2016 were not different from previous years. text:
The main user is the KIM.

[SECTION BREAK]

The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers practical nautical skills necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, focusing on team building and character development. The ship is used as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. It is also deployed during the annual sailing period, during which a longer training voyage of about five weeks is undertaken together with a flotilla of minehunters; the cruise. Besides the KIM, the Operational School is also a major user. For this, practical sailing sessions are provided for the training of non-commissioned officers' sailing qualifications for minehunters. Marines also learn to operate landing craft with it. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Civil maritime schools also make good use of the Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Technical training on board is also possible. Upon request, bridge teams from individual ships can use the Van Kinsbergen for tailored training or as part of a training trajectory. Occasionally, the ship is used for scientific research (TNO, universities) or for informational purposes. MOV Van Kinsbergen Jan-Dec For a few years now, the Van Kinsbergen has been sailing with a fixed schedule aligned with the Vocational Technical Education (VTO) periods. As a result, January of each year begins with the first sailing weeks for the beginning midshipmen on the Van Kinsbergen. The VTO period lasts a total of two years, during which these midshipmen undertake a sea service practicum (ZPR) on board the Van Kinsbergen three times for one week. The last ZPR lasts two weeks. The sailing week, together with a week on the Ship Handling Simulator (SHS), concludes a theoretical block. This allows for a progressive learning line to be realized, where the knowledge gained from the previous block serves as the basis for the subsequent block. This is also reflected in the program designed for the midshipmen. ZPR 1 is filled with the elementary aspects of navigation, such as learning to determine a position; evasive maneuvers; taking bearings; the operation of a 'leading line', and to break the week, a port visit.

This is also the moment to provide the midshipman with summative feedback on their performance thus far. In 2015/2016, there was a transitional year. Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Training and Support A variety of exercises and training sessions took place in the Caribbean over the past year. This was to maintain the operational readiness of the own units, but also served as an ideal training location for CZSK, CLSK, and CLAS units or partners in the region. In addition to its own training, CZMCARIB also supported training of important strategic partners in the Caribbean, such as the United States and France. Units from CZMCARIB also trained abroad, for example at Camp Lejeune in Jacksonville, United States (Military Operations in Urban Terrain) and in French Guiana and Martinique (Unit Cohesion Training).

[SECTION BREAK]

The Fight Against Drugs Prompt action to ensure safety at sea and from the sea requires continuous vigilance. CZMCARIB is a '24/7 organization' where the Operations Center of the Maritime Headquarters Caribbean is staffed 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. This results in operational successes each year. Over the past year, approximately 7000 kg of contraband was removed from the market, with Zr.Ms. Groningen having the largest 'catch' (2000 kg).

[SECTION BREAK]
