Pulles EMSD The Maritime Headquarters Caribbean (MHKC) has coordinated and directed all operations and exercises of the military units present in the West and a growing number of visiting domestic and foreign units since 2016 as an operational center in the Caribbean. MHKC also frequently acted as the commander of military resources (CMM) for various military assistance requests from local authorities of the (island) countries in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. The execution of Main Task 3, support of civil authorities, has significantly increased in recent years at CZMCARIB, thereby supporting the vision of enhancing its position as a maritime and security partner in the Caribbean. Holland did not have a shipboard helicopter, which allowed the collaboration established in 2014 with the US helicopter squadron (USCG) HITRON to continue.

International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in maintaining the international rule of law in the Caribbean. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy in the Caribbean is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization 'Joint Interagency Task Force South' based in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4., one of the task groups of this organization. Upon the arrival of the station ship Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën in Willemstad, Curaçao, the crew is assembled in parade formation.

Command of the Naval Force in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Force in the Caribbean Counter Drugs All three station ships patrolled for both the Caribbean Coast Guard (KWCARIB) and Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4). Various successes were achieved in this regard. In cooperation with international units, CTG 4.4 removed approximately 7,000 kg of contraband from the market in 2016. These international operations are conducted with various countries, including the United States, France, Colombia, the United Kingdom, and the Dominican Republic. Hurricane Relief During the annual Hurricane Relief Exercise (HUREX) in the Windward Islands, CZMCARIB once again demonstrated that it is ready to provide emergency assistance if necessary. During the exercise in June, at the beginning of the hurricane season, intensive collaboration took place with local aid organizations, and the ties for further cooperation in the future were strengthened. After the passage of Hurricane Matthew, CZMCARIB provided international emergency assistance in Haiti from October 12 to October 26. Due to excessive rainfall and wind, large parts of the country were devastated, and some areas became inaccessible to the outside world.

The Audit Service of the Ministry (ADR) issued an unqualified audit opinion following the annual audit. The 'Payment Office CARIB', which is temporarily housed under the Directorate Controller CARIB pending the FABK reorganization, paid invoices totaling more than 56 million euros in 2016, including those for the Coast Guard, CZMCARIB, the KMar, and DMO. The payment office will be formally housed under FABK starting in 2017. 2016 was financially challenging for CZMCARIB. This was entirely due to the low euro-dollar exchange rate. The euro budget series made available therefore yielded significantly less local currency than previously anticipated. CZMCARIB could not carry out the assigned operational activities and support within the allocated budget of 21.6 million euros. Despite savings measures amounting to 0.9 million euros, the final realization amounted to 24 million euros. This was accommodated within the total budget of CZSK, allowing local suppliers in Curaçao, Aruba, and Sint Maarten to be paid in the fourth quarter as well. During the annual open day of the Marine Barracks Savaneta, visitors were also able to view the ship. Of the 10,000 (!) visitors, a large number took advantage of this opportunity.

In mid-May, the Pelikaan was again in Aruba, this time to support the Ronde van Aruba. Two teams from the ship's crew participated in this event. One of those teams even secured a third place. In addition to these events, the Pelikaan facilitated the transport of the CIDW to and from Bonaire and conducted its amphibious operations with the 32RSQN. As part of the preparation for providing emergency assistance, the Pelikaan participated in the annual HUREX from June 13 to 29. This year, French units stationed in Martinique also trained in the Windward Islands. In addition to work in Aruba and Curaçao, the Pelikaan also facilitated the transport of French vehicles and soldiers from Martinique to and between the Windward Islands. Over several days, operational snipers from the Korps Mariniers and snipers in training were able to hone their skills in maritime sniping. After the summer leave, minor maintenance was carried out to ensure that all ship systems were functioning optimally again.

text:
This was immediately put to the test by supporting the visit of a unit from the United States Marine Corps Force Reconnaissance. In cooperation with the FRISC troop and other elements of the 32RSQN, the Pelikaan conducted amphibious training and practiced boat drills. The ship also served as a diving platform while logistical support was provided. On September 21, the transport of the CIDW from Bonaire was combined with a port visit and an open day. On this day, not only the Pelikaan visited the island, but also a cutter from the coast guard, the CURMIL, the KMar, and the CIDW were present during the open day. A large number of island residents, particularly several classes of elementary school students, visited the units and enjoyed the demonstrations.

[SECTION BREAK]

In the following week, a tropical disturbance developed over the Atlantic Ocean. This intensified to hurricane strength heading towards the Caribbean. Upon reaching the easternmost Caribbean islands, the forecast indicated that this hurricane Matthew would find its way to the Lesser Antilles. All units of the Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean prepared for a passage of the Lesser Antilles. Ultimately, Matthew passed as a Category 3 hurricane about two hundred miles north of the Lesser Antilles. The expected damage in Curaçao did not occur. Aruba and Bonaire particularly experienced extreme rainfall. On Monday, October 10, the Pelikaan departed with aid supplies, vehicles, and additional personnel towards heavily affected Haiti. The first stop was Aruba to pick up the marines from 32RSQN, along with extra supplies and vehicles. From October 10 to 30, the ship was deployed in close cooperation with marines from the 32RSQN to provide aid supplies to the most severely affected villages along the coast. The Pelikaan visited Port-au-Prince multiple times to take on aid supplies from various aid organizations. The crew members and marines then distributed the goods with the FRISC’s and carried out recovery projects in the affected villages. Government representatives and representatives from aid organizations were also on board to ensure that aid supplies reached the right places and could be distributed safely and in a coordinated manner. By the end of October, most communities had received emergency aid, and aid organizations took over the further structural rebuilding.

In 2016, MBPAR housed and supported four rotations of the CIDW.

Furthermore, MKSUF continued to focus on personnel development and well-being.

text:
Various workshops and training sessions were organized to enhance the skills and knowledge of the personnel. The command also emphasized the importance of physical fitness and mental resilience, leading to the implementation of several initiatives aimed at promoting a healthy lifestyle among the staff. Overall, 2016 was a year of significant activity and development for the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean region, with a strong focus on training, operational readiness, and personnel welfare.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean also saw ARUMIL trainees participating in the training. Ultimately, 23 trainees reached the finish line. After the summer leave, approximately 25 personnel from both CURMIL and ARUMIL started the Advanced Vocational Training (VVO). Until the Christmas leave, the trainees regularly went into the field to apply the knowledge they had gained in practice. This training will conclude at the end of February 2017. Finally, a start has also been made with the Practical Officer Training (POTOC) for CUR and ARUMIL. Following a recruitment and selection process, along with six weeks of preparation for the candidates, four candidates (two for CURMIL and two for ARUMIL) began the POTOM in Rotterdam. In the spring of 2017, the remaining trainees will come to Curaçao to complete their training. Social Development Trajectory (SVT) The SVT is a training trajectory of approximately five months. This trajectory is aimed at instilling a positive behavioral change in 'social dropouts' or 'underprivileged youth'. The training is military-oriented and focused on developing various competencies. The trajectory is part of a larger program from the Ministry of Education in Curaçao. In 2016, two SVTs took place at MKSUF. A limited number of youths were offered, which meant that the SVT could not be optimally utilized. Despite the small 'classes', the youths were enthusiastically applauded by their proud families at MKSUF at the end of both trajectories, after a grueling march.

[SECTION BREAK]

Due to a reorganization at the Ministry of Education, the next trajectory (2017-1) has been canceled, leaving the future of SVT uncertain.

The Green Platoon CURMIL The green platoon is the CURMIL unit that is actually operationally deployable. An important development for the platoon is that it falls under the MHKC as an operational unit. From here, the unit has been deployed for, among other things, manning observation posts. Additionally, the platoon has been on standby twice for deployment. The first time to support the KPC during potential unrest among striking Isla personnel. The second time because Hurricane Matthew was heading towards Curaçao.

[SECTION BREAK]

However, in both instances, actual deployment was not necessary.

During this period, they followed a military-oriented training course at the barracks. The Aruban militia was responsible for carrying out this task. Some of the trainees completed the entire program and have already found jobs in the Aruban labor market. There are also five internship positions at MSKSAV, where they can participate for four months at the barracks and thus prepare for a role in society. Open Day Approximately 30,000 visitors enjoyed the annual open day of MSKSAV. The purpose of the open day is twofold. On one hand, it is intended to familiarize the Aruban population with the work of the Royal Netherlands Navy (including the Marine Corps), the ARUMIL, and the Caribbean Coast Guard. On the other hand, this day is meant to raise money for a good cause. The proceeds of 30,000 Aruban guilders were donated to the Fundacion Ban Uni Man Pa Cria (school breakfast) and Stichting Turtugaruba (protection of the sea turtle).

[SECTION BREAK]

32nd Raiding Squadron (32RSQN) 32RSQN in the Caribbean (MCC) successfully fulfilled the operational annual program. This included the following exercises: An extensive MOUT training (operations in urbanized areas) lasting 14 days at Camp Lejeune in Jacksonville (North Carolina, United States), utilizing the facilities and support of the Force Recon II Marine Expeditionary Force and the US Riverine Squadron. They worked with paint ammunition and role players in various scenarios. • Reception of Force Recon, USMC for training in Aruba • HUREX (disaster exercise after hurricane) in Sint Maarten • DISTEX (general disaster exercise) in Aruba for the station ship. • Various exercises with the local security partners of the KIA (prison), KPA (Aruba Police Corps), K9 (dog teams), and the Arrest Team of the KPA. • In total, 32RSQN provided a training week in Aruba for the CIDW three times. • As a conclusion of the year, the unit conducted an exercise in Curaçao. At the end of September, Hurricane Matthew passed through the Caribbean, narrowly missing the Leeward Islands. The Aruban government requested military assistance in preparation for the possible consequences of the hurricane. The crew was ready at the barracks to provide military assistance during the passage of Hurricane Matthew.

Haiti, on the other hand, was severely affected.

[SECTION BREAK]

From October 6 to 30, 32RSQN, together with the patrol ship Zr.Ms. Holland and the support ship Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, provided emergency aid to the affected island. For two weeks, the King's Company faced significant challenges during the Kings Isle exercise. In Bonaire, the men prepared by training attacks, medevacs, patrols, and 'controlling disturbances' further for their task in the West: defense of territorial integrity and maintenance of law and order.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean In March and October, the Training Center of the Royal Military Constabulary provided training in crowd control. Through this training, the Marine unit is prepared to assist the local police in maintaining public order as part of military assistance. Logistics and Equipment This year, it was decided to place the equipment service (MD) under the Chief Logistics Service (HLD) to streamline support. The LD and the MD are thus managed under a single command to optimize operational support.

[SECTION BREAK]

The boat group Aruba made extensive use of FRISC’s. In total, there are four of the 12-meter version (Raiding Craft) and two of the 9-meter version (Support Craft Caribbean) in Aruba. The utility and necessity of the 'boat lift' have also been recognized, and an additional boat lift is expected to be realized in 2018. Infrastructure The construction of the new office building is progressing steadily. The new office building was supposed to be in use by the end of 2016, but due to gaps in planning, it has now been postponed to early 2017.

[SECTION BREAK]

Sports The Ronde van Aruba, which takes place every year in early May, has now grown into an internationally recognized running event in the Caribbean region. The 75 km race can be completed with 4- or 2-person teams or even as an individual. Every year, many military personnel and civilians from Aruba participate in the sporting event. MSKSAV is the start and finish for the event.

Marine Support Point Pointe Blanche (MSTPPB) Commander: Major (majmarns) R. Witteveen In 2016, the MSTPPB further standardized the training program and worked on making operations more robust. The focus was on spreading the workload; working on robust communication; reducing single points of failure; a more flexible training program; and working with SAP. Cooperation In 2016, MSTPPB focused on strengthening partnerships. In particular, cooperation was sought with the security partners on the island. Several workshops were held in 2016, during which specific knowledge was transferred to the security partners. At the end of the year, a good relationship was also established with the Gendarmerie. Visibility In the second half of 2016, the 'rotating elements' placed significant focus on the visibility of the Marine detachment in Sint Maarten.

[SECTION BREAK]

They did this through an open day at the Learning Unlimited Preparatory School, several social patrols on the boardwalk, and by participating in other events. Additionally, visibility in Saba and Sint Eustatius was increased by visiting at least once a month. These visits were focused on a military exercise and/or supporting civilian partners. Military Assistance In 2016, the MSTPPB also provided military assistance several times at the request of the governor. This primarily involved searches in the prison in the form of hard assistance. Each assistance resulted in the seizure of knives, drugs, and other prohibited items.

[SECTION BREAK]

Observation As part of the annual plan, the support point contributed to improving the information position of CZMCARIB by carefully observing and reporting on the security situation in the area. This was done, for example, by conducting observation exercises on the SSS islands. These exercises were carried out in close consultation with local security partners. The observation skills of the rotating element are one of the capabilities that the security partners do not possess but for which there is a great need. (Military) Tracking In recent years, military assistance has been provided several times by (Military) Trackers at CZMCARIB. Since there is also a need for this capacity in the Windward Islands, the MSTPPB trained two individuals as Military Trackers within the permanent element at the end of 2016.

Materiel Maintenance Head: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) D. van den Bosch, MSc, MA The Materiel Maintenance (MI) department is responsible for the maintenance and management of equipment, including vehicles, vessels, shore (communication) systems, and other operational resources such as weapons and ammunition under CZMCARIB and the Director KWCARIB. Additionally, the MI department is also responsible for transport support and all logistical processes. Finally, the department is responsible for acquiring and providing equipment and services as well as local disposal. The Materiel Maintenance department consists of three offices: Technical Support (TO), Logistics & Transport (L&T), and Procurement.

[SECTION BREAK]

SAP Operations In November 2015, the operations of Carib transitioned to SAP. This had a significant impact on the various departments throughout 2016. In addition to regular activities, the processes transitioned to SAP under the guidance of a project group from the Naval Chain.

[SECTION BREAK]

Zr.Ms. Pelikaan The support ship Zr.Ms. Pelikaan was in Named Maintenance at the beginning of 2016. This was fully carried out alongside the Rima pier at MBPAR. FRISC Since early 2014, CZMCARIB has had access to ten FRISC vessels. These are present at CZMCARIB in two variants, namely the Raiding Craft (RC) and the Support Craft Caribbean (SCC). A point of concern in 2016 was the delivery and availability of spare parts for maintenance. A partial cause of this was that SAP was insufficiently filled with the correct data.

[SECTION BREAK]

The end of the technical lifespan has been reached, and they will be systematically replaced by Metal Sharks in 2017. In 2016, two cutters underwent a periodic docking in Suriname. The docking was completed with a maintenance period by MICAR at MBPAR. Additionally, new tenders for the cutters were delivered. SEWACO Systems The beam path connection system experienced regular failures in 2016. The maintenance of this system can no longer be guaranteed, particularly due to the lack of spare parts. Logistics & Transport The L&T department has the executive capacity to support the operational logistical activities of the units, such as (strategic) movements of equipment and personnel. This applies to both the own units of CZMCARIB and visiting national and international units. In this context, various exercises and training were conducted from Curaçao and on-site. Needy Haitians approach Zr.Ms. Holland.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean was supported. Furthermore, the urgent deployment in the context of emergency aid on the island of Haiti was also logistically supported by Logistics & Transport (L&T). In a very short time before departure, a large and diverse emergency aid package of vehicles and other equipment was assembled and subsequently loaded onto Zr.Ms. Pelikaan and Zr.Ms. Holland.

[SECTION BREAK]

The L&T department is also responsible for the supply of all units of CZMCARIB and the management and maintenance of all vehicles within CZMCARIB.

[SECTION BREAK]

In terms of supply, the migration to SAP has been a fundamental change in operations that proved to be very labor-intensive. Primarily, the data migration from a number of unique CZMCARIB legacy systems made this project complex. Regarding the vehicles, the availability throughout the year was under pressure due to personnel shortages among the mechanics and regularly stalled deliveries of parts (combined with the aging vehicle fleet). For the upcoming year, it is planned to deliver 33 new trucks for the islands of Curaçao and Aruba.

text: Procurement The Procurement department faced a long period without a Head of Procurement in 2016, while the SAP operations also needed to be initiated here. DCIOD The planned reorganization of International Support Caribbean (RIO CARIB) has, following previous years, not yet been completed in 2016. As in previous years, the usual briefings took place both in the Netherlands and on the islands in the Caribbean. For newcomers in 2016, these were provided at the Marine Establishment in Amsterdam. In November 2016, the information officer of the Americas/Caribbean cluster of DCIOD provided briefings for the repatters on the islands of Sint Maarten, Curaçao, Aruba, and Bonaire during a trip through the Caribbean. text:
A.C.F. Melaet In the annual plan for 2016, the goal was set to take the next step towards a robust operational product. The employees of P&O Advice Caribbean shaped this, entirely in line with the objective of P&O to provide the organization with sufficient, well-motivated personnel. Timely and active personnel filling policy in good consultation with line managers and P&O CZSK, and a critical view on labor qualifications have proven essential to getting the right employee in the right place. The training backlog for SAP must not go unmentioned as a standout issue for 2016. Especially within a small organization like CZMCARIB and the great distance to the Netherlands, being trained in a timely manner before departure has repeatedly proven to be extremely important. P&O Advice Caribbean has proven to be an indispensable source of information for line managers and employees. Additionally, collaboration with HR staff of local personnel was further expanded to gain better insight into the shared issues of shortages and to provide for current and future needs to retain knowledge within the Caribbean personnel. In the spring, various career counselors from the LBB P&O CZSK department made a working visit to CZMCARIB. The career counselors primarily spoke with military personnel who will regularly repatriate to the Netherlands in 2017. The discussions aimed to provide these military personnel with more clarity about their future opportunities. Unfortunately, the absence of a new service termination regulation as well as personnel shortages within the organization affected the timely provision of clarity regarding future opportunities.

[SECTION BREAK]

On December 2, 2016, the total filling of Dutch Defense personnel at CZMCARIB was 98%. Within CZMCARIB, the filling on Aruba was 90%, on Sint Maarten 98%, and on Curaçao 99%. The filling rate of local personnel at CZMCARIB was 97%, with 98% filling among local personnel on Curaçao, 94% at CURMIL, 100% among local personnel on Aruba, and 84% at ARUMIL.

text:
In February 2016, the digital Personnel Information System AFAS Profit was introduced and put into use by the HR staff of the Local Personnel Bureau. The first step towards a clear formation and staffing of local personnel was taken.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean (CZMCARIB) was thus established, with the professionalization of the CURMIL being implemented in the formation. Protocols and procedures, particularly in HR, have largely been described, and simultaneously, the proposed organizational structure change within the HR department has been implemented. The updating of personnel files and the preparation of digital files for input were daily tasks in 2016. The year concluded with the submission of the 'Vision Note for the Future CURMIL/ARUMIL' for further decision-making, so that an action plan can be established to fix the chosen direction in the operations of CZMCARIB. The common thread for 2016 was bringing to the agenda and securing the target group of local personnel in the (existing) consultation forums. Safety and Environment In the area of Safety and Environment, the focus in 2016 was on three sub-areas. Firstly, in the context of 'safe working', efforts began to better and more structurally carry out operational and non-operational activities. In addition to the existing Risk Inventories and Evaluations, the introduction of Task Risk Analysis was new.

[SECTION BREAK]

Secondly, managing the asbestos issue within the Caribbean was central. Examples include the asbestos contamination of the obstacle course and the Operations in Urban Areas training location at MKSUF, and the removal of the asbestos-containing pipeline at MSKSAV. The inventory of hazardous substances, particularly the so-called CMR substances (carcinogenic substances), is the third sub-area that has been addressed. Based on the reported incidents, five Committees of Inquiry (CVO) have been established.

[SECTION BREAK]

Energy Saving Insight into energy consumption (water and electricity) received full attention from CZMCARIB. The costs of energy are a substantial part of the Caribbean budget. If 1% can be saved on the energy bill, it results in a saving of approximately 60,000 guilders.

text:
In the autumn of 2016, MSKSAV began a pilot project in which four air conditioning units were equipped with Plugwise Stealth Switches. The initial results indicate that the investment is recouped in two months and thereafter provides a saving of 45 guilders per month per air conditioning unit. A rollout of these Plugwise Stealth Switches across CARIB could result in significant savings.

[SECTION BREAK]

The 'Phase 3 Solar project' - the installation of 650 kW of solar panels - at MBPAR has been completed, achieving a total capacity of 1 Megawatt. MSKSAV (300 kW) and MKSUF (350 kW) also have solar panels. Through various measures, such as replacing the drinking water network, installing osmosis systems, and improving environmental awareness, the Caribbean achieved a water saving of 30% in 2016. Environment After a lengthy process, MBPAR and MKSUF received a ministerial decree from the Minister of Health, Environment, and Nature. As a result, based on the 'Curaçao 1994 Environmental Protection Act', a package of permit regulations has come into effect for both locations. Final exercise of the CURMIL at Santa Martha, Curaçao. Final exercise of the CURMIL at Santa Martha, Curaçao.

text:
On Wednesday, January 20, 2016, the Zika virus was first detected in Curaçao. Because this virus can be harmful to the unborn child, the staff of CZMCARIB immediately addressed this situation.

[SECTION BREAK]

In consultation with the Defense leadership in the Netherlands, a preliminary action plan was devised. A number of measures were established to allow women the opportunity to travel to the Netherlands. Approximately thirty pregnant women voluntarily went to the Netherlands for a certain period during their pregnancy. These were mainly partners of military personnel stationed in the West, but also some pregnant female military personnel. This situation was significant for the families, and where necessary and possible, DC BMW provided support. As long as there is no clarity, this situation will also remain relevant in 2017.

[SECTION BREAK]

DC BMW provided psychosocial assistance to employees and their families throughout the Caribbean region in 2016. Unlike the regional offices in the Netherlands, there is often a need for long-term assistance in the Caribbean region. This is partly due to the special situation of overseas postings and the inability to fall back on alternatives such as General Social Work or other forms of civil assistance. In 2016, regular work visits were made to Bonaire (KMar) and Sint Maarten to be more accessible to personnel and their families on these islands. In the context of services to commanders, information and advisory reports were prepared, and participation in the Social Medical Team of CZMCARIB and KMar took place. In October 2016, at the request of the Head of Operational Personnel Care CZSK, DC BMW organized a follow-up program in both Aruba and Curaçao for the personnel of the units involved in the emergency aid for Haiti. In 2016, there was also attention for the initiative of DC BMW to jointly address issues involving domestic violence more effectively. This year, DC BMW provided information to a number of teachers from local schools where many children of Defense employees are placed. The goal of this collaboration is to recognize signals at an earlier stage and, if necessary, to provide support. The official guidelines provided by Dutch law and the Professional Association of Social Work Professionals (BPSW) were, of course, taken into account.

text:
DC BMW is also involved in local veteran care. In the spring, a thematic meeting for veterans was organized in collaboration with the DGV at Landhuis Ascencion. In Curaçao, the 'Veterans Association Curaçao' is active; this organization represents the interests of veterans on the island. DC BMW has contact with this association to provide access to veterans residing in Curaçao from the position as a partner within the National Veterans Care System (LZV). In this context, there are also contacts with the Veterans Care Desk of the ABP in the Netherlands. Additionally, contact is maintained with caregivers from the local Mental Health Care (GGZ). Spiritual Care The Spiritual Care in the Caribbean this year consisted of Pastor J. Wójcik, Chaplain F. van Grimbergen, Humanistic Counselor Norbert de Kooter, and Chaplain P. Vlaar. The first three are based in Curaçao, while Chaplain Vlaar is stationed in Aruba.

[SECTION BREAK]

N. de Kooter replaced Humanistic Counselor R. Donker in July 2016. Donker returned to the Netherlands after four years of service in Curaçao.

[SECTION BREAK]

The spiritual caregivers go where the men and women of Defense go. And in the Caribbean, this also applies to partners, families with children, and veterans. Every first Saturday of the month, a spiritual service is held.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean took care, together with a number of veterans, to maintain the military cemetery on Roodeweg. A commemoration also took place there on May 4. Later in the year, the IGK visited to lay a wreath. There was also a speech by a spiritual caregiver during the commemoration on May 4 at the monument by the Waaigat. The humanistic counselor (HuRa) regularly travels to the Windward Islands and Bonaire to visit KMar personnel. The KMar has over 150 personnel working on various islands in the Caribbean. In addition, the HuRa can also be found at the KMar brigade in Suffisant.

Brummelaar Royal Netherlands Institute for the Navy Commandant: Captain (ktz) P.P. van den Berg Dean Faculty of Military Sciences: Prof. dr. H. Rudolph On Monday, September 5, 2016, the Maritime Introduction Period (MIP) began for one hundred aspiring naval officers at the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM). This intensive period took place, as last year, at various locations to make the MIP more maritime. The initial training of the aspirants took place at the KIM, under the guidance of the permanent staff, but with the assistance of naval officers from the 2015 promotion. In this way, young people learn what it is like to lead and to pass on knowledge to the aspirants.

[SECTION BREAK]

After a short period at the KIM, a two-day bivouac was organized at Marine Barracks Erfprins, followed by five days on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, after which they departed for the well-known Texel for the final part of the first maritime-military training. On September 28, the aspirants returned to the KIM. The conclusion of an intensive period, where family and friends could be present, took place on Friday, October 14. On this memorable day, the aspirants were installed as naval officers. Another important day in the life of a (future) naval officer is the day of the Grand Oath. This took place this year on Friday, June 17, at the exercise ground. Annually, a three-day gala, the Assault, is held in Den Helder for the naval officers of the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM).

[SECTION BREAK]

Attachments

The Assaut was held in Willemsoord and was attended by the Commander of the Navy, Lieutenant General (ltgen) R. Verkerk. It is well known that the Royal Netherlands Navy and the Royal Institute for the Navy are filled with traditions. Therefore, it must be pleasing for many naval officers to see the Assaut return this year in winter. After eleven years of the Assaut being held in spring, it was decided in 2016 to bring this annual event back to its original time in December.

From December 15 to 17, 2016, the cadets were able to showcase what they had built, learned, and developed at the KIM. Hospitality is an important part of this, and during the Assaut, the cadets successfully put this into practice.

[SECTION BREAK]

Under the leadership of Captain (ktz) P.P. van den Berg, the KIM has further professionalized its education. The formation of files and guidance of the cadets has been a focal point and continues to develop every day. As more cadets with a higher professional education/university background join, the operations have been further adjusted to provide optimal guidance in the future. This guidance must result in the delivery of officers who are immediately deployable at the Royal Netherlands Navy upon completing their training.

Coast Guard Netherlands
Director: Captain (ktz) R.J. Blok MSc The Coast Guard protects and promotes the responsible use of the North Sea and monitors the Dutch borders, but it does not do this alone. The Coast Guard operates on behalf of five ministries: Infrastructure and Water Management, Defence, Security and Justice, Finance, and Economic Affairs. In 2016, Coast Guard personnel, together with staff from the participating services – Rijkswaterstaat, Royal Netherlands Navy, Police, Customs, Royal Marechaussee, Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority, Royal Air Force, Inspectorate for the Environment and Transport, and the State Supervision of Mines – worked for the safety (safety & security) and economic interests of our country. Steps towards modernization
For the Coast Guard, 2016 was a busy and challenging year. A year in which important decisions were made regarding the modernization of the Coast Guard, the reorganization came into effect, and the regular Coast Guard tasks in the areas of service provision and enforcement were carried out. The decision-making for the development and acquisition of the Maritime Operations Center Coast Guard, to replace the existing Coast Guard center, was an important step towards a modern and future-oriented Coast Guard that can operate information-driven and is equipped for its tasks. Contribution to European operation 'Triton'
FRONTEX, the European agency for the management and coordination of external borders, requested the Netherlands to deploy the Coast Guard aircraft for the European operation Triton. Therefore, in April, the Coast Guard aircraft was stationed on the Italian island of Lampedusa to conduct surveillance over the Mediterranean Sea. The task of the aircraft and its crew was to detect and map illegal migration flows from North Africa to Europe during patrol flights, so that the responsible authorities could anticipate the situation. In case of emergencies, the aircraft could be requested to contribute to search and rescue activities, in accordance with international obligations. Search and Rescue
Drowning victims, shipwrecked individuals, or others in distress or danger are located and rescued by the Coast Guard. Coast Guard ships, helicopters, and aircraft are ready for this Search and Rescue (SAR) task 24 hours a day. The Coast Guard carries out its SAR tasks in the North Sea (in the territorial sea and within the Dutch Exclusive Economic Zone), the Wadden Sea, the IJsselmeer, the Randmeren, and the South Holland and Zeeland rivers.

In 2016, 1,565 assistance and rescue operations were carried out. Missing kitesurfer
On October 5, 2016, the Coast Guard center in Den Helder coordinated a large-scale search operation for a missing kitesurfer. Based on various data, such as current and wind, the operators determined the search plan for the rescue units. Searching continued late into the night in the hope of finding the man alive. Unfortunately, the units found the lifeless body of the kitesurfer in Krabbendijke (Zeeland).

[SECTION BREAK]

Attachments

Emergency Situations

In emergency situations on ships, the Coast Guard is called for assistance. Examples of these situations include when a ship has run aground, has had a collision, or has become unmanageable. The Coast Guard is reachable 24 hours a day via various communication lines.

text:
Inland Vessel Sunk

The Coast Guard Center (KWC) received a report on July 5, 2016, of a sinking inland vessel on the IJsselmeer. The KWC summoned the Coast Guard aircraft, a rescue helicopter, and six rescue boats to provide assistance. There were three people on board, who were in the wheelhouse. This had filled with water, causing one crew member to become hypothermic. The crew members were brought ashore at Stavoren and treated by ambulance personnel once there.

[SECTION BREAK]

Coast Guard Enforcement

To ensure safe and smooth processing of maritime traffic in the North Sea, the Coast Guard supervises compliance with applicable traffic and behavioral regulations. Enforcement officers at the Coast Guard Coordination and Communication Center carry out this task. They take action based on information from computer systems or direct Coast Guard units to conduct inspections or controls and take enforcement action. Although much information is available through various automated systems, surveillance using ships, aircraft, and helicopters provides important additional (detailed) information about, for example, potentially criminal discharges of polluted wastewater or oil. In 2016, a total of 34 criminal discharges were observed according to the criteria of the Bonn Agreement Report. Customs officers and members of the Royal Marechaussee work together on board the Coast Guard patrol vessels to inspect ships in the North Sea. Together with the Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA), the Coast Guard checks fishing logs, catch composition, storage space, and prohibited net equipment. In 2016, 1,218 inspections were carried out, resulting in 254 criminal offenses being detected and 172 reports being drawn up. There were 36 warnings issued and 16 administrative measures taken. SAR Operation Becomes Drug Case

A fishing boat encountered problems on the evening of January 14, 2016, during a severe storm and sent out a distress signal. Various units were immediately alerted. It was not until the course of the night that the crew could be rescued at the mouth of the Westerschelde after a joint effort by the Coast Guard, the Belgian Air Force, and the Royal Netherlands Rescue Society (KNRM). Due to the bad weather, the boat could not be towed, and the wreck washed ashore at Cadzand during the night. When Customs officers, together with the police, boarded the wreck, they made a remarkable discovery: one thousand kilograms of cocaine.

Reorganization of the Technical Domain RN (HTD)  
Project Leader: Captain (ktz) ir. J.W. Hartman  

The Royal Netherlands Navy has the ambition to remain an innovative navy in the future, even with scarce technical personnel, increasing technical complexity, and limited financial resources, while ensuring its material readiness effectively. To achieve this goal, the program for the Reorganization of the Technical Domain RN (HTD) was initiated in 2013 after thorough research. An important first step in the HTD program was the merger of the Technical Service (TD) and the Armament Technical Service (WD). This step took place on May 7, 2014.

[SECTION BREAK]

With the merger, the existing personnel was consolidated into one service, the Technical Service (TD). In 2016, various projects and trials aimed at changing the technical operations on board the operational units and streamlining training were completed, and the results were subsequently integrated into the line organization. Furthermore, the reorganization plan was established to optimally align the job profile for TD personnel with the changes brought about by the HTD program. This was done after extensive consultation with employee representation and trade unions. The implementation of the reorganization will start in 2017. With the integration of the results into the line organization and the upcoming implementation of the reorganization in 2017, the HTD program in its current form has been terminated, and the further development of the TD will be shaped within the TD committee, the advisory body of the Flag Officer Technical Service.

text: In 2016, the navy was deployed in major international operations and exercises. Prominent this year was the provision of emergency aid. After the devastating force of Hurricane Matthew, Haiti was particularly in ruins, leading to significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected country to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines also took action to ensure that the aid could be distributed safely among the population. Additionally, the navy showcased its capabilities in the Mediterranean by rescuing migrants in perilous situations at sea. As part of drug enforcement, several ships participated in the Counterdrug Operation Carib Venture. Furthermore, participation occurred in large international exercises such as Black Alligator and Emerald Move.

[Jaarboek 2016 (p.133) — narrative]
In 2016, the navy was deployed in major international operations and exercises. Prominent this year was the provision of emergency aid. After the devastating force of Hurricane Matthew, Haiti was particularly in ruins, leading to significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected country to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines also took action to ensure that the aid could be distributed safely among the population. Additionally, the navy showcased its capabilities in the Mediterranean by rescuing migrants in perilous situations at sea. As part of drug enforcement, several ships participated in the Counterdrug Operation Carib Venture. Furthermore, participation occurred in large international exercises such as Black Alligator and Emerald Move.

FOREWORD In your hands, you have the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2017. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The Navy made a significant impression during SAIL and the Marine Days in Den Helder. Old sailing ships and new war vessels were simultaneously on display in and around the Nieuwe Haven. Additionally, marines landed with heavy equipment onshore for the interested public. With thousands of visitors, it was a great success and a wonderful opportunity to showcase what the Navy has to offer.

text:
After the devastating hurricane Irma, Sint Maarten was particularly in ruins and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various ships set course for the affected island to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines were also deployed to ensure that the aid could be distributed safely among the population. The personnel underwent many new training courses and participated in (international) exercises. At the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and ships to introduce visitors to the naval forces.

text:
The expenditures by CZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher than expected. This increase was largely caused by additional expenses for maintenance and higher salary costs due to the agreed labor conditions agreement. With the establishment of the coalition agreement, there is a turning point after years of cutbacks and a rising budget. At the beginning of 2017, however, savings measures were still necessary, such as reducing the number of sailing days by replacing the ship in the West not in the Caribbean but in the Netherlands and accepting a short absence in the operational area during transit. Throughout the year, financial space re-emerged, which the Navy has used among other things to

[SECTION BREAK]

Organizational overviews were used to purchase additional spare parts and to increase the stocks that had diminished in recent years in order to improve material readiness. With the coalition agreement, it was also decided to incorporate the budget of the Coast Guard in the Caribbean into the Defense budget, and CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command) processed these adjustments in the administration throughout the year. To improve cost insight, various studies were conducted. As part of the 'Replacement of the Walrus Class' project, a cost-benefit analysis was carried out, and interdepartmental cooperation was involved in completing a policy study on the costs of readiness. One of the recommendations was to develop a cost-to-readiness model. CZSK contributed to this by developing a standards system to better substantiate the budget in terms of activities and products. A standardized approach is increasingly being used in the Policy, Planning, and Budget Cycle. In terms of personnel, this is done with averages and standards for other personnel expenditures, and for weapon systems, defense-wide established standardization sheets are used.

[SECTION BREAK]

Finally, F&C (Finance and Control) conducted many analyses for the growth plans in the context of the Development of Armed Forces (DOKM). Many types of ships will be replaced in the coming years, which requires further analyses of the expected future operating costs. The department is also taking many measures, for example, in the context of the safety organization, with personnel expansions and intensifications of activities, resulting in higher expenditures.

Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV) is the supporting directorate within the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) and the Coast Guard in the areas of personnel, training, healthcare, organization, operations, and information provision. Additionally, the directorate serves as an important link to the Defense Staff/Administrative Staff through the Integration department. For 2017, the focal points of the directorate were: Optimizing operations in the broadest sense of the word. An important step was taken with the establishment of a new business plan, which will be further developed in the coming years. Personnel from Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman working on the bridge.

[SECTION BREAK]

Simplified organizational chart of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV).

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-3 22 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Ensure that the personnel establishment of CZSK is fully filled in 2020, with a target of 98% in permanent positions and 2% flexible deployment consisting of reservists and hired personnel. To achieve this, the P-continuity project started in 2015, aimed at further professionalizing personnel management and care within CZSK. This involved matters such as Professionally Oriented Training (BGO), employability, leadership development, and ensuring integrated healthcare. Intensifying collaboration between (internal) Defense, civil regional (in training), and international partners. Intensifying the management role of CZSK for the Coast Guard Netherlands and CARIB, with special attention to long-term sustainability. Further developing the adaptability of the CZSK organization to changing circumstances, both within Defense and in society.

[SECTION BREAK]

This particularly applied to the supporting and administrative processes. In practice, this proved to be considerably more challenging, but the organization must be sufficiently prepared for the future, and therefore it is deemed necessary for this process to continue.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-4 23 Directorate Personnel and Operations Legal Affairs (JUZA) Head: Captain (ktz) mr. G. Souer The JUZA department is part of the DP&O, one of the five line directorates of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and state and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different bureaus.

[SECTION BREAK]

Thus, every employee at JUZA can function as a first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department.

[SECTION BREAK]

JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel, but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. Should a military member be involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from the Ministry of Defence in this matter. It was decided to make the organization more adaptive, a start was made with DOKM, and in November an agreement was reached on a collective labor agreement for 2017-2018. As part of the Adaptive Armed Forces, the Bureau Flexible Capacity was established within P&O. This bureau originated from the Bureau Reservists. The latter agency was engaged until June in the deployment and administrative support of the reservists of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve. In addition to continuing this task, the Bureau Flexible Capacity was established as the coordinator for external hiring and deployment of temporarily available military and civilian personnel.

[SECTION BREAK]

In 2017, CZSK began with DOKM. A project organization was set up for this purpose. DOKM for CZSK involves: the expansion of operational (combat) support. In the coming years, these expansions will be implemented, which will lead to an increase in mine countermeasure capacity, the establishment of a Fleet Marine Squadron, and the construction of a Combat Support Ship.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-5 24 Directorate of Personnel and Operations After a long negotiation process, an agreement was reached at the end of November between the Defense leadership and the trade unions regarding a new Collective Labor Agreement for Defense. The biggest change is the new termination of service regulation, which links the retirement age to the AOW (state pension) age. Military personnel will now be dismissed five years before the AOW age. Working longer is no longer only the norm for civilian personnel, but also for military personnel. In 2017, the shortage of personnel (technical and operational) was painfully felt, resulting in many temporary transfers and replacements to meet the required deployment. The frequent transfers led to unrest, and in some cases, it was a reason for departure.

[SECTION BREAK]

To break this downward trend, it was decided to allow only voluntary replacements and to work on extending the duration of assignments where possible.

text: Career Guidance Career guidance is the alignment of personnel wishes with the possibilities that the organization offers regarding career paths. This alignment takes place in the form of a career conversation, which is held during each function or once every three years. This conversation encompasses the personal developments of the involved official in the near future, as well as in the medium and long term. Personal development of the employee is necessary to remain valuable to the organization. In addition to this internal mobility, the career counselor pays attention to external mobility for employees who will not progress in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section included four military offices for the operational service groups, Marines, technical service, and logistics service, and one office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of 2017, this section had 37 military and 3 civilian positions. Since mid-year, the career guidance office for civilian personnel has been fully staffed, allowing for career conversations for civilian personnel on a larger scale. Furthermore, as of October 1, career guidance for civilian personnel has been implemented and established across Defense.

In addition to this internal mobility, the career counselor pays attention to external mobility for employees who will not progress in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section included four military offices for the operational service groups, Marines, technical service, and logistics service, and one office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of 2017, this section had 37 military and 3 civilian positions. Since mid-year, the career guidance office for civilian personnel has been fully staffed, allowing for career conversations for civilian personnel on a larger scale. Furthermore, as of October 1, career guidance for civilian personnel has been implemented and established across Defense.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-6 25 Directorate of Personnel and Operations This year, various groups experienced personnel shortages. This was particularly evident among the junior officers and the middle management of the non-commissioned officers. The 'Technical Allowance' introduced in 2016 was applied unchanged this year, meaning that technical personnel in the rank of corporal to and including warrant officer receive a retention bonus under certain conditions. The idea is that a retention bonus over multiple years will have more effect than the usual one or two years. Another implemented measure for personnel retention is that the 'recycling' of this personnel should be kept to a minimum. An excessively high number of first lieutenants of the Marines and corporals of the Technical Service has been maintained to eventually fill the shortage in the next higher ranks.

Everything was done by the staff to contribute maximally to "Safety at and from the sea" by placing the right people, with the right training, in the right positions. Integration (INT) The Integration department (INT) is part of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DPBV), one of the three line directorates of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). The INT department aims to manage the operational and supporting process chains of the CZSK integrally on behalf of C-ZSK, focused on delivering deployable units in accordance with the assignment of the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS). The INT department consists of three bureaus: Bureau Strategy and Advice (S&A), Bureau Policy, Planning & Budgeting (BPB), and Bureau Investments (INV). Bureau Strategy & Advice The Bureau S&A supports C-ZSK in its role as maritime military advisor to the CDS and the Minister of Defence. Bureau S&A operates in two teams: the Advice team and the International Military Cooperation team. The Advice team acts as the first point of contact (mailbox) for the Executive Staff (Defence Staff and Main Directorates) regarding policy documents, studies, parliamentary matters, and the so-called Hague consultations. Important tasks this year included activities related to DOKM and the Defence Memorandum. This team also supported the Head of the Policy Directorate in the development of the 'Work Program Maritime Strategy & Ports 2018-2021', an interdepartmental work program initiated together with the Maritime Cluster based on the Maritime Strategy 2015 - 2025.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, this team provides analysis of inspection reports from the Inspector General of the Armed Forces regarding visits to CZSK units. The International Military Cooperation (IMS) team supports C-ZSK in maintaining its international contacts and working relationships.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-7 26 Directorate of Personnel and Operations in collaboration with the Defense Staff (IMS). In addition to the preparations for regular meetings within the framework of the Belgian-Dutch cooperation (BENESAM) and the Naval Steering Group (NSG) with Germany, an important step has been taken in Dutch-German cooperation. Regarding the operational integration of the German Sea Battalion into the Marine Corps, the Initial Operational Capability of the first mission sets (Force Protection, Very Shallow Water Diving MCM, Non-combatant Evacuation Operations) was achieved on September 22, 2017. A cooperation agreement in the field of submarine search, escape, and rescue has been signed with Sweden, allowing collaboration in the execution of escape exercises using a Swedish rescue submarine.

[SECTION BREAK]

Bureau Policy Planning & Budgeting The Bureau BPB is the first point of contact for the Defense Staff regarding the BPB cycle and the Commandant of the Armed Forces' Directive on Readiness (AGCDS). Bureau BPB is composed of three sections: Planning Integration (PLINT), Programs (PROG), and Material Support (MOST). The PLINT section is responsible for the integral planning process within CZSK. Due to financial constraints, PLINT proposed several measures at the beginning of 2017, in close collaboration with F&C and the AR, to enable more hiring in 2017. The Defense Staff has urged throughout the year to obtain sufficient financial space to address existing backlogs in the supply chain logistics (logistics debt). This space was subsequently also offered to CZSK, after which the Directorate of Material Maintenance (DMI) was able to make significant progress in 2017 and actually overachieved on the budget.

In preparing the business plan for 2018/2019, a deepening was carried out on the activities; these are now provided with a (primary) action owner and, moreover, formulated more concretely in many cases. An integration of the short-term activities from the Sailplan 2030 CZSK into the Business Plan also followed, allowing progress to be monitored through the regular Business Reports. The structure of the Business Reports was significantly changed in 2017. Furthermore, the directorates no longer prepare their own reports as input for the CZSK business report, but provide direct input for the CZSK report itself. In this way, the volume of reporting per quarter was halved, and the administrative burden was also reduced.

[SECTION BREAK]

In the Implementation Note, attention was requested from the Executive Staff for the structural shortfall in maintenance, the shortages in various personnel allowances, and the structural lack of staffing space for students in initial training (unavailability for function) as input for the BPB process 2019.

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS 27 Directorate Personnel and Operations The Programming section is responsible for drafting the Readiness Plan (GSP). This GSP is the long-term plan of the CZSK and looks approximately ten years ahead. It forms the basis for various sub-plans within the CZSK, including the Maintenance Plan of the DMI, the Operational Year Plan of the DOPS, the Filling Plan of P&O, and the Training Plan of the Royal Netherlands Navy Training (OKM). This year, the development proved to be a dynamic process in which all parties involved had to regularly adapt flexibly to rapidly changing environmental factors, which affected both the GSP and the various sub-plans. The integration of maintenance capacity for the Portuguese M-frigates and the prolonged unavailability of various units due to technical problems are examples of this.

[SECTION BREAK]

The responsibility for planning and monitoring the material exploitation lies with the MOST section. In 2017, the section was closely involved in the first defense-wide synchronized Supply and Demand Management (VAM) cycle. Additionally, both internally and externally, efforts were made to improve the VAM structure and processes. Under the leadership of the CDS, contributions were made to further develop and numerically populate the Defense Exploitation Plan – Weapon Systems (DEP-W). The inventory of C-systems that is in use by CZSK, which started in 2016, was completed this year. This inventory serves as input for a military-wide inventory of C-systems, allowing for better budget allocation to address the bottlenecks in the replacement of such systems.

[SECTION BREAK]

The expansion of the section with Project Coordinators for New Material has been accelerated in the context of DOKM. The Project Coordinators will be intensively involved in preparing the CZSK organization for the arrival of new material, which is planned in the various replacement projects within DOKM. Also, this Armory at the Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks.

In 2017, the Personnel and Business Operations Directorate functioned regularly as 'Haarlemmerolie' to smooth out difficult-running material processes. Investment Office The INV is responsible within CZSK for the planning and realization of the bandwidth budget allocated to the defense components from the Defense Investment Plan (DIP). The Bandwidth Investment Plan (BIP) applied here lists all bandwidth projects of the CZSK, with a five-year outlook.

[SECTION BREAK]

The overrealization of the 2017 budget was partly due to the Seamanship Trainer (ZMST) at Fort Harssens, for which the official opening is scheduled for February 2018. A large number of innovation projects have also been financed, including lifting aids, 3D printers, and applications to improve business operations. Several (financially) significant projects, such as the replacement of the submarine Thetis and the transformer stations at the docks, have been submitted to the Defense Staff for consideration. Furthermore, an increase is observable in the number of files jointly financed by the Operational Command (OPCO), especially in the area of small caliber weapons, optical devices, and drones. Also in 2017, the needs were again greater than the allocated budget, and several large projects were postponed to 2018.

In September, Hurricane Irma struck the Leeward Islands, followed within two weeks by Hurricane Maria. In preparation for the likely needed assistance, three General Military Nurses (AMV) and one General Military Doctor (AMA) were relocated from the Primary Health Company (EGB) Caribbean and distributed across the Leeward Islands together with the other units. After the hurricanes passed, the devastation on all islands was significant and there was a great need for emergency assistance. Military support scaled up during that period, and the staff doctor CZMCARIB/EGB Carib, Medcell, and Head Command Group role 1 consulted frequently with DOPS J-med to ensure that sufficient medical support and HPG care for the own units on the islands was available. Initially, EGB Carib provided the medical support, but soon units flown in from the Netherlands took over to ensure that the health centers in Curaçao and Aruba would not face capacity issues. On the first flight to Curaçao, part of the Marine Spearhead Task Unit (MSTU) accompanied a doctor. After a few days, a dedicated HPG member followed. Additionally, the medical staff capacity at CZM Carib was strengthened with a staff doctor. Zr.Ms.

Throughout 2017, several staff members were involved in emergency deployment/humanitarian assistance to the Caribbean during Hurricane Irma and its aftermath. Physical Training and Sports The year 2017 consisted of maintaining ongoing matters and organizing a total of 35 sports events, including four National Military Championships (NMK) in Basketball, Indoor Soccer, Swimming, and Half Marathon, five Open Military Championships (OMK); Dutch Marine Trail, Centaur Sailing, Sloop Sailing, Weightlifting, 20 Marine tournaments and championships, and four Sports Promotion events; the Half Marathon of Den Helder, Mud Masters, Dam to Dam run, and the Amsterdam City Swim. 2,372 personnel participated in the events, some of which had over 200 participants. The most popular events were the Royal

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Personnel and Operations Institute for the Navy (KIM) Cross in which 235 personnel members of CZSK participated, the Half Marathon of Den Helder with 221 participants, the Dutch Marine Trail with 175 participants, and the Marine Run with 168 participants. In addition, the sports promotion events Mud Masters and Dam to Dam Run were well attended. With the latter event, participants raised sponsorship funds for a good cause. After the event, the CZSK participants were able to present a check of €3,500 to the Make A Wish Foundation. Furthermore, CZSK managed to win various championships or individual participants representing CZSK achieved good performances. For instance, the CZSK NMK Basketball team and the veterans and ladies won silver at the NMK Half Marathon. In the West, the CZSK sports instructors were also active.

[SECTION BREAK]

For the 25th time, the Round of Aruba was organized from the sports office of the Marine Barracks Savaneta.

[SECTION BREAK]

With nearly 400 participating teams, 72 km was run across the island during the night of May 18 to 19. Women, mixed, duo teams, men, women, and individual runners braved the extremely diverse course with temperatures around 30° C and high humidity. Notably, the performance of the winning individual runner was remarkable, as were the initiators of healthier food and exercise for the Navy in Den Helder.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-17 36 Directorate Personnel and Operations a sergeant of the Marines who completed the distance just above 10 hours. In addition to the sports events, the Training Unit Physical Training & Sports (FT&S), part of the MOC, has trained various instructors and specialists, namely: 19 Physical Trainers Instructors; 24 Physical Trainers and Sports Instructors; 20 Medical Personal Trainers; 2 swimming specialists. Diving Medical Center Personnel Staffing The year 2017 was primarily characterized by (under)staffing. Unfilled vacancies and only one administrative employee meant that tasks had to be carried out with fewer people. Efforts were made to address this on an administrative level through certain arrangements, involving a total of five individuals. This has affected the continuity and quality of care.

[SECTION BREAK]

A diver during the exercise Joint Protector in Eemshaven.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-18 37 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Two of the four diving doctors were transferred at the end of 2017. The personnel plan did not account for a timely replacement of these two diving doctors. Given the training duration of a diving doctor (an average of 18 months), this will lead to problems in the future, considering the disproportionately high workload for the doctors who were not transferred. In addition to the increased workload, they must support any new "diving doctors in training." A similar problem existed with the diving medical nurses. Given the relatively larger pool of this type of personnel, the effects of this issue seemed milder; however, due to frequent changes among diving medical nurses and the need to train specialists, this placed significant pressure on the qualitative filling and support capabilities of the Diving Medical Center (DMC). Duty System For the treatment of victims of both Defense and civilian diving accidents, a diving doctor, a diving medical nurse, and a technician are on standby 24/7. Since only two technicians were qualified in 2017, this was a point of concern and a weak link in the diving medical care chain. Inadequate staffing of the diving duty has consequences for the diving activities of the armed forces. Due to this occupancy rate, the DMC decided in 2017 to discontinue 24-hour care for civilian (sport) divers.

Equipment The measuring equipment in the examination department (lung function, exercise ergometry) has long been depreciated and is in urgent need of replacement. The procurement process was difficult, and when in December the procurement of new examination equipment finally seemed to be concluded, the remaining supplier did not meet the requirements.

Expanding Tasks Despite the above, the DMC was able to deliver more output in scientific areas and support than in previous years. This is the result of a reorganization of personnel and resources and the optimization of operations. Thanks to an employee, a management information system has been established, allowing the DMC to utilize all available capacities more effectively. To align the actual job content with the job descriptions, a reorganization is conceivable in the long term.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-19 38 Directorate Personnel and Operations Social Medical Service In 2017, the Social Medical Service (SMD) provided occupational health care and personnel support, as part of the reintegration policy of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK), assisting clinical and outpatient patients. This year, a total of 360 military personnel registered with the SMD.

[SECTION BREAK]

The clinical patients primarily consist of military personnel with injuries or ailments related to the musculoskeletal system. They are internally guided to reach the high fitness level of their operational unit, so that they can recover from their injuries and resume their work without falling behind in fitness. The Physical Profile for Marines (FMP) describes the required fitness level per rank and is divided into three levels. The expected physical profile for fleet personnel, who operate together with marines and must meet a higher fitness level than when assigned to the fleet, has not yet been published. Fleet personnel who become unfit are rehabilitated to fitness in accordance with the requirements of the Defense Fitness Test (DCP).

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-20 39 The Directorate of Personnel and Operations, as an independent unit of CZSK, provides primary occupational health care outside the EGB. The requirements plan was completed in March 2017, and based on that, alternative locations were considered. The Korporaal van Oudheusden Barracks (KVOK) in Hilversum was found to be suitable, and in April 2017, the green light was given for the relocation of the Service to the KVOK.

[SECTION BREAK]

Utilizing existing buildings required extensive modifications, which still did not meet the requirements plan. It was decided to place two new buildings constructed from prefab units on the open grounds of the KVOK where the Marine Examination Center previously stood. This met the required delivery in July 2018, allowing the relocation to begin on time. For the future, cooperation is being sought with, for example, the MRC department of occupational rehabilitation, so that at the end of the lifespan of the prefab housing at KVOK, a new purpose for the SMD is ready. Unfortunately, it became clear that it would not be possible to have the final design ready in time and thus to tender the project. At the beginning of December, it was stated that the delivery of one of the two buildings could perhaps take place on time, but by the end of the year, it became clear that this was also impossible. Additionally, the phased delivery of the two buildings was not feasible without disrupting the training program of the internally placed patients. It is further unclear what the effect of the above will be on the planned closure of the MEA. What is certain is that the SMD cannot relocate in time to vacate the current building by July 1, 2018, for transfer to the project office marine area Amsterdam. Relocation to a temporary location is pending.

[SECTION BREAK]

40 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Zr.Ms. Walrus arrives in Den Helder.

[SECTION BREAK]

41 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Management does not see the readiness of the buildings at the KVOK as a feasible alternative. The Service has provided much input and cooperation in the development of the support tool for line managers regarding the reintegration of sick employees. Line managers are assigned tasks through this tool in PeopleSoft, making the employer's reintegration efforts more transparent and timely. The first user tests took place at the end of 2017 and were promising. Personnel Care Just like in previous years, the Personnel Care department supported the operational units regarding personnel care. Employees are and remain the most important success factor for effective task execution of the Naval Forces.

In this consultation, contact persons from various defense components come together to discuss diversity and learn from each other. Coordinator Projects Personnel Care In close collaboration with colleagues within and outside the Personnel Care department, on May 18, the ninth memorial meeting for KM military personnel and civilian employees of the CZSK who died in active service was organized. This year, it was also a valuable and memorable day for the bereaved.

[SECTION BREAK]

Bureau Operational Personnel Care The Bureau Operational Personnel Care (OPZ) is responsible for communication regarding family circumstances, home front care, briefings, children's activities (this year three CZSK-wide and one for the children of marines), and support during the CZSK memorial. The bureau also supports the operational units and individually deployed military personnel. For prolonged deployments, home front information and contact days are organized. Thanks to the various home front committees, creative actions for the crews have been conceived and executed. Care for, during, and after deployment has been discussed and organized through care plans with the units. For the two mission units, an adaptation program was organized and executed by OPZ. Additionally, various adaptation discussion leaders participated in both CZSK adaptations and adaptations from other OPCOs. Bureau Mental Resilience The Mental Resilience Cluster (MV) is responsible for the Collegial Network Royal Netherlands Navy (CN KM) and stress management. MV focused over the past year on training new Collegial Networkers (CN-ers) and Trauma Risk Management (TRiM) team leaders. This involved ensuring the quality of the already trained CN-ers and embedding the CN KM within the CZSK. The CN KM saw several deployments in 2017 where the TRiM protocol was applied. Quality assurance has taken place, among other things, through skills days and organizing a study day.

Furthermore, individually deployed military personnel were introduced to the concept of gender awareness in preparation for their mission, based on UN Resolution 1325.

[Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.23) — narrative]
The VPAPZ also conducted research into finding more synergy between the various veterans and post-active reunion associations. This effort will be further developed in 2018. Coordinator Projects Personnel Care In close collaboration with colleagues within and outside the Personnel Care department, on May 18, the ninth memorial meeting for KM military personnel and civilian employees of the CZSK who died in active service was organized. This year, it was also a valuable and memorable day for the bereaved.

[Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.23) — narrative]
Bureau Operational Personnel Care The Bureau Operational Personnel Care (OPZ) is responsible for communication regarding family circumstances, home front care, briefings, children's activities (this year three CZSK-wide and one for the children of marines), and support during the CZSK memorial. The bureau also supports the operational units and individually deployed military personnel. For prolonged deployments, home front information and contact days are organized. Thanks to the various home front committees, creative actions for the crews have been conceived and executed. Care for, during, and after deployment has been discussed and organized through care plans with the units. For the two mission units, an adaptation program was organized and executed by OPZ. Additionally, various adaptation discussion leaders participated in both CZSK adaptations and adaptations from other OPCOs. Bureau Mental Resilience The Mental Resilience Cluster (MV) is responsible for the Collegial Network Royal Netherlands Navy (CN KM) and stress management. MV focused over the past year on training new Collegial Networkers (CN-ers) and Trauma Risk Management (TRiM) team leaders. This involved ensuring the quality of the already trained CN-ers and embedding the CN KM within the CZSK. The CN KM saw several deployments in 2017 where the TRiM protocol was applied. Quality assurance has taken place, among other things, through skills days and organizing a study day.
