4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-24 43 Directorate Personnel and Operations In the AGCDS 2018, it is stated that all defense components must implement the Directive 'psychosocial support for uniformed personnel' (Impact directive) by establishing a Collegial Network. CZSK has partially set up this network. There is currently no network for civilian personnel.

[SECTION BREAK]

The MV Bureau has supported other defense components in establishing various networks by opening up training sessions and participation in working groups. As part of stress management, briefings were held in preparation for various missions. Collaboration has been sought with various schools/trainers such as KIM, SMVBO, MOC, Maritime Team Training and Applied Leadership (MTTL), and Netherlands Maritime Special Operations Force (NLMARSOF). Within this collaboration, a way was explored to uniformly offer a stress management tool. NLMARSOF operators are about to jump during an exercise above Leeuwarden.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-25 44 Directorate Personnel and Operations. To this end, NLMARSOF has initiated the training pilot "Mental Strength." Within this pilot, various stress management tools were offered, including those from sports psychology. The goal of all this is to enhance performance and reduce dropout rates by making participants more resilient.

[SECTION BREAK]

Case Management Office CZSK The office handles individual cases with an irregular character that require special attention and recognition from the employer. Typically, these involve complex care issues that may be politically and/or media-sensitive, have a high risk of failure, are multidisciplinary in nature, and therefore require coordination. The year 2017 was marked by an increase in the number of cases and the corresponding workload per case. The cause of this may be that the functionality of case management is increasingly proving itself or that more and more supervisors and employees are finding their way to the office. Another possible reason for the increase could be the effect of the reorganization on regular processes at centrally allocated services of Defense. This year, the Case Management Office also received several new (alleged) article 4 (employment under special circumstances) reintegrants in its portfolio.

text: Maritime Team Training and Applied Leadership MTTL is a small office with seven FTE, specializing in team training in the maritime-military domain.
text_with_context:
Source: KM+jaarboek+2017.epub  ·  Chapter: Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering

[Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.25) — narrative]
Maritime Team Training and Applied Leadership MTTL is a small office with seven FTE, specializing in team training in the maritime-military domain.

text:
It provides three 'products' to teams of the CZSK.

[SECTION BREAK]

Since 2013, the focus has shifted from guiding individual leaders to guiding leaders and their teams. The first of these is the Team-APK training, and after the summer of 2017, the new 'Building Trust' team training. These trainings are conducted at an external training location at the Old Rijkswerf in Den Helder. The second product is the Coaching Course for Supervisors CZSK (LCC). In this course, civilian and military supervisors (from the rank of Lieutenant at sea 2nd Class) learn to coach as a form of leadership. The third product involves two MTTL members working on training Crew Resource Management (CRM) instructors for the fleet and marines and guiding teams on CRM. Training CRM instructors is the first step in integrating CRM within all training and education of CZSK. This is done in close cooperation with a Mobile Training Team from the US Navy. The essence of CRM is that, in addition to the usual training of technical skills, teams are viewed in a different, broader way. The collaboration between people and not so much non-technical skills is central to this. The services provided by the MTTL office are adjusted as much as possible to the needs of the teams.

[SECTION BREAK]

text:
Unfortunately, the planned team training sessions in the West were largely canceled this year due to Hurricane Irma passing over the Leeward Islands. In 2017, collaboration was sought in the area of CRM with the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM) and the SMVBO. For the first time, Flag Officer Sea Training (FOST) staff members were guests as students at the Immunization (IMM) CRM training course in November. In 2018, MTTL will continue discussions with FOST on whether CRM can be used as 'the' evaluation tool for non-technical skills throughout the entire operational chain (including FOST). There was also more intensive collaboration with Belgian marine colleagues by opening the LCC and IMM CRM training courses to their leaders. In 2017, approximately 800 personnel from CZSK were trained by MTTL trainers in various training sessions/LCCs. NH90s hunting a submarine during the FOST exercise near Heston, United Kingdom.

Koerse The year 2017 was primarily focused on further securing and developing the changes initiated in 2016. The internal Training Royal Netherlands Navy Schools (OKMS) organization is solid but is understaffed in certain areas to meet all training requests. Vacancies and numerous personnel changes exacerbated this shortage of available capacity. The effects of this are increasing training backlogs and lagging educational development.

[SECTION BREAK]

Recruitment Assignment The recruitment assignment indicates how many students from a specific (sub) service group need to be recruited and undergo initial training. In 2017, the recruitment assignment was fulfilled for most (sub) service groups. Bottlenecks Steering, Control & Coordination Training Royal Netherlands Navy (SBC-OKM).

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, the high dropout rate in the First Marine Training is a problem. For the corporal training programs, there were too few students in the (sub) service groups Operational Service Operations (ODOPS), Marine General (MARNALG), and Marine Connections (MARNVB).

Development of the Armed Forces In early 2017, the first meeting was initiated, aimed at the transition that the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) organization would have to undergo as a result of the intended cabinet decision to substantially and structurally increase the defense budget. One of the measures eligible for additional funding was the strengthening of the training domain. In collaboration with the schools, a plan was developed with three tracks. Track 1 concerns outsourcing training (allowing scarce Royal Netherlands Navy capacity to be deployed elsewhere), track 2 involves the purchase of educational materials, and track 3 focuses on expanding the OKMS organization with job positions. Additionally, a temporary transition organization has been defined to oversee the implementation of the three tracks on behalf of the Chief Training Royal Netherlands Navy (HOKM). It must also provide for the development of education for new systems that will eventually be introduced within CZSK as part of DOKM. Educational Affairs This calendar year, Steering, Control & Coordination of Royal Netherlands Navy Training (SBC-OKM) provided information to all Authorities with Jurisdiction (mostly department heads) about their role in the needs assessment process. During this information round, the Authorized Authority is informed about the process for establishing a Qualification Profile when developing and providing training. The Workplace Qualification List (AKL) indicates who needs which qualification to perform their function. The AKL is an important building block for gaining insight into the qualitative personnel readiness of CZSK employees. This year, the AKL was digitized, making it accessible via the Software Application for Standard Reports (COGNOS).

[SECTION BREAK]

In consultation with the schools, the evaluation calendar was established, which records when each training should be evaluated. The Authorized Authority is also involved in determining the calendar and the prioritization included in it.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Training and Individual Training proposal (O&iT) is the concept (the offer) of a training program, from which O&iT can be further developed. The Expertise Center Training

[SECTION BREAK]

The Directorate of Personnel and Business Operations (ECOD) has designed a format for the O&iT proposal that is used across Defence. The OB&E office created a user manual for this purpose. The ECOD has used this instruction as a basis to develop the Purple O&iT proposal (new version with filling instructions).

Quality in Image The Court of Audit wants to know what the qualitative operational readiness of Defence personnel is. Since the branches of the armed forces have different systems for this, the project 'Quality in Image' was initiated, with the aim of improving the quality and accessibility of Personnel Readiness (-related) data.

[SECTION BREAK]

For this, it is necessary to ensure that the process of determining qualifications and assigning qualifications to personnel is secured. A complete and accurate list of job qualifications is an indispensable tool for this. Professionally oriented training Following the implementation of Professionally Oriented Training (BGO), a communication plan for BGO was drawn up. To implement this, the final exercise of the Marine Corps took place in Rotterdam.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-30 49 Directorate Personnel and Operations is establishing a BGO Communication working group. This group is intended to provide information about BGO on board ships, to listen to issues, and where possible, to offer solutions. The overarching goal is to create support for the implementation of BGO and the resources used for it.

[SECTION BREAK]

The operational units are assisted in setting up 'workplace learning' by the Bureau Praktijkleren (BPL). BPL staff embark during the Safety and Readiness Checks 2 (SARC) on board to provide information to the leadership for establishing an adequate support structure for the trainees. Research by SBC-OKM into the support structure at the operational units revealed that there are still various challenges regarding guidance. BPL has been invited to work together with the BGO working group to promote the project more broadly across the operational units. This is done through interviews and presentations. Gamified, Peer to Peer, Adaptive, Learning In November 2015, the company MAD Multimedia won the Defense Innovation Competition (DIC) for training & education with the concept Gamified, Peer to Peer, Adaptive, Learning From Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman's perspective on Zr.Ms.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-31 50 Directorate Personnel and Operations (GPAL). The prize was a monetary amount with which the Pilot GPAL 1.0 could be financed across all branches of the armed forces, including CZSK. The pilot was successfully concluded in 2016. In 2017, the Steering Group Training and Individual Training (RO&iT) decided to organize a second pilot GPAL 2.0. OKM was even assigned two pilots. These are being supervised by the Bureau Educational Affairs of SBC-OKM. One pilot is being held at the School for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense, Damage Control and Occupational Safety (SCBRNDCBV) (various courses) and the other pilot at the Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) for students and users of the Safety and Craftsmanship (VeVa) learning pathway.

[SECTION BREAK]

For both schools, expert staff are creating short instructional videos that will be placed on the defense-wide GPAL app. Students can access the videos on location via a QR code or I-beacon, but can also create their own videos. The GPAL concept facilitates learning in the workplace and peer-to-peer interaction among learners. Common instructions or actions can be recorded and shared as needed. An advantage is that this reduces the burden on instructors and practical trainers.

[SECTION BREAK]

Simulation symposium Navy.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-32 51 Directorate Personnel and Operations Interns An important task of the BPL is to create internship positions for students who apply for an internship at the CZSK through the 'Defence Internship Bank'. The office processes the applications, searches for internship positions within the CZSK organization, and coordinates the administrative handling. The table below indicates how many internship positions and of what type have been realized: Number WO/HBO 51 MBO students 34 School visits by Steering Control & Coordination (SBC). On average once a month, HOKM, along with the Chief of the Crew and, if possible, several department heads, pays a working visit to one of the OKM schools. During this visit, HOKM meets with the school management team, the participation council, and the person responsible for the buildings and grounds. The SCBRNDCBV, the Netherlands-Belgium Operational School (NLBEOPS), the Belgian-Dutch Competence Center Support Department Catering in Bruges (BEL), the Belgian-Dutch Mine Countermeasures School Eguermin in Ostend (BEL), the School for Maritime Training, Operations & Education, the DDS, the KMTO, the Training and Education Center Logistics (OTC-Log) in Soesterberg, and the MOC at the van Ghent Barracks in Rotterdam were visited, with the DDS being visited on-site aboard the submarines Nautilus and Soemba in the Grevelingenmeer. From December 10 to 13, a visit was made to the Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean (CZMCARIB) in Curaçao.

[SECTION BREAK]

Among other things, Marine Barracks Suffisant was welcomed as the ninth OKM school. The commander of MK Suffisant is responsible for the training of the Curaçao and Aruban militias and has a training department for this purpose. It was agreed that there is a functional relationship between HOKM and C-MK Suffisant. The name by which this organizational part is designated in this role is the Training Center CARIB (OCC).

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-35 54 Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Belgian-Dutch catering school (CCSp Dept Catering BENL) Commandant: Major R. Dejaghere Commandant NL-DET: Lieutenant (junior grade) (SD) H.C.M. Feitsma From October 26, Lieutenant (junior grade) (LD) R.

[SECTION BREAK]

Vervelde In 2017, the continued existence of the school was under scrutiny. On the Belgian side, restructuring took place, during which the catering concept was also examined. Given the potentially far-reaching consequences for the training of Belgian catering personnel, consideration was given to the possible outsourcing of the training to civilian parties. This approach proved unfeasible; the timeframe in which the school could prepare students for their (Defense) tasks was much shorter than that of a civilian trainer.

[SECTION BREAK]

The company restaurant at the barracks in Bruges sought collaboration with the school in 2017. Initially driven by personnel challenges, but also from the perspective of the school, the company restaurant seemed a welcome opportunity to better simulate everyday practice. The initial experiences raised some points of attention, but the agreement followed to continue this initiative in the coming period.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the request of the coast guard, the school trained cooks for Aruba. Thus, it fulfilled the concept of 'learning everywhere and always.' The involved trainer, who was familiar with the workings on the island, was able to provide customized training, tailored to the prior knowledge of the student cooks, with the program focused on the specific situation of the galley aboard a cutter. This process resulted in well-deserved certificates with social significance. The civil qualification of Dutch sailors and prospective corporals increasingly demands more from the training time. While the school had previously faced additional requirements in the areas of mathematics, English, and Dutch (REN subjects), attention is now being requested within the Secondary Vocational Education for so-called 'elective components.' These training programs provide the necessary broadening or deepening of the fixed curriculum for level 2 and level 3 training. In consultation with ROC Midden Nederland, the school sought to determine where these elective components could be integrated into the existing training content, so that additional training time was minimized. In co-creation, elective components have now been developed, and another is on the horizon.

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-37 56 Directorate Personnel and Operations This year, the SCBRNDCBV has also focused on filling long-standing vacancies by attracting and internally training new instructors. They will further develop their skills during their placement. Additionally, personnel from elsewhere within the CZSK, who may be interested in following the internal instructor training (UA04), have been sought. Through modernization in equipment with two new simulator trainers, realistic training can be conducted in the 'one-line extinguishing technique', which reduces water consumption for firefighting. The nozzle trainer, which can simulate a hot gas layer using gas (the layer of hot air that rises during a fire and eventually ignites), is functioning properly and is an important component of the training simulators. The fire progression trainer (flash-over trainer) is also being extensively used. A significant advantage of the new simulator trainers is that they are equipped with a post-combustion system, allowing training to occur under nearly all meteorological conditions and resulting in less environmental impact.

[SECTION BREAK]

School for Maritime Education and Operations (SMVBO) Commander: kltz R.M.

[SECTION BREAK]

Platel This year, the Intake Department ensured that out of the 326 enrolled EMMV students, 268 successfully completed this training. For the Flow Department, the year 2017 was primarily focused on facilitating the renewed training programs. In 2016, significant substantive changes were implemented within the SMVBO-Flow training programs. For instance, the Management Training Course (LMV) structure was overhauled, reducing the total number of LMVs from eight to six, and these programs are now tied to a specific rank and career path. This meant that starting this year, following an LMV was no longer voluntary but a mandatory part of the career path to be followed. After a year full of innovation, the time had come to reap the benefits of this, and despite a shortage of trainers, a significant number of training programs were conducted. The Flow Department trained 1690 out of 1744 registered participants, spread over 149 training programs.

Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training in Den Helder (KMTO) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) ing. D.J.M Meijer EMSD Students All new entrants to the Technical Division (TD) of the navy begin their careers at the KMTO. In 2017, 95 sailors graduated with the EVO and 61 with the First Adjustment Module (AEM). Additionally, 34 non-commissioned officers, who have already gained operational experience as sailors, started their technical MBO3 training in Mechatronics at the ROC Kop van Noord-Holland. Besides the 'regular' entrants, there are also VeVa students. The KMTO collaborates with ROC's spread throughout the country, which provide the VeVa training, specializing in Mechatronics level 2 and 3. These students participate in the exercise Port Defender, where the diver is launched into the water.

[SECTION BREAK]

60 Directorate of Personnel and Operations provides vocational education at the ROCs and during their training, they receive the Vocational Practical Training (BPV) at the KMTO. This year, the KMTO had a total of 192 VeVa students. In addition to the new intake, the KMTO also provides education for the already serving technical personnel. Various staff members follow various technical vocational and/or functional training courses at different times in their careers, both in groups and individually, ranging from one-day to long-term courses. Given the many international collaborations of the CZSK, the KMTO also trains foreign naval colleagues. For example, in 2017, Chilean colleagues attended the Technical Central (TC) Procedures MF module at the KMTO, a German naval staff member completed the Basic Knowledge Unix and APAR courses, and several Belgian staff members participated in, among others, Generic Functional Education and the System Responsible Officer (SVO) training. It is an app that allows employees to consult instructional videos created by colleagues, supervisors, and/or instructors using QR codes and iBeacons (Bluetooth transmitters), for example, with a mobile phone. Over the past year, the KMTO has supported seven learning tasks from the learning task book of the Assistant Mechanic with videos during a pilot, and three students were onboard Zr.Ms. Evertsen for technical training at the KMTO at Marinekazerne Erfprins.

operational needs of the Royal Netherlands Navy. Representatives from the units unanimously concluded that they were very satisfied with the capabilities of the app and its alignment with the current training philosophy. All parties involved in the project reported in GPAL seeing added value as a tool within the BGO.

[SECTION BREAK]

In 2017, the first students of the pilot learning trajectory 'distance learning' succeeded. Two corporals were the first to complete the program positively in June, thereby obtaining an MBO-4 qualification. The group that started in September 2016, consisting of 24 technical corporals, can achieve an MBO qualification at level 4 upon successfully completing this trajectory.

[SECTION BREAK]

This learning trajectory in the form of distance learning is provided by ROC Kop van Noord-Holland with support from KMTO. The new form of technical education, the Continuous Technical Learning Lines (DTL), was also a topic that occupied the staff of the school in 2017. The DTL is becoming increasingly known within the technical department of the navy, and the changes in technical education are steadily becoming noticeable within the organization. To properly guide and support these changes, KMTO launched the communication campaign DTL, Tell-Tell-Tell! Intensive communication was conducted from KMTO with all relevant target groups, such as organizing information sessions and (ship) visits. Additionally, significant efforts are being made in the development, phasing in and out, and implementation of the DTL.

Er zijn verschillende workshops en trainingen georganiseerd voor personeel om hun vaardigheden en kennis te verbeteren. Dit omvatte onder andere leiderschapstrainingen en cursussen gericht op persoonlijke ontwikkeling. Belgian-Dutch mine countermeasures school EGUERMIN Dutch leadership: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) M.M. Lambregts In 2017, the separation of EGUERMIN and the Centre of Excellence Naval Mine Warfare was completed. EGUERMIN has retained its prominent status as a binational naval mine countermeasures school within NATO. This has resulted in a well-filled training catalog that is also known and recognized by the allies. The naval mine countermeasures school EGUERMIN is the training center for operational training and specific technical aspects for the minehunters of the Netherlands and Belgium. The training and courses provided there are tailored in consultation with the HOKM, the Competence Center of the Naval Component (CCMAR), and NLMARFOR Sea Training Command (STC) according to the needs.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Personnel and Operations of the Commander of the Naval Forces and the Commander of the Belgian Naval Component. Binational training and exercises The crews of the Belgian and Dutch mine countermeasure units go to EGUERMIN to follow functional training: Personnel and non-commissioned officers of the Operational Service and naval officers learn to use various systems to detect and clear naval mines; Military personnel from the Technical Service receive instruction on, among other things, the Degaussing System, which reduces the magnetic signature of the ships; Divers receive training on deck work and the operation of naval mines; Personnel responsible for the deployment of the Remote Environmental Monitoring Unit System (REMUS) Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) are trained at EGUERMIN to become REMUS 100 AUV Operators; Team training in the Team Training Facility (TTF). Demonstration of the Light Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (LAUV).

text:
Ultimately, it was decided to deploy an operational unit in Doorn to generate sufficient cadre members to fill a training unit EMV MARNS. In addition to this challenge, the staff of the MOC was confronted with the start of the OKM-wide ISO re-certification, the mandatory compliance with the working hours stipulated in the Working Hours Act (ATW), the start of preparations for the DOKM, and the business plan for 2018. In addition to these operational matters, the MOC had a first in 2017 with the first female candidate who passed the Marine selection and assessment, and the idea of the Incoming Finex POTOM at the Marine Training Center.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2017_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-53 72 Directorate of Personnel and Operations even military personnel from other branches of the armed forces would transfer to the Marine Corps.

[SECTION BREAK]

Ideas regarding this were extensively discussed. The actual implementation could possibly take place in 2018. The MOC, together with the Van Ghent Barracks (VGKAZ), was also fully operational in 2017, training hundreds of students through the Initial Training Departments, Career Training, Functional Training, and the Physical Training and Sports unit. This was prepared and supported by the Quality Assurance, Innovation, and Knowledge Management Department (KIK) and LOG/PLANS. In addition, the usual ceremonial tasks were carried out, such as during Prinsjesdag, the wreath-laying on December 9 at the Oostplein in Rotterdam, various arrivals and swearing-in ceremonies, and even a contribution was made to National Operations in maritime border control during the migrant crisis. text:
Therefore, during the Jungle Training from April 2 to April 22, 2017, improvements were made to the communication systems. The training took place in the jungle environment of the Caribbean, specifically on the island of Curacao. The focus was on enhancing the operational capabilities of the Marines in challenging environments. The training included various scenarios that tested the Marines' skills in navigation, survival, and combat in jungle conditions. The exercise was conducted by the Marine Corps with the support of various units, ensuring that all participants were well-prepared for future deployments in similar environments.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-6 81 Operations Directorate desired level. This year's training took place in Belize, which presents a significant challenge regarding communications due to the dense vegetation and the unpredictable nature of the terrain. NIMCIS Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) are virtually unusable here, making reliance solely on HF communications necessary. In response to the concerning situation regarding these communications during the last training in Belize in 2015, the JKCMOX requested extensive communication tests to be conducted in the various training areas in Belize. Therefore, the HF Test Team (HFTT), consisting of eight personnel, successfully tested and mapped the HF communications over a period of fourteen days. The goal was to ensure that tactical and safety communications could be maintained throughout at least JW(I)C 2017 by thoroughly testing HF communications both day and night. With the necessary improvements and solutions implemented, the creation of a Standard Operations Procedure (SOP) for "communications in a jungle environment" is currently in progress.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-9 84 The Operations Directorate oversees naval units and the Coast Guard Cutters in the Caribbean region and additionally provides support to the fleet and NATO allies. The STC consists of six departments: GBW, Submarine Service, Mine Countermeasures Vessels Mine Operational Sea Training (M(CMV)OST), Force Protection and Boarding Operations (FPBO), Weapons System Management (WSM GBW), and STC-Shore. The Shore department comprises the Ship Operations Bureau (SBV), the Bureau for Consolidation, Preparation, and Sustainability (CG&B), and the Safety and Environment Bureau (V&M). Sea Training Command: Shore In 2017, five larger naval units began their operational training trajectory. After completing their SARC-1 and SARC-2, these units were further trained at sea by the GBW department or the MOST. For the smaller units, including tugs, training, diving, and landing craft, the transition to the PvB system has commenced. This involves separating the training of the crew from the platform.

[SECTION BREAK]

Ten of these smaller platforms have been delivered as operationally ready, and twenty personnel have obtained their PvB certification. Even during the operational period of the units, they are monitored and corrected where necessary. Five so-called CTs have been conducted, part of which took place in the West. Additionally, thirty-one readiness checks have been carried out to assess whether the units still meet the high standards established during their training trajectory. For four units, it was determined after inspection that the operations were sufficiently in order to commence scheduled maintenance and then resume the training trajectory. Finally, ten major safety presentations were given on location as part of various P-weeks, and a contribution was made to five VMS-Def training courses.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directie Operaties embarked Allouette III. On June 20, the staff debarked in Augusta, after which the ship was ready for its mission. After the summer leave, the staff embarked on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam to also conduct a PDT with this ship. This training was carried out during the outbound journey to the Anti-Piracy mission Atalanta. For this, several enablers were embarked, including a Cougar helicopter from the 300 Squadron DHC, a Swedish Enhanced Boarding Element (EBE), an EBE from the Corps of Marines, a Swedish CB90 squadron, three FRISC’s from SATG, and an ART. Since all these modules needed to be prepared for the mission, a diverse staff was assembled consisting of personnel from KMTO, DMI, the SCBRNDCBV school, MTC, Defence Intelligence and Security Institute (DIVI), Defence Helicopter Command (DHC), and MHKC. The first part of the PDT focused on fire, damage control, and the individual preparation of the enablers. After the staff change in Malaga, the focus shifted to the mission and the integration of the enablers. A transit to Malta followed, where a two-day exercise program took place with the Maltese Defence Force. After part of the staff was dropped off in La Valetta, Malta, the ship continued its journey towards Crete to conduct two large boarding exercises at the NATO Maritime Interdiction Operations Training Centre (NMIOTC).

[SECTION BREAK]

Sea Training Command: MOST 

MOST provided training for 27 units from eight different countries during 58 sailing weeks in 2017. The mobile MOST team was deployed four times in four different countries in 2017. The year began with the CT for BNS Primula, while the Sea Acceptance Trials (SATs) and the SARC 3 for Zr.Ms. Makkum were conducted simultaneously. In early February, MOST provided support to Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 1 (SNMCMG) while it was in Zeebrugge. During this execution, two Italian seariders from La Spezia were guests at MOST as observers. At the end of February, a CT for BNS Godetia was conducted, and training was provided for Willemstad. Subsequently, CTs for Zr.Ms. Snellius, Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen, and BNS Lobelia were conducted. The mobile team underwent an extended Fast Cruise (FC) of Zr.Ms. Mercuur in week 13 in Den Helder. An extended FC was necessary because the Varende Materieels Beproevingen (VMBs) commenced immediately after extensive maintenance and significant propulsion modifications. At the beginning of spring, the SARC 3 and 4 for Zr.Ms. Luymes were scheduled, while the other team conducted the CT for BNS Narcis. Immediately after, the FC and VMBs for Zr.Ms. Urk were on the agenda. In May, a NATO test of the Latvian ship Virsaitis was planned; for its execution, a mobile team flew to Liepaja, Latvia. At the same time, the other team was deployed in Zeebrugge for the execution of the SARC-3 of Zr.Ms. Mercuur, followed by the SARC-3 of Zr.Ms. Urk and the VMBs of BNS Bellis. On June 6, the German minehunter Sulzbach Rosenberg was present in Zeebrugge for a NATO test. The other training team conducted a CT for BNS Castor and BNS Bellis.

The Maritime Headquarters ABNL (MHK ABNL) is part of the Operations Directorate of the CZSK. The MHK is responsible for Belgian and Dutch operations and exercises of fleet and marine units. The MHK ABNL: Programs, plans, directs, coordinates, and supports operational readiness activities. Prepares mandated operations, executes them, and supports these operations. Drafts the bi-national operational year plan (OJP) and oversees the realization of the assigned activities. Additionally, the MHK ABNL serves as the 24/7 point of contact and coordination within CZSK for operational matters.

Karel Doorman made a brief port visit to Haakonsvern, after which it returned to Den Helder for the next event; the Marine Days. It was the first time the ship was open to the public during the Marine Days. The event coincided with SAIL, and the ship also hosted the Captain's Dinner. During these days, over 20,600 visitors were welcomed on board. On June 8, Zr.Ms. Tromp sailed for a demonstration of Replenishment at Sea with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman for a working visit from the outgoing Minister of Defence J.A. Hennis-Plasschaert. Most of the time was spent on Assisted Maintenance, during which the Technical Service and the involved shore authorities made significant efforts to prepare the ship for the autumn voyage. This autumn voyage kicked off in Rotterdam with the World Port Days, where Zr.Ms. Tromp, together with other units and civilian parties, welcomed approximately 430,000 visitors during the first weekend of September. Following the World Port Days, the ship, along with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, and BNS Louise-Marie, steamed towards the Baltic Sea. This task group would participate over a period of seven weeks in three major international exercises: Northern Coasts, Joint Warrior 17-2, and Formidable Shield 2017. The staff of the task group, this time under the command of Commander (cdr) J.H. Hulsker, was once again embarked on Zr.Ms. Tromp. After a weekend in Karlskrona, Northern Coasts commenced. This exercise focused on international cooperation in the Baltic Sea, with the secondary goal of the SARC-4 of Zr.Ms.

On April 4, the ship conducted a DISTEX at the Marine Barracks Savaneta in Aruba, and the next day it ceremonially entered the port of Oranjestad. There, the USCG LEDET was embarked. After departing from Oranjestad on April 9, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel began its CTG 4.4 period. On April 11, the ship conducted a Naval Surface Fire Support exercise with the 76 mm gun north of Aruba. Holland Commander: kltz P.C.B. Dijkhuizen EMSD The deployment of Zr.Ms. Holland this year consisted of three parts: a training program led by C-STC, Coast Guard duties, and counter-drug operations. After the maintenance period in Curaçao, Zr.Ms. Holland conducted CD operations from December 13, 2016, to January 20, 2017, with support from the USCG LEDET and a Guard Aviation Detachment with an MH-65 Dolphin helicopter. After completing a joint training/integration period, the ship was ready for Operation Carib Venture under the leadership of CTG 4.4. During this period, two drug transports were disrupted, and the ship was closely involved in a controlled overload of contraband. During the Coast Guard operation periods, daily FRISC patrols were again conducted around the Windward Islands and in the waters around Anguilla and Saint Kitts. On January 21, in close cooperation with the DASH-8, an interception of a Go-Fast was carried out, resulting in the seizure of 220 kg of cocaine and the arrest of three individuals by the Coast Guard boarding team.

text:
Zr.Ms. Urk Commander: Lt. G.E.

[SECTION BREAK]

Fretz In mid-January, the ship was taken to Zeebrugge for major maintenance. Subsequently, a training period began, during which crew members attended courses, completed tests, and made preparations. In early March, part of the crew boarded Zr.Ms. Urk in Zeebrugge. They ensured that the ship completed SARC 1, after which the rest of the crew embarked to complete SARC-2. Furthermore, Lieutenant (ltz) G.E. Fretz took command. In May, SARC-3 was scheduled for two weeks. Despite many material defects, the status Ready for Sea was achieved. Before the leave, several SATs were conducted, and a signature measurement took place on the Haringvliet. After the summer leave, the crew began the second half of the training trajectory. In August, the ship worked on an exercise program in Zeebrugge as part of SARC-4, during which a lot of diving took place. After successfully completing this week, Zr.Ms. Urk set course for Scotland for two weeks of exercises in the Firth of Forth.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-43 118 Operations Directorate near Edinburgh. Here, mine hunting was practiced intensively, and due to the deeper waters around Scotland, the Self Propelled Variable Depth Sonar (SPVDS) was well utilized. As a break from the training program, a weekend stop was made in Leith near Edinburgh.

[SECTION BREAK]

Upon arrival in Zeebrugge, it became clear that we had successfully completed SARC-4 and that Zr.Ms. Urk received the designation Ready for Exercise. In October, the final phase of the training trajectory began. SARC-5 consisted of four weeks filled with scheduled exercises in firefighting, mine hunting, force protection, and multiple emergencies. This was good preparation for SARC-6, which immediately followed SARC-5. During this week, various exercises were conducted, but this time the exercises were unexpectedly initiated by the MOST. Despite a good start to SARC-5/6 and the enthusiastic commitment of the crew, this period unfortunately concluded with an unsatisfactory result, meaning that Zr.Ms. Urk will conduct SARC-5/6 again in March 2018.

Although several technical problems arose throughout the year, Willemstad and her crew dedicated themselves to training and education, displaying the Dutch flag, and promoting the Royal Netherlands Navy in general. After completing the annual maintenance in Zeebrugge, the year for Zr.Ms. Willemstad began in March with participation in the international exercise Joint Warrior near Scotland. In the spring, the ship contributed to testing future mine countermeasure equipment in cooperation with the Belgian Navy. After this, she represented the Dutch Navy during SAIL Den Helder and Marine Days in Den Helder, where approximately 1,500 people were guided on board. Willemstad also participated in July in the Cadet Cruise, focusing on training six future officers. After taking part in

The Operations Directorate participated in the World Port Days in Rotterdam in August, where an estimated 2000 people were on board. text:
Walrus made three voyages during the year 2017. From January 30 to February 17, the voyage took place in which the submarine facilitated the Commanding Officers Course Qualifying Exercise (COCQEX) in Norwegian waters for both the NLSMCC and the British SMCC. During this voyage, students were tested in safely operating a submarine at periscope depth among warships maneuvering at high speed around the submarine. During this voyage, a port visit to Bergen took place.

[SECTION BREAK]

Zr.Ms. Walrus in British waters.

This period was also used to carry out a crew change. Crew Orange, previously working on Zr.Ms. Bruinvis, exchanged with Crew Blue, who were working on Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Walrus. Crew Orange would later carry out the CDS operation with the Walrus later in the year following this exchange. After the crew change and maintenance period, trials after maintenance, Combat Training (CT), and a Pre Deployment Training took place in preparation for the CDS operation. The Walrus had to carry out the BNO program intermittently due to several significant malfunctions that required a return to Den Helder.

[SECTION BREAK]

After completing the trials, Zr.Ms. Walrus successfully executed the CDS operation. From November 19 to December 2, the third voyage took place, focusing on Zr.Ms. Mercuur near Plymouth.

[SECTION BREAK]

124 Operations Directorate provided support to FOST and 7 SQN. In addition, there was a focus on training our own personnel. The program during these two weeks mainly consisted of CASEX B2 with air units and several CASEX A24 with surface and air units. The NH90s from 7 SQN participated in the serials at various times. Additionally, Zr.Ms. Walrus advanced crew members with an INDEX program in their training trajectory. Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw Commander: Lt. Cdr. E.G.J.

Operational units Marine Corps 1st Marine Combat Group (1 MCG) Commander: Lt. Col. I.D.L. Moerman, from September 1 Lt. Col. E.

[SECTION BREAK]

Piwek The first half of 2017 was largely focused on supporting the training of 13 Raiding Squadron (RSQN) and 22 RSQN. In the first quarter, the Joint Arctic Training 2017 (JAT17) demanded all attention. 12 RSQN began its training program in August. After the summer leave of 2017, the training of the MCG staff commenced.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-50 125 Operations Directorate Individual Deployments Various personnel from 1 MCG participated in individual deployments in 2017, including the Capacity Building Mission Iraq (CBMI, both regular and Special Operations Forces (SOF)). Very High Readiness Joint Task Force (Land) (VJTF(L)) The VJTF(L) is a rapidly deployable brigade and is under British command. The Netherlands contributed a Raiding Squadron Task Unit (RSTU) in 2017, consisting of approximately 180 personnel. The main body was formed by 1 RSQN, supplemented by enablers from 10 Combat Service Support Squadron (10 CSS SQN), 14 Combat Support Squadron (14 CS SQN), and 15 Reconnaissance Target Acquisition Squadron (15 RSTA SQN).

[SECTION BREAK]

From January 1 to December 31, 2017, the entire VJTF(L) was on 48 hours notice to move for deployment within NATO territory. Marine Spearhead Task Unit (MSTU) The MSTU is a rapidly deployable unit of the Marine Corps that can be deployed within 48 hours. The core of the unit is a Raiding Squadron, supplemented with enablers in Sint Maarten after Hurricane Irma.

[SECTION BREAK]

Operations Directorate of Combat Service Support Squadron, Combat Support Squadron, and Reconnaissance Target Acquisition Squadron. Command & control is provided by a staff element of the MCG staff. In 2017, this task was assigned to 1 MCG. FPME-4 From July 18, a composite unit from 1 MCG participated for three months in the Force Protection Middle East (FPME) mission number 4 in Jordan. The unit was responsible for providing security for a Belgian squadron of F-16s. The CLSK was unable to execute rotation 4 due to the fact that the appropriate security personnel were on deployment protection.

text:
Not providing Force Protection was not an option because the Netherlands had an agreement with Belgium that if they supplied the F-16s, the Netherlands would provide ground security.

[SECTION BREAK]

Colleagues from the CLSK were also added to the security detachment of 1 MCG. During the mission, there was excellent cooperation. Emergency Assistance Sint Maarten 11 Raiding Squadron (including the reinforcement of a Troop from 23 Raiding Squadron), BME, and logistics personnel from 1 MCG provided emergency assistance in Sint Maarten following Hurricane Irma from September 8 to the end of September. In addition, 1 MCG supplied the majority of the staff officers, together with personnel from 2 MCG, to form the command and control element of the Joint Task Force Sint Maarten.

[SECTION BREAK]

VPD (Vessel Protection Detachment) As in previous years, VPD teams were also deployed in 2017 to secure Dutch ships. This year, 2 MCG provided the six primary VPD teams and 1 MCG was required to provide five secondary VPD teams. This led to several deployments. National Assistance Personnel from 1 MCG also saw deployment in the national domain in 2017. For example, from August 12 to August 20, a Maritime Advanced Search Team (MAST) provided support for an operation in Curaçao. Atalanta 2017 From August 27 to December 3, personnel from Recce Sniper, supplemented by personnel from 22 RSQN, participated as EBE in the Atalanta mission aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam as part of the European Union's anti-piracy mission.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-52 127 Operations Directorate Training and Exercises The larger exercises of 2017 included the JAT in the vicinity of Harstad (Norway), the Black Horse shooting training at Twentynine Palms (United States), and the mountain training in Garelochhead (United Kingdom). 10 CSS SQN was on 48 hours notice to move for the VJTF in 2017 with approximately half of the squadron, personnel as well as equipment. The squadron had logistical resources ready for 30 days to enable an expeditionary operation, entirely independently. At the same time, the squadron supported the other exercises of 1 MCG, in support of the MTC and also 2 MCG. Despite a significant shortage of trained personnel and the absence of many mid-level staff, all assignments were able to proceed.

text:
When activating emergency aid to the Windward Islands following Hurricane Irma, 10 CSS SQN, partly due to the preparation for VJTF, was able to prepare and push out all necessary materials and supporting personnel within 24 hours via Eindhoven Airport and the port of Den Helder. 11 RSQN underwent parachute training in the first half of 2017 and supported 2 MCG with the Eagle Niala exercise. In the context of preparation for the VJTF(L), 11 RSQN participated in the ALERT EX in the Netherlands and the DEPLOY EX in Romania. After the summer leave, 11 RSQN was deployed as MSTU for emergency aid to the Windward Islands following the passage of Hurricane Irma. Shortly after the emergency aid, novices from the unit were able to participate in the mountain training.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the end of 2017, 11 RSQN prepared to provide 5 VPD teams starting January 1, 2018. Throughout the year, 11 RSQN was on standby in the context of the VJTF and the MSTU. 12 RSQN carried out various smaller activities in the first half of 2017 such as VPD deployment, boarding training in the Nieuwe Haven, Hunter Force, participation in the Cutlass Express exercise in Djibouti/Mauritius, support for training and exercises, and various ceremonial tasks including the Normandy commemoration. Furthermore, 12 RSQN phased out in the first half of 2017 to start with a newly formed crew in August 2018 for the preparation year. Due to insufficient outflow from the EMV, 12 RSQN began the preparation year with only two Troops instead of three.

[SECTION BREAK]

From August to October, functional training for the various specialists within the squadron, such as infantry engineers (IE), marksmen, and section commanders, was the focus. The unit also conducted SOP training during this period. In October-November, 12 RSQN participated in mountain training. Subsequently, the unit conducted shooting training in Otterburn, United Kingdom.

text:
13 RSQN completed its training cycle in the first half of 2017. The squadron consisted of a staff and two Troops (due to underfilling during formation in 2016). Training during this period included winter training in Norway, SOUT training in Germany, Basic Helicopter Training, and fast rope training in the Netherlands, culminating in Maritime Interdiction Operations (MIO) training and MARSOC certification exercise. With the completion of the training cycle, 13 RSQN was certified MARC-4 in July 2017. In the second half of 2017, 13 RSQN conducted the Black Horse exercise at the US Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center in Twentynine Palms (Mojave Desert, California). The objective of this exercise was to conduct tactical shooting exercises up to squadron level. In the autumn, 13 RSQN carried out, among other things, the military tracker course in Aruba. For the CBMI mission, 13 RSQN assembled and trained a training team to be deployed in Iraq in January 2018.

[SECTION BREAK]

14 CS SQN consists of three Troops: Anti Armour (AA) Troop, Armoured All Terrain Vehicle (AATV) Troop, and Assault Engineers (AE) Troop.

[SECTION BREAK]

Throughout 2017, these Troops followed their own training programs. AE and AATV supported, with each a section, the training year of a RSQN. As a result, they participated in several exercises of the training system, such as the mobility week and the certification exercise. AE also conducted cold weather training for Marines in Norway.

[SECTION BREAK]

the Zr.Ms. Zeeland provided support during the operation. The Directie Operaties (Operations Directorate) also conducted several diverse national operations. For example, they were deployed twice before the summer, including for the search for a missing person. In August, they were deployed in Curaçao. As part of the MSTU, AE Troop provided emergency assistance in Sint Maarten after Hurricane Irma. 2017 concluded with a large MAST deployment in Hoogeveen.

The MCG staff achieved Operational Readiness status in the first half of 2017. In mid-2017, a Jungle Warfare Instructors Course was conducted in Belize, which also involved a platoon from the Air Mobile Brigade. Furthermore, various training activities of the sub-units were planned and executed. Due to the deployment of many personnel, the MCG primarily conducted small-scale exercises. Hurricane Irma led to a rapid deployment to Sint Maarten of the 2 MCG staff supported by personnel from 1 MCG, 11 RSQN, a Troop from 23 RSQN supplemented by units from the Air Mobile Brigade and engineers from the Royal Netherlands Army. An EBE was also deployed aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam in operation Atalanta. Finally, a Guard Team was deployed with Zr.Ms. Zeeland. They provided support from the Zr.Ms. Zeeland during the operation.

Netherlands Maritime Special Operation Forces (NLMARSOF) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J. van Nee Caribbean as an underwater training location During the spring, the frogmen, placed within the operational squadrons of NLMARSOF, conducted the diving course 2017 in Curaçao. Unique to this training was the participation of operators from both M-squadron (National CT operations) and C-squadron (International SOF operations). Throughout this training, the most diverse aspects of SOF operations in a maritime environment were practiced. Port Defender The Port of Rotterdam served as the stage for this large port protection exercise for three days in the second week of April. Here, the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM), the Special Intervention Service (DSI), the Port of Rotterdam Authority, the Rotterdam Police Unit, and the Rotterdam-Rijnmond Safety Region trained together to be able to respond to a large-scale disaster or a terrorist attack in the port area of Rotterdam in the future. M-squadron participated in this exercise as part of the DSI and as a specialist in Maritime Counter Terrorism. Live Fire Exercises (LFX) M-squadron, NLMARSOF conducted two rotations of one week of LFX at the Sig Sauer Academy in Epping, United States. Due to the acquisition of the MCX weapon platform from Sig Sauer, M-squadron was able to utilize these facilities. During these weeks, they fired with this new weapon platform, and in the evening, a visit was made to the weapon factory to see how an MCX is made from a piece of lightweight metal.

The Operations Directorate received guidelines to use during the preparation. This naturally creates high expectations, but unfortunately, not everyone was equally well-prepared, and it was inevitable that some marines would drop out. The requirements based on the Defense Condition Test and the Physical Profile of Marines are 'hard' requirements. This means that there can be no compensations made and no exceptions granted.

By the end of the first week, only twenty-two candidates remained in the running for a spot in the NLMARSOF training. Seventeen marines stood in great uncertainty on the exercise ground in Doorn on the morning of Monday, July 3, waiting for what was to come. The following two weeks, an Operator from NLMARSOF jumps from a Hercules C-130 during an exercise.

Peters In the past year, the Seabased Support Group (SSG) provided second-line logistical support in support of a challenging Operational Year Plan (OJP), combined with various 'real-world deployments'. This had a significant impact on the necessary personnel and material support. As a result, various specialists from SSG participated in exercises and 'real-world deployments' with other units to support them worldwide. This included logistics and munitions management, armaments technicians, communications service, and automotive mechanics. Due to the challenging OJP, the essential completion of an exercise or the execution of necessary maintenance on used materials was regularly under pressure. For some already scarce operational pool resources, this meant that they were less available for certain units.

Second Landing Craft Task Unit (LCTU-2) The first half of 2017 was focused on the preparation for LCTU-2. This unit was the second unit to be certified according to the intended preparation system. After the summer leave, the various assets of LCTU-2 undertook several serious deployments with Zr.Ms. Rotterdam during Operation Atalanta and emergency aid in the Caribbean with Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman. Marines landing on the beaches of Texel.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-60 135 Operations Directorate Training and Exercises At the beginning of the year, the unit was not yet certified. Therefore, all training was focused on preparing and being ready for the certification moment in July. For the LCTU, the first joint training was a unit training at the Stuifdijk on Texel, where the Amphibious Beach Unit (ABU) was deployed and the vessels operated according to a Surface Assault (SURFALT) to and from the beach. At the end of February, the unit departed for ISHK to maintain individual skills and drills on various weapon systems. In March, the CERTIFEX for the 22nd RSQN took place. LCTU-2 had to support this training, which was also a good dress rehearsal for its own certification in July. The first part of the exercise took place in the vicinity of Vlissingen, using the Marine barracks as a Forward Operating Base (FOB). The second part of the exercise was at the Kop van Noord-Holland, where we operated from Zr.Ms. Rotterdam.

[SECTION BREAK]

After the CERTIFEX, LCTU-2 conducted some of its own training sessions. These included a training on Vlieland; a medical training and a communications week. Additionally, LCTU-2 repeated several annual activities in May and June, including the Military Basic Skills (MBV) and the FPM. LCTU-2 provided the amphibious demonstrations at the end of June during the Marine Days and SAIL Den Helder. Furthermore, the unit was responsible for coordination on the water.

[SECTION BREAK]

Subsequently, we proceeded to the CERTIFEX. During this CERTIFEX, not only the 11th RSQN was certified, but also LCTU-2.

The staff of the GOMD expanded with an additional officer for WSM and now consists of four people (Chief of the Crew, two Weapon System Management officers, and Ship Manager in Conservation) and the Binational Support Team with 11 Dutch personnel remotely in Zeebrugge. The staff developed future mine countermeasures policy in anticipation of the replacement of the current Alkmaar-class mine countermeasures vessels. An important part of this policy is mine countermeasures at greater distances from the mother ship using underwater, surface, and aerial drones. The staff also initiated a plan to bring the DDG back under the Mine Service to improve efficiency and clear responsibility within the mine countermeasures organization. On March 21, the Chief of the Crew of Hr.Ms. Urk, SMJRODOPS Berentsen, was awarded the 'De Ruyter Medal' by Minister of Infrastructure and Water Management M. Schultz van Haegen, in recognition of the significant commitment and involvement of the Mine Service in maritime operations. On April 21, the team from the broad mine countermeasures community became champions in rowing. The GOMD staff organized a very successful Mine Service reunion on May 17 for actively serving personnel, veterans, and former members, which also included the former mine sweepers Naaldwijk and Mahu from the Floating Heritage Royal Netherlands Navy.

Naval Aviation Service (MLD) Group Leader: Commander (cdr) G.A. Polet The increasing availability of NH90 helicopters continued in 2017. With this upward trend, expertise in the Netherlands also increased, positioning our country at the forefront among NH90 users worldwide.

[SECTION BREAK]

However, the large number of different configurations still negatively impacted availability, as various components were insufficiently stocked. Meanwhile, the update of the NH90 from Full Operational Capable (FOC) to Full Radar Capable (FRC) and Maintenance Release 1 (MR1) continued. This latest upgrade is still taking place in Italy during the Retrofit. With the increasing availability, we were also able to meet more of the demand for NH90 on board ships during deployments. Operations This year, a total of 1968 flight hours were performed with the NH90 helicopter. Additionally, our simulator was still in Italy, where we trained a total of 998 hours that year. The first half of the year was partly focused on supporting Zr.Ms. Evertsen in its training trajectory (SARC-4 & NOST), followed by an SNMG1 deployment from May 8 to July 13 with the N319. Part of this deployment included participation in exercises such as BALTOPS and Dynamic Mongoose. From March 4 to June 17, the N324 was deployed on board Zr.Ms. van Amstel during SSCG1. The ship was relieved in the Caribbean by Zr.Ms. Zeeland for SSCG2. In the OPV concept, where the patrol vessel was supported by 2 FRISC’s and an NH90 helicopter, the added value of an NH90 as a game-changer was once again proven. On board was the N325, which was embarked for the period from June 19 to November 10.

In this overview, we highlight only a few highlights from 2017.

text:
The MWC projected the existing template of the defense doctrine discussions onto CZSK. Based on VCZSK 007 Doctrine Development, the doctrine committee of the Royal Netherlands Navy (DCKM) was established under the chairmanship of the Chief of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (PC-CZSK) as a counterpart to the Doctrine Committee of the Armed Forces (DCK). This committee is intended to guide the development of operational knowledge products of CZSK. This involves standardization (doctrine, the way we currently perform our tasks) and concept development (future task execution). Logically, MWC retains the coordinating role in these activities, but the Commander of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (C-ZSK) took ownership of the steering of that process. Associated with this was a new department for Change Management and Innovation, which was strongly connected in communication with MWC.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-67 142 Operations Directorate For the coordination of the external development of knowledge, MWC has been contributing to the Knowledge Network Sea for several years, together with S&A. This body, under the leadership of DMO, aligns the national development of specific scientific knowledge and technology for the benefit of CZSK, particularly within the Golden Triangle (Defense, Industry, Knowledge Institutions). The increasing political demand for international cooperation means that projects in NATO funds such as PESCO, but especially the EU Defence Fund, must also be coordinated. In addition, the national coordination of activities from the growing number of maritime Centres of Excellence means that the Knowledge Network Sea is becoming an increasingly important forum to maintain oversight and provide direction for external knowledge development.

[SECTION BREAK]

Operational highlights this year to which MWC made a significant contribution include: Exercise Formidable Shield 2017, the participation of Zr.Ms. De Ruyter in live multinational BMD scenarios under the command of USN 6th Fleet. JPOW 2017; participation with a SIM-LCF in a multinational BMD exercise organized in collaboration between Germany and the Netherlands. Field briefing during jungle training in Belize.

[SECTION BREAK]

text:
Among the niches to be developed is the Maritime Ballistic Missile Defense (MBMD) capability, which has been under consideration for some time. A DMP-A identified the need for a sensor on board the LCFs, but to generate a truly operational Early Warning Capability for ballistic missiles, a complete set of prerequisites must be fulfilled.

[SECTION BREAK]

To this end, the AR decided to establish an introduction committee, for which MWC would provide the framework. This IC-MBMD must coordinate the generation of prerequisites and simultaneously demonstrate and integrate the capability in the Integrated Air and Missile Defence systems of NATO during periodic exercises such as Formidable Shield (FS) and JPOW. H-MWC is the chair, and a new MBMD section under the Department of Doctrine and Tactics is carrying out the working group actions. The JKCMOX is working hard on the development of military-wide regulations regarding Working at Height within Defense.

[SECTION BREAK]

The knowledge center plays a pioneering role for the other OPCOs in this regard. The result is that they have decided to use the methodology employed by JKCMOX as the standard. By providing instructors for various training courses, JKCMOX ensures knowledge retention within the MOX domains at Defense. Examples include support for the Sign Awareness Instructor Course in Reek and the Jungle Warfare Instructor Course conducted in Belize. By incorporating input from various After Action Reports into new instructions, JKCMOX enhances the safety of training, exercises, and operations in the MOX domain. The aforementioned motion by Van der Staaij and the MBMD initiative led to some strengthening of the MWC organization. An information manager and a cyber officer were added to the organization, and (partially through reorganization) a BMD section was formed. The strengthened organization continued to produce knowledge products, the most notable of which were: Functional Concept Air and Missile Defense Green Paper Low Frequency Active and Passive Sonar Advisory Note on the establishment of C-IED organization Handbook on Boarding Operations Handbook on Military Operations in the Mountains BEL/NLD Handbook on MCM operations.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-71 146 Operations Directorate the MEIC products and methodology. The team invested a lot of time in modernizing and presenting the environmental products differently to the customer. The goal is to make it easier for the customer to gain situational awareness in the lead-up to and during deployment in an operational area. Given the limited number of exercises in 2017, it was possible for the METOC and Hydrographic sea riders to follow additional courses and training without compromising operational support. In addition to supporting units during the NOST, SNMG-1, and exercises such as Joint Warrior and Northern Coasts, the emphasis from 2017 for the METOC sea riders was on ASW. The goal was to structurally elevate the knowledge and skills of all ASW specialists, and the first step towards this was the Active Anti Submarine Warfare (ACT ASW) in November 2017.

[SECTION BREAK]

Furthermore, the MEIC sea riders worked with the Geography Service on land-water maps, so that the customer can use these integrated maps for overview and planning purposes.

[SECTION BREAK]

Civil Production After the completion of the SHIP2 project at the end of 2016, the new system was further evaluated and put into use in 2017. This department generated the first depth images from the new database for depth storage and processed these into the products. A total of 69 new ENC cells were published, along with twelve paper nautical charts and four 1800 atlases for the corresponding area. Thus, all 1800 atlases have now been produced from the new Hydrographic Production Database (HPD). Additionally, the annual editions of HP7, HP1D, HP33, and HP33D were published. In total, we published 390 "Notices to Mariners." A more logical map layout was designed for the paper charts for the approaches to Scheveningen and IJmuiden, which better takes into account the location of the new traffic separation schemes that had come into effect earlier. These charts were published in December.

text:
5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-72 147 Operations Directorate It is of great importance to have up-to-date information. Especially in the Caribbean, this remains a point of ongoing attention. Two cartographers therefore made a working visit to the Leeward Islands. Due to Hurricane Irma, the Windward Islands were not visited.

[SECTION BREAK]

The visit was successful. Not only were agreements made to better secure the information provision in the future, but a wealth of information was also gathered. Participation was made in the Hydrographic Services and Standards Committee (HSSC) and various related working groups under the IHO framework. In addition, we held working meetings with colleagues from neighboring countries. At the request of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management (I&M), a staff member from the service participated in a working group under the Sub-Committee on Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue (NCSR) of the IMO. This working group assesses proposals for routing measures (new traffic separation schemes, etc.) submitted by IMO member states.

[SECTION BREAK]

The service participates in this as a subject matter expert. Geodesy and Tides The Knowledge Center for Geodesy & Tides (KCG&G) section provides knowledge for the measurement processes and publications of the Hydrographic Service, as well as for other branches of defense and government. The geodetic expertise is applied at sea, where the water level is of great importance. Tide knowledge is linked to marine geodesy. An important application is determining the correct coordinate systems and enabling conversions between them. This concerns both horizontal and vertical references. Another application is providing geodetic and tide data for general use, such as calculating boundaries at sea and publishing tide predictions.

[SECTION BREAK]

Support for Hydrographic Publications KCG&G hosted the Data Quality Working Group (DQWG) from May 13 to 15 at the Frederikkazerne in The Hague. The DQWG is a working group of the HSSC of the IHO. The working group is responsible for developing a standard for representing the quality of hydrographic products. Finland transferred the chairmanship of this working group to the Netherlands for a period of three years.

148 Directorate of Operations At the initiative of the Netherlands, the HSSC approved new Terms of Reference for the DQWG during the annual meeting from November 9 to 10 in Ottawa, Canada. Its objective is now to ensure that aspects of data quality are applied in an appropriate and harmonized manner within future IHO standards.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, the KCG&G participated in the Tides, Water Levels and Currents Working Group (TWCWG) from May 8 to 12 in Victoria, Canada. The TWCWG is another working group of the HSSC. The goal of this working group is to develop a standard for the delivery and representation of surface currents and vertical reference levels. The standard to be developed is based on components of the S-100 product specifications.

[SECTION BREAK]

Support for hydrographic surveys An internal project has been initiated to clarify the relationship between the planned, executed, delivered, and published hydrographic surveys. This research will lead to a better understanding of the effort required to measure the current seabed position and the observation of significant objects on the seabed, as well as the eventual publication in the navigation chart. The result is expected by the end of 2018. Work on the bridge of Zr.Ms. Snellius.

[SECTION BREAK]

Operations Directorate Other The Service consulted with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding the periodic determination of the extent of the Eems-Dollard treaty area. This file will be further addressed in 2018. Hydrographic Information Provision and Management In 2017, the deployment of the Hydrographic Information Provision & Management (HIB) section was primarily focused on maintaining the new Hydrographic production system. This followed the completion of the so-called SHIP 2 project on December 31, 2016. In continuation of this SHIP 2 project, several tasks for the next increments were also carried out under its own (regular) management, particularly for nautical publications, management information, and messages to mariners.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, the Hydrographic Service began the transition to Windows 10. This also marks a phased farewell to the "old Hydrographic Windows XP environment." Furthermore, following the ISO-9001 certification of the Service at the beginning of 2017, quality management within the HIB section has been further expanded and refined. The resulting processes and measures have now largely been integrated into the daily operations of the section.

The auditor found no deviations, and thus the Hydrographic Service was certified as of April 27, 2017, with a validity of three years. 5_KM_Annual_Report_2017_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-75 150 Operations Directorate The second half of the twentieth century has been marked as a risk. All nautical charts have been scanned and will be transferred to the Semi-Static Information Management department of the Ministry of Defence. Charts older than the second half of the twentieth century have already been archived at the National Archive. Distribution On November 23, 2017, the harmonization deadline set by the European Directive INSPIRE for the online availability of a number of spatial datasets expired. From that date, the web services provided by the Hydrographic Service through its partner Teledyne CARIS must comply with the standardization guidelines for maritime boundaries and zones, and for geographical names at sea and in large inland waters. This has been achieved.

At both fairs, we presented ourselves together with other safety organizations such as the Coast Guard, Rijkswaterstaat, and Varen Doe Je Samen, to promote safe navigation at sea and in the extensive inland waters. This year, we highlighted the changes in the traffic separation schemes around the new wind farm to be constructed at Borssele, particularly the publication of this in our nautical charts.

Hydrographic survey vessels Zr.Ms. Snellius (A802) Commanders: Lt. Commander (ltz1) G.T. Mollema (HOV-A) from January 1 Lt. Commander (ltz1) S.M. Duineveld (HOV-B) from January 1 to May 2 Lt. Commander (ltz1) S.R. Maureau (HOV-B) from May 2 The first weeks after the holidays, Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Snellius was undergoing maintenance. From January 30, it resumed collecting hydrographic data. At that time, the ship operated on a rotation schedule of two crews, the A-crew and the B-crew. Although conducting hydrographic days is core business for a hydrographic survey vessel, general proficiency for the ship's crew is also necessary to ensure safe working and living conditions on board.

[SECTION BREAK]

To train this proficiency, a CT is scheduled once a year, conducted under the inspiring leadership of one of the MOST teams. The B-crew had the honor of kicking off at the end of February, followed by the A-crew a few weeks later. The A-crew combined this training with a port visit to Antwerp, after which the sailing program continued. After these educational periods, it was time to conduct some hydrographic days, interspersed with a number of foreign ports for necessary relaxation.

[SECTION BREAK]

Thus, the B-crew visited Newcastle in June. This port was also at the top of the A-crew's list of foreign ports to visit. Consequently, the ship visited Newcastle again in July in a short time, now with the A-crew on board. Stavanger was the port visited in the autumn by the A-crew, where a visit to the Preikestolen was, of course, a must. Afterwards, the B-crew then visited Stavanger. By early November, the sailing days were over, and Zr.Ms. Snellius went to Delfzijl for maintenance for the rest of the year.

text:
Following the maintenance, a training period commenced to restore operational, personnel, and material readiness by completing the training trajectory Safety and Readiness Checks (SARC-1 to 3). SARC-4 took place from April 24 to 26.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Belgian-Dutch MOST provided the leadership and training for this and also assessed the crew's capabilities. During this period, various exercises were conducted, such as maneuvering, navigation, and fire drills. On May 2, Zr.Ms. Luymes departed for sea; however, it had to return to Den Helder on May 3 due to problems with the diesel generators. These issues were resolved on May 7, and the ship returned to operational area HY17201. This was located in the shipping lane north of the Wadden Islands.

Luymes was part of the group of ships that opened to the public during SAIL Den Helder from June 22 to 25. On Sunday, June 25, the ship departed for sea in connection with the exercise Sandy Coast, in which it would participate until July 5. For the exercise, Zr.Ms. Luymes placed various exercise mines at predetermined positions on the seabed. Several minehunters found these during the exercise and were subsequently picked up by Zr.Ms. Luymes with the help of divers. The diving team also brought a decompression tank on board. In the remaining time between placing and picking up the exercise mines, surveying was conducted in the operational area HY17201. Five days later, Zr.Ms. Luymes departed for ten days at sea for hydrographic work. Just like earlier in 2017, there were standby watches during this trip.

[SECTION BREAK]

During this period, the ship went to Den Helder to take on the new Chief of the Crew and there was a change of the watch officers. On September 4, Zr.Ms. Luymes departed towards Brünsbuttel for the Northern Coasts (NOCO) exercise, where the vessel served as the flagship. Sailing in a formation with Zr.Ms. Schiedam, Zr.Ms.

After this port visit, the NOCO exercise commenced. The ship deployed various exercise mines, which were subsequently searched for by the minehunters. At the end of the exercise, from September 22 to September 25, a port visit was made to the capital of Denmark, Copenhagen, for Rest and Recreation. On September 29, Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Luymes docked again in Den Helder.

To verify our current method of tide reduction and to allow the students to experience how to deploy a tide gauge buoy, this was done in the new work area HY17516. This area has 45 effective sounding days and is located just above the northernmost traffic separation scheme, bordering British waters. From October 23 to October 27 and from October 30 to November 9, the C-crew was active in this area. On November 13, the B-crew transferred their belongings from Zr.Ms. Snellius to Zr.Ms. Luymes to subsequently operate in a two-on-two off schedule with the C-crew. On November 15, the B-crew departed to sea with Zr.Ms. Luymes. They conducted sounding operations in a combined area HY17108_229_209, after which they began work in area HY17225. This area is located south of the approach to Rotterdam at Steenbank Vessel Traffic Service. On November 18, she

[SECTION BREAK]

The Operations Directorate directed Zr.Ms. Luymes to Vlissingen via the Oostgat, to anchor in the roadstead of Vlissingen and shelter from the stormy weather. During the time the ship was anchored, the crew continued to collect data with the hydrographic boat. On November 21, Zr.Ms. Luymes moored again in Den Helder. During the transit to Den Helder, the Multibeam Echosounder was tested near IJmuiden.

[SECTION BREAK]

Due to the bad weather, the departure of the C crew was postponed, and they left for sea on December 1. Because of the still marginal conditions in the North, the ship began operations in area HY18115 just above the Wadden Islands.

[SECTION BREAK]

On December 4, Zr.Ms. Luymes returned. The B crew set sail on December 11 and returned on December 20. The final loading operations in work area HY17108_209_229 were carried out, and the work continued in HY17225.

Navy Days and SAIL 2017 The Navy Days coincided this year with SAIL Den Helder. Therefore, the first half of the year was focused on the preparation and execution of SAIL and the Navy Days. To safely carry out this large event, a lot had to be arranged. In June, we held a large-scale multidisciplinary operational exercise called Sailing Home 2.0, in preparation for the Navy Days and SAIL. Approximately 350 emergency responders and actors were involved, and the working methods of the various crisis partners were practiced, improving mutual cooperation.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Navy Days and SAIL 2017 took place from June 22 to June 25. To prevent parking problems and traffic jams on the access roads and the marine area, a transfer point was set up near MVVK De Kooij, where visitors' vehicles could park. The area and docks of the Mine Service were part of the SAIL area. In addition to the modern navy, divers demonstrated their skills during the Navy Days.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Directorate of Material Maintenance of ships found the Tall Ships from distant continents and ships from the national Floating Heritage in the harbor. Approximately 350,000 people visited the Navy Days and SAIL in Den Helder. For the first time this year, naval soldiers from the German Sea Battalion participated in these events. Completion of renovation of barracks Mid-year, following the completion of the renovation of the barracks MBDH Nieuwe Haven, the buildings IJsmeeuw, Kokmeeuw, Stormmeeuw, and Mantelmeeuw were put into use. This provided 450 sleeping places, allowing the residents of Sneeuwmeeuw, Mantelmeeuw, and COA’s to be distributed among the renovated barracks Kokmeeuw, Stormmeeuw, and IJsmeeuw.

[SECTION BREAK]

During the renovation, only the outer facades and the construction walls remained standing, and the rest was renewed. As a result, the buildings received a modern contemporary appearance on the inside.
