5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-5 56 Operations Directorate Marine Training Command (MTC) Commander: LtCol (ltkolmarns) J.P.O. de Jong Shooting Competition in Poznan After a relatively quiet period, the shooting teams of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) – two teams from the Royal Netherlands Marine Reserve (KMR) and the Marine shooting team – participated again in September in the international NATO shooting competition Snajper in Poznan, Poland. Each team consisted of four shooters. In addition to the Dutch teams, teams from the United Kingdom, Czech Republic, Switzerland, Italy, France, Germany, and of course Poland also took part in the competition. A considerable international gathering with, as it turned out, many top shooters. This time, the competition took place at the outdoor range Biedrusko Military Training Ground near Poznan. The competition consists of seven events, where shooting is done with weapons supplied by and from the Polish army. Before a team begins shooting with a weapon, the procedures with the weapon are first practiced under the guidance of a Polish instructor. The instructor also assists the shooters at the shooting point.

[SECTION BREAK]

Although the Marine team achieved good results, they just missed out on the prizes. Fortunately, the KMR teams managed to win three awards; the second prize overall foreign team, the second prize overall individual, and the first prize for rifle.

The ship was declared 'seaworthy' after many setbacks in the preliminary phase, but will continue its SARC trajectory only in 2019 due to a different program. With a SARC-4 from June 24 to July 4, HNLMS Friesland was prepared for deployment as SSCG. In addition to the integration, the JSS had to be assigned and all personnel and materials embarked. The PDT and the final integration between units of Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman were completed in one and a half weeks and concluded with a boarding on the Italian Navy ship ITS Orione. Among ten authentic tall ships and under the watch of thousands of spectators, the ship ceremonially entered the Annabaai as part of the maritime event Velas Latino America Curaçao (VLAC) on Sunday, July 15. In September, Friesland prepared for possible emergency aid to Dominica following tropical storm Isaac.

text:
Zr.Ms. Friesland was tasked by the Maritime Headquarters Caribbean Area (MHKC) for the preparation. The ship immediately suspended its operations and steamed to Curaçao to load supplies. On the way, 24 marines also embarked in Aruba. In just over five hours, the ship was loaded with emergency aid supplies, including several 1000-liter containers for drinking water, medical supplies, and generators, and was then ready for deployment. Due to the limited impact of storm Isaac, actual action ultimately was not necessary. During its responsibility as SSCG, Zr.Ms. Friesland conducted six successful drug interceptions, both with the Coast Guard Caribbean Area (KWCARIB) and the American organization Joint Interagency Taskforce South.

[SECTION BREAK]

In this process, Zr.Ms. Friesland intercepted about 3900 kilograms of contraband.

Groningen was primarily focused on BO and training for most of the year. At the beginning of January, the crew provided several weeks of personnel support to the Royal Marechaussee in executing Maritime Border Control in Europoort. In mid-February, the ship emerged from dry dock. After a successful SARC-1 in early June, the vessel was towed from the naval yard to the operational berths on June 19. Starting in September, the training period for the ship and crew began. This started with the schooling period in which crew members attended various service-related refresher courses. On September 20, one of the life rafts was tested. The crew was very enthusiastic, and marine vlogger Annelotte Zwart was present to document the test. From October 22 to 30, the crew was able to demonstrate what they had learned during the SARC-3 under the guidance of the STC. Due to issues with the main propulsion diesel, this did not go smoothly. Nevertheless, Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Groningen managed to complete the SARC-3 within five days. Following the SARC-3, there was a four-week period of Varende Materieels Beproevingen (VMB). This went well. During these weeks, the VLICO Zee was also successfully concluded. The weekend between the third and fourth week, the ship was in the port of Antwerp. This was the first port visit for the crew in this composition. It was unexpected that Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Groningen received the assignment to assist with NATO sailing practice. This meant an additional week of sailing after the VMBs. It became a busy week with many navigation exercises, while part of the crew remained behind to attend various training courses.

[SECTION BREAK]

On December 18, the traditional Christmas tree ceremony took place. A Christmas tree was previously hoisted in the mast to indicate that the ship was in port during the holidays so that other ships could send mail home. A delegation from the Stichting Veteranen and Postactive Militairen Groningen was present at this ceremony.

text: In December, the ship facilitated the theme day of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean (CZMCARIB). This theme day focused on the (simplified) military assistance requests and strengthening cooperation with local authorities in Curaçao. One of the three main tasks of Defense in the Caribbean is to support local and civil authorities. At the initiative of CZMCARIB, discussions were held on board regarding how and in what situations military assistance can be of added value. Additionally, the procedure for requesting certain assistance in Curaçao was simplified. This allowed for quicker action. The simplified assistance procedure applied to the deployment of military search, military tracking, diving operations, and static observations with binoculars and drones. With an attendance of nearly seventy partners from the security chain, including (representatives of) the government, Curaçao Police Corps (KPC), the public prosecutor's office (OM), Justice, Coast Guard, Royal Marechaussee, the Governor's cabinet, Customs, and representation from the Netherlands, the theme day was a success. As a result, a similar day will be organized next year for the chain partners in Aruba. During the port visit to Kralendijk in Bonaire, Zr.Ms. Zeeland, in the context of the 'Open Day of Defense', held an open ship together with Zr.Ms.

text: 5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-25 76 Operations Directorate Exercises An important aspect of the first chain year for a Raiding Squadron (RSQN) is conducting operations with subordinate enablers from Combat Support (CS) and the Reconnaissance Surveillance and Target Acquisition (RSTA) squadron. The marines of 12 RSQN conducted the Special Operations in Urban Terrain (SOUT) training in March of this year in Oksbøl, Denmark. Additionally, 12 RSQN participated in the Maritime Interdiction Operations (MIO) training from May 28 to June 15. During these three weeks in Den Helder, various skills and drills were taught. These are necessary for various types of operations in the maritime domain. The training is provided by Marine Training Command (MTC) Maritime Special Operations Capable (MARSOC). A Dutch marine instructs during the training mission CBMI Kurdish Peshmerga.

[SECTION BREAK]

Operations Directorate Stormtide Stormtide is an annual exercise organized by the Belgian Armed Forces. In previous years, training took place with a company or battalion. This edition (from September 12 to 21) was an exercise at brigade level.

[SECTION BREAK]

The participating units consisted of a battalion of paratroopers and a battalion of commandos, both part of the newly established Belgian 'Special Operations Regiment'. This SO Regiment was supplemented by a unit of British 'pathfinders' and a Troop of marines from the 13th Raiding Squadron (13-RSQN).

[SECTION BREAK]

Burmese Chase The second edition of the exercise Burmese Chase took place in May at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, United States. Following earlier participation in 2017, the Reconnaissance, Surveillance and Target Acquisition Squadrons (RSTA) of the Marine Corps received another invitation to participate in the Joint Fires exercises of the year. Due to the many training opportunities and the international character, it was decided to send the operationally ready Joint Fires Cell from the 15th RSTA Squadron and a Fire Support Team from the 25th RSTA Squadron to the US. 81mm mortar of the Marine Corps in action.

Exercises Hurricane Hits Texel 20 Combat Service Support Squadron (20CSS SQN) practiced high quality standards during a biweekly exercise on Texel.

[SECTION BREAK]

What do you do when you urgently need to pack your medical equipment and find yourself in an area that has been 'hit' by a natural disaster 48 hours later? Thus, the medical personnel of 20 CSS SQN received a 'warning order' at the end of their first Medical Spec week. The first week focused on theoretical and practical knowledge. During the second week, an ideal location for a humanitarian disaster exercise was sought, and local authorities were approached to support this.

[SECTION BREAK]

21 RSQN When the last Marines from the EMVMARNS were integrated in March, the formation of 21 RSQN was a fact on April 1, and the buildup could begin. To prepare everyone for the tasks associated with their roles, the unit started the functional training period. Three important courses that the Marines underwent during this period, depending on their roles, were the Sierra (fire support), Infantry Engineer, Designated Marksman, and Combat Life Saver courses. Later in the year, the Standard Operating Procedure Training (SOP 1) and Live Fire Tactical Training (LFTT) followed. The year concluded with training aboard Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt off the coast of Great Britain. 22 RSQN Throughout 2018, 22 RSQN was responsible for providing the Rotating Element (RE) in Sint Maarten. Since 2014, Marines have been permanently stationed on the Dutch part of this island to carry out all three main tasks of the armed forces (defending territory, promoting international rule of law, supporting civil authorities), with a focus on the third main task.

[SECTION BREAK]

Operations Directorate 23 RSQN After a large-scale certification exercise last July, 23 RSQN earned the coveted badge of the United States Marine Corps Forces Special Operations (MARSOC). Following this, a busy program ensued, including two retention weeks, a shooting week, support for the GSI training, and support for the Amphibious Nautical Operational Sea Training ((A)NOST). In November, there were also the Automatic Opening (Parachute) and Military Tracker courses. 24 SQN The second section of 24 Assault Engineers Troop (AE Tp) gathered on September 15 at Schiphol for departure to its first international exercise.

Final destination: Ásbrú, Iceland; a small village in the otherwise desolate volcanic landscape on the southwestern coast of the island. The area around the base of the Icelandic Coast Guard in Ásbrú was the scene of the exercise Northern Challenge 2018 (NC18) for two weeks. 25 RSTA Two sniper teams from the Reconnaissance Sniper Troop (RS Tp) of 25 RSTA were with the 21st Raiding Squadron during an exercise in Denmark.

80 Operations Directorate September 28 in Canada to participate in the 'Canadian International Sniper Concentration' (CISC). This is a biennial competition aimed at allowing sniper teams from various countries to compete, thereby gaining insight into the procedures and techniques employed by the respective countries. It also serves as a valuable assessment moment for the operators of the RS-Troop and provides information on possible improvements for training and education. That RS is on the right track was particularly evident from the fact that one team succeeded in winning the first prize for international teams.

At Camp Åsegarden, 20 CS SQN prepared for the arrival of the units and the start of the Joint Arctic Training (JAT 18). Equipment and personnel were gathered from various locations to optimally and completely support 20 CS SQN.

To achieve this result, a four-week training course was completed, partly in Breda and partly in Eloy, Arizona, USA.

Netherlands Maritime Special Operation Forces (NLMARSOF) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J.B.W. van Nee, from July 4 Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) J.W. van Dijk For NLMARSOF, 2018 was a busy and eventful year, both in terms of operations and in terms of training, education, and exercises. In the spring, a Special Operations Task Group (SOMTG) participated in 'Operation Inherent Resolve' in Iraq, with the primary task of training and educating Iraqi special units. Additionally, a Special Operations Task Unit (SOMTU) was part of a Combined Joint Special Operations Task Group (CJSOMTG) during Operation Sea Guardian. A combined Belgian, Danish, and Dutch task group was temporarily embarked aboard Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman during her Blue Waves deployment in the eastern part of the Mediterranean Sea. The operation aimed to provide Military Assistance and enhance Situational Awareness in the region. For the Dutch elements of the CJSOMTG, this was

[SECTION BREAK]

The Operations Directorate also provided a good opportunity to maintain skills as they were on standby throughout the year as part of a Spanish-Dutch SOMTG for the NATO Response Force (NRF). This year, NLMARSOF contributed to Military Assistance operations in Africa, including Obangame Express, Phoenix Express, and Flintlock. The objective of these deployments was to elevate local special units to a higher operational level so that they could better address local issues independently. An important added value for the own units was the ability to collaborate with various international partners from different cultures and under diverse circumstances. Nationally, M-Squadron has been part of the Reaction Concept of the Special Operations Service (DSI) for several years now. Nevertheless, M-Squadron remained responsible for the termination of large-scale terrorist activities.

[SECTION BREAK]

Within the reaction concept, they were part of so-called Rapid Reaction Teams (RRT) and the Quick Reaction Force (QRF) on a daily basis. This allowed them to intervene in situations with increased threat in direct cooperation with the police at any moment.

[SECTION BREAK]

In addition to operational deployment, individuals and (sub)units have followed several training courses and conducted exercises to maintain and improve operational readiness. Marines during winter training in Norway.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-31 82 Operations Directorate Many operators have individually acquired various specializations or have further developed in these areas.

[SECTION BREAK]

Examples include the free-fall (para) training and the weapon and demolition training. Noteworthy was the training for Special Operation Combat Medic (SOCM). This NATO training prepares the SOF-Medic to a particularly high level, enabling SOF teams to have the necessary medical capacity in situations where additional medical care is not immediately available. A large number of trainings and exercises have also been conducted.

[SECTION BREAK]

During the winter months, C-Squadron participated in the exercise Polar Neptune in Norway. The focus was on conducting long movements, reconnaissance, and raids under winter conditions. The exercise was particularly challenging due to the presence of a 'hunting force' from the Norwegian army. In the second quarter, NLMARSOF participated in the exercise Night Hawk in Denmark. In this large international exercise, the staff of NLMARSOF and a SOMTU from C-Squadron formed the nucleus of an international SOMTG, together with a team. Visit by Secretary of State for Defence Barbara Visser to NLMARSOF in Den Helder on August 27.

The M-Squadron organized a large-scale exercise in the spring on a 'hijacked' passenger ship off the Dutch coast. This maritime anti-terror operation was carried out in cooperation with, among others, the police, coast guard, and emergency services. Throughout the year, various anti-terror exercises were held on mass transportation modalities such as airplanes and trains. On this occasion, the outgoing commander of the C-ZSK received the Bronze Medal of Merit for his contribution to the development of the Navy's special units.

Amidst the busy activities, a reorganization process was prepared that would take effect in 2019. Through a formative expansion and restructuring of existing capabilities, the staff and support capabilities will be strengthened. In addition to a reorganization of the operational squadrons, a medical support element will be introduced as well as a fire direction capacity for the Seabased Support Group (SSG). Commander: Major (majmarns) S. Peters.

In the past year, SSG provided second-line logistical support to support a challenging Operational Year Plan (OJP), combined with various 'serious deployments'. This had a significant impact on the necessary personnel and material support. It ensured that various specialists from SSG accompanied other units.

text:
After a process of intensive development and in collaboration with TNO, the MWC was able to declare the new Maritime Battlelab (MBL) Initial Operations Capable (IOC) in April 2018. The battlelab is an innovative concept to conduct high-end virtual simulations of (maritime) warfare scenarios. Applications for which the MBL was designed include concept development, pre-testing of launch scenarios, and post-simulation of executed launches. This can be done stand-alone, but also connected to a network of similar capabilities, primarily for concept development. Now the MWC has that capacity structurally in-house and could work on possibilities to generate the same capacity for underwater warfare. The possibilities that this capacity offered were endless, and given the attention that the MBL attracted, it was expected that more and more partners would work with this capacity and that more applications would be discovered. Departure of an NH90 from Zr.Ms. De Ruyter in the Mediterranean Sea.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-39 90 Operations Directorate In February, the amphibious operations section was finally ready to publish its Maritime Doctrine Publication on Amphibious Operations. In March, the AR decided to continue the study on the Future Littoral Operating Concept (FLITOC). This process quickly became known as the 'roadmap mastering the littoral' (MTL). This was intended to lead to a complete revision of how operations from the sea are shaped. Given the small size of the MWC amphibious section, these activities are coordinated between MWC, S&A, and the group leader of the Marines.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-40 91 The Operations Directorate took on tasks without personnel expansion. This was achieved with a Full-Time Equivalent (FTE), and as a result, JKCMOX began inventorying, building networks, seeking external knowledge, and conducting a multitude of risk analyses. Last year, the MWC also produced a series of publications. In Maritime Ballistic Missile Defence and Submarine Warfare, new concepts for future operations were established. Knowledge was documented for the CZSK-wide reader in the manuals Above Water Warfare and Use of Tactical Data Links in CZSK. Lastly, knowledge was also documented for a specific target group in the Manuals Military Tracking and Avalanche Safety.

[SECTION BREAK]

Hydrographic Service Chief Hydrographer: Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck Offer Development Within IHO cooperation, new standards were developed for the unlocking of hydrographic data. This was based on S-100, the Universal Hydrographic Data Model. The transition to S-100 and the associated product specifications will commence in the coming years. It remains to be seen how the service will prepare for this and what the implications will be for processes, products, and services.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Hydrographic Service (HYD) decided to discontinue several products, including a paper chart of the Northern coastal area. A difficult decision was the termination of the innovative product Digipilot, which had been on the market for about ten years.

[SECTION BREAK]

As a legacy from the paper era, the Electronic Naval Charts (ENC) had long followed the layouts and naming conventions of the paper charts. However, the connection between paper and electronic charts is fading. Additionally, the organization of ENCs had become confusing due to changes in paper chart numbers and the combined use of 1800 charts and nautical charts. Therefore, a new, grid-oriented organization of the ENC portfolio will be implemented gradually. Demand Development The trend from paper to digital continued in 2018. The expectation is that next year the trend will level off due to the requirement to carry ENCs for SOLAS ships >500GT by July 2018.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-41 92 Operations Directorate The ratio between our own products and products under license has further decreased over the past year. The reuse in systems for SOLAS ships, in addition to the use of paper nautical charts, has declined as more and more ships are using ENCs. Reuse has also decreased due to the emergence of products for small shipping that have been made without a license.

[SECTION BREAK]

Renewal of distribution channels Distribution through chart agents has been formalized again thanks to the conclusion of new agent agreements (Dutch and English; A-agents and B-agents). Two important improvements have been made, which were agreed upon during the agents' meeting on October 22: The delivery of non-updated nautical charts is now described; The arrangement for returning expired copies has been expanded. The distribution of co-production charts with the United Kingdom Hydrographic Office (UKHO) was improved by connecting to their Print on Demand (PoD) system. HYD and UKHO made agreements about this in 2018 that will now be implemented. The formalization of those agreements will take place as part of the renewal of the Bilateral Arrangement with UKHO.

The reuse of HYD's open data was further promoted through joining the collaboration Information House Marine (IHM). This collaboration already existed between Rijkswaterstaat (RWS) and the Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality (LNV).

The partners wanted to further develop the IHM portal into a central place for maritime environmental information of the Dutch part of the North Sea, including the open data from HYD. The command transfer took place at the recreation center De Witte Raaf in the presence of all staff of the Naval Base Den Helder (MBDH) and invited guests. New Parking Policy MBDH – First Wheel Clamp Placed at Naval Base Den Helder On Wednesday, October 10, the first wheel clamp was placed at the Naval Base. An Amarok that was parked incorrectly near the company restaurant Meeuwennest was the first victim. This was in accordance with 'Announcement MBDH 2018/2019 parking policy'. This new policy was established due to issues caused by illegal parking. This blocked emergency exits and access routes for emergency services. Additionally, illegal parking caused significant irritation among colleagues and hindered the emptying of waste containers. There was frequent parking on the docks, leading to dangerous situations. Large vehicles faced additional obstacles. These are all issues that were also noted by the Inspectorate for the Environment and Transport (IL&T).

[SECTION BREAK]

The parking policy has also created additional parking spaces and established a temporary parking arrangement using a blue disc. This prevented people from staying too long but allowed them the opportunity to load or unload at the barracks. Demolition of OPSCHOOL Last year, the demolition of the old OPSCHOOL began after the completion of a new NLBEOPS school in building Zeearend.

[SECTION BREAK]

Until 2018, the work was delayed due to unexpectedly discovered asbestos. After a storm, asbestos-containing panels blew off building Condor and caused contamination up to the mudflat. The necessary involvement of an asbestos remediation company led to a thorough cleanup operation, resulting in further delays of several months. Unfortunately, asbestos was also found in the adjacent building Raalte, which meant that work could not be carried out in these buildings either, in this case by NLMARSOF, until inspection and remediation had been completed.

Directorate of Material Maintenance Floating Docks for KBW The Ministry of Defence has allocated additional budget for overdue maintenance and for making adjustments to infrastructure. By installing floating docks at pier 60, a mooring capacity for small vessels such as FRISCs and LCUs has been provided. Minor maintenance on these small vessels can now be carried out on-site, and boarding and disembarking have also become safer. Additionally, the old portacabins have been demolished and replaced with a building for 140 workstations to better center the personnel of KBW around CASCO-2. This building has been named Bezaan. All future buildings on the site will be given names related to sailing. For example, the newly constructed shed of the Submarine Service (OZD) has been named Genua.

[SECTION BREAK]

Environmental Station With the reorganization of 2013, the environmental station at the Nieuwe Haven has become a forgotten and neglected issue. Personnel were not included in the new organization. The environmental station continued to operate solely through makeshift arrangements, such as in the past year thanks to a workforce of temporary staff.

[SECTION BREAK]

With an environmental coordinator and two forklift drivers, the environmental station has become a well-known entity at the naval harbor. Furthermore, through a collaborative project with the Employee Insurance Agency (UWV), work has been found for three individuals in terrain management. Preparations are being made for exercise Trident Juncture by loading Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt.

[SECTION BREAK]

the lighting, and the heating system have been improved. Additionally, the flooring in the gym was replaced. The participation in these events was high, and they contributed to team building and morale within the Royal Netherlands Navy. Overall, the year was marked by significant efforts in maintaining and improving facilities, while also ensuring that personnel remained engaged in physical training and sports activities.

6_KM_Annual_Report_2018_DIRECTORATE_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-7 102 Directorate of Material Maintenance Development & Recreation (O&O) Bureau O&O MBDH is the point of contact and information hub for all defense personnel at the Nieuwe Haven, crews of inland vessels, and foreign colleagues. A newsletter is published every two months containing all new information about workshops, events, and discounts. Furthermore, O&O organized several activities this year, such as pub quizzes, sushi-making workshops, and beer tastings. The organized Activity Day MBDH was highly appreciated by all participants. The discount vouchers for admission tickets to the swimming pool, cinema, and theater performances were also popular. By creating and distributing pamphlets and newsletters, everyone was made aware of the opportunities offered by O&O.

[SECTION BREAK]

Logistical Support KST and Steiger 19 (OZD) This bureau provided logistical support in various areas and to different units for both KBW units and units that fall under the Group Senior Submarine Service. The current numbers are: Administrative support for 26 ships, including sailing lists, port fees, etc.; Nutritional support for 24 ships; Store support for 23 ships; Support to the Group Senior Small Above Water and Group Senior Submarine Service; Customs clearance for all naval ships entering or leaving Den Helder. Additionally, a lot of work was done by the head of Facilities (OZD) and the facilities/provost staff (KBW). As a result, the shortcomings identified in the IL&T report have been addressed and improved.

[SECTION BREAK]

Increase in Users JKDAZ The number of registrations for team-building days from all units within the armed forces increased last year. This was partly due to many co-users of the Joost Dourleinkazerne (JDKAZ) such as the KIM introduction, VeVa, EVO marines, EMMV fleet, army units, and foreign units. It remained a challenge to provide all users with the necessary support.

6_KM_Annual_Report_2018_DIRECTORATE_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-8 103 Directorate of Material Maintenance Staff FMS at JDKAZ For years, there has been a need for a Fleet Marine Squadron at CZSK. Last March, the first discussions took place, during which several milestones were established. It was not possible to accommodate the entire FMS at JDKAZ, but a portion of the staff was chosen to be housed there. Physically, the entire FMS will need to be part of the SATG. Marine Championship Run Swim Run at JDKAZ From an amphibious perspective, the Run-Swim-Run was established within the SATG at JDKAZ two years ago. This is a distance running event with a swimming segment in between. This took place in the backyard of the barracks through the dunes, on the beach, and in Mok Bay. It was a sporting activity on the operational terrain of the SATG, the boundary between water and land. This sporting event grew, and the decision was made to hold the first marine championship in this regard. This year, it was once again a success.

[SECTION BREAK]

Marine Establishment Amsterdam (MEA) Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) N.P. Vermaire The crucial question that loomed throughout the spring was whether the definitive closure and evacuation of the barracks would proceed on July 1, 2018. This caused a lot of tension among the personnel.

[SECTION BREAK]

Until mid-June, the intention was to close and transfer the entire site, with the exception of building 014, to the Project Bureau Marineterrein Amsterdam. They would carry out the redevelopment on behalf of the State and the Municipality. On June 14, the relieving news came: the Minister of Defense decided to retain the barracks for Defense as support for public order and safety in Amsterdam, as a defense center for conferences and events in the capital, and as a home base for several units. This would fit on a smaller part of the site, resulting in buildings 027 and 039 being transferred on July 15. In consultation with the Municipality of Amsterdam, it was decided to transfer the helipad and part of the empty ring on January 1, 2019.

The MOC is housed at Van Ghent Barracks. The main training courses at the MOC are the EMV, the corporal training, and the POTOM. In addition, the practical weeks of VeVa and various career and specialist training courses take place. The barracks also played an important role this year in organizing events with a social character, such as supporting various youth projects in Rotterdam South, the King's Games, and the Sophia City Run. text:
In April, the implementation of the first energy management system within the defence organizations of nine EU member states was completed. The implementation took a year and concluded with a visit from the auditors of the European Defence Agency (EDA) to the locations of the individual participants to conduct an audit. They also visited the Nieuwe Haven as the first defence location in the Netherlands with an energy management system.

[SECTION BREAK]

This pilot was led by Mr. R.J.L. Put from the EDB. The outcome of the audit of the Nieuwe Haven was positive, which means that the Ministry of Defence will implement this system at several major defence locations. In the KWS power plant, a replacement of part of the automation took place in May. The servers and programming setup were replaced, followed by an update of the software. To make the EDB more effective and prepare the organization for the future, after many consultation sessions, HMAROST on July 10 commissioned the organizational change, named EDB 2.0, to be implemented. In September and October, two compact transformer stations were installed, one at Erfprins for a temporary deployment and one at Maritime Airbase De Kooy for the new radar tower. Finally, in November, the 12kV main distributor in the KWS was extended with three additional fields. This allows the EDB to expand the 12kV network that the ships use, which is necessary given the increasing load from the ships.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Directorate of Materiel Maintenance took place at the Van Ghent Barracks in Rotterdam, and the commemoration at the Indisch Monument in Roermond followed on September 18, Prinsjesdag. As usual, the Marine Band and Drummers & Pipers were positioned in front of the Ridderzaal to play honors and the Wilhelmus upon the arrival of the king. At the end of September, during the National Tattoo in Ahoy Rotterdam, collaboration occurred with fellow musicians from the Royal Netherlands Army and Royal Netherlands Air Force in a piece celebrating 100 years of Leonard Bernstein. The own show received a beautiful extra highlight from a drill team of Norwegian torchbearers. Each year, the installation service for the new cadets takes place in Den Helder, accompanied by a presentation march through the 'stelling'. This year was no exception. There were also many concerts in the autumn. Examples include Capelle aan den IJssel, the pension fund of the Holland-America Line in Rotterdam, and for the centenary of the Marine Sanatorium Fund in Den Helder.

In addition to soloists from the own orchestra, Charly Luske, Ronald Douglas, and Francis van Broekhuizen also performed. Guest conductor Per-Otto Johansson led a jubilee concert in a sold-out sports hall in Uddel.

6_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-21 116 Directorate of Material Maintenance Training Vessels Marine Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen The Marine Training Vessel (MOV) Van Kinsbergen was used for nautical practical training. The ship was specifically built and equipped for this purpose. It accommodates sixteen trainees.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Van Kinsbergen has, in addition to the regular navigation bridge, a fully equipped secondary training bridge. This makes the ship suitable for safely practicing mooring and unmooring maneuvers, and it is equipped with a RHIB. The ship was used as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. It was also deployed during the annual sailing period, during which a longer training voyage of five weeks was undertaken together with a flotilla of minehunters, known as the cruise. Each year, the Van Kinsbergen sails for approximately two hundred days.

[SECTION BREAK]

Zr.Ms. Urania Commander: LtCdr (ltz1) W.W. Wester On board Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Urania, naval officers in training are prepared for their future seafaring roles. On the ship, they learn all the necessary nautical skills. The upcoming officers learned about the sea last year, for example, and learned skills such as navigation and sailing. Team building and character development were also high on the agenda. Cadets sailed on board to gain sailing experience and to familiarize themselves with the navigation equipment on board. Furthermore, representative sailing trips were made with various groups from the Ministry of Defence, raising the sails whenever the weather permitted.

[SECTION BREAK]

text:
These international operations were undertaken with various countries including the United States, France, Colombia, the United Kingdom, and the Dominican Republic.

[SECTION BREAK]

Hurricane Relief In preparation for the hurricane season, which ran from June 1 to November 30, CZMCARIB, together with local authorities, conducted the annual Hurricane Exercise (HUREX). These HUREX exercises were carried out at the unit level in Aruba and Curaçao and CZMCARIB-wide in the Windward Islands. Hurricane Relief Exercise On September 7, 2018, Hurricane Isaac developed over the Atlantic Ocean. Given the forecasts, it was possible that Isaac would pass through the Caribbean Sea as a hurricane, potentially causing damage to Dominica or the Windward Islands of the Kingdom. In preparation for this, CZMCARIB provided assistance to International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in maintaining international law and order in the Caribbean. Due to the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The Navy is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is also the commander of Task Group 4.4, one of the task groups of this organization.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Sint Maarten. Military personnel have been deployed in advance to ensure public order and safety. A task group has also been formed to potentially assist Dominica if a request for military assistance is submitted. This task group consisted of the station ship Zr.Ms. Friesland and the 32nd Raiding Squadron (RSQN) from Aruba.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, a liaison has been established with the Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency (CDEMA), the disaster response organization in Barbados. Ultimately, Isaac passed the islands as a tropical storm, and the effects remained limited to inconvenience.

[SECTION BREAK]

Military assistance from CZMCARIB provided both soft and hard military support to the authorities of the islands of the Kingdom several times in 2018. Some examples are described below: Ta Basta Awor. CURMIL was deployed multiple times in 2018 for crime fighting as part of Ta Basta Awor, setting up vehicle checkpoints together with the KPC.

Search. In Aruba, the 32 RSQN contributed to investigations by the Korps Politie Aruba (KPA) and the Recherche Samenwerkingsteam (RST) by providing search capacity. Also in Curaçao, engineers from the CidW provided support to the KPC in searching the prison, residences, and properties as part of judicial investigations. Support was also provided from the Netherlands in the form of the Maritime Advance Search Team (MAST) of the Korps Mariniers.

[SECTION BREAK]

SARGASSUM. The CidW and CURMIL provided assistance in Bonaire and Curaçao by clearing large amounts of washed-up sargassum. Carnival and Harvest Festival. CURMIL provided assistance to the KPC during the carnival and harvest festival by patrolling together with the KPC. On Sint Maarten, the Marine Detachment on the island assisted in securing the penitentiary institution. In Bonaire, the CidW supported the relocation of the penitentiary institution. The 32 RSQN and the CidW provided assistance several times through static observations. In Curaçao, assistance was provided multiple times to safety partners with diving capacity. Soft military assistance was also provided by storing vehicles at barracks that had been confiscated by so-called seizure teams.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Army Company in the West Rotations of the Army CidW carried out a varied and challenging exercise program. The rotations were provided by C-Para Company 13 Infantry Battalion 'Regiment Stoottroepen Prins Bernhard' from Assen (CidW26), C-Tijger Company 11 Infantry Battalion 'Garderegiment Grenadiers en Jagers' from Schaarsbergen (CidW27), Defense Ground-Based Air Defense Command/DGLC (CidW28), and A-Madju Company 13 Infantry Battalion 'Regiment Stoottroepen Prins Bernhard' (CidW29). All CidW rotations undertook various integrated exercises with the CURMIL. Engineers from CidW executed various projects, including the construction of a jump bunker and a hand grenade range at the Wacawa training area and various activities at Marine Base Parera (MBPAR), Marine Barracks Suffisant (MKSUF), and MS-KSAV.

text:
Command of the Navy in the Caribbean In June, the ship provided support during the sniper training and the EMV. The snipers were able to hone their skills in maritime sniping while the ship dropped off the trainees from the EMV for an exercise in Bonaire.

[SECTION BREAK]

Furthermore, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan participated in the HUREX in the Windward Islands that same month. Due to several technical defects, the ship was only able to participate partially in the exercise. During the stay in the Windward Islands, the crew of the Pelikaan was decorated for their efforts in hurricane relief assistance in Sint Maarten and Dominica in 2017. For the maritime event VLAC, similar to SAIL Amsterdam, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan picked up additional personnel from Aruba in July. The Marine Band also boarded from Aruba for a musical performance during VLAC. During the summer leave, a large part (six out of fifteen) of the crew of Zr.Ms. Pelikaan changed.

[SECTION BREAK]

Immediately after the leave, the ship was deployed for the transport of the CidW to Bonaire. An intensive training program followed to onboard the new crew members. During this program, the port of Saint George, Grenada was visited. The program was also combined with transporting the CidW to Aruba and the 32RSQN to Willemstad. In October, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan departed for the Windward Islands for regular transport weeks. The first stop was Sint Eustatius. Onboard, teaching materials from Curaçao were taken, which were donated to the Gwendoline van Putten school, the technical school on the island. The students of this school also received a tour onboard Zr.Ms.

text:
Velas Latin America Curaçao From Sunday, July 17 to Wednesday, July 19, the port of Curaçao hosted nine tall ships. The reason for their visit was the maritime event VLAC. In the spring of 2018, MBPAR facilitated the organization of this maritime event. The local Sail Foundation Curaçao had overall leadership but relied heavily on CZMCARIB. A large part of the requested support was also provided by MBPAR, including a project leader. In the preparation and execution, the naval base maintained liaison with the VLAC organization and directed the project team of CZMCARIB. It was a successful event, during which an informal request came from the Curaçao Sail Foundation to CZMCARIB to participate again in 2022 or to provide support.

[SECTION BREAK]

Personnel - Accommodation Last year, the accommodation at MBPAR had 205 beds, spread over 114 rooms. The accommodation met the standards of the time and was, as already indicated, used intensively. Although there was ample capacity for sleeping places, the demand for accommodation increased throughout the year. As a result, external hotel accommodation was regularly called upon. Emergency sleeping accommodation in the sports hall of the naval base was also utilized.

[SECTION BREAK]

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-15 132 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean For now, we maintain the current accommodation with the utmost care. The barracks Landkrab and Zeeschildpad were painted during the past period, as well as the Goudenbal. All rooms are equipped with a faster wifi connection, and construction is underway for a new bar in the Longroom. The Personnel - Physical Training & Sports and Development & Recreation (FT&S/O&O) Bureau O&O reflected on a successful 2018 filled with enjoyable events for young and old. One of the highlights was the staff party on May 5. In the context of Liberation Day, this was organized at the training ground of the MBPAR, with approximately 1,400 colleagues and their family members.

text:
The Personnel - Marine Sports Association (MSV) The Marine Sports Association (MSV) offered its members eleven different sports in 2018. Judo for children was restarted this year after no instructor could be found in 2017.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, the Auto Hobby Club was integrated into the MSV this year. Again this season, there are plenty of defense employees, partners of defense employees, children of defense employees, and even so-called external members who are eager to join the MSV.

[SECTION BREAK]

Administration Based on the idea of “relieving the customer,” the Administration Bureau was merged with the Defense International Support Service Center (DCIOD) into a joint support point. With the project “Reorganization International Support Caribbean,” a start was already made at the end of 2017, and this was further developed in 2018. The service to employees and their families has thus been further optimized. Additionally, cross-pollination between the various departments is important for the continued development of the services that this office can provide. SAP Service Desk/central needs assessment support In 2018, the service desk/central needs assessment support, also known as the Bureau Support Needs Assessment (BOB), was launched. This translated the needs of employees into the SAP environment, in order to fully “relieve” the customer. The “complex” processing procedure for services and goods in SAP was assigned in 2018 to the specialists of the service desk. BOB took over the tasks for creating “requests for needs assessments” and orders from customers who had no access to

[SECTION BREAK]

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-16 133 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Area SAP access. In addition to SAP requests, BOB was involved in the replacement of the Defense pass types 1 and 2 and with the application and issuance of type 4 Service Provider/Family Member passes. Lastly, BOB played a key role in providing residential security. BOB was responsible for the (de)installation of the systems by CVD, the company that provides residential security for defense personnel. As part of the new Food & Beverage system, BOB will manage food requests for MBPAR in the future. Over time, BOB will also manage accommodation for MBPAR and MKSUF in Planon via Digi-on self-service.

Company Restaurant Lamunchi At the end of 2017, the company restaurant Lamunchi was reopened after a long period of maintenance work. In January 2018, this was celebrated with a classic key handover during a festive reopening.

[SECTION BREAK]

This was accompanied by a solidarity meal for all of MBPAR. Since then, the Logistics Service Provision (LDV) has taken up residence in this renewed, but especially improved restaurant. Additionally, the LDV personnel supported various exercises with the Mobile Field Kitchen. Infrastructurally, several projects were realized, but a lot of preliminary work was done for infrastructural new construction and improvement projects in 2019.

Examples of this included charity actions such as work on the children's care pavilion at the Christian foundation Siloam; organizing and executing various sports activities for elementary school children; conducting recruitment programs at secondary schools; supporting national holidays; and carrying out many ceremonial tasks.

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-19 136 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Security, Environment, and Health As a barracks in general and as a training center in particular, (physical and social) safety was a high priority on the MKSUF agenda in 2018. Risk assessments provided good insight into the measures to be taken to ensure that training, exercises, and regular operations were conducted as safely as possible. Environmental issues were also a topic where Dutch and local environmental regulations were adhered to. The nuisance regulation-based permit requirements were implemented and complied with, with special attention paid to food safety. Through fixed contracts, the barracks and its individual spaces were kept clean, safe, and free of pests. The intrinsic perception of the MKSUF personnel regarding these issues was high in 2018, as evidenced by the results of inspections and audits conducted by (external) defense and government services; all were passed with a (well) sufficient rating. For primary healthcare, the MKSUF personnel utilized the Primary Healthcare (EGB) health center at MBPAR.

[SECTION BREAK]

Military ceremony during the annual Opening of the States in Curaçao.

[SECTION BREAK]

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-20 137 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Additionally, the right to general practitioner care for all OCC trainees was enshrined in a covenant in 2018, which is a significant improvement in the safety and health situation for this target group. The MKSUF medical bay, led by the CURMIL nurse and excellently supported by the EGB, plays an indispensable role in this aspect. Infrastructure MKSUF is a barracks where the roads wind between buildings amidst well-maintained gardens. Unfortunately, several of these buildings, namely the barracks, did not meet the Defense accommodation standards at all. In 2018, a lot of time and energy was invested to advocate for the necessity of accommodation improvement. The start of the cafeteria renovation has been on the agenda throughout 2018. Unfortunately, this project has been postponed time and again. There is cautious hope that a start can finally be made by mid-2019. The beautiful but dated Longroom will be restored to its "authentic" state after serving as a temporary restaurant.

text:
Command of the Navy in the Caribbean 32nd Marine Squadron In line with the ambition to strengthen partnerships, the 32nd Marine Squadron (32 RSQN) invested in collaboration with local partner services in 2018. To ultimately become the relevant security partner in the region in general and Aruba in particular, further engagement was sought with the local disaster management staff; police, fire brigade, and coast guard. This collaboration led to various forms of deployment in 2018. With the simplified application procedure, several capabilities of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZM-CARIB) were quickly deployable for the Caribbean islands within the Kingdom. As a result, the 32 RSQN was deployed several times for searching objects, tracking, and observing. Ultimately, the unit was deployed three times for static observation in support of the Public Prosecution Service and the coast guard. Additionally, it provided support three times for search operations in Curaçao and once in Aruba in support of the Public Prosecution Service.

[SECTION BREAK]

In 2018, the marines supported the coast guard in large-scale operations and specific assignments. Marines also assisted on the coast guard cutters in carrying out coast guard tasks. In 2018, the unit began providing a Guard Team for the station ship. This team can conduct boardings on vessels as part of anti-drug operations.

[SECTION BREAK]

The 32 RSQN was also on standby to carry out any emergency assistance operations, including humanitarian aid. As Tropical Storm Isaac approached, the units were moved to the Windward Islands in preparation for assistance after a possible destructive passage. A troop was moved to Curaçao and embarked on the station ship Caribbean Area, and a troop including squadron staff was flown in advance to Sint Maarten. The unit on this last island provided support to the local police. Due to the weakening of the storm, the unit on board the station ship was ultimately not deployed.

[SECTION BREAK]

In Aruba, the 32 RSQN provided support for the readiness of various safety services. The unit supported or organized various disaster exercises. For example, the unit participated in March in the exercise Carib Wave with different scenarios, ranging from a tsunami that had caused damage to the island to a tabletop exercise involving a bomb threat on board a cruise ship. For the runway overshoot exercise, the unit provided simulated casualties, simulating an aircraft accident. The unit also organized a hurricane exercise on the island, sharing experiences from Hurricane Irma in 2017.

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-23 140 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean 32 Raiding Squadron during VLAC.

[SECTION BREAK]

Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied The unit received and supported several units in Aruba during training and education. Together with the barracks, it provided support in 2018 for: A diving training from the United States Marine Corps; The military tracker (instructor) course; The Basic and Advanced training of the local militias; The training for frogmen; The training of the CidW of Curaçao; Ceremonial tasks during Dia di Bandera, Dia di Betico, King's Day, Remembrance Day, and the three arrivals of the station ship in Aruba; The events Highwinds (surf and wakeboard event) and the Aruba Regatta (sailing). In addition to deployment and support, the unit conducted various training sessions in 2018 to maintain or improve training and operational readiness. With the exercise Caribbean Urban Warrior at Camp Lejeune in the United States, the unit carried out its annual exchange with the American Marines in March. In this exercise, the unit was trained in operations in urban areas. The unique training location and opportunities at Camp Lejeune provide added value to the training level of the unit.

[SECTION BREAK]

In June, the unit underwent its annual preparations for the hurricane season. With the exercise in Aruba, the entire unit was deployed. Subsequently, the staff of the unit traveled to Sint Maarten for the hurricane exercise in the Windward Islands. Here, further agreements were made with the island authorities regarding support and military assistance in the event of a possible hurricane passage, together with the Marine detachment Sint Maarten. Due to the support during tropical storm Isaac, the annual tactical and dynamic shooting exercise in Curaçao could not be carried out.

[SECTION BREAK]

This was then adjusted and executed in Aruba. The tactical exercise was subsequently expanded in preparation for the exercise Tres Kolos.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Logistics and Equipment Head: Lieutenant Commander (ltz1) M.C. Philipse-Breitenstein Due to the procurement office being understaffed throughout the year, needs could not always be met in a timely manner. By the end of the year, the department was fully staffed, allowing for a catch-up. A contract was signed for universal and Toyota parts for the white vehicle fleet. The mechanics and carpenter received large water-cooled fans, modeled after those in Curaçao, to improve working conditions.

[SECTION BREAK]

The IVECO was successfully introduced, and at the beginning of next year, the Anaconda will replace the MB280. The Supply Office received an environmental container to responsibly store chemical waste until it can be disposed of. The lighting in the warehouse is now compliant with Occupational Health and Safety (ARBO) requirements and energy-saving, and the fans in the warehouses have been repaired by the Rijks Vastgoedbedrijf (RVB). Sustainability This year, further steps were taken in the area of energy savings. In 2018, there was a 15% reduction in electrical energy consumption compared to the previous year. This was achieved by replacing air conditioning remote controls in combination with the use of timers between the air conditioners.

[SECTION BREAK]

Next year, savings could be expanded to 25 to 30% through further rollout. After that, we will depend on the RVB to meet the need for energy neutrality or even energy independence. To achieve this, approximately 4000 solar panels of 1.2MWp need to be added alongside the current panels of 100kWp. Together with battery capacity and the reconfiguration of generators and transformers at the barracks, this could lead to energy independence. This plan has been approved by the Minister of Defence. Furthermore, the Minister of Energy of Aruba, Elmar, has requested the electricity company in Aruba to cooperate.

SAP The backlog in SAP training was reduced this year by providing various training sessions. The Key Users and Super Users were also able to attend several training sessions in Curaçao at the end of 2018. Material Maintenance Caribbean (MICAR) has created six additional FTEs to strengthen the SAP organization, one of which went to Aruba. This acted as the front office for the supply office from the newly established

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Area Facility Coordination Point (FCP). Finances Despite the fact that Defense had more money available for equipment this year, this did not lead to the timely replacement of vehicles that had reached their replacement age. Priorities still had to be set, but due to limited purchasing capacity, not everything was realized. Infrastructure The armory of MKSAF has received better lighting and two dehumidifiers have been installed, bringing the humidity below the mandatory 55%. Additionally, the central air conditioning of the central warehouse has been turned off and replaced with split-unit air conditioners.

[SECTION BREAK]

Furthermore, DMI has replaced the locks and fittings of the safe doors, allowing the door to open again in case of emergency. General Service The barracks has transitioned to On Guard security after delays. Unfortunately, this has not yet resulted in the significant improvement that was expected. When taking the new office buildings Tribon Preto and the building of the Royal Marechaussee into use, MKSAF cleared all old buildings in a major cleaning operation. As a result, there is no longer a workplace in a building with asbestos roofs, except for the carpentry workshop. In the context of delegating tasks in the operations, the buildings managed by the operational unit were handed over to the barracks. This resulted in all infrastructure and facility matters being transferred to the barracks. The company restaurant was scheduled for major maintenance and kitchen replacement last year. Unfortunately, this was postponed by the RVB.

Commander: Major (majmarns) R. Witteveen  

General  
In 2018, the focus for the Sint Maarten Detachment (DETSXM) was on supporting the civil authorities. For this purpose, intensive contact was sought with strategic security partners on the island, such as the Coast Guard, the police, the fire department, and the ambulance service. An inventory was made of the needs and the possibilities and capabilities of the detachment were brought to attention. This intensification of cooperation with security partners resulted in successful military assistance. For the second objective 'getting the basics in order', the detachment worked on improving basic readiness by establishing standards and authorizations. In addition, the detachment was closely involved in the renovation of apartment complex Gonzalo and the developments for new construction. Furthermore, MULAN was rolled out at the naval support point and the two FRISCs damaged during Hurricane Irma in 2017 were replaced. There was a significant personnel turnover within the permanent element during the summer period.

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2018_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-29 146 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Cooperation One of the highlights of 2018 was the military assistance during storm Isaac. Leading up to this, there was no military assistance provided, causing the 96-hour deadline for the hurricane to pass. In the subsequent Emergency Operational Centre (EOC) meeting, it was decided to request military assistance. CZMCARIB managed to deploy the requested units before the expected passage. The task for this assistance was also clear beforehand: to support the local authorities in maintaining public order and safety. For this purpose, the Sint Maarten Police Corps (KPSM) shared their operational plan with CZMCARIB, and this was executed jointly with KPSM.

[SECTION BREAK]

Fortunately, the impact of storm Isaac was limited.

text:
Also, in 2018, a HUREX was conducted on Sint Maarten where, at the operational level, marines from the 32 RSQN, the Marine Detachment Sint Maarten (DETSXM), and all safety partners went through a multidisciplinary scenario. Visibility In 2017, military deployment ceased after hurricane Irma, and the detachment operated an adjusted program until the end of that year. As a result, in 2018, with a regular training program, extra attention was still paid to visibility in the Windward Islands.

[SECTION BREAK]

Each rotating element (every four months) carried out a so-called charity week. During these weeks, several small community projects were undertaken. Additionally, the detachment was also active on Saba and Sint Eustatius. On Saba, at the beginning of 2018, the triathlon was supported with participants and volunteers, marking the start of a collaboration between the organization and DETSXM. Disaster exercises on Saba and Sint Eustatius were also supported. Observation As part of the annual plan, the support point contributed to improving the information position of CZMCARIB by closely observing and reporting on the security situation in the area. This was done by conducting observation exercises on the SSS islands. These exercises were carried out in good consultation with the local safety partner. The observation skills of the rotating element were one of the capabilities that the safety partners did not possess, but for which there was a great need.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Force in the Caribbean Sports Activities In 2018, the DETSXM started a New Year's run, which all defense personnel in Sint Maarten could participate in. Additionally, this year the Marine Run Sint Maarten was organized for the first time. This year it was only accessible to defense personnel, but next year it will be open to everyone.

[SECTION BREAK]

A team from the rotating element also participated in the Aruba Round in the military category, achieving a commendable third place. As is customary, the year was concluded with the event Beat the Marines on December 8. This year marked the fourth time. This event celebrated the corps anniversary with an amphibious obstacle course, challenging the safety partners to defeat the marines.

Pelikaan The support ship with transport capacity underwent an Annual Maintenance (JO) and docking in the first period of the year, as usual. The docking was carried out in Cartagena, Colombia, and the JO alongside the Rima dock at MBPAR. The Maintenance Program, scheduled for 2020, also required capacity. This project is being executed by shipyard DAMEN in the Netherlands under the auspices of DMO/Projects. FRISC CZMCARIB had temporary access to fourteen FRISC vessels. The outdated analog installation is only still used for the fire alarm system.

Logistics & Transport The Logistics & Transport (L&T) department had the executive capacity to support the operational logistical activities of the units, such as (strategic) movements of equipment and personnel. This involved both the own units of CZMCARIB and visiting national and international units. The department was also responsible for the FRISC’s of the Coast Guard.

[SECTION BREAK]

Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied is responsible for the supply of all units of CZMCARIB and the management and maintenance of all vehicles within CZMCARIB. In 2018, the replacement for the 40 MB280s was acquired by DMO/Projects: the Dutch Military Vehicle (DMV) Anaconda 4x4. The new tactical vehicle fleet will be delivered in two (partial) shipments. The first delivery of 36 vehicles will take place in January 2019, and the second delivery of 10 vehicles will follow before the start of the 2019 hurricane season. The introduction, the setup of maintenance, and the familiarization of drivers and mechanics will be implemented in the first half of 2019. After the rollout of the Anaconda 4x4 within CZMCARIB, the MB280 vehicles will be transferred to the CLAS.

This means that part of the identified P-multi-need from DOKM, the Executive Staff, and the SAP evaluation has been converted into twenty physically fillable positions within MBPAR, MHKC, MICAR, and MSTP Point Blanche. Additionally, in 2018, the first steps were taken in the reorganization of MICAR and MSTP Point Blanche. Prior to the reorganization of MICAR, the Purchasing Department CARIB was transferred to DMI to better and more effectively utilize the purchasing capacity within CZSK. Furthermore, the purchasing office from the inflow pool of civilian personnel was successfully strengthened with one purchaser. Young and old were able to visit Zr.Ms. Friesland during VLAC.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean The emergency assistance following Hurricane Irma in 2017 has resulted, from a lessons learned perspective, in an initial draft of a role plan for emergency assistance, in which personnel are assigned to a basic organization that must be supplemented from the Netherlands in the event of major disasters. CZMCARIB-wide, the organization has proven capable of fulfilling its vision and gaining more insight into its own shortcomings. P&O Advice CARIB has proven to be an indispensable link in the chain, serving as a point of contact for line managers and employees, as well as being an added N1 team to MHKC. In light of the professionalization of Caribbean military personnel, collaboration with HR staff of the local personnel has been intensified in this area. As in previous years, various career counselors from the Career Counseling Department (LBB) P&O CZSK visited CZMCARIB in 2018. The LBBs primarily spoke with military personnel who are scheduled to repatriate to the Netherlands in 2019. Additionally, collective briefings were provided, and there were opportunities for informal meetings. The discussions and briefings aimed to provide these groups with more clarity regarding developments within their service and the ongoing negotiations about employment conditions throughout 2018.

CZMCARIB-wide, the organization has proven capable of fulfilling its vision and gaining more insight into its own shortcomings. P&O Advice CARIB has proven to be an indispensable link in the chain, serving as a point of contact for line managers and employees, as well as being an added N1 team to MHKC. In light of the professionalization of Caribbean military personnel, collaboration with HR staff of the local personnel has been intensified in this area. As in previous years, various career counselors from the Career Counseling Department (LBB) P&O CZSK visited CZMCARIB in 2018. The LBBs primarily spoke with military personnel who are scheduled to repatriate to the Netherlands in 2019. Additionally, collective briefings were provided, and there were opportunities for informal meetings. The discussions and briefings aimed to provide these groups with more clarity regarding developments within their service and the ongoing negotiations about employment conditions throughout 2018.

Percentages On January 8, 2018, the total fill of Dutch defense personnel at CZMCARIB was 94%. Within CZMCARIB, the fill was 91% in AUA, 100% in Sint Maarten, and 95% in Curaçao.

[SECTION BREAK]

With these percentages, the fill rate was lower than in 2017. However, this presents a distorted picture, as a large part of the unfilled positions was planned for succession in 2019.

[SECTION BREAK]

The fill rate of local personnel at CZMCARIB was 93%, with 96% fill among local personnel in Curaçao, 82% in CURMIL, 100% among local personnel in Aruba, and 89% in ARUMIL. Staff Officer Local Personnel STOLP: Lieutenant Commander (ltz2) C.E. van der Eerden-Borsboom, from July 7, Lieutenant (ltz1) (LD) mr. E.J. Stoel In 2018, the focus for HR Caribbean Personnel was primarily on CARMIL, consisting of CURMIL with 111 positions and ARUMIL with 65 positions. The reason for this is that turnover among local civilian personnel is very limited.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean has, over the past few years, made significant progress in addressing the backlog of national decisions (appointment decisions). In the autumn of 2017, HR Caribbean Personnel, in consultation with representatives from HRM Caribbean Personnel, ARUMIL, and the Departmento Recurso Humano of Aruba, developed a renewed flow policy for ARUMIL. This new policy has led to considerable improvements in the legal status of ARUMIL. A positive flow decision is now linked to the militia of ARUMIL when their initial employment contract is nearing its end. In practice, this positive flow decision was often associated with a decision to participate in the VVO (Voluntary Military Service). Upon completion of the VVO, militia members of ARUMIL were appointed as civil servants rather than as contract workers. This civil servant status provided a preferential position when the involved militia member transitioned to the Government of Aruba. By decision of March 6, this new policy was established by the Council of Ministers of Aruba.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Furthermore, in the autumn of 2017, an outplacement policy was established for CARMIL. The HR departments in Curaçao and Aruba initiated the creation of a Personal Outflow Plan (PUP) approximately two years prior to the planned outflow, in collaboration with the individual concerned. Based on this PUP, preparations were made for transition to a (executive) government service or external mediation. In the context of this PUP, courses and training were also followed to achieve a better starting position. Since this policy was established in the autumn of 2017 and the intention was to create a PUP two years before outflow, a catch-up was made in 2018 in the preparation of PUPs.

[SECTION BREAK]

On August 24, C-ZMCARIB established a memorandum titled 'Development of Caribbean Militias' and submitted it to C-ZSK. This memorandum outlined the current position of CARMIL, the barriers, and the long-term vision for CARMIL. The goal that C-ZMCARIB has in mind regarding CARMIL is: CARMIL can be fully integrated and deployed as a full-fledged unit of Defense that can also cooperate with Land Services; CARMIL has equivalent and adequate material resources and accommodation, comparable to Dutch military personnel; CARMIL receives appropriate remuneration both in relation to Land Services (base salary) and Dutch military personnel (allowances); CARMIL has a suitable and future-proof legal and legal position system within the Countries and Defense. On November 11, the Admiralty Council discussed the memorandum 'Development of Caribbean Militias' and approved it in principle.

[SECTION BREAK]

Some aspects still needed to be supplemented before the memorandum could be submitted for final approval to the CDS from CZSK. It is expected that this will happen in the course of 2019. In particular, points three and four are expected to have an impact on HR Caribbean Personnel, as much work needs to be done here. This will take place in consultation with representatives from the countries of Curaçao and Aruba, the Ministry of Defense, and CARMIL. Since the autumn of 2018, a growing interest has been observed at CARMIL to transition towards Defense in the Netherlands, often towards the Marine Corps. In consultation with the P&O department of CZSK and the Special Appointments office of the Personnel Logistics Service Center, an initial process has been set up to facilitate this transition.

text:
In the first quarter of 2018, the evaluation of Hurricane Irma from 2017 was written and completed. The safety aspects related to this natural disaster played an important role. Many improvement proposals were linked to a safety aspect. From the drinking water supply to the exposure to asbestos and from the air transport of hazardous materials and munitions to communication aspects.

[SECTION BREAK]

These improvement proposals were later processed in 2018, under the leadership of the MHKC, into lessons learned. Following the evaluation of Hurricane Irma, CZMCARIB continued to systematically map the risks of operational activities. In 2018, the risks of approximately 35 training courses, operational processes, and deployments were inventoried and evaluated. These primarily relate to the training provided within MKSUF and to the units stationed at MBPAR, MS-KSAF, and MSTP Pointe Blanche.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean In relation to the Task Risk Analysis (TRA), the Subject Matter Expert (SME) established the control measures and guided the Safety & Environment (V&M) officer through the process. The outcomes were recorded in the TRA format. The TRA was added to the Operation Order (OPORD) by the Officer in Charge (OBL). It was the responsibility of the OBL to implement the established control measures. This aimed to further embed CZMCARIB safety in the line, the so-called first line of defense. With this method of working, the tasks and responsibilities regarding safety were particularly assigned and aligned with the element of 'structure'. In 2018, a portion of all operational TRAs was completed. Due to issues with the availability of the renewed SharePoint environment, these TRAs could not yet be published. Various technical and organizational causes underlie this.

Then, CARIB-wide, the completed TRAs could be used easily and uniformly. With this, CZMCARIB was able to partially fulfill the element of 'system'. The system could not function properly due to the lack of central accessibility in the new SharePoint environment.

[SECTION BREAK]

After drafting TRAs, V&M officers and third-year HBO interns regularly monitored in practice. There were monitoring moments during, among others: Engineer Exercises; Shooting Exercises; Amphibious Cross; King's Day; Drone Flying; Working at Heights; Sail Curaçao 2018. During these activities, the relevance of the associated TRA was assessed, and the implementation and compliance with the established control measures were evaluated. After the activity, discussions were held with the SME to determine whether the control measures were indeed effective. This assessed whether the TRA was implemented and functioning in practice. Based on practical experiences, adjustments or additions to control measures were made. In this way, the Plan Do Check Act (PDCA) cycle was completed. At the level of CZMCARIB, the element of 'system' for exercises, training, and deployments was thus secured.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Within CZMCARIB, all decentralized employers had an up-to-date Risk Inventory & Evaluation (RI&E).

[SECTION BREAK]

MSTP Point Blache is an exception to this. In 2018, an RI&E was prepared for MSTP Point Blanche and submitted for assessment to the Coordination Center for Expertise in Occupational Health and Safety (CEAG). Four Safety Councils CARIB and one Thematic Safety Council for Incidents were organized. Here, the CARIB-wide safety, environmental, integrity, and security aspects were addressed. In 2018, the following aspects were discussed: Chromium-6 contamination in FRISC warehouses MICAR and MK Savaneta; VGB policy CARIB; Oversight by external authorities; Preventive Medical Examination (PMO); Asbestos obstacle course and the OVG training location MK Suffisant; Onboard handling of hazardous substances (Zr.Ms. Pelikaan); Daily inspections by the Coast Guard along the Aruban coast.

text:
Company Social Work (BMW) region CARIB Head: Lieutenant (ltz) 1 (SD) H.J.H. Goetzee The main tasks that Company Social Work (BMW) performed in the Caribbean region include assistance, services, reporting, support after traumatic events, and crisis intervention. For the CARIB region, BMW, together with the Spiritual Care (GV) and in Aruba also with P&O, is responsible for notifying family communications. BMW/GV/P&O was always available at the base for personnel and their families. Since June 1, 2017, BMW at Defense has been under the Personnel Care Service Center (DC PZ) of the Defense Support Command. BMW provided psychosocial assistance to employees and their families throughout the CARIB region in 2018. Unlike the regional offices in the Netherlands, there is often a need for long-term assistance in the Caribbean region. Additionally, there is more contact with the families of the employees who have left their social network in the Netherlands. This was also related to the special situation of overseas postings and the difficulty of relying on alternatives such as local General Social Work or other forms of civil assistance.

[SECTION BREAK]

In 2018, regular work visits were made to Bonaire, where the Royal Marechaussee was active. These visits were also made to Sint Maarten to be more accessible to personnel and their families on these islands and to provide assistance and services in this way. In the context of providing services to commanders, information and advisory reports were prepared and participation took place in the Social Medical Team (SMT) of the various units at CZMCARIB, DBBO, and the Royal Marechaussee.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Due to the aftermath of Hurricane Irma, the BMW personnel from BMW CARIB were called upon for support in 2018. There were several requests for assistance both from the home front and from the military personnel themselves. In 2018, attention was also given to BMW's initiative to better address issues related to domestic violence and/or aggression within the family system.

Since June 1, 2017, BMW at Defense has been under the Personnel Care Service Center (DC PZ) of the Defense Support Command. BMW provided psychosocial assistance to employees and their families throughout the CARIB region in 2018. Unlike the regional offices in the Netherlands, there is often a need for long-term assistance in the Caribbean region. Additionally, there is more contact with the families of the employees who have left their social network in the Netherlands. This was also related to the special situation of overseas postings and the difficulty of relying on alternatives such as local General Social Work or other forms of civil assistance.

In the context of providing services to commanders, information and advisory reports were prepared and participation took place in the Social Medical Team (SMT) of the various units at CZMCARIB, DBBO, and the Royal Marechaussee.

In 2018, fourteen children in Curaçao received their First Holy Communion, and eight children were able to receive the sacrament of Confirmation from Chaplain Paul Vlaar. Throughout the year, nine children were baptized, either in the chapel of Ascencion or in the Noah chapel on Parera. There were also various church activities organized in Aruba.
