text: C&A Competitions In the early summer of 2018, the Cadets and Midshipmen competitions were held in Breda. C-KIM secured the first points with the victory in the fencing competition. Over two days, many sports were practiced, but unfortunately, the medal this year went to the cadets. The rematch will take place in 2019 in Den Helder. POTOM The goal of the POTOM is that every student is capable of functioning as a Troop Commander of a Raiding Troop. The training had a logical progression in the responsibilities assigned to students, starting with small team drills and culminating in leading (complex) operations at the Troop level. The emphasis was on taking responsibility, learning to collaborate with fellow students and operational marines, managing stress, and developing tactical insight. A relatively large amount of attention was also given to the theoretical aspect of warfare for a practical training program. The guiding document for this was the British All Arms Tactical Aid Memoire (AAT-AM). From this document, the students issued their orders to their troops. This was standard in English to enable students to collaborate internationally with other countries such as the United Kingdom.

C&A Competitions In the early summer of 2018, the Cadets and Midshipmen competitions were held in Breda. C-KIM secured the first points with the victory in the fencing competition. Over two days, many sports were practiced, but unfortunately, the medal this year went to the cadets. The rematch will take place in 2019 in Den Helder. POTOM The goal of the POTOM is that every student is capable of functioning as a Troop Commander of a Raiding Troop. The training had a logical progression in the responsibilities assigned to students, starting with small team drills and culminating in leading (complex) operations at the Troop level. The emphasis was on taking responsibility, learning to collaborate with fellow students and operational marines, managing stress, and developing tactical insight. A relatively large amount of attention was also given to the theoretical aspect of warfare for a practical training program. The guiding document for this was the British All Arms Tactical Aid Memoire (AAT-AM). From this document, the students issued their orders to their troops. This was standard in English to enable students to collaborate internationally with other countries such as the United Kingdom.

text:
In addition to the combined training and exercises for operational readiness, the voyage also focused on the education and motivation of second-year cadets from the Naval Service Corps. After completing the basic theoretical naval training at the Royal Naval Institute (KIM), they were tasked with translating this into practical skills as naval officers on a naval ship. Last year, a group of 35 cadets participated in the deployment. After two weeks, a rotation took place to provide all aspiring naval officers with an equal practical experience. The emphasis was on safe navigation in busy shipping areas, accurate positioning, seamanship exercises, and participation in the large international exercise BALTOPS 18. The planned port visits provided the cadets with an opportunity to present themselves as good ambassadors of the Dutch Armed Forces during various courtesy visits. The sailing program of the six-week voyage took place in the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and around the Danish islands. Installation of cadets.

[SECTION BREAK]

the cultural revolution. The Assaut was a celebration of this era, with participants dressed in period costumes, reflecting the glamour and struggles of the 1920s. The event included various activities and performances, allowing the attendees to immerse themselves in the spirit of the time. The Great River Race took place in London on the first weekend of September. Each year, a rowing team of cadets and midshipmen participates in this massive event. They rowed for three hours along the Thames.

[SECTION BREAK]

The results were commendable, and once again, the team finished in the top ranks. Ceremonial events this year included several occasions where the presence of the Corps of Cadets was requested, such as Prinsjesdag and the Command Transfer of C-ZSK. The Corps responded positively to these requests. The banner of the Corps of Cadets is the oldest banner of the Royal Netherlands Navy. In 1904, Queen Wilhelmina presented the banner to the Corps. This banner is unique in the Dutch armed forces as it is the only one that is not orange but red, as the cadets had a corps flag in those colors before 1904.

[SECTION BREAK]

During the May days of 1940, it was even brought to safety by some cadets and taken to Great Britain.

text: The Coast Guard Network has initiated the writing of a Vision 2030. Significant progress has also been made in the establishment of a new Regulation Organization Coast Guard Netherlands (ROKN). This has led to major steps in shaping the contours of future developments in the operational area and the corresponding administrative embedding of the Coast Guard. An important national development was the upcoming large-scale construction of wind farms in the Dutch Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) under the energy agreement "Wind Energy at Sea." This presented significant challenges for the Coast Guard due to the increasingly busy use of the North Sea, an increase in larger vessels and cargo volume, and developments in autonomous navigation and cybersecurity. Additionally, international developments will also demand the attention of the Coast Guard in the future. Examples include Maritime Security, the European Coast & Border Guard, and the implications of Brexit. 2018 was an eventful year, with many multi-year developments that will increasingly affect the personnel of the Coast Guard, the Coast Guard Network, and Dutch society as a whole.

2_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_PREFACE-in_memoriam-1 8 Personnel Directorate Preface NH90s from 860 Squadron in action from Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt.

[SECTION BREAK]

FOREWORD In your hands is the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2020. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, and the actions the shore organization took to facilitate these deployments.

[SECTION BREAK]

The year began as in previous years. This changed when, at the end of February and the beginning of March, COVID-19 also affected the Netherlands. Virtually the entire society came to a standstill, and the Royal Netherlands Navy had to adapt significantly. The lockdowns and safety regulations had a major impact on the workplace. The departments and units improvised and quickly regrouped so that the organization could function properly. In a safe manner, personnel followed many new courses, training sessions, and participated in (international) exercises. This was done differently than usual; sometimes from home, or in the workplace at a distance of one and a half meters.

[SECTION BREAK]

We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy. Foreword Commander of the Naval Forces Vice Admiral Rob Kramer.

[SECTION BREAK]

19 Organizational overviews shock-resistant budget. The expenditures by CZSK (Article 2 of the defense budget) were higher in 2020 than initially allocated at the beginning of the year. Compared to the draft budget, more was realized in readiness.

[SECTION BREAK]

The main reason is the usual interdepartmental transfer from the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management for payments to the Rijksrederij by the Coast Guard Netherlands for buoying tasks and emergency towing assistance. Within the maintenance category, various increases occurred throughout the year, leading to higher expenditures. This was partly due to the year-end margin of 2019, higher VAT receipts, various reallocations within the navy to reduce the deficit in maintenance, and several other mutations (€5.6 million). The under-realization elsewhere in the budget was also utilized for expenditures on the maintenance process. In personnel expenditures, more was spent overall than indicated in the draft budget. The cause lies mainly in additional expenditures on pension premiums from Article 10, higher employer costs, and labor conditions. On the other hand, less was spent due to the effects of COVID-19 on activity-related allowances, training, business trips, other personal expenses, and budget was made available for maintenance issues.

[SECTION BREAK]

Legal Affairs (JUZA) Head: Commander (cdr) G. Souer, LLD The JUZA department is part of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DP&O), one of the five line directorates of the CZSK. The department advises and supports the CZSK, the directors of the CZSK, and unit commanders on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within the CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within the CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and constitutional and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different offices.

[SECTION BREAK]

Thus, every employee at JUZA can serve as the first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department.

[SECTION BREAK]

JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of the CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. Should a military member be involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from the Ministry of Defence in this matter.

Personnel and Organization (P&O) Head: Captain (ktz) E.C.W. Jansen General Last year saw significant changes in the P&O domain. To retain more personnel for the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM), efforts were made to focus more on the individual. Additionally, COVID-19 had a considerable impact, and employees often worked 'remotely' and from home. Many changes had already been initiated, funded by the Second Chamber Motion Van der Staaij, further development of the armed forces (DOKM), and defense-wide projects such as Retention and Recruitment. Various measures that were implemented have now been secured in operations. For instance, an Oceangoing Patrol Vessel (OPV) remained in the Caribbean and was manned with a relief crew (the so-called multiple-crewing concept).

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-4 23 Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Bi-national Support Team (BST) Multipurpose Frigates received further development this year. Many organizational parts grew, either from the Van der Staaij motion or DOKM measures (temporary or not), as well as from strengthening the security chain. Furthermore, the measures from the Labor Conditions Agreement 18-20 were translated into regulations, from which HR measures followed. Part of this was the new Human Resources (HR) model developed by the Directorate of Personnel. The new model was intended to provide more opportunities for flexibility and customization for agreements between employees and supervisors. In fulfilling positions, the needs of the organization and the talents of employees in relation to the organization were better mapped and combined. New appointment and contract forms, strategic talent management, and the remuneration model are topics in the new HR model that affect the legal status of employees. A pilot environment at the Submarine Service has started to test some of these topics for feasibility.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Royal Netherlands Navy continued to face a significant personnel shortage this year.

text:
Measures to promote personnel retention were articulated in fourteen Personnel measures, drafted in September 2019 by the AR. The implementation of these measures received much attention alongside regular work. The measure to develop and implement a new HR system for CZSK was the most impactful. The old job allocation process was no longer functioning and needed to be simplified.

[SECTION BREAK]

To this end, a research study was conducted last year that will be further developed in 2021. It was investigated whether the Royal Fleet Auxiliary concept is applicable to a Hydrographic Survey Vessel (HOV), and the possibilities of 'alternative manning' for Combat Support Ships were mapped.

[SECTION BREAK]

The job vacancy bank was cleaned up to improve its functionality and transparency. Furthermore, it has been incorporated into operations that military personnel working at CZSK will be assessed once in their position. This could contribute to personnel retention, allowing for better alignment with the long-term objectives and development needs of military personnel. Units of the OPE fleet are manned task-oriented (warfare), with a guaranteed minimum staffing of CoCe. The effect is that high-end warfare, single threat can be secured, and not always multi-threat. In the career guidance section, starting qualifications (MBO3 level) have been established for the sub-service groups Logistics Service and Marines. A 'reflection moment' pilot has been conducted as part of retention, aimed at corporals in their second function.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-5 24 Directorate Personnel and Operations provided officers in their second position at the rank of Lieutenant Commander (kltz) insight into their development opportunities. The pilot was successful and 'the reflection moment' will be incorporated into operations in 2021. Following the evaluation report 'Mentors Officers' from 2019, this was expanded to all officer corps, at the rank of Lieutenant Commander (kltz) / First Lieutenant of the Marines (1st Lt mar) and the mandatory pairing between mentor and mentee was removed. An action plan to improve awareness for mentors for non-commissioned officers was implemented. To make the use of the flexible workforce, consisting of reservists and externally hired civilian personnel, more manageable, a process was established whereby the directorates received a drawing right on funding for external hiring. The Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve increasingly succeeded in binding military personnel who irregularly exit as reservists to the RN, and has thus grown significantly in size.

Measures to promote personnel retention were articulated in fourteen Personnel measures, drafted in September 2019 by the AR. The implementation of these measures received much attention alongside regular work. The measure to develop and implement a new HR system for CZSK was the most impactful. The old job allocation process was no longer functioning and needed to be simplified.

[Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.4) — narrative]
To this end, a research study was conducted last year that will be further developed in 2021. It was investigated whether the Royal Fleet Auxiliary concept is applicable to a Hydrographic Survey Vessel (HOV), and the possibilities of 'alternative manning' for Combat Support Ships were mapped.

[Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.4) — narrative]
The job vacancy bank was cleaned up to improve its functionality and transparency. Furthermore, it has been incorporated into operations that military personnel working at CZSK will be assessed once in their position. This could contribute to personnel retention, allowing for better alignment with the long-term objectives and development needs of military personnel. Units of the OPE fleet are manned task-oriented (warfare), with a guaranteed minimum staffing of CoCe. The effect is that high-end warfare, single threat can be secured, and not always multi-threat. In the career guidance section, starting qualifications (MBO3 level) have been established for the sub-service groups Logistics Service and Marines. A 'reflection moment' pilot has been conducted as part of retention, aimed at corporals in their second function.

text: Advantages of choosing VeVa for young personnel include: guaranteed internship placement, starting qualification, and job security with physical and psychological approval. There is also time for maturation for youthful aspiring military personnel. VeVa is by definition a Vocational Support Learning Path education. The disadvantages of VeVa for the student include boredom during the training and repetitions. For the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM), the different training approaches of the MBO schools and the low level of practical experience in the technical fields are particularly disadvantageous. Due to the shortage of practical hours in Vocational Support Learning Path programs, there are developments towards Vocational Accompanying Learning Path. In these programs, a student receives more practical hours. Other advantages of Vocational Accompanying Learning Path include better recruitment of young personnel since the student receives youth wages instead of an internship allowance and more intensive guidance at the learning workplace within Defense. VeVa is a strategic success due in part to the anchoring of Defense in education within society.

Intake & VeVa In March 2020, the first outbreak of COVID-19 occurred in our country. The first intake of the year was then in the last week of the EMMV. This meant that the students could complete the final exercise the Volharding and the last activities of their thirteen-week training, but with a very limited ceremonial beret parade. This was also the case for the other EMMV intakes of the year 2020.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-15 Directorate Personnel and Operations The EMMV operated in 2020 largely from the "EMMV bubble" to avoid contact with the outside world. From the second intake, the EMMV took place entirely internally at Marinekazerne Erfprins this year.

[SECTION BREAK]

Because the training also took place during the weekends, the duration of the training could be shortened from thirteen to nine weeks. Despite a reduction of one month, the intakes this year required a lot of extra effort from the cadre members and their families. Not only were the students away from home for nine full weeks, but this also applied to the cadre members. In addition to the students and cadre members being away from home for an extended period, the recreational opportunities were very limited due to the "EMMV bubble." The students received a nice boost halfway through the year. In the day room of the EMMV, a test setup was installed in collaboration with E-sports KM, featuring ten gaming PCs that allowed students to entertain themselves.

Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training in Den Helder (KMTO) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) ir. M. Flaman EMSD The Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) stands for "Inspiring". The motto of the Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) is: "We train maritime technicians." The KMTO provides vocational and functional education for the personnel of the Technical Service (TD), but also for the (technical) personnel of other services and defense components. In addition, the school makes an important contribution to the training and development of crews of operational units, both above and below water. For training and development purposes, the KMTO has representative practical resources and simulators. Students All new sailors and non-commissioned officers of the Technical Service (TD) of the Royal Netherlands Navy begin their careers at the KMTO. In 2020, 23 sailors started with the Entry-level Vocational Education (EVO) and 43 with the First Adjustment Module. Additionally, 26 non-commissioned officers, who already have operational experience as sailors, began their technical MBO 4 training in Service and Maintenance at the ROC Kop van Noord-Holland.

The VeVa students follow their vocational education at the ROC's and receive their Practical Vocational Training (BPV) at the KMTO. In 2020, 38 VeVa students started their BPV at the KMTO. text:
Due to travel restrictions related to COVID-19, the number of foreign students this year was significantly smaller than in previous years. In 2020, lessons were still provided for two German and five Belgian colleagues. Impact of COVID-19 on activities COVID-19 also affected the activities of the KMTO.

[SECTION BREAK]

By implementing measures such as reducing class sizes and allowing everyone who was not directly involved in teaching to work from home, (almost) all training could continue safely. Within the KMTO, the following three basic principles were applied: lessons that could take place remotely were conducted via distance learning; practical lessons that required in-person instruction took place on-site within the RIVM guidelines; and if compliance with the RIVM guidelines during in-person instruction was impossible, these lessons only took place after a task-risk analysis weighed the necessity against the risks. For all lessons requiring in-person instruction, procedures were established that outlined which specific measures applied to that particular lesson. To ensure that distance learning received the best possible support, the room was transformed into a virtual classroom. This allowed instructors to conduct distance learning while it felt as if they were in front of a normal class. Since the infrastructure for the project was already almost fully in place, Zr.Ms. Willemstad docked in Den Helder after four months of deployment in NATO context.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Personnel and Business Operations Directorate started the virtual classroom just one week later. The practical education also made adjustments to enable lesson activities within the RIVM guidelines. For example, a body camera was used in combination with a tablet to ensure that an instructor or examiner did not have to stand close to the student to assess the practical work.

text:
Developments and Innovation The management of the KMTO noted that the intake of sailors had stagnated in recent years and that the market forecast indicated this was a structural trend. Additionally, the training pathway to sailor and corporal TD was experienced by the students as too long and too theoretical. To address these issues, the management of the KMTO developed a plan for the Technical Vocational School CZSK, which significantly restructured the training approach. An important change was that the education primarily took place at the workplace and that education at school was only provided when it could not be done (safely) on board or in the workshop. Since this change in education also affects the operations on board and the HR organization, it is being developed in conjunction and is a change that will take several years. In anticipation of the new structure of education and in response to the needs of the fleet, the vertical VVO was transformed from MBO3 Mechatronics to MBO 4 Service and Maintenance. For this, it was necessary to set up a revised VVO in collaboration with the ROC Kop van Noord-Holland. The experiences gained from this will be used in the Technical Vocational School CZSK. Due to COVID-19, it was impossible to continue the research with other institutions. An example of this was the joint research with the Katholieke Universiteit Leuven, Kortrijk department, and the Belgian Navy.

[SECTION BREAK]

In 2020, the polytechnic lessons with a new teaching method were scheduled to take place. However, since this teaching method requires close collaboration in groups, it was unfeasible within the RIVM guidelines, and it was decided to conduct the polytechnic lessons in the traditional manner until the end of the COVID-19 crisis.

De Ruyter. Dutch-Belgian Operational School (NLBEOPS) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) E.J. Horstman EMSD The year 2020 was a tumultuous period for the NLBEOPS. COVID-19 posed a significant additional challenge for the school starting in March. In a very short time, the management and staff took the necessary steps in the spring to ensure both the continuation of the planned training and the operational readiness of the NLBEOPS. Many control measures were implemented to increase hygiene and to maintain sufficient distance – one and a half meters – in the classrooms, training areas, and common spaces. This was the last year in which the CCO training consisted of a basic and type training. Netherlands Submarine Command Course (NLSMCC) From November 2019 until mid-April, the 26th edition of the NLSMCC took place. Due to the operational planning of the sea phase, the SMCC started before the Christmas leave. This was a unique situation, which provided the participants and trainer support with more flexibility and depth in preparation for the sea phase. The course was attended by three participants: two Australians and one American student. With the earlier development of the Guardion Submarine Trainer, this SMCC was the first edition to take place entirely in the new trainer. The NLSMCC worked closely with the SMCC of Great Britain and Norway with the aim of efficient deployment of available resources and sharing of acquired knowledge and experiences. This collaboration and the crew member of Zr.Ms. De Ruyter takes a sounding while approaching the port of Dubai.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-25 44 Directorate of Personnel and Operations synchronization of the German training at the tri-nation SMCC again led to unique training opportunities for the students. Despite the significant impact of COVID-19 on the execution of the final part of the training, such as limited numbers of units for Joint Warrior, national travel restrictions for the students, and infections on board, an Australian and an American candidate successfully completed the training in early April. Air Warfare Course (AWC) Due to COVID-19 measures, both the work visits and the support of Operation Gammel Dansk could not be realized, and there were too few opportunities left to conduct a thorough AWC. Therefore, the course leaders and commanders of the German and Dutch operational schools decided to cancel the AWC in 2020.

For the ICT office, 2020 was marked by the transition from Cisco R&S version 6 to version 7. The integration of a Cyber module was further implemented. The renewed network administrator training kicked off this year. A Cyber office was established that will develop a cyber training package for CZSK starting in 2021 from a working group. The emphasis here is not only on the technical side but also on the operational side of Cyber and the synergy with ICT and IM. The Information Command & Control Management training had to be temporarily interrupted in the spring due to COVID-19. By extending the second part of the training by one week, all participants still passed.

[SECTION BREAK]

The VVO Operational Service Communications (ODVB) for beginning non-commissioned officers of the communication service took place amidst adjustments and COVID-19 measures. The training has been modernized on many fronts, with a strong focus on distance learning. Following the VVO ODVB, the Typemodule ODVB OOFF training for beginning non-commissioned officers is also implemented in 2020.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-26 45 Directorate of Personnel and Operations Defense Naval School (DVS) As with all departments, the COVID-19 crisis had a significant impact on the DVS. Through maximum effort and a flexible approach from the personnel, the damage to education remained limited. The DVS was previously a forerunner in providing distance education and modernizing school education, particularly through the use of GPAL. As a result, the training calendar was able to proceed almost unchanged. In the navigation department, all training courses continued, with only the NATO Klein Bovenwater (KBW) course needing to be canceled. The seamanship department conducted three EVO ODND and one VVO ODND. Furthermore, many RHIB and crane training sessions were held. The seamanship trainer was in full use. More and more ships utilized the trainer, and the VeVa also made frequent use of the new possibilities.

[SECTION BREAK]

No solution has yet been found for the rejected Dependance. New construction has been postponed again and is now scheduled for 2022, with commissioning planned for the first quarter of 2023.

The training unit of the Surface Assault and Training Group (SATG) conducted amphibious navigation training in Texel. In 2020, it provided four Landing Craft Rubber Motorized (LCRM), four Fast Raiding Interception and Special Forces Craft (FRISC), three Landing Craft (LC) BASIC, and two LC3 training courses. The LC2 course was not held this year; an LC2 course is scheduled for the spring of 2021.

[SECTION BREAK]

VeVa The importance of VeVa Maritime for the CZSK organization was widely supported both within and outside the NLBEOPS. Due to COVID-19, the reduced instructional capacity and increase in the quota made 2020 a challenging year.

[SECTION BREAK]

The ambition to facilitate an engaging and binding program by deploying the sailing ships Morgenster and Eendracht did not materialize. The VeVa internships could not take place from week 12 to week 37 due to COVID-19. Nevertheless, several steps in the right direction were taken. Maximum effort was shown to adjust the programs in such a way that the impact for the ROCs was minimized. This required flexibility and understanding from all VeVa Maritime partners. The final touches were also put on the VeVa Maritime script in collaboration with the OO&P department. Engaging and binding will take on new forms in 2021: the development of a maritime learning line for VeVa; the relocation of the VeVa section NLBEOPS to the Lieutenant Colonel Maaskamp barracks; and the provision of VeVa internships aboard Navy ships. Preparations for this were carried out in 2020.

From an educational perspective, 2020 has been fruitful for the Educational Development & Planning department.

International Training and Exercises Training and exercises at EGUERMIN are not only offered to Dutch and Belgian military personnel but also to those from other NATO partners. These training sessions include components of the binational training, supplemented by the use of the Naval Mine Warfare Gaming System. These trainings prepare personnel for roles as Principle Warfare Officers in Naval Mine Warfare and Staff Officers. Additionally, training is facilitated for personnel within the Naval Coordination And Guidance for Shipping and Allied Warning for Navigation and Information System offices. Wargaming On the wargaming system, members of a Naval Mine Countermeasures staff can plan, execute, and evaluate a mine countermeasure operation. The wargaming system of EGUERMIN is a unique tool within NATO.

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-30 49 Directorate of Personnel and Operations The Marine Training Centre (MOC) in Rotterdam Commander: LtCol (ltkolmarns) P. Damen Last year saw the interim evaluation of the 'Houtskoolschets' (Charcoal Sketch). The cultural change within the MOC led to a decrease in personnel turnover. When the effectiveness of the training finally increased, COVID-19 hit hard. Initially, everything came to a standstill, and the leadership assessed what could and could not continue. The question arose of how long this would last and when activities would resume as usual.

[SECTION BREAK]

Unfortunately, it turned out that all activities abroad were halted, and only a ML training and support for mountain training could be provided. During this mountain training, the final part of the recce operator course was completed. The Practical Training for Marine Officers (POTOM) was halted, and the personnel were sent back to the KIM. Coster In 2012, the three-director model was introduced within Defense. This was the result of the defense-wide reorganization following the measures from the defense memorandum “Defense after the Credit Crisis, a Smaller Armed Forces in an Unstable World” (April 8, 2011). This reorganization was carried out based on pressing financial, personnel, and organizational frameworks. Based on this, it was decided at that time to divide staff, operational, and governance tasks of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) among the directors of Personnel and Operations and Material Maintenance, with the P-CZSK expected to fulfill the central coordinating role.

[SECTION BREAK]

In practice, it soon became clear that this organizational investment brought structural shortcomings in the areas of governance integrity, span/scope of control, allocation of responsibilities, oversight, and the absence of escalation levels. Furthermore, attention to personnel, operations, governance risks, and oversight increased significantly, and the intensity of governance coordination between internal and external interfaces grew. To achieve more balance in the governance organization of the CZSK, clarity in ownership, and in operations, C-ZSK requested the Chief of Defense Staff (CDS) to agree to the expansion of the framework of the three-director model. This provided the opportunity to establish a new directorate under a single leadership,

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Personnel and Operations focused on governance, operations, and oversight of the CZSK as a solution to the identified structural flaws and vulnerabilities in the organization. In November 2019, the new Directorate of Integrated Operations & Governance was established.

Moerman) The S&A department supports C-ZSK in its role as maritime military advisor to the CDS. The S&A department operates in three teams: the Advice team, the International Military Cooperation (IMS) team, and the Strategy team. The Advice team acts as the first point of contact (mailbox) for the Executive Staff regarding policy documents, studies, parliamentary matters, and the so-called Hague consultations. This team is also actively involved in the network of the foundation ‘Netherlands Maritime Country’ and the analysis of the reports from the Inspector General of the Armed Forces regarding visits to CZSK units. The IMS team supports C-ZSK in maintaining its international contacts and working relationships, in collaboration with the Defense Staff and DGB (IMS/DIA). The Strategy team advises C-ZSK as maritime advisor to the CDS on concept & capability development and plays an important role, particularly in the initial phase of the (larger) replacement projects of the Navy. For the first time this year, S&A facilitated the Strategic Foresight process through a pilot to support the strategic narrative and strategic thinking within CZSK. This year was marked by the onset of the COVID-19 period. This had an impact on work but certainly also on international contacts. All staff talks for this year were canceled due to COVID-19.

text:
De inzet van nieuwe technologieën en innovatieve benaderingen zal hierbij een cruciale rol spelen. Daarnaast heeft de afdeling aandacht besteed aan de mentale en fysieke gezondheid van het personeel. Er zijn initiatieven opgezet om het welzijn van de medewerkers te bevorderen, waaronder sport- en welzijnsprogramma's. Dit is essentieel voor het behoud van een gemotiveerd en gezond team dat in staat is om de uitdagingen van de toekomst aan te gaan. In het kader van personeelsontwikkeling zijn er ook diverse loopbaantrajecten en opleidingsmogelijkheden aangeboden. Dit stelt medewerkers in staat om zich verder te ontwikkelen en hun carrière binnen de Koninklijke Marine vorm te geven. De afdeling blijft zich inzetten voor een goede balans tussen werk en privéleven, wat bijdraagt aan de tevredenheid en betrokkenheid van het personeel. Al met al was 2020 een jaar van verandering en innovatie binnen de Directie Personeel en Bedrijfsvoering, met een sterke focus op het verbeteren van processen, het implementeren van nieuwe technologieën en het ondersteunen van het personeel in hun ontwikkeling en welzijn.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Personnel and Operations participated in official E-sports competitions. Mewe During 2020, MBS, under the leadership of C-NLMARFOR, served as the staff of the Amphibious Task Group that was on standby for the NATO Response Force. To maintain readiness, three major exercises were planned in which MBS would participate in the Commander Amphibious Task Group formation.

[SECTION BREAK]

During Arctic Archer 20, including Cold Response 20, COVID-19 made its entrance, and this exercise was prematurely terminated. Mediterranean Archer 20, including Dynamic Mariner 20, was conducted in a scaled-down form without port visits. Additionally, Tyrrhenian Archer 20, including Mare Aperto 20-1, was scheduled but this exercise was canceled. To maintain proficiency in sailing in a squadron, the deployments Continuation Cruise 20 and Baltic Breeze 20 were prepared and executed. Furthermore, MBS was ready to provide personnel to the Caribbean and supported MTC for the Computer Aided Staff Training (CAST) of 1 Marine Combat Group (MCG).

[SECTION BREAK]

de Jong New chain Raiding Squadrons (RSQN) have been filled and developed annually since 2013 according to a fixed system. After the average formation of a new RSQN per MCG every six months, a training year begins before a squadron becomes operational. This year was better known on the work floor as 'the chain' and was carried out under the leadership of its own MCG, but also with guidance from the MTC. After years of fixed routine through which the chain has been followed, the decision was made to adjust the current training system starting in 2020. Thus, the 22nd and 13th RSQN formed in 2019 were the last warriors to have the honor of going through the 'traditional training chain.' text: She was deployed in the context of the European-led Mission Awareness Strait of Hormuz (EMASOH). During the outbound journey, the STC staff embarked from January 28 to February 10. Integration training was conducted with the boarding team of RSQN 23 as well as with the embarked NH90 helicopter. Various PASSEX exercises with French and Spanish training partners were also scheduled. The training program was briefly interrupted for a port visit to Palma de Mallorca. After this, the course was set for Malta for boarding exercises with the Armed Forces of Malta (AFM). During the subsequent transit to Crete, mission-specific training was also conducted. C-STC declared the ship 'operationally ready' before he and the staff disembarked during the Brief Logistic Stop (BLS) on the aforementioned island. Following this, a PDT training was conducted from February 23 to February 27 on BNS Leopold I. This training was in preparation for her two-month deployment with the French carrier group, Groupe Aero Naval. The program was largely executed during her outbound journey to the Mediterranean Sea in the South Coast Exercise Areas with FOST. The proficiency improved after five days, after which the ship was able to address the remaining points of attention itself to further enhance operational readiness. On March 8, the crew of Zr.Ms. Zeeland OPV-R departed to sea from Aalborg, Denmark. The goal was to conduct a PDT in preparation for her deployment.

Operations Directorate 2nd Marine Combat Group (2 MCG) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) E.E.R.M. Thomeer Joint Arctic Training (JAT) This year, many participated in the JAT. Marines experienced severe weather conditions, such as rapidly changing temperatures and precipitation. This made operations more difficult. JAT ensured that marines learned to cope with extreme conditions while carrying out their work. Both the Anti Armour Troop and the Assault Engineers Troop participated in the JAT. This year, these specialized units worked with both the snowmobile and the BV-206 tracked vehicles. From a new base location in Skjold, 2MCG, supplemented by units from the German Seebatallion and the Belgian Special Operations Regiment, completed a challenging training in extreme terrain since early January. Joint Mountain Training In September and October, the marines of 2MCG participated in the annual mountain training in the north of Norway, approximately 300 kilometers above the Arctic Circle. About 470 marines, including 154 novices, completed a physically and mentally challenging program in which units were trained to successfully conduct operations in Military Operations in eXtreme conditions (MOX) terrain. Operating under extreme climatic and geographical conditions requires specific knowledge, skills, and experience to perform under these circumstances and to be independently deployable for longer durations.

[SECTION BREAK]

This mainly involved planned support for basic training in the OJP, alongside support for SAIL Amsterdam, the World Port Days in Rotterdam, and training support for the LC-3 training. It was striking to see how the annually recurring meetings became increasingly limited in size and setting. Of the large meetings, the NATO Maritime Operations Working Group in Albania still took place more or less normally, but the Amphibious Operations Work Group was a virtual meeting. The Steering Group Meetings of the maritime COEs could take place in Ostend, Norfolk, and Kiel due to a temporary easing of the restrictions. However, various conferences, seminars, and working groups dwindled, were postponed, or were organized virtually (if possible). The Maritime Battle Lab remained very active despite all COVID restrictions and conducted activities for the MTMD forum, Spartan Windmill 3, Ship in the Loop test, Augmented Reality Tests, and Connectivity tests with the F-35. For the latter, the lab has recently acquired a mobile version of itself, which can be safely transported from Den Helder to any work location using Pelican cases (hard plastic cases).

5_KM_Annual_Report_2020_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-37 96 Operations Directorate For the CZSK organization, personnel shortages are becoming increasingly pressing. This is especially true for specialists; the shortage is particularly significant in this area. Despite these challenges, the MWC was able to meet most support requests: Various ships were provided with seariders; The MWC supplied replacements for gaps in the crews of operational ships; Direct support for training and exercises was provided; The Advanced Acoustic Analysis Course was conducted. The MWC provided extensive expertise for various wargames, including Silver Kraka as part of the Marine Corps PL 2025 and Force Design. A safety and environmental advisor officer strengthened the Joint Knowledge Center Military Operations under Extreme Conditions (JKCMOX) this year. The transition to S-100 and the associated product specifications was initiated with the adoption of the S-100 Roadmap during the second IHO Assembly. Naval Base Den Helder – General Service Tide and Ebb Jetty near Jetty 5 On Monday, January 6, the floating jetty near Jetty 5 was struck by a commercial vessel. The floating jetty and mooring posts sustained significant damage as a result. This jetty is also important for patient transport/ambulance/KNRM/Coast Guard. The spud poles have been replaced and the jetty has been made operational again.

[SECTION BREAK]

Pre-winter training MCG1 MCG1 held a pre-winter training at the MBDH. Due to limited space in the barracks at the MBDH, MCG1 was stationed on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. Solar panels at the Naval Base The Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate has allocated 25 million euros for five years for the Solar on Rooftops Program. The goal is to install as many solar panels as possible on government rooftops. The Marine Complex Nieuwe Haven has been designated as one of the first three locations of the government. The solar panels are intended to be installed at the Accutestcentrum and building IJsduiker at Nieuwe Haven.

[SECTION BREAK]

Resuscitation by BHV On January 28, an external person who was receiving a tour became unwell near building Kaiser and was resuscitated. The first responders were the BHV members and the Marine Fire Brigade. The civil ambulance arrived quickly to further stabilize the victim and transport them to the hospital. Storm damage At MBDH, hurricanes Ciara and Dennis caused significant storm damage. Many bicycle sheds lost roofs and/or walls, roofing from a temporary building came loose, and facade panels were detached and blown away. Furthermore, a number of

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Material Maintenance doors were blown off, cladding came loose, containers were blown away, winch houses were blown away, and a scaffolding was blown over at the ship lift complex. Several buildings also had water leaks, and a bollard on pier 21 was torn loose. Water Damage Due to frequent and extensive rainfall, a high groundwater level developed throughout the Nieuwe Haven in mid-2020. As a result, the basement spaces of various buildings were flooded.

When a TV is turned on in the barracks room, the information screen of the MBDH appears immediately. text:
Events and activities in 2020 This year again featured major events on the calendar, but 2020 would primarily be marked by SAIL. The CZSK New Year's Reception successfully kicked off the year, and Vice Admiral Kramer was eager to return to MEA for the KM's year start. At the end of January, the barracks hosted the Safety Day of the Directorate of Defense Safety with three hundred guests, including many VIP guests such as the CDS, State Secretary Visser, and Dutch astronaut André Kuipers. From spring onwards, operations were set to fully support the annual events, such as the SCIANDRI King's Games, the Amsterdam Veterans Day, and the 5th of May Concert. New activities were also planned, including the NATO panel business meeting and the MWK Lifesaving led by the Bureau for International Military Sport.

[SECTION BREAK]

Until COVID-19 broke out: cancellations flooded in. MEA faced a global pandemic that was expected to last more than a few months. Before long, the entire annual schedule was canceled, including events such as SAIL, the Canal Pride, Amsterdam City Swim, and the Sinterklaas arrival. That the pandemic would last more than a year and bring the events sector to a standstill was unexpected. No reservations, no visitors, no catering, and no full halls. Operations were thus put on a low flame, but at the same time, the COVID-19 crisis also provided an opportunity to carry out significant overdue maintenance in and around the ECA. The event complex underwent a true transformation, with the reintroduction of the shop, the arrival of the new all-ranks bar 't IJ, and the installation of a reception desk at the entrance.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Material Maintenance This year, we processed over 2886 reservations for "Short-Term Berthing" for activities on and around the MEA, and there were 14124 visitors during 662 events, meetings, and conferences. Port Visits The number of port visits decreased significantly this year due to COVID-19.

Most requests for berths came from the port and towing service in Den Helder and the DDG. Nevertheless, various foreign units also visited Amsterdam this year; the most notable was the Standing NATO Mine Countermeasure Group 1 in September. Future and Infrastructure In the summer of 2020, the working group "Redevelopment Marine Establishment Amsterdam," consisting of members from Defense, the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf, and the Rijksatelier, started its work. This working group began developing plans for the revitalization of the barracks section.

[SECTION BREAK]

Meanwhile, the State and Municipality are working on a Note of Principles, which outlines the urban planning, zoning plan, and the conditions for the future of the entire site. This note is to be submitted to the municipal council and the ministers in the summer of 2021. This will determine the future of the barracks. A portion of the former Marine area in the center of Amsterdam has received a partially temporary new designation.

In 2020, the conversion of the barrack rooms for the personnel began. Marine Band of the Royal Netherlands Navy Commander: Major (maj) C. Knegjens Conductor: Major (maj) H.J.C. Tien Bandmaster: Lieutenant (lt) P. Bongaert, from September 1 Lieutenant (lt) D. Kuiper Besides the 75th anniversary of liberation, the Marine Band also celebrated its own anniversary in 2020, as August 1, 1945, is the 'administrative birthday' of the band. The season was festively opened on January 10 with the world premiere of 'Un momento dado' by composer Johan de Meij, specifically written for the Calefax reed quintet with wind orchestra.

[SECTION BREAK]

A promotional campaign and radio/video recording surrounded the presentation in Tilburg, followed by a reprise in Groningen. Furthermore, in January, an educational concert was held for primary school students and a refugee center in Den Helder, where spontaneous clapping, singing, and dancing occurred. A performance in the most beautiful concert hall in the Netherlands, the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, is always special. Here, the Marine Band performed as the first military orchestra ever in the prestigious Sunday Morning Concert series (January 26), simultaneously broadcast on NPO Radio 4. For the musicians, it was no problem to showcase foreign national anthems with equally beautiful sound a week later during the ceremonial guard of Credentials in the forecourt of Palace Noordeinde. A benefit gala concert took place in Arnhem on February 15. Together with the newly appointed assistant conductor Adjutant (adj) G. Bellefroid and soloists Francis van Broekhuizen and Romy Monteiro, a performance was held for a sold-out audience at Musis Sacrum.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Material Maintenance The trilogy of CDs featuring music by Russian and German-speaking composers was completed with recordings of American repertoire in Hilversum. Notably, the pianola recorded by George Gershwin in 1925 served as a soloist. The CD 'Rhapsody in Navy Blue - Originals' was released in the autumn on the international label Channel Classics.

text:
The busy schedule continued with a performance on March 6 in Woudenberg. Together with guest conductor Ivan Meylemans, a varied classical and show program was performed for over 600 enthusiastic visitors, including the Liberation Medley specially composed for this season.

[SECTION BREAK]

What was supposed to be a fantastic anniversary year was abruptly disrupted by a lockdown and tightened measures due to the pandemic. Physical ensemble playing was no longer possible, and many planned activities were canceled until further notice. Military ceremonies could only take place during the following period with many restrictions in mind. The Military Music Agency chose to carry out several important events with musicians from different orchestras and in a small ensemble. The National Remembrance on May 4, the American commemoration in Margraten on May 24, and the National Indonesia Remembrance on August 15 were performed in 'purple'. Among others, Veterans Day and the National Tattoo were canceled. From the end of June, some ceremonial services could temporarily resume under strict rules and with a maximum of thirty people. On June 28 in Den Helder, live ensemble playing occurred for the first time again, followed by a guard of honor for Letters of Credence. The ceremonial change of function of the Military Adjutant in Ermelo could also be accompanied.

[SECTION BREAK]

Due to guidelines from the RIVM regarding air circulation and aerosol spread, it was not possible for a wind orchestra to play collectively for a long time. Therefore, the whole was split into ensembles that could rehearse with a prescribed distance. Several incidental presentations took place in the Grote Kerk in The Hague and in the theaters of Zutphen and Maastricht. The commemoration service for the Leiden Liberation was also performed with a small ensemble.

In place of the annual Princess of Orange concert, which also included congratulations from the mayor of The Hague, the highlight in this digital age was an alternative Corps concert that was recorded by orchestra sections in different shifts aboard Zr.Ms. Rotterdam in Den Helder. [SECTION BREAK]

A number of musicians had to say farewell to the orchestra in small circles in the autumn due to FLO (Force Reduction). Among them was clarinetist First Lieutenant Marine (eltntmarnskap) P. Bongaert. He had led the band as conductor for over eleven years at many occasions, including the inauguration of King Willem-Alexander, state visits, three Prinsjesdagen, and countless ceremonial presentations of credentials. text:
Marine Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen The Marine Training Vessel (MOV) Van Kinsbergen is used for nautical practical training. The ship has been specially built and equipped for this purpose. It accommodates 16 trainees. Zr.Ms. Urania.

[SECTION BREAK]

6_KM_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-21 122 Directorate of Material Maintenance Navigation and Training Bridge The Van Kinsbergen has, in addition to the regular navigation bridge, a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for practicing all navigation procedures and safe mooring and unmooring. Deployment The Van Kinsbergen sails approximately 200 days per year. The main user is the KIM (Royal Netherlands Naval College). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. The ship serves as a supplement to theoretical and (bridge) simulator lessons. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, including team building and character development.

[SECTION BREAK]

Besides the KIM, the Dutch-Belgian Operational School is also a major user. Students at the OPSCHOOL receive practical sailing training for the qualifications of non-commissioned officers for minehunters, hydrographic survey vessels, and submarines. Civil Maritime Schools The civil maritime school on Terschelling, the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB), also makes good use of the Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Within the framework of the agreement, the MIWB has access to the training vessel for several weeks. Second-year Maritime Officer students undertake short practical voyages on this ship. During their stay on board, navigation is particularly practiced. Additionally, the MIWB uses the ship for Advanced Fire Fighting training, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. Instructors from the MIWB provide lessons for the adelborsten of the KIM in Den Helder.

[SECTION BREAK]

These include subjects such as loading technology and maritime law. Within the framework of the agreement, there is an exploration of how to expand cooperation to further modernize and improve education within both institutions.

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-1 124 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Area Organizational Chart CZMCARIB.

[SECTION BREAK]

the role of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean region. The Command of the Navy in the Caribbean is responsible for maritime security, law enforcement, and disaster relief operations. The operational area is characterized by various factors such as the significant distance from the Netherlands, a large maritime accountability area, tropical climatic conditions, numerous direct political and international contacts, and culturally locally determined circumstances. Additionally, we observe three developments in the environment in which CZMCARIB operates that significantly influence our actions.

[SECTION BREAK]

Firstly, there is geopolitical destabilization in the region, particularly due to developments in Venezuela. A second development relates to the situation in Venezuela and concerns the increasing influence of criminal organizations. The country is in a humanitarian and economic crisis, resulting in an increase in migration of undocumented individuals and smuggling of contraband such as drugs and weapons. Finally, we see an increase in climatic extremes as a result of global warming.

[SECTION BREAK]

Whether CZMCARIB can adequately fulfill the three main defense tasks with its current capabilities is a legitimate question. In light of the above developments, the Advisory Council on International Affairs, at the request of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, is conducting a study on the role of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean region.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean "Security and political developments in the Caribbean and their impact on the Kingdom." In addition, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is conducting a crime image analysis that examines transnational crime in the Caribbean region. The results of both studies are expected in 2021 and may influence the future task and priority setting of CZMCARIB. Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as: "Providing security in the Caribbean." This one sentence articulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB is responsible for the territorial integrity of the Caribbean countries of the Kingdom and Caribbean Netherlands.

text:
The own and visiting operational units have a so-called threshold function. Arrival of Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman in the port of Philipsburg, Sint Maarten.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean states that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability is part of our second main task, which also includes the deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and drugs by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, conducting counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this regard.

[SECTION BREAK]

C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. It supports civil authorities. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. With its highly developed specialized and unique capabilities, the armed forces now have broader support options. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB.

[SECTION BREAK]

It also provides emergency assistance in disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB also supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba.

International Drug Enforcement
In addition to the territorial defense of the six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in upholding the international rule of law in the Caribbean. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy in the Caribbean is closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South based in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4, one of the task groups of this organization.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Vision In order to realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the changes around it, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK.’ This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. ‘Relevant maritime’ and ‘security partner’ in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third core tasks.

The SSCG is equipped with an NH90 onboard helicopter, which acts as a force multiplier in the various operations. On Sunday, July 19, the onboard helicopter of Zr.Ms. Groningen crashed at sea during a routine fly exercise. This occurred approximately seven nautical miles northwest of Aruba. At the time of the tragic accident, the helicopter was making approach routes and landings to train the flight deck officer and pilot. There were four crew members on board. Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Curaçao and Aruba in support of KWCARIB, focusing on illegal landings due to the deteriorating (COVID-19) situation in Venezuela. text:
The base houses the staff of C-ZMCARIB and the Search and Coordination Center of the Coast Guard Caribbean Area. MBPAR also provides accommodation for a rotating company of the army. They are initially in the Caribbean for a training program. If necessary, they also provide humanitarian assistance, for example after a hurricane or to maintain public order. The company is also deployed for ceremonial tasks, such as at the Opening of the States. This boat group at MBPAR is primarily used to support various operations and exercises. In addition, they can also conduct beach reconnaissance and river operations. The Navy Operations Center is also located at Marine Base Parera. This center directs all counter-drug operations in the Caribbean. The base has workshops where all sailing and rolling equipment is maintained. Anaconda vehicles at Marine Base Parera.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean During the pandemic, the GGD opened a testing facility at the base. COVID-19 meant that certain maintenance tasks could not be carried out. For example, the replacement of the ICT cabling in the buildings on the staff hill did not take place.

[SECTION BREAK]

However, the deployment of Securitas to improve access control at the gates was able to continue. Marine Barracks Suffisant (MKSUF) Commander: Major (majmarns) C. van Dinteren, from August 27 Major (majmarns) S. Baan Like the rest of the Kingdom, 2020 was entirely focused on COVID-19, yet the barracks continued to operate without interruption. In fact, due to the pandemic, the demand for additional enforcement capacity in Curaçao was greater than ever before. This led to improved collaborations with local authorities (notably the KPC) and strengthened the position of the CURMIL. The deployment of local military personnel in enforcing the curfew, combating unrest in downtown Willemstad, and addressing whale threats was successful. After years of efforts to professionalize the CURMIL, MKSUF (particularly the CURMIL) could count on the respect of the local population as well as that of local authorities such as the KPC in 2020. The long-term professionalization of the CURMIL characterized internal operations through inventiveness and flexibility, with barracks personnel making significant contributions. Without a substantial budget, the results this year were visible through the deployment of CURMIL as an operational unit.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Support Vessel Zr.Ms. Pelikaan Commander: Lt. D.M. Boom The year began for Zr.Ms. Pelikaan differently than any other year. The ship was not in Curaçao after more than ten years, but in the Netherlands for the Midlife Update (MLU).

text:
In the first months, everything went smoothly. The maintenance progressed steadily, and the crew regularly returned home to Curaçao in small groups to keep work and home life in balance.

[SECTION BREAK]

Unfortunately, starting in March, things changed from what was planned. Due to COVID-19, Curaçao went into lockdown. The crew that was in Curaçao could not return to the Netherlands and vice versa. Fortunately, the Netherlands did not go (completely) into lockdown, and all maintenance work on the ship could continue as planned. The crew worked hard on the renewed ship, and it paid off. What followed were the sailing material tests and seaworthiness tests. For the crew, it was mainly getting used to working with the newly installed much larger crane. After this, the signal was given to start the workup. With many new personnel, the learning curve for SARC 3 was steep, but the crew also overcame this hurdle.

[SECTION BREAK]

On September 17, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan departed towards the sea to Curaçao. The ship Zr.Ms. Pelikaan at the dock at Damen Shipyard for a Midlife Update.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean maneuvered steadily between all hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean and arrived, ahead of schedule, in Willemstad on October 1. At a proper COVID-19 distance, the vessel was warmly welcomed. Transport between the islands had, of course, been at a standstill for some time. Therefore, the familiar trips to Aruba and Sint Maarten followed.

[SECTION BREAK]

The boat group practiced to reacquaint everyone with the platform and the changes that the crane had brought. Finally, at the end of the year, a voyage to Bonaire took place for various inspections that needed to be conducted on Dutch territory. Fortunately, COVID-19 had been somewhat contained, and the crew was able to enjoy a short port visit, of course with the necessary PCR tests beforehand.

In 2020, the care provided by EGB CUR was primarily focused on COVID-19. The support that had been provided to the local Public Health Service (GGD) since July 2019 continued in 2020 (setting up GGD testing sites, assisting with contact tracing among their own personnel, and opening their own COVID-19 testing site at MBPAR). They also provided daily care to personnel who tested positive and were placed in quarantine at MKSUF. This support was ongoing throughout the year. In addition to all COVID-19 care, the EGB made every effort to continue daily care. Training and exercises also continued, often medically supported by the EGB. As a result, operational readiness was guaranteed. A work agreement was signed with the local ambulance service, Fundacion Kuido Di Ambulans Korsou, on September 18. By appointment, they ensure the availability of a civilian ambulance at the training area Wacawa. This provides broader medical support for shooting training there.

Due to the aging of the systems and travel restrictions related to COVID-19, it has proven very difficult to have the current chain perform to standard in 2020. Throughout the year, various malfunctions occurred on all islands. These were partly caused by the climbability of the masts, a crucial factor in safely carrying out maintenance, not always being guaranteed. For this reason, the Coast Guard invested in 2020 in a minimal solution to keep the masts safely and independently climbable until their replacement takes place in 2021. The average material availability across all eight radar locations in 2020 was 80%, compared to the standard of 95%. Bonaire At the end of 2019, it was agreed with the chain partners and the Governor of Bonaire to start in 2020 with the establishment of a joint location for all chain partners.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is involved in maritime enforcement, a so-called Multidisciplinary Maritime Hub Bonaire. The intention is to better support multidisciplinary cooperation in Bonaire. The contribution of the Coast Guard to this project consists of a boat dock that is financed from the available financial resources of the Spring Memorandum 2019. The construction of the boat dock was delayed in 2020 due to the coronavirus crisis.

text:
Nevertheless, in this exceptional pandemic year, it proved possible to welcome a group of approximately 100 aspiring cadets at the KIM. During the maritime introduction period (after the quarantine weeks), the future leaders learned how to act as team players within the armed forces in general and specifically within the KM. On Texel, the focus was on basic military training and pushing physical limits. This was followed by a sailing period aboard the Norwegian three-masted sailing ship Statsraad Lehmkuhl. Here, the aspiring cadets became acquainted with the sea and the elements. In addition, they learned how to safely perform seamanship tasks aboard a ship. The Maritime Introduction Period (MIP) formed the first part of the training curriculum at the KIM. This curriculum focused on competencies such as decisiveness, teamwork, communication, stress resilience, and sense of responsibility. Leadership is the common thread throughout the training. The aspirants are expected to ultimately be able to lead, guide, support, and delegate. This professional training is an essential part of the officer training program. Therefore, despite the ongoing pandemic, it was decided to carry out the MIP as fully as possible. To do this responsibly, the KIM implemented risk-mitigating measures, including a two-week quarantine period. The installation is an annual tradition, which unfortunately had to take place this year without the parents of the 2020 graduates and without the cadets from the 1970 graduation class who were installed 50 years ago (a drama for this graduation). text:
Coast Guard Netherlands Director: Captain (ktz) J. van Zanten COVID-19 largely dominated the life and work of the Coast Guard personnel in 2020. The protection of personnel in crucial functions during the execution of Coast Guard tasks was central to this. Through timely internal measures, good cooperation, and flexibility of the partners, the Coast Guard was able to carry out its tasks, even during the pandemic. Last year was characterized by developments in the area of operations and business operations in execution of the 2030 vision. An important step in this development was the reorganization of the Coast Guard Center, which took place in 2020.

[SECTION BREAK]

The organization has been fully staffed with the influx of personnel. An important national development was the large-scale construction of offshore wind farms under the energy agreement "Wind Energy at Sea." The supervision and security of these farms and ensuring the safety of the North Sea in and around these farms will require a significant contribution from the Coast Guard and its partners starting in 2021. International developments in the field of Maritime Security, the European Coast & Border Guard, and the consequences of the pandemic will increasingly demand attention from the Coast Guard in the coming years. These multi-year developments will have implications for the Coast Guard to ensure the safe and responsible use of the North Sea.

2_Navy_Annual_Report_2021_FOREWORD-in_memoriam-1 8 Personnel Directorate Foreword Divers in training in Den Helder.

[SECTION BREAK]

FOREWORD In your hands, you have the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2021. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The year began with COVID-19 measures, which caused many planned activities to be canceled. Nevertheless, the units managed to pick up the pace by creatively and responsibly resuming their work. Throughout the year, the measures were relaxed, allowing the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) to deploy more extensively. In a safe manner, personnel followed many new courses, training sessions, and participated in (international) exercises. This was done differently than usual, sometimes from home or at the workplace while maintaining a distance of one and a half meters.

[SECTION BREAK]

After the devastating earthquake in Haiti, part of the island lay in ruins, and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various units of the KM set course for the affected island to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines were deployed to ensure that aid could be distributed safely among the population.

text:
The vast majority of the work was conducted from home.

[SECTION BREAK]

During the General Political Debates, a motion from the VVD was adopted, providing an additional €300 million budget for Defense. This budget is intended to reduce maintenance backlogs in military equipment, barracks, other buildings, and ICT. For the Navy, this means an increase in the maintenance budget by €40 million structurally to reduce maintenance backlogs. Furthermore, at the end of 2021, the coalition agreement was presented, which includes a structural investment of €3 billion more in Defense. This is a substantial amount, with which C-ZSK will also...

[SECTION BREAK]

Organizational overviews years can take important steps towards both recovery and renewal of the organization. In 2021, in addition to the operational budget, the Defense Materiel Budget Fund (DMF) was used for the first time. The expenditures by CZSK were higher in 2021 than initially allocated at the beginning of the year. Compared to the draft budget, the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) achieved more in readiness. Within material expenditures, the military component spent more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The draft budget included a contribution to, among others, the Defense Materiel Organization (DMO) for the procurement of ammunition. This contribution was financed through the reallocation of personnel expenditures. Also, in personnel expenditures, KM spent a net million more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The cause was the additional expenditures for hiring. The hiring included not only temporary workers but also the hiring of operational management and IT consultants.

[SECTION BREAK]

Within the Navy, there was a shortfall in the personnel roster. The hiring was necessary to bring in essential personnel to prevent stagnation.

[Organisatieoverzichten (p.7) — narrative]
During the General Political Debates, a motion from the VVD was adopted, providing an additional €300 million budget for Defense. This budget is intended to reduce maintenance backlogs in military equipment, barracks, other buildings, and ICT. For the Navy, this means an increase in the maintenance budget by €40 million structurally to reduce maintenance backlogs. Furthermore, at the end of 2021, the coalition agreement was presented, which includes a structural investment of €3 billion more in Defense. This is a substantial amount, with which C-ZSK will also...

[Organisatieoverzichten (p.8) — narrative]
Organizational overviews years can take important steps towards both recovery and renewal of the organization. In 2021, in addition to the operational budget, the Defense Materiel Budget Fund (DMF) was used for the first time. The expenditures by CZSK were higher in 2021 than initially allocated at the beginning of the year. Compared to the draft budget, the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) achieved more in readiness. Within material expenditures, the military component spent more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The draft budget included a contribution to, among others, the Defense Materiel Organization (DMO) for the procurement of ammunition. This contribution was financed through the reallocation of personnel expenditures. Also, in personnel expenditures, KM spent a net million more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The cause was the additional expenditures for hiring. The hiring included not only temporary workers but also the hiring of operational management and IT consultants.

[Organisatieoverzichten (p.8) — narrative]
Within the Navy, there was a shortfall in the personnel roster. The hiring was necessary to bring in essential personnel to prevent stagnation.

[SECTION BREAK]

P.F. Willemse The Directorate Personnel and Organization (DP&O) is the supporting directorate within the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) in the areas of personnel, training, healthcare, and organization. DP&O is the directorate that, within its scope and resources, ensures that the personnel of the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) have every opportunity to further develop and grow and adequately responds to those matters in the environment that can contribute to good employment practices.

[SECTION BREAK]

For 2021, the focal points of the directorate were: Restructuring towards future-proof training and individual instruction. This includes developments in the areas of simulation, the learning environment of the future, and studies related to the organizational structure of the Operational Command (OKM). Ensuring that inspiring vocational education takes place within CZSK by modernizing training through the use of modern learning tools, innovation, and establishing a connection between the operational and training domains. Restructuring training for flexible working, ensuring the social and physical safety of students and staff, and the practical application of Diversity & Inclusion (D&I). Simplified organizational chart of the Directorate Personnel and Operations (DPBV).

[SECTION BREAK]

Personnel and Organization The intensification of cooperation with industry and employment agencies as part of recruitment. Transition of P&O KM to a more sustainable personnel system in which personnel are more central. The development of a CZSK Policy Plan on Diversity & Inclusion. Further development of alignment between the CZSK training calendar and the Operational Year Plan (OJP). The disentanglement of the Bureau Flexible Capacity and the implementation of further professionalization of the Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve. Ensuring that we contribute sufficiently to the recruitment and retention of personnel according to a strategic communication plan.
