30 Directorate of Personnel and Organization Due to existing training backlogs on one hand and an increased need for education/training and a broader availability of budgets on the other, OKM/CZSK has a need for (possible) hiring of educational and training services. OWZ contributed multiple inputs to the process surrounding the European public procurement to establish a framework agreement. The formal designation is "Educational and training services, didactic training services, and services for designing, building, and maintaining custom digital learning interventions." The CDS commissioned the realization of the Quality in Image program in 2017. A Defense-wide project aimed at gaining better insight into the individual Personnel Readiness of the staff. The outcomes of the Note Results Quality in Image (2019) resulted in the Qualification Chain for individual Personnel Readiness and is articulated in the Directive CDS-703. Since March 2021, a number of additional educational and training professionals have been separately appointed at OKM to achieve, among other things, the intended generalization of CZSK Qualification Profiles (KP) and the design of one or more CZSK templates. Changed and/or expiring contract(s) and evolving insights led to the functional management being shifted to OWZ from October 2022. Safety and Craftsmanship (VeVa) Within the CZSK, this year saw the start of Safety and Craftsmanship (VeVa) with the exit direction Care level 4. This occurred alongside the existing directions Maritime, Mechatronics, Ground Operations, Automotive Technology, and Aircraft Maintenance Technology.

[SECTION BREAK]

The reason for this was the shortage of care personnel within CZSK.

In 2022, the improvement of the Maritime training began by offering integrated vocational practical training, in which the components of military basic skills (previously offered in separate weeks by the SMVBO) are offered in the same week as the vocational skills (previously offered in separate weeks by NLBEOPS). In this way, the student has vocational practical training every week in which vocational skills are alternated with military basic skills, such as collaborative assignments, exercises, etc. This should raise the knowledge level of the student.

[SECTION BREAK]

In addition to the integration of VeVa, a work organization started this year with SMVBO and NLBEOPS, in which all FTEs for the training are housed in one organization. By implementing the VeVa work organization under the leadership of the coordinator, the training became increasingly visible. Previously, external parties had different contacts, making it unclear who was responsible for what.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Directorate of Personnel and Organization was now clear about these lines. The ROCs were also satisfied with the communication and content of the integrated program. Through communication and team-building days, there is increasingly more understanding of each other's work. VeVa also supported the Maritime Technician trajectory by conducting (part of) the internship weeks with their knowledge and personnel. The training further offered secondary school students a number of weeks per year for an orientation internship. VeVa also worked on a civilian training trajectory for 15/16-year-old students to become a logistics service sailor.

text:
Despite the restrictions this brought, SCBRNDCBV made an important contribution to realizing its mission: "We make naval ships safe" and thus to the operational output of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). The Training and Exercises department supported the training trajectories of Zr.Ms. Tromp, Zr.Ms. De Ruyter, BNS Louise-Marie, and Zr.Ms. Mercuur. The crews of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, Zr.Ms. Van Amstel, and the Oceangoing Patrol Vessel (OPV)-W and OPV-R underwent a Continuation Training (CT). This is an interim training for a ship that is not on a mission but has lost some proficiency and can use an extra boost. Additionally, the crews of BNS Leopold I, OPV-B, and OPV-R underwent a Pre-Deployment Training (PDT). This training is conducted for a ship before it goes on a mission and aims to prepare it for various possible emergencies and other events it may encounter during the mission. The school also provided customized training for OPV-W and OPV-B. An important component of the initial training is the D-officers training. SCBRNDCBV completed three sessions of this in 2022.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-12 33 Directorate of Personnel and Organization This year, the school also focused on filling long-standing vacancies by attracting and internally training new instructors. This personnel will further develop their skills during their placement. SCBRNDCBV also made use of reservists and personnel from Navtrain International. In the context of introducing hydrogen, there was an innovation in equipment. Near the school, the first hydrogen electrolyzer module was installed. SCBRNDCBV also provided introductory and safety lessons on this. All of this is part of the project flying, sailing, and driving on hydrogen. 4_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-13 34 Directorate of Personnel and Organization This resulted in more flexibility and a better work-life balance. This created a new normal. Intake This year, 326 First Maritime Military Training (EMMV) students arrived, and the SMVBO successfully trained 293 of them. The school bid farewell to the partially overlapping five intake moments and transitioned to four intakes per year. Intake 1 was the last group to experience the drastic COVID-19 measures. SMVBO divided the group in such a way that half started two weeks later and ultimately swore them in together with intake 2. This also marked the start of this ceremony at the Kampanje location.

[SECTION BREAK]

To reduce early and possibly unnecessary dropouts, the school adjusted the structure of the EMMV and introduced "the soft landing." As part of this, SMVBO developed the Pre-Intake. In this program, students undergo a three-day program four to six weeks before the intake date, during which a baseline measurement for the Physical Fitness Test and swimming is taken, and a fitting moment at the KPU allows the student to break in their combat boots and better prepare physically. Additionally, the school changed the structure of the EMMV by no longer going directly to Texel for the relatively demanding bivouac program for untrained students. It involved a more balanced buildup in the number of marching kilometers and the weight of the carried equipment. From now on, an introductory bivouac of three days will be conducted at Marine Barracks Erfprins, followed by a mid-bivouac of five days on Texel, and concluding with the Volharding, which has been extended from two to three days. The program has also been adjusted to "lead" the students in the first two weeks, then "guide" them for two weeks, and finally work them up towards the Volharding by "supporting" them.

The training and courses provided are tailored in consultation with the Head of Training Royal Netherlands Navy, the Competence Center of the Naval Component, and the NLMARFOR and STC according to the wishes of C-ZSK and the Commander of the Belgian Naval Component. Binational Training and Courses The crews of the Belgian and Dutch mine countermeasure units go to EGUERMIN to follow functional training: Personnel, non-commissioned officers, and officers of the Operational Service learn to use various systems to detect and clear naval mines; Staff from the Technical Service receive instruction on, among other things, the Degaussing System, which reduces the magnetic signature of the ships; Divers receive training on deck work and the operation of naval mines; Personnel responsible for the deployment of the Remote Environmental Monitoring Unit System (REMUS) and Autonomous Underwater Vehicle are trained at EGUERMIN to become REMUS 100 AUV Operators; Team training takes place in the Team Training Facility. International Training and Courses Training and courses at EGUERMIN are not only offered to Dutch and Belgian military personnel but also to those from other NATO partners.

[SECTION BREAK]

These training and courses include components of the binational training, supplemented by the use of the Naval Mine Warfare Gaming System. These courses prepare personnel to become Principle Warfare Officers Naval Mine Warfare and Staff Officers. Additionally, training is facilitated for personnel within the Naval Coordination And Guidance for Shipping and Allied Warning for Navigation and Information System offices. Wargaming On the wargame system, members of a Naval Mine Countermeasures staff can plan, execute, and evaluate a mine countermeasure operation. The wargame system of EGUERMIN is a unique tool within NATO.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_OF_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-18 39 Directorate of Personnel and Organization Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training in Den Helder (KMTO) Commandant: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) ir. M. Flaman EMSD The motto of the Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) is: 'We train maritime technicians'. The KMTO provides vocational and functional education for the personnel of the Technical Division (TD), as well as for the (technical) personnel of other services and defense components. Additionally, the school makes an important contribution to the training and development of crews of operational units, both above and below water. For training and development purposes, the KMTO has representative practical resources and simulators. Students All new sailors and non-commissioned officers of the TD of the navy begin their careers at the KMTO. In 2022, sixteen sailors started the First Vocational Training (EVO) and 42 started the First Adjustment Module. Additionally, twelve non-commissioned officers, who have already gained operational experience as sailors, began their technical MBO4 training in Service and Maintenance at ROC Kop van Noord-Holland.

[SECTION BREAK]

Besides the regular entrants, there are also VeVa students. The KMTO collaborates with ROC’s spread throughout the country, which provide the VeVa training with a specialization in Mechatronics at levels 2 and 3. The VeVa students follow their vocational education at the ROC’s and receive their Practical Vocational Training (BPV) at the KMTO. In addition to the new intake, the KMTO provided education for the existing technical personnel. Various employees participated at different times in their careers in various technical vocational and/or functional training courses, both in groups and individually, ranging from one-day to long-term training. Through international collaborations, KMTO also trained foreign naval colleagues.

[SECTION BREAK]

After the lifting of travel restrictions due to COVID-19, the number of foreign students this year was higher than in the pandemic years. In 2022, the school provided lessons for three Belgian and nine German colleagues.

Developments and Innovation In September, the first class started with nineteen students at the maritime schools and they undertook internships at the KMTO. The experiences that these young people shared with other students from the maritime schools were enthusiastically received, leading to the expectation that the number of applications for the following academic years will increase.

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-19 40 Directorate Personnel and Organization Personnel and Organization The number of vacancies remained significantly high in 2022, which forced the school to cancel a considerable number of training courses. Although this meant that no technical personnel could be trained for some weapon systems, it was necessary to keep the workload for the instructors at an acceptable level. Furthermore, it was not always possible to provide specific lessons, as the necessary knowledge was lacking at the school due to the vacancies. There was also a backlog in the area of educational development due to the large number of vacancies.

[SECTION BREAK]

Upskilling and Training An important aspect within the KMTO (Royal Netherlands Navy Training Organization) is the connection of technical training to operational management. In addition to conducting ship visits in this context and providing training on board, it also regularly supports the upskilling unit of STC (Sea Training Command) by preparing naval vessels for mission-specific readiness, sailing readiness, and exercise readiness.

[SECTION BREAK]

Due to the many vacancies, KMTO was unable to provide all the requested support during peak times. This was particularly the case when the management training for system chiefs, system responsible officers, and heads of technical services took place. Zr.Ms. Van Amstel launched the Low Frequency Active Sonar (LFAPS) during the exercise Atlantic Archer.

41 Directorate of Personnel and Organization Dutch-Belgian Operational School (NLBEOPS) Commander (kltz) E. Horstman EMSD, from March 1 kltz S.E. Glaser The year 2022 was once again a year full of challenges for the NLBEOPS. The pandemic had less impact in the first semester and hardly any influence in the second half of the year. The crew of the school was therefore able to operate in the normal mode, and secondary activities such as All Hands, team-building moments, a successful annual sports day, emergency response exercises, and joint coffee breaks finally took place again without restrictions. Within the various departments, they drew lessons from the operational management they employed during the past period and the use of remote working. The personnel filling of the NLBEOPS was approximately 90%. An additional challenge for the NLBEOPS was the necessary assignment of personnel for deployments and support of the fleet. In response to the war in Ukraine at the end of February, the defense staff and the AR instructed to achieve a better/higher personnel filling of the ships and to significantly increase contributions to the Standing NATO Maritime Groups. This also impacted the personnel filling of the school. The necessary expertise and resources were made available by the NLBEOPS to the fleet and to international allied organizations.

[SECTION BREAK]

In terms of material readiness, the quality did not improve in 2022. The main concerns involved the (again) postponed planning for the replacement of the Schooff, the water leakage and stormwater drainage at the seamanship trainer (Poolster), the deteriorating condition of the trainer park at the NLBEOPS, and the often sluggish and complex process of maintenance, repair, and replacement of equipment and trainers/simulators. More reports were made of defects and failures of trainers – also multiple times due to reduced operator knowledge – which affected the smooth operation of the trainer runs.

[SECTION BREAK]

The number of enrolled students increased significantly to 2,370, and the overall pass rate was 79%. The largest dropout was noted in the Advanced Vocational Training (VVO) ODOPS and the EVO ODOPS.

Netherlands Submarine Command Course (NLSMCC) The NLSMCC was able to proceed this year with three students after a year of absence. In addition to a Dutch student, a Brazilian and a Swedish student participated in this training to become submarine commanders. Although somewhat hindered by COVID-19 restrictions, a complete training cycle was conducted consisting of a training phase and a sea phase. Unlike previous years, the final phase of the NLSMCC took place this year during the Cold Response exercise in northern Norway. The combination of narrow fjords, challenging navigation conditions, and active simulated threats provided a challenging environment for the students.

[SECTION BREAK]

All three candidates successfully completed the training. The cooperation between the countries of the tri-nation Submarine Command Course (SMCC) (United Kingdom, Norway, and the Netherlands) remained strong, and this year Germany was added to the Memorandum of Understanding. This allows the involved allied navies to exchange even more ideas about submarine training. Furthermore, the sea phases of the various national training programs will be better coordinated, optimizing the use of supporting units such as submarines, frigates, helicopters, and maritime patrol aircraft. This synergy will lead to an excellent period of Underwater Warfare training for all involved during the NLSMCC.

[SECTION BREAK]

the practical applications of their studies. The course included visits to various organizations and facilities, enhancing their understanding of the maritime operational environment. The training culminated in a series of exercises that allowed participants to apply their knowledge in realistic scenarios. 

In 2022, the Royal Netherlands Navy (Koninklijke Marine) continued to focus on the development of personnel through various training programs, ensuring that they are well-prepared for their roles in both national and international operations. The Personnel and Organization Directorate for new construction is high, but a date for the start of construction is not yet available. It is clear that the new annex will be built on the site of the old one. The wet section was active in supporting the new vessel Alunaut and in further training Ukrainian colleagues. The dry section of seamanship saw significant updates in training regarding digitalization over the past year. Not everything is ready yet, but the initial setup and experiences were positively received by the trainees. The Navigation Office is fully operational again and is active in various areas. A major ongoing project (in collaboration with Surface Assault and Training Group (SATG)) is the new High Speed Navigation training and the new simulator NavSim. This simulation has been developed by SimCenMar into a first prototype, which will be put into use at the beginning of 2023.

[SECTION BREAK]

On the NavSim, procedures can be trained for high-speed sailing between a helmsman and a navigator. Additionally, the training for boating license 1 has been fully digitized, allowing individuals to opt for e-learning. Boating license 2 is nearly fully prepared in the digital environment.

[SECTION BREAK]

A minor setback for the Navigation Office is the inability to use the BOS/ECDIS trainer due to technical issues. Fortunately, this has not affected the training programs, but it did impact the number of instructors required for the courses. A significant advancement for the training of naval officers was made by the school through the development of the Ship Handling Course. This one-week course is provided to watch officers who have sea watch standard A. In this training, students can gain experience in navigation and maneuvering in a short time frame. The first courses were immediately fully booked, and they are already fully filled for 2023 as well. Throughout the year, it has become evident that the demand is increasing due to Subject Matter Expert (SME) requests. This is not only in the various trainers but also in the development of, for example, new construction. A new project that DVS was only involved in quite late was SEACROSS.

4_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-26 47 Directorate Personnel and Organization Education Development & Planning With the addition of the Education Innovation office in 2022, the department now consists of four offices. These are: the Training and Individual Training office (O&iT), the Assessment office, the Training Path Guidance office (OTB), and the Education Innovation office. The O&iT office is responsible for all O&iT proposals developed or adjusted at the request of H-OKM in collaboration with the knowledge departments of NLBEOPS. The approach of developing O&iT proposals in educational development teams has been a success. C-NLBEOPS assembles a team per Institutional Designation for a specific duration. This team may consist of an L&D officer (educationalist), various experts/SMEs from the involved knowledge department, a staff member from the OTB office who can provide didactic advice, an O&iT developer, and a staff member from the Education Innovation office. Over the past year, several teams were active simultaneously. This approach allows for better application of the principles of BGO in developing the core and sub-tasks in the O&iT proposals.

The newly established non-commissioned officer training program started, and the MOC, as well as P&O and Operational Units Marines (OPEMARNS), invested a lot of time and energy into filling this quantitatively. After all, the shortage of personnel needs to be addressed. The collaboration with units was also intensified to create more synergy in the area of integration. In this way, both organizations attempted to cope with the significant personnel shortage on both sides. To delve deeper into personnel shortages, the MOC looked for other possibilities to still make progress. This resulted in personnel being recruited from Society College and Defensity College, and interns and graduates were frequently deployed to work on (sub)projects. The MOC also strengthened its ties with its British counterpart, the Commando Training Centre Royal Marines. There was a mutual need for more integration and knowledge sharing. Thus, both officer training programs jointly participated in several exercises, Marines attended the All Arms Commando Course, and knowledge sharing occurred between both Fieldlabs, particularly on the theme of reducing dropout rates. Additionally, it offered the

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-28 49 Directorate Personnel and Organization training center various courses that can be followed by cadre members and officers. In addition, in 2022, Force Design took more shape. Therefore, the MOC (Military Operational Command) has taken on a more active role in its development by participating in several working groups such as Training and Education, as well as Leadership. One of the objectives from the defense memorandum was to increase the connection with society. The MOC fulfilled this, partly due to its geographical location and connection with the city of Rotterdam. The center held many discussions with strong brands in the area, such as football club Feyenoord, Port of Rotterdam, Erasmus University, and Rotterdam University of Applied Sciences.

[SECTION BREAK]

The result of this intensification will pay off starting in 2023 with joint activities that will benefit both these companies, the MOC, and society. Furthermore, the MOC also contributed this year to many ceremonial activities such as: Prinsjesdag, wreath-laying at Oostplein, May 4th, and various arrivals.

This resulted in personnel being recruited from Society College and Defensity College, and interns and graduates were frequently deployed to work on (sub)projects. The MOC also strengthened its ties with its British counterpart, the Commando Training Centre Royal Marines. There was a mutual need for more integration and knowledge sharing. Thus, both officer training programs jointly participated in several exercises, Marines attended the All Arms Commando Course, and knowledge sharing occurred between both Fieldlabs, particularly on the theme of reducing dropout rates. Additionally, it offered the

In addition, in 2022, Force Design took more shape. Therefore, the MOC (Military Operational Command) has taken on a more active role in its development by participating in several working groups such as Training and Education, as well as Leadership. One of the objectives from the defense memorandum was to increase the connection with society. The MOC fulfilled this, partly due to its geographical location and connection with the city of Rotterdam. The center held many discussions with strong brands in the area, such as football club Feyenoord, Port of Rotterdam, Erasmus University, and Rotterdam University of Applied Sciences.

[Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.28) — narrative]
The result of this intensification will pay off starting in 2023 with joint activities that will benefit both these companies, the MOC, and society. Furthermore, the MOC also contributed this year to many ceremonial activities such as: Prinsjesdag, wreath-laying at Oostplein, May 4th, and various arrivals.

van Rijn In November 2019, the Directorate of Integrated Operations & Governance (IB&B) was established. The aim of this consolidation of departments focused on operations and governance within the CZSK was: to achieve greater integration and effectiveness in operations and governance; to provide improved management of the safety organization; to realize a better distribution of the workload within the various directorates of CZSK.

[Directie Personeel En Bedrijfsvoering (p.34) — narrative]
From December 2020 to March 2021, the directorate conducted an evaluation. One of the conclusions was that the above objectives had not been fully achieved. This has various causes.

text:
At the establishment of the directorate, it was based on the existing structures. At that time, no organizational improvements were made other than an administrative reorganization. The intended synergy between the different departments was not yet fully achieved through this reorganization. Additionally, the Governance Staff initiated various developments in recent years that directly impacted the organization of the IB&B directorate. This includes the establishment of the CIO system, the embedding of Portfolio and Program Management (P3O), the strengthening of short-cycle innovation, and the strengthening of Safety and Environment (V&M). As a result of the introduction of the new top structure within Defense, the interfaces between the directorate and the Governance Staff also changed. For effective realization of the objectives, it was necessary to logically cluster the tasks. This clustering had to align with BBD2020 and DN 2022.

[SECTION BREAK]

4_KM_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_PERSONNEL_AND_OPERATIONS-35 56 Directorate of Integrated Operations and Governance The clustering included, among other things, the embedding of the CIO system and the establishment of the P3O organization. In addition, this clustering led to a future-proof investment in short-cycle innovation, the change capacity of the organization, and the establishment of an organizational unit focused on the physical living environment and sustainability. In this way, a decisive, future-oriented organization emerged with the capacity for change to contribute to the further development of the CZSK. All of this made it necessary to reorganize the directorate to achieve the desired integration and effectiveness in the operations and governance of the CZSK. Therefore, in the second half of 2022, a reorganization process was initiated with an intended completion date of December 2023.

[SECTION BREAK]

Booij The year 2022 was characterized for the department by providing support to developments occurring elsewhere within the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) and Defense, such as reorganizations within the CZSK, the development of configuration proposals for new developments, and CZSK contributions to major IT programs such as GrIT, TEN/Foxtrot, and Roger. This year also heralded the modernization of the Information & Technology (I&T) domain and organization at CZSK as a result of the focus on the digital domain in the Defense Memorandum 2022. The Digital Transformation of Defense, and thus also within CZSK, commenced. Finally, various larger and smaller IT projects were initiated or executed. During the year, the department did significant preparatory work for the necessary changes in the I&T domain, such as the evaluation of BVIV as part of the evaluation and reorganization of the Directorate IB&B. The development of the decentralized part of the defense-wide system of the Chief Information Officer (CIO) also took place. Additionally, the department worked on configuration proposals for embedding or improving the I&T subdomains of data science, robotics, and modeling & simulation.

[SECTION BREAK]

The ERP Competence Centre CZSK (EC3) focused in 2022 on supporting reorganizations in ERP M&F and the introduction of new equipment. Furthermore, the bureau supported various improvement trajectories in the Materiel Logistics domain of CZSK, including participation in the Roger program (SAP S4/HANA) CZSK, the conversion from R3 to S4 HANA database, and the go-live of SAP Ariba.

Change and Innovation Management (V&I) Head: Captain (ktz) B. Stoelinga The department supported various innovative projects, with the maritime drones project standing out the most. In this regard, V&I collaborated at the national level with maritime partners such as the Coast Guard and the Royal Netherlands Rescue Society. This year, the project - with direct contributions from, among others, the Maritime Drone Team of DMI and the Maritime Systems Department of DMO - made a restart from the familiarization phase, during which a successful experimental program was conducted.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Directorate of Integrated Operations and Management was carried out with commercially available drones from Dutch startups. In particular, V&I continued in 2022 with the experimentation of a drone developed by TU Delft; the NederDrone. This device is intended to be able to take off and land autonomously from a moving deck in the future, and it should also be able to perform longer flights powered by hydrogen propulsion, allowing it to operate at greater distances, Beyond Visual Line of Sight, from a mother unit.

GENIUS is a built-in module that allows drones to communicate and collaborate with each other. This enables them to autonomously decide how to best execute a given task after it has been assigned. This is called intelligent swarming. Launching of the mid-body segment of the Combat Support Ship Den Helder in Romania.

Vooijs The Russian invasion of Ukraine on February 24 underscored the necessity to strive for as many operational units as possible for the highest spectrum of violence. However, within the unit, the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) still experienced some hindrance from the pandemic at the beginning of 2022.

Nevertheless, due to the flexibility of the STC, the program was able to be executed almost entirely in accordance with the Operational Annual Plan (OJP). In January, the training year began with a CT/PDT for OPV-B on Zr.Ms. Friesland from January 24 to February 1.

Due to the ongoing shortage of OPV platforms and crews, this was the first of four CT/PDT periods for this class of ships, which had to be conducted from Curaçao. Tromp ready for exercise during an 'All Hands' Ready For Exercise (RFE), and the ship was ready for its Netherlands Operational Sea Training (NOST). In preparation for the safe crossing of Zr.Ms. Groningen to the West, the ship conducted a CT from April 4 to April 8 in the North Sea. The last training effort of the STC staff and personnel before the summer leave was a CT/PDT on Zr.Ms.

Groningen in the West. During the period from July 5 to July 13, they carried out an intensive program off the coast near Willemstad. After the concluding patrol exercise, which included various exercise incidents and the interception of a smuggling vessel, C-STC again declared the ship 'mission specific ready' for counter-drug operations. After the summer leave, from September 6 to September 15, the interim training of Zr.Ms. Rotterdam continued with a second CT. At the end of this period, readiness increased by identifying points of attention and making the necessary next steps.

Maritime Headquarters ABNL The Maritime Headquarters ABNL (MHK ABNL) is part of the Operations Directorate of the CZSK. The MHK is responsible for Belgian and Dutch operations and exercises of fleet and marine units. The MHK ABNL: Programs, plans, directs, coordinates, and supports operational readiness activities. Prepares mandated operations, executes them, and supports these operations. Prepares operations on behalf of the CDS and supports them. Advises generally on maritime military operations. Drafts the binational OJP and oversees the realization of the assigned activities. Additionally, the MHK ABNL is the 24/7 point of contact and coordination within CZSK for operational matters. Maritime operations with Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) Since the introduction of UAS in the Marine Corps, these military unmanned systems have been flown at the boundary of land and water. Not long after, flying from ships followed. In the past two years, there has been frequent flying from the LPDs, and the OPVs have now become familiar territory for the UAS section. This section is a specialized unit of the Marine Corps, consisting of seven marines including leadership members, who together form two UAS teams. The UAS section has various systems at its disposal to provide the commander with the necessary information. The UAS operators of the section fly, among other things, with the PUMA, RAVEN Marines training in Norway during a Joint Mountain Training.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-24 85 Operations Directorate and WASP is authorized to operate the various available Commercial off the Shelf and Military off the Shelf systems. 2nd Marine Combat Group (2 MCG) Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) C.G.J. Wigger PRE Joint Arctic Training (JAT) Prior to the winter training of 2022, all JAT candidates underwent a preparatory course to prepare themselves as well as possible, both physically and mentally, for this challenging training of the Marine Corps; the so-called PRE JAT. To survive in arctic conditions, it was of great importance to send the involved military personnel with sufficient knowledge into the field. This is all related to the extreme weather conditions under which the marines must operate.

[SECTION BREAK]

The establishment of a serious preparatory course is therefore not without reason. For the marines, having sufficient knowledge is a matter of life and death.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_NM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-25 86 Operations Directorate JAT 2022 A large group of marines departed on February 9 from Eindhoven Airport to Norway for the annual JAT, also known as the 'cold weather training' of the Marine Corps. The Whiskey Company was established in the 1970s to provide marines with cold weather experience. This was in preparation for the NATO mission to defend the northern flank of the area of operations together with the Royal Marines. This was already relevant during the Cold War, but with the current situation in Ukraine, it is more important than ever.

[SECTION BREAK]

This year, 21RSQN from 2MCG also participated in the JAT.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-30 91 Operations Directorate exercises return on an annual basis. In the last quarter of 2022, LCTU-1 prepared for the JAT of 2023. Second Landingcraft Task Unit (LCTU-2) LCTU-2 was the operational unit in 2022 and was therefore scheduled to carry out the JAT.

[SECTION BREAK]

Despite several training sessions in 2021 being canceled due to the pandemic, the unit conducted the JAT, Cold Response, and various training support activities.

[SECTION BREAK]

Training, exercises, and deployments After the JAT, LCTU-2 prepared for its own training in Instow. Due to the limited availability of vessels within the SATG, it was necessary to combine this training with the LC-1 and LC-2 courses. LCTU-1 also participated so that as many LCs as possible could benefit from this unique training opportunity. Although it was a combined training in a relatively short period, this did not detract from the training objectives of LCTU-2. In the second half of 2022, the unit supported various basic Marine training courses and two LC-3 courses, in addition to several of its own training weeks. Additionally, the reconnaissance team of LCTU-2 participated in the exercise Coptic Whisper organized by 47 Commando Raiding Group Royal Marines in Cyprus. Fast Raiding Interception and Special forces Craft (FRISC) Squadron The unit primarily supported NLMARSOF in 2022, such as making a significant contribution to the exercise Port Defender in Rotterdam in the first half of the year. The squadron also conducted various of its own training sessions. A section of Raiding Crafts participated in the JAT and Cold Response with LCTU-1. Simultaneously, the unit assisted with two Military Assistance assignments. The Raiding Craft sections also supported Jungle training in Suriname in the first half of the year, where a training of its own preceded it in the same area. In the second half of 2022, the FRISC squadron began a Live Fire Exercise (LFX) in Tarva, Norway. This location offers a unique environment to conduct shooting exercises from the water to the land with Landing Craft units, in addition to providing ample challenges for high-speed navigation.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-34 95 Operations Directorate Submarine Service (OZD) Group Commander: Captain (ktz) J. van Zanten In 2022, the submarines trained in both Scandinavian waters and the Mediterranean Sea. For Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw, the focus in the first half of 2022 was primarily on completing the NLSCC. Zr.Ms. Dolfijn crossed the Atlantic Ocean for exercises in American and Caribbean waters. The submarine also participated in the filming of the feature film 'Invasie'. In the second half of the year, Zr.Ms. Zeeleeuw visited Scheveningen during Flag Day and Rotterdam during the World Port Days. Zr.Ms. Mercuur regularly accompanied the submarines during these events. The ship also supported the Royal Institute for the Navy by participating in the midshipmen's training cruise. For the service as a whole, 2022, in addition to the sailing and training program, was also characterized by further professionalization of the staff. Furthermore, at the end of 2022, the DMO sent out a request for proposals to three candidate shipyards for the replacement of the Walrus class. Many employees of the Submarine Service were involved in the preparation of this extensive and complex document. Large Above Water Units (GBW) Group Commander: Captain (ktz) F.J.G.

For a number of detachments, the squadron chose to deploy Lieutenant Commander (kltz) pilots or Lieutenant (lt) OC instructors from 7SQN. This was all done to simultaneously build the squadron's personnel and its flight units. Amphibious Operations 2022 was the first year that Flight 2 worked on operational readiness. In the spring, they practiced at Deelen Airfield. During this exercise, they focused on multi-ship operations during low-flying exercises in various low-flying areas. The unit used the new crew concept and training program as a guideline. This concept consists of two pilots in the cockpit and one or two loadmasters in the back. In the third quarter, the Flight Test Office conducted tests to equip the NH90 with a so-called Modular Aircraft Survivability Equipment system. This system primarily protects against incoming missiles, is equipped with a countermeasure system, and is mounted in pods on a newly designed heavy store carrier.

[SECTION BREAK]

From week 44 to week 46, the MLD participated for the first time in the DHC exercise Falcon Autumn with two NH90 helicopters. In this exercise, the service collaborated with the other squadrons of DHC and operated multi-type. During this exercise, the NH90s and their crews seamlessly participated in the scenarios, and the performance of the helicopters exceeded expectations.

[SECTION BREAK]

Short detachments and assignments In addition to the single deployment, the MLD participated in short assignments, exercises, and deployments. The service facilitated several HQ weeks for pilots, Helicopter Direction Officers, and Flight Deck Officers for CZSK. Unlike in previous years, Flight 2 required Helicopter Qualification weeks on the so-called Big Decks.

[SECTION BREAK]

Only Zr.Ms. Rotterdam, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, and Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman were suitable for this. The MLD often combines these Big Deck weeks with 300SQN. Coordination between the squadrons regarding the following procedures, which sometimes differ due to type-specific capabilities, proves to be essential. 860SQN is the lead unit in this regard. 5_KM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-38 99 Operations Directorate Maritime Warfare Centre (MWC) Head: Colonel (ltkolmarns) J. de Wolf The year 2022 was primarily focused on rebalancing for the MWC, restoring balance after the pandemic. This involved restructuring part of the capacity to better meet the demands of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). It led to the establishment of a Subject Matter Expert (SME) for Maritime Unmanned & Autonomous Systems, the creation of an additional SME for Anti-Submarine Warfare (VTE filled after four years of vacancy), and the merging of capabilities for Maritime Ballistic Missile Defence and Above Water Warfare. This did come at the expense of the VTE SME Operational Technology, which means that CZSK must draw on expertise elsewhere for the Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear dossier. Driven by personnel shortages, the centre must apply a more forced and sharper delineation of tasks.

text:
The MWC's core task is to support the Force Development of the operational navy broadly, developing the contemporary navy into the navy of tomorrow. The focus is on practical support at a low-tactical level with a conceptual approach. Strategic issues are primarily addressed in The Hague and at S&A, while hard technology development is mainly the responsibility of the Defence Materiel Organization (DMO), with the understanding that the MWC remains in continuous consultation with the aforementioned departments. However, the centre also continues to work on a strong network of knowledge partners. The rebalancing here mainly involves re-establishing contacts that were lost during COVID-19.

[SECTION BREAK]

The external pressure on the MWC as a knowledge provider increased significantly this year. Due to the growing tensions in the world, the Defence budget steadily rose, creating more opportunities for new projects, as well as expansion, re-evaluation, and/or acceleration of ongoing investment projects. Wherever maritime capacity review was concerned, Defence called upon the MWC to provide capacity and expertise to support planning.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the same time, more regular (inter)national meetings could again be organized physically. This was done extensively to restore ties between various knowledge parties. A summary of the key meetings: From March 8 to 10, the Head of Maritime Battle Lab (H-MBL) participated in the User Group Meeting for Evolved SeaSparrow Missile Block 1 and 2 at the Naval Air Warfare Center China Lake in the United States.

This was in preparation not only for the Maritime Operations Working Group but also for the harmonization of all NATO Maritime working groups. Development of Offerings Within the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO), new standards are being developed for the delivery of nautical datasets, based on S-100, the Universal Hydrographic Data Model. HYD actively contributes to this, among other things by leading the writing of the Guidelines for following the Worldwide Electronic Navigational Products Database for S-100 Principles. These were adopted by the Council in 2022. The IHO Council evaluates the S-100 Roadmap annually, in which the Netherlands has been re-elected for the period 2023-2025. At the initiative of the Netherlands, the Assembly addressed the command transfer at the Hydrographic Service.

[SECTION BREAK]

5_KM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-44 105 Operations Directorate Council for the period 2020-2023 focused on the theme “the effective implementation of the Revised Strategic Plan keeping in mind to apply the principles of ISO9001.” The Council subsequently decided that “ISO9001 principles will be experimented on the development of the Product Specification for ENCs, S-101 ed. 2.0.0.” The S-100 implementation project at HYD commenced in 2022. National alignment of tasks and responsibilities regarding S-100 received attention, with the service collaborating with the Directorate-General for Civil Aviation and Maritime Affairs of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management.

[SECTION BREAK]

Demand Development The trend of a decrease in paper products in favor of digital products (2014-2019) continued after a stable period (2019-2021). In absolute terms, the sales of 2022 returned to the level prior to the COVID-19 measures. The ratio between the use of the service's own nautical products and derived products under license has remained approximately stable for several years (2017-2022). In 2022, the Electronic Chart Distribution Service of the International Center for Electronic Navigational Chart (ENC) made a fresh start under better usage conditions, which will increase the distribution of ENCs via electronic navigation products from commercial producers. Thanks to the introduction of the new Open Data Viewer from the Marine Information House, the reuse of source data via INSPIRE web services shows an eightfold growth. The ENCs also became available as a view service in this Open Data Viewer. This fulfills the mandate to manage data for the North Sea Agreement and contributes to the data provision necessary for Marine Spatial Planning.

Renewal of Distribution Channels The International Centre for ENC, where the Chief Hydrographer served as chair of the Steering Group until July 2022, is preparing for the distribution of S-100 series products. The distribution of ENCs (S-57 and S-101) is also being redesigned, with the center's Distribution Working Group acting as a sounding board. The Amstel team of the Amsterdam-Amstelland police unit left building 012 in the summer, leaving the Jordaan team still housed in the building. The renovation of the Lijnbaansgracht police station progressed more slowly than planned, causing the departure of the Jordaan team, scheduled for December, to be postponed to 2023. The portacabins placed in 2021 for building 014, which were necessary because building 012 had insufficient changing facilities for 2 basic police teams, were removed in mid-2022. The area was converted into a parking lot. From the end of April, the Central Agency for the Reception of Asylum Seekers used the B-wing of the barracks building for crisis emergency shelter for asylum seekers. Trigion Security Corporation provided security for this wing.

[SECTION BREAK]

As a result, there was limited accommodation available for own units and short-term overnight stays. This crisis emergency shelter Command transfer Service Center Personnel Logistics at the MEA.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Directorate of Material Maintenance lasted until the end of the year, and nearly constantly, 250 asylum seekers and status holders made use of it. Events and activities in 2020 This year, various events were again on the calendar. The event center was able to fully operate this year, if necessary, according to COVID-19 restrictions, allowing meetings and small conferences to proceed in a scaled-down form with ample spacing, should the number of COVID-19 infections require it. Major events such as the Canal Pride and Amsterdam City Swim took place this year for the first time in two years as usual. With large numbers of participants, it was quite busy at the barracks.

[SECTION BREAK]

Only the arrival of Sinterklaas was presented in a completely new format, resulting in MEA playing a much less prominent role than before the pandemic. Thus, for the first time since 1965, Sinterklaas no longer disembarked from the steamboat at the barracks to ride into the city on horseback.

[SECTION BREAK]

The end of a long tradition, as the new format will also be the basis for the future.

The event center was able to fully operate this year, if necessary, according to COVID-19 restrictions, allowing meetings and small conferences to proceed in a scaled-down form with ample spacing, should the number of COVID-19 infections require it. Major events such as the Canal Pride and Amsterdam City Swim took place this year for the first time in two years as usual. With large numbers of participants, it was quite busy at the barracks.

Only the arrival of Sinterklaas was presented in a completely new format, resulting in MEA playing a much less prominent role than before the pandemic. Thus, for the first time since 1965, Sinterklaas no longer disembarked from the steamboat at the barracks to ride into the city on horseback.

[Directie Materiële Instandh (p.7) — narrative]
The end of a long tradition, as the new format will also be the basis for the future.

In 2022, there were 30,699 visitors during 816 events, meetings, and conferences at the barracks. However, due to occasional resurgences of COVID-19 infections, 269 events and meetings with over 10,000 planned participants were also canceled at the last minute. Port visits The number of port visits increased again this year but had not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels. Most requests for berths came from the harbor and towing service in Den Helder and DDG. For the first time in years, a diving vessel also visited the barracks, in support of a large diving and port security exercise. The ship was moored at the quay along the Dijksgracht for over a week. This year, several foreign units also visited Amsterdam. The most notable were the visits of the training sailing ships INS Tarangini, which was moored at the Sumatrakade for over a week, Shabab Oman II of the Royal Navy of Oman, which docked at the Passenger Terminal in the city center, and the visit of the Irish naval ship Le Samuel Beckett. The visit of HMS Kent caused some commotion in November because the ship docked at the same quay where a cruise ship was moored for the reception of asylum seekers. This was viewed by local and national press as less desirable due to potential traumatic experiences of asylum seekers. After consultation with the authorities, HMS Kent was relocated to Houtveemkade in Mercuriushaven.

The main training programs at the MOC are the EMV, the Corporals' Course, and the POTOM. Additionally, the practical weeks of VeVa and various career and specialist training courses take place.

[SECTION BREAK]

Characteristic of the year 2022 were the many ceremonial activities. In addition to the traditional entries marking the conclusion of the Final Exercise EMV and POTOM, several function and command transfers took place. One of the highlights was that on June 1, various dignitaries presented the Defense Memorandum from VGKAZ. It was an honor to host the event where the new significant plans, which will have a major impact on the defense organization, were announced. Presentation of the new Defense Memorandum at Van Ghent Barracks on June 1.

[SECTION BREAK]

6_KM_Annual_Report_2022_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-9 116 Directorate of Material Maintenance Van Braam Houckgeest Barracks (VBHKAZ) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) R. Clermont In 2022, the barracks staff, in consultation with the users, further developed the reorganization of the Mobilization Complex Maartensdijk. The Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve received its own storage facility for their equipment this year, including an armory at the barracks.

[SECTION BREAK]

On October 19, a large-scale sewage leak was detected in building Algiers. The management evacuated the ground floor for two weeks, which put a lot of pressure on the barracks. This was due to the ongoing renovation of the barracks, which is scheduled to continue until 2025. The Defense Operational Clothing System project concerns the introduction of new combat clothing for the armed forces. All military personnel will receive a new combat uniform executed in the new camouflage pattern developed for the Defense Operational Clothing System, Netherlands Fractal Pattern, based on the combat uniform currently worn by the Marine Corps. The rollout of this new combat clothing and the selection concept for combat boots can already be found here and there at the barracks. Finally, the major events gradually resumed, starting with the Oktoberfest of the Identity Group Marine Special Operations, the reunion of the W-Company, and a spectacular conclusion with the Corps anniversary on December 10 for the units stationed at the barracks. Marine Fire Brigade Commander: Deputy Chief Commander A.F.M.

Both new vehicles were procured through a national tender and were delivered in May. Product group port facilities Head: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) A.J. Schuitmaker Last year, the product group supported the Marine Days, which took place again after the pandemic. This event was spectacular as always. During SAIL-Harlingen, the department was also present with two tugboats and other equipment. Following the container disaster with MS Zoë in January 2019, the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management decided to establish a Vessel Traffic Service (VTS) for the North Sea. As a result, the Traffic Center Den Helder expanded further with an additional VTS sector and an extension to a two-person post. The Marine Fire Brigade was present at Maritime Airbase De Kooy.

6_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE_DIRECTORATE-11 118 Directorate of Material Maintenance Product Group Energy Distribution Company (EDB) Head: Drs. Ing. R.J.L.

Put In March, the EDB connected the new health center to the heating and electricity grid, and a few weeks later, the department, as the first within Defense, installed an innovative charging station. This is specifically intended for electric trucks. These two projects are part of the energy transition that the EDB is implementing regarding energy supply for the Navy. It actually took until December for the first electric truck to be introduced and to start using the charging station.

[SECTION BREAK]

On Friday, March 11, the EDB met with local partners, such as the municipality and Housing Foundation DH, for the first time physically since the outbreak of COVID-19. During this meeting, the participants signed a letter of intent to concretize the sustainable heating network. Additionally, the EDB laid the 12kV connection from Erfprins/Harssens from pier 13 to the KWS and the department made primary and secondary cable connections for the new rectifiers so that these could be tested.

text:
Marine Band of the Royal Netherlands Navy Commander: Maj. Marine Band C. Knegjens Conductor: Maj. Marine Band H.J.C. Tien Bandmaster: Lt. Marine Band D. Kuiper 2022 began cautiously for the Marine Band due to the tail end of the pandemic. Nevertheless, the band was able to fill the vacancies for tenor saxophone and piccolo in the first weeks of the year. Corporals J. Rousschop and E. Tuik-Vogel filled these positions. The entire orchestra transitioned to using the iPad instead of paper sheet music for sustainability reasons during this period.

[SECTION BREAK]

Initially, this was a bit awkward, but with the classroom explanation from Sergeant Major E. Kramer, everyone quickly embraced the device. In March, the always well-attended Night of Military Music took place again, where the Big Band and the Trumpet Team represented the Marine Band at this edition.

[SECTION BREAK]

119 Directorate of Materiel Maintenance participation. Finally, the moment arrived on April 2, when a concert with full attendance took place again. In Urk, the audience enjoyed, in a full Ichtus church, live and via a live stream for the first time again the sounds of the entire orchestra.

[SECTION BREAK]

Later that month, an even larger audience could do so during the closing ceremony of the Invictus Games in The Hague. A wonderful evening with much attention for the exceptional athletic performances of the many participants. In addition to a live performance by Di-rect and an emotional speech by British Prince Harry, it was a grateful task for the chapel to serve as a live band for the many accompaniments and tunes. Regarding the ceremonial part of the chapel's duties – always outdoors – there had fortunately been permission for some time to play with the full ensemble. After a number of honor guard Credentials for Palace Noordeinde, a state visit awaited on April 5. King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima officially welcomed Indian President Ram Nath Kovind and his wife at the Royal Palace on the Dam with musical accompaniment from the chapel.

[SECTION BREAK]

Sergeant Major J. Schippers played the Signal Tattoo. New electric truck with the innovative charging station.

text: 120 Directorate of Materiel Maintenance Once launched from the starting blocks for the public concerts in full attendance, a series of these followed in Rijswijk, Den Helder, and Breda. One of the highlights of 2022 was Velas Latinoamerica 2022 in Curaçao. This event took place in Willemstad from June 7 to June 12, during which Defense was present with a lot of equipment. The Marine Band, along with the Drummers and Pipers, and a torch guard consisting of the Curaçao Militia (CURMIL) opened the event on June 7 with a tattoo at Brionplein. As a warm-up for the big concert on Friday evening at this square, another concert was held on June 9 at Marine Barracks Suffisant, featuring soloists Tamara Nivillac and Merietza Haakmat. The following morning, the brass quintet MAR V provided musical support for the wreath-laying ceremony for Admiral Louis Brion, in the presence of commanders from various ships visiting Velas Latinoamerica and the Minister of Economic Development of Curaçao. On Friday evening, the highlight of this service demand was a large concert in Willemstad in the middle of Brionplein. In tropical temperatures, the square filled with people enjoying the Antillean sounds amidst the many nautical activities.

Urania also participated in events in Ostend and anchored in Kiel for the Kieler Woche. The summer was marked for the ship by participation in the Tall Ships Races. This annual sailing event attracts dozens of ships, which compete in various races to different European ports.

[SECTION BREAK]

This year, Zr.Ms. Urania started the race in Esbjerg. During the race to Harlingen, the sailing ship encountered various weather conditions, ranging from calms to wind force six. After this first race, Zr.Ms. Urania participated in SAIL Harlingen with the Tall Ships fleet. The second leg of the Tall Ships Races consisted of the Cruise in Company from Harlingen to Antwerp. During this leg, Zr.Ms. Urania took the initiative to explore the IJsselmeer with the ships with (relatively) shallow draft. This led to a convoy of twelve vessels that jointly lay in the lock and entered Enkhuizen with a sail-in parade. During this leg, there was ample opportunity for crews from the various ships to exchange, sail together in the evenings, and anchor together.

Marine Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen Commander of military crew: Lieutenant (ltz2) T.D. de Brouwer Master: M. de Wijn The Marine Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen is used for nautical practical training. The ship has been specially built and equipped for this purpose. It accommodates 16 trainees. Navigation and training bridge The Van Kinsbergen has, in addition to the regular navigation bridge, a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for practicing all navigation procedures and safe mooring and unmooring.

[SECTION BREAK]

6_KM_Annual_Report_2022_DIRECTORATE_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-19 126 Directorate of Material Maintenance MOV Van Kinsbergen.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directorate of Material Maintenance Deployment Each year, Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen sails for approximately 200 days. The main user is the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills. These skills are necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. The vessel serves as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, including team building and character development.

[SECTION BREAK]

Besides the KIM, the Dutch-Belgian Operational School is also a major user. Students at the OPSCHOOL receive practical sailing training for the qualifications of non-commissioned officers for minehunters, hydrographic survey vessels, and submarines. Civil Maritime Schools The civil maritime school on Terschelling, the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB), also makes good use of Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Within the framework of the agreement, the MIWB has access to the training vessel for several weeks. Second-year Maritime Officer students undertake short practical trips on this ship. During their stay on board, navigation is particularly practiced. Additionally, the MIWB uses the ship for Advanced Fire Fighting training, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. Instructors from the MIWB provide lessons for the adelborsten of the KIM in Den Helder. These lessons cover subjects such as loading technology and maritime law.

[SECTION BREAK]

Within the agreement, there is an exploration of how to expand cooperation to further modernize and improve education within both institutions.

Van Kinsbergen for tailored training or as part of a training program. Occasionally, the ship is used for scientific research (TNO and universities) or for informational purposes. Two Crews Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen has two crews of five persons each; a military and a civilian crew. The latter consists of a captain, a first and a second mate, a chief engineer, and a cook. The military crew consists of a commander (kltz), a senior officer, a skipper with sailing qualifications, a chief technical officer, and a cook.

[SECTION BREAK]

Directie Materiële Instandhouding Zeedienst Practicum (ZPR) 1 For the first sailing period of 2022, the MOV was deployed for the KIM for the so-called ZPR1. In this practicum, the leadership establishes a foundation for safe (visual) navigation in combination with GPS and traditional nautical charts from point A to point B. This is the first sailing period for the cadets aboard the Van Kinsbergen. This journey lasted four weeks and was with the Zeedienst intake year 21. This period was from January 27 to February 23. The ship began its journey with high hopes, but the crew soon faced several setbacks. The so-called Delta variant of COVID-19 spread rapidly worldwide, and unfortunately, the crew and personnel of the Van Kinsbergen could no longer fend off the virus. Despite the measures taken, the ship was forced to return to Den Helder and adjust the sailing program. The weather was also uncooperative during this time of year. Storms Dudley, Eunice, and Franklin swept over the MOV, causing multiple schoolings in various ports, and the sailing area was later even restricted to only the Wadden Sea and the roadstead of Den Helder. Storm Eunice ranks among the top three heaviest storms in over fifty years.

Lems Directorate Controller CZMCARIB: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) (LD) P. Borsje-Senders from August 1: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) (LD) M.C. Philipse-Breitenstein Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as: 'Providing security in the Caribbean.' This one sentence articulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB is responsible for the territorial integrity of the Caribbean countries of the Kingdom and Caribbean Netherlands.

[SECTION BREAK]

The own and visiting operational units have a so-called threshold function. This means that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability. The second main task also includes deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and drugs by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, carrying out

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean for counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this regard. C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. The support of civil authorities. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. The armed forces now have broader support capabilities with their highly developed specialist and unique capabilities. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB.

[SECTION BREAK]

It also provides emergency aid during disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB also supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba.

CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, carrying out

[Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.3) — narrative]
Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean for counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this regard. C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. The support of civil authorities. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. The armed forces now have broader support capabilities with their highly developed specialist and unique capabilities. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. text:
Vision To realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the surrounding changes, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK.’ Arrival of Zr.Ms. Friesland in Willemstad.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. 'Relevant maritime' and 'security partner' in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third primary tasks. Due to national and international agreements, it aims to promote the international and local rule of law with its own resources, for example by contributing capabilities to (inter)national organizations or by providing military assistance. Reflection on 2022 With the global decline of the pandemic, activities in the CARIB (both military and civilian) gradually gained momentum. The number of training activities in the CARIB as a training hub increased throughout the year, as did the participation of its own units in exercises elsewhere in the region. This provided a positive boost to operational readiness.

Just as in the Netherlands, the Alert State was raised in the West, a situation that was maintained throughout the year. Zr.Ms. Dolfijn and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan also made their presence known. International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in upholding the international rule of law in the Caribbean region. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South in Key West. The Commander (kltz) of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Taskgroup 4.4., one of the task groups of this organization.

text:
The SSCG did not have access to an NH90 this year.

[SECTION BREAK]

Therefore, for the duration of two rotations, the collaboration established in 2014 with the United States Coast Guard's Helicopter Interdiction Tactical Squadron continued. During these rotations, an MH-65 helicopter was embarked on board. In addition to the regular cooperation with the Dash-8 of the Caribbean Coast Guard, the SSCG had air support from the Dutch MQ-9 of 306 Squadron of CLSK this year. This improved aerial coverage was experienced by the SSCG as a force multiplier and a good step towards more intensive cooperation with the Air Force.

[SECTION BREAK]

Counter Drugs All three ships were deployed under both the flag of KW CARIB and for CTG 4.4 and were very successful during these periods. In cooperation with international units, CTG 4.4 and KWCARIB seized approximately 19,500 kg and 14,200 kg of contraband from the trade market respectively this year. Thus, 2022 is a record year. These international operations were conducted by KWCARIB in coordination with various countries including the United States, France, Colombia, and the United Kingdom in the US-led collaborative framework Joint Interagency Task Force South. Salute shots were fired upon the arrival of Zr.Ms. Friesland in Aruba.

[SECTION BREAK]

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-8 137 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Hurricane Relief The hurricane season, which ran from June 1 to November 30, did not lead to large-scale deployments this year. During the passage of tropical storm Bonnie in the Windward Islands, the Marine Squadron CARIB (MSC), the Aruban Militia in Aruba (ARUMIL), as well as CIDW and CURMIL in Curaçao, were on standby and worked together with the local police during the passage. Additionally, the units provided small-scale assistance during the annual exercise Windward Express in Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius during the passage of tropical storm Fiona.

text:
Throughout the exercise, the military worked intensively with local authorities and aid organizations. Land Units The MSC, rotations of CIDW, and the Sint Maarten Detachment (DETSXM) completed a full and challenging readiness and training program. The MSC practiced Military Operations in Urban Terrain in the United States during Caribbean Urban Warrior. They also participated, together with the Boat Platoon and the Marine Detachment Sint Maarten, in the international exercise Tradewinds in Military of CurMil in Curaçao.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Belize and Mexico, where they practiced Riverine and Jungle operations. In August, the units received the long-awaited Improved Operational Soldier System package. In October, the international exercise Tres Kolos took place in Aruba, in which, alongside the French and Americans, all land units of CZMCARIB participated. DETSXM participated in the Commando Training in Martinique in November. The three rotations of CIDW were provided in 2022 by the 12th Infantry Battalion Air Assault Regiment of Heutsz and the 104th Reconnaissance Squadron Joint ISTAR Commando. During the rotations, they trained in Aruba, Curaçao, and Bonaire. Local authorities frequently utilized the CIDW search team.

[SECTION BREAK]

Additionally, CURMIL and ARUMIL took a first step in professionalization in 2022, based on the Ambition Document CZMCARIB. These units consist of personnel employed by the countries of Aruba and Curaçao and are directed by CZMCARIB. Military Assistance In 2022, CZMCARIB provided 24 soft and hard military assistance operations to the authorities of the countries and islands of the Kingdom. Some examples are described below: In January, CURMIL provided hard military assistance in Curaçao to enforce COVID-19 measures, including enforcing the curfew. In January, the Primary Healthcare Company opened a vaccination site at Marine Base Parera for booster vaccinations.

text:
The EOD supported the investigation into the cause of an explosion in Curaçao. In Bonaire and Curaçao, the search team assisted in searches of prisons, homes, plots, and vehicles. Among other things, phones, money, drugs, weapons, and documents were found.

[SECTION BREAK]

During the summer leave, CIDW assisted in Curaçao in the search for a missing Dutch tourist in Christoffelpark. During Tropical Storm Bonnie, CURMIL, CIDW, MSC, and ARUMIL provided assistance in Aruba and Curaçao. During Tropical Storm Fiona, MSC and DETSXM provided support in Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius. In Curaçao, CIDW conducted static observation twice at the request of the Public Prosecution Service. CURMIL collaborated with the local police during the harvest festival in Curaçao and performed traffic guidance tasks.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Visiting Units Throughout 2022, several units came to the Caribbean to conduct their training. Among others, NLMARSOF, other units of the Marine Corps, the Commando Troops, 43 Mechanized Brigade, and 101 Engineer Battalion utilized the Training Hub CARIB. Various courses were also offered, such as the sniper course, tropical medicine, diving training, and shooting training. Finally, several international partners came to the Caribbean for training and exercises, including the French and Americans.

text:
Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied Finance In 2022, the Finance department of CZMCARIB had a budget of 22.9 million euros, which was in accordance with the submitted budget. The final realization of the budget was 23.4 million euros, partly due to the currency claim of 4 million being paid by itself. The realization fell short due to limited travel opportunities as a result of COVID-19, but there were more business trips and training activities, including Caribbean Engineer, than in 2021. Due to a catch-up in training, 220% of this budget was realized. The country package still resulted in a 12.5% reduction in the salaries of local staff. Management Information In the area of Management Information, CZMCARIB made further progress in implementing the Business Intelligence and Improved Management Information dashboard for management information and reporting to CZSK. In the spring, the department published the information management plan CZMCARIB, the first information management plan of CZSK. The management also adjusted the annual plan for 2023 so that it aligns with the business reporting and is better secured internally.

[SECTION BREAK]

Marine Base Parera (MBPAR) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) M.J.M. Hezemans MSc The year 2022 was marked by the end of the COVID-19 measures.

[SECTION BREAK]

This meant that MBPAR welcomed units again for exercises and that colleagues came on business trips to conduct audits or provide support in other ways. The many months of working from home, remote meetings, and maintaining distance affected the mutual bond. Therefore, the barracks invested a lot of energy in organizing joint activities in 2022. Booster location This year began with the establishment of a local COVID-19 booster vaccination site in the sports hall of MBPAR. On January 8, staff, their family members, and those of various partner government agencies were given the opportunity to receive their booster vaccination.

Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied VLAC 2022 Until June, the base assisted the Curaçao Sail Foundation in organizing VLAC 2022; a four-yearly sailing event that lasted six days and is comparable to SAIL Amsterdam. From June 6 to June 12, CZMCARIB ensured that the Marine Band performed a continuous tattoo and that they performed for the public at Brionplein. Additionally, on Friday and Saturday, a defense village was open to the public at Motetwerf, where the Roadshow also contributed. On these days, they also provided demonstrations on land, in the air, and on the water.

Lines Loose 2.0 In the past, a large party was regularly organized for all personnel of CZMCARIB and the Coast Guard in Curaçao. After a year full of effort, on December 9, Zr.Ms. Friesland and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan were moored at the Marinebasis Parera.

[SECTION BREAK]

Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied therefore organized the 'Trossen Los 2.0' party. With the help of various Truk’i’Pan and musical performances from, among others, the Sleeves, it was a successful evening. Other events On King's Day, the traditional Grand Parade was held.

This time in the presence of C-ZSK. For the first time since the pandemic, there was an opportunity to celebrate Christmas together again. Military personnel and the local population attended mass together at the exercise area of the naval base. On New Year's Eve, the Pagara was also lit together while enjoying an oliebol and a drink. This million-firecracker is ignited annually in the days leading up to the new year to drive away evil spirits.

[Commandement Der Zeemacht Carib (p.13) — narrative]
This time in the presence of C-ZSK. For the first time since the pandemic, there was an opportunity to celebrate Christmas together again. text: In collaboration with the Sint Maarten Police Corps, MSTPPB established a shooting range. All other safety partners on the island also made use of this facility. Despite some bureaucratic processes, the shooting range can now also be used for static shooting skills. Raiding Section (RS) In August, the RS, in a new composition, conducted a shooting training and the drivers obtained the necessary driving licenses for the new Anaconda vehicles. This was the unit's top priority. The RS participated in the exercise Barracuda Warrior together with the MSC. This was followed by the exercise Caribbean Urban Warrior at Camp Lejeune. During training, the unit learned combat techniques in Military Operations in Urban Terrain. The unique training location and opportunities that Camp Lejeune offers provided the team with experience in Three Block War. This was of added value for the training level and junior leadership of the unit. In the coming year, the RS also prepared for the hurricane season and participated in the exercises Hurricane Relief Exercise (HUREX) and Windward Express. In this context, the unit, together with the MSC, made further arrangements with local partners on the island regarding how to cooperate in the event of a possible hurricane passage. FRISC Section In the first quarter of 2022, there were various movements towards Saba and Sint Eustatius to transport equipment and personnel. Furthermore, the team supported the RS multiple times with exercises and assisted MSTPPB and Gonzalo.
