Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Support Vessel Zr.Ms. Pelikaan Commander: Lieutenant (ltz1) M.J.C. Jereskes MSc The year 2022 began for Zr.Ms. Pelikaan with a long period at the dock at MBPAR for the modernization of both the high and low classified networks. With support from the Netherlands from the DMI and the DMO, the hardware and software were modernized. By mid-February, the work was completed and the ship was free to move again. Due to the fact that some time had passed since the last training period, the leadership opted for an internal training period of two weeks. During this time, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan made a port visit to Tobago over the weekend to improve international relations. Due to strict COVID-19 measures, the leadership, in consultation with the Dutch ambassador in Port of Spain, chose a dinner instead of a reception. Dignitaries from Trinidad & Tobago were present, including representatives from the coast guard, armed forces, island government, and the crisis center for (natural) disasters. After the training period, the ship was in Curaçao from early March to mid-April for annual maintenance. During this period, technicians renewed the satellite communication system thanks to a temporary solution. Together with the previous maintenance on the networks, this ended a period of many malfunctions that made operations and command and control difficult. The maintenance concluded with approval from the classification bureau Lloyds, the retrieval of the CIDW, and the sailing material tests.

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2022_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-21 150 The Command of the Navy in the Caribbean reflected on how they deal with this theme and where improvements are possible. They considered how laws and regulations are applied in daily work. To conclude that week, a two-day Safety Leadership Course was held for various commanders and department heads from Curaçao, Aruba, and Sint Maarten. This training focused on the role of the commander regarding safety in a broad sense: reporting and investigating incidents and applying risk management. Department of Organizational Social Work (DBMW) region CARIB Team Leader: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) H.J.H. Goetzee The main tasks that Organizational Social Work (BMW) performs in the Caribbean region are assistance, service provision, reporting, support after traumatic events, and crisis intervention. For the CARIB region, BMW, together with the Spiritual Care Services and in Aruba also with HR, is responsible for notifying family announcements. With the lifting of COVID-19 restrictions during the year, it was again possible to conduct work visits to Bonaire and Sint Maarten. Here, colleagues from the Royal Marechaussee and DBMW work to be more accessible to this personnel and their families on these islands and to provide better assistance and services. Additionally, there were also more work visitors from the Netherlands.

text:
In 2022, the Coast Guard saw an increase in the number of undocumented individuals from Venezuela; this year, 170 persons attempted to enter the islands illegally. Drug Smuggling The Coast Guard made several significant drug seizures in 2022, either in collaboration with Defense or third parties, intercepting 29,274 kg of cocaine and 5,116 kg of marijuana and hemp. Several chain partners with whom intensive cooperation took place in 2022 included CTG 4.4, SSCG, USCG, and the American Joint Inter Agency Task Force-South. Cooperation in 2022 varied from initial detection by flying units of the Coast Guard to joint operations and the use of the service's powers in international waters under the San José Treaty. Search and Rescue Cases In 2022, the Coast Guard rescued 598 persons from emergency situations. The service itself recorded 46 deceased and 11 missing persons in its area of responsibility. COVID-19 The Omicron wave of COVID-19 infections reached the Caribbean region in early 2022 and, like previous variants of the virus, also impacted the Coast Guard. This resulted in a temporarily reduced operational availability of operational units. Additionally, several planned initiatives for early 2022 could not be realized.

[SECTION BREAK]

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Cooperation with Defense The structural cooperation with Defense is described in a covenant between the CZSK and the Coast Guard. The covenant outlines mutual support in the form of personnel, resources, and services, and implements the management task by Defense and the execution by the Coast Guard, as established in the National Coast Guard Act. In 2022, this was also put into practice, and the cooperation was positive. The SSCG was available to the Coast Guard in 2022, in accordance with the operational availability of the ship. However, this meant that the vessel was deployed less in 2022 compared to the number of sailing days established in the covenant.

of May. The various promotion years compete for honor and see this as preparation for the annual midshipmen and cadet competitions. These took place this year in the second weekend of May. The KIM also organized a sports day, which was well attended and contributed to team spirit among the students. In June, the KIM hosted the annual open day, allowing prospective students and their families to explore the institute and learn more about the programs offered. The event was a success, with many visitors expressing interest in joining the Royal Netherlands Navy. In July, the KIM participated in the annual Navy Days in Den Helder, showcasing various naval capabilities and engaging with the public. The event featured demonstrations, ship tours, and opportunities for visitors to meet personnel from different branches of the Navy.

[SECTION BREAK]

Throughout the year, the KIM continued to focus on the development of its students, with an emphasis on leadership, teamwork, and operational readiness. The faculty worked diligently to ensure that the curriculum remained relevant and aligned with the needs of the Royal Netherlands Navy.

[SECTION BREAK]

In December, the KIM concluded the year with a festive gathering to celebrate the achievements of the students and staff. This event served as a reminder of the importance of camaraderie and the shared mission of the Royal Netherlands Navy.

[SECTION BREAK]

The attachments from July (unfortunately coinciding with the Navy Days) were won by the cadets. A remarkable athletic achievement. The evening before the grand swearing-in ceremony, the now traditional Marine Band concert took place. This event was held outdoors and is intended for the parents of the cadets, staff of the KIM, and their partners. On Friday, June 30, the grand swearing-in ceremony took place, where a total of 84 young officers took the oath or made a promise. Following this, in the afternoon, the officers' diplomas were awarded.

To strengthen the connection with the residents of Den Helder, the KIM held the KVMO-Winnubst concert this year on November 15.

[SECTION BREAK]

This was possible for the first time in two years. This tradition is a free concert by the music association Winnubst. They make an important contribution to the socio-cultural life in Den Helder and within the region. The harmony orchestra consists of advanced musicians. Every year, in the second half of December, the Assaut takes place at the KIM. The Assaut is a tradition that dates back to 1871. The Corps of cadets transforms 't Zaaltje and the surrounding areas into a richly decorated gala; each year with a different theme. The Corps of cadets works 24 hours a day in two shifts during this period to realize this theme. Originally, the Assaut was established by the Cadet Fencing Association Olympia as a fencing tournament, but it has since evolved into a three-day gala that returns annually. In 2022, the Assaut had the theme "Arabian Nights." For two years, the grand gala ball of the KIM could not take place, but from December 15 to 17, it finally happened again. The Assaut featured three festive evenings. On the first evening, the Pre-Assaut took place, during which the Corps of cadets thanked the parents and permanent staff for all the support they provided throughout the year. The second evening is dedicated to the Gala Ball. The final evening is the Corps Assaut, an evening for the Corps of cadets.

Kuipers EMSD The year 2022 was marked by the conclusion of the Covid-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which had a significant impact on the security awareness in Western Europe.

[SECTION BREAK]

The explosions in September in the Baltic Sea around the Nord Stream gas pipeline exposed the vulnerability of vital infrastructure at sea and focused attention on Maritime Security in general. The Maritime Information Node of the Coast Guard made an important contribution to the security picture for Dutch shipping and to the enforcement of sanctions against the Russian Federation from its information position. The node is an example of successful collaboration as it takes shape within the Coast Guard organization with various services and partners. The service tasks of the Coast Guard were carried out in 2022 in accordance with the standards. From August 1, a third Emergency Response Towing Vessel was put into service to ensure shipping safety in and around (under construction) wind farms, which has proven its value from day one. On November 3, an event took place at Schiphol.

For the new task under the Act for the Protection of Merchant Shipping, an initial permit was issued in June by the Inspectorate for the Environment and Transport to a Private Maritime Security Company. This company is allowed to offer the deployment of armed security teams to ship managers of Dutch-flagged vessels, for which the Coast Guard handles the assessment of the applications. In the second half of 2022, the service received many requests for the deployment of Privately Contracted Armed Security Personnel.

[SECTION BREAK]

The renewal and modernization of the Coast Guard is taking shape, with a significant milestone being the start of the shadow operation of Guardion Coastguard release 1.0 on July 1. The final rollout of Guardion Coastguard (in 2023) will lead to a significant limitation of the reporting capabilities of the Coast Guard. The latter will only be resolved in a later release, which may result in an incomplete picture being provided of the execution of tasks by the Coast Guard for 2023. However, the renewal and modernization of the Coast Guard also brings the realization that in order to continue executing current and new tasks in the future while also getting and keeping the operations in order, the current staffing of the Coast Guard is far too tight. This was already evident in the execution of Maritime Security tasks in 2022, and Coast Guard personnel felt a high workload and significant demand from clients and collaborating partners on a daily basis. Together with the challenges on

Page 11 11 FOREWORD Since 1488, we as a navy have provided security at sea and from the sea. We do this with fleet and marine units, supported by all those naval men and women on shore. And we do this with our national and international military and civilian partners. We do this far away and close to home. Since 1488, we have been at the center of history, adapting to new developments and learning from our experiences. By learning from history and the developments within it, we ensure that we remain future-proof, that we can effectively deter and fight to win. It is only logical that we document that history. The result of that logic can be found in this yearbook.

Defense Materiel Budget Fund (DMF) In the DMF, expenditures in 2023 were higher than the budget allocated at the beginning of the year (€ 179 million). The budget increased during the year due to additional allocations (€ 84 million) for, among other things, the policy framework for operational stocks (BKI) for main tasks 2 and 3, the effect of higher revenues, and a cash shift from 2024. Due to delays in the realization of, among other things, BKI and projects, the budget (€ 48.3 million) was added to the budgets of 2027 and 2028 through a cash shift. As a result, a surplus of € 21 million was presented as of December 31. The surplus is mainly due to a higher reliability of delivery of goods and services than was estimated at the time of the cash shifts, but also due to higher outsourcing costs than previously budgeted. The budget shifted to 2027 and 2028 will be used for the delayed projects from 2023. Additionally, within the DMF in 2023, € 29.6 million more was received.

[SECTION BREAK]

This includes incidental receipts for, for example, the maintenance of the Portuguese Multipurpose Frigates (M-frigates). Due to the extra efforts in the collection of work for third parties, CZSK has also achieved structurally higher revenues. These additional revenues are and will be used for the maintenance of maritime materiel.

The Directorate Personnel & Organization (P&O) plays a crucial role as a Human Resource (HR) partner in realizing the ambitions of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) regarding personnel readiness and good employment practices. It supports personnel in their development and growth, thereby contributing to career progression within the organization and a positive impact on both Defense and the labor market. By engaging and retaining employees, P&O creates space for flexible deployment in the future and promotes innovative initiatives. Schelkers  
The JUZA department is part of the DP&O, one of the four line directorates of CZSK. The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on legal issues that arise. Traditionally, the main areas of law that the department deals with are international law, including the law of the sea, (military) criminal and disciplinary law, and constitutional and administrative law. In addition, JUZA coordinates the handling of complaints within CZSK. For several years now, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has also been an essential part of the department's responsibilities. Given the increasing substantive and political complexity in 2023, an additional civilian official has been appointed for this area of law. In close collaboration with colleagues in the P&O department, advice is also provided regarding (military) civil service law and labor law within Defense. The department has focused more on operational and international law than before, a year after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Although the JUZA department has its own responsibilities, the role of the head of the department as a subject group leader is broader. This official oversees, among other things, the accumulation of experience and the knowledge level of all military lawyers of the Royal Netherlands Navy, regardless of location.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 28 28 Directorate of Personnel and Organization In this capacity, a broad and structured retraining program has been developed for all military lawyers of the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM), aimed at increasing knowledge of international (maritime) law and the law of the sea, in light of the aforementioned geopolitical developments. This program is set to commence in 2024. In 2023, the department invested in work relationships, both within and outside the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) and Defense. This has led, among other things, to the department increasingly connecting with interdepartmental and international forums on this subject, based on its knowledge of the law of the sea.

Kempers P&O contributes as an expert Human Resource partner to the realization of CZSK's ambitions regarding personnel readiness and good employment practices. The department does this by providing personnel with the opportunity to develop and grow. In this way, P&O, as a career development organization, makes a relevant contribution to Defense and the labor market. By engaging and retaining employees, the possibility for flexible deployment in the future is created, allowing for (innovative) initiatives.

Setting up and executing Management Development (MD) up to the level of Lieutenant Commander (kltz)/Lieutenant Colonel (ltkol)/scale 13, in conjunction with and aligned to the MD policy for the levels of Captain (ktz)/scale 14 and higher. Setting up and executing the job allocation process and personnel management for military personnel within the frameworks of the Flexible Personnel System. Setting up and executing career guidance for military personnel within the frameworks of this system and for civilian personnel.

text:
Developments  
The CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command) was in a difficult situation regarding personnel in 2023. Despite significant salary increases in 2022, particularly for sailors and corporals, the military branch still struggled to find enough new personnel to fill the growing organization. The civilian workforce did increase, which kept the total personnel count nearly stable. In 2023, to combat personnel shortages, the Defense Personnel Plan (DPP) and the Defense Component Personnel Plan (DOPP) were implemented. These aimed to significantly improve the personnel staffing of Defense. The DOPP included measures to increase intake, enhance personnel retention, accelerate career progression, and adjust the operations of CZSK.

[SECTION BREAK]

Some measures from the DOPP included:  
Introduction of the Service Year: on August 21, 2023, the first 12 service year military personnel began the First Maritime Military Training (EMMV). The service year personnel were assigned on board for a period of 9 months after the EMMV and basic training at the School for Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Defense, Damage Control, and Operational Safety (SCBRNDC&BV).

[SECTION BREAK]

More focus on lateral entry and accelerating career progression. Various programs were developed to make officers and non-commissioned officers deployable more quickly. This includes accelerated programs for the sergeant Network Manager, sergeant Operational Service Operations (ODOPS) Weapon Controller, watch officer, and command center officer (CCO). More freedom of choice for future corporals after the corporal training. Implementation of the Marine Technician program, in which a partnership has been established with various Dutch maritime schools. Technical labor market allowance for certain groups of technical personnel.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 30 30 Directorate of Personnel and Organization Additionally, the HR renewal gradually gained momentum with the development of various HR renewal projects such as: Human Resources Analytics Strategic Workforce Planning Strategic Talent Management HR Service Delivery Model HR Information Technology The ambition that Personnel and Organization (P&O) had in 2023 was to make the Royal Netherlands Navy an attractive modern employer with sufficient and deployable personnel. The department advises military personnel on the operation of the ship.

The Center is also responsible for the monitoring and enforcement of a safe (hyperbaric) working environment on board submarines, as well as the medical supervision of exercises and providing medical advice regarding escape and survival at sea for submarine crews. Social Medical Service (SMD) The Social Medical Service provides absenteeism guidance and support for the reintegration of military personnel from CZSK with absenteeism or a deployability limitation, or after medical repatriation. The Service follows the deadlines set out in the Improvement of Gatekeeper Act and the reintegration memorandum of Defense. The staff collaborates with the Reintegration Service Center (DCR) of the Defense Support Command (DOSCO).

[SECTION BREAK]

The SMD handles the application and processing of the Military Medical Examination and has contacts regarding this with the Bureau for Special Medical Assessments (BMB). Medcell Fleet and Role1CG Based on the Operational Annual Plan (OJP), medical personnel is made available. The coordination of the execution takes place through the Role 1 Command Group and the Medical Cell Fleet in collaboration with the operational units and the Maritime Headquarters (MHK). Prior to a deployment (in the home port or home base), advice is given to operational units regarding the medical precautions to be taken, in the context of Hygienic and Preventive Healthcare (HPG). The medical measures, such as vaccinations, are coordinated with and carried out by the Primary Healthcare Company (EGB).

[SECTION BREAK]

Maritime Medical Operations (MGO) The Maritime Medical Operations department is responsible for securing and developing maritime medical knowledge in order to provide advice within and outside the CZSK, such as to the Maritime Warfare Centre (MWC), the SCBRNDC&BV, and the Defense Medical Training and Education Center (DGOTC). The MGO is also involved in developing and teaching medical skills education through the skills labs, with the aim of maintaining and expanding medical personnel knowledge and skills, assessing reserved actions of General Military Nurses (AMV’ers), providing retention training for Combat Life Savers (CLS’ers) through the skills labs, and conducting the Operational Business Introduction (OBI) for the AMV and General Military Physician (AMA).

Meijer EMSD Bureau for Training Needs Assessment & Evaluation (OB&E) The OB&E bureau periodically supported the Competent Authority in cleaning up the Workplace Qualification List (AKL) and provided insight into the qualification level of CZSK units. The qualification level is the degree to which officials meet the required qualifications. Furthermore, the bureau coordinated the training or qualification needs assessment process for all service groups and the DMI, and supported the OKM schools in cleaning up outstanding development assignments.

[SECTION BREAK]

As a result of the subproject Implementation Qualification Chain Individual Personnel Readiness (KiPG), the Implementation Regulation KiPG CZSK was written. This implementation regulation provides clarity and transparency regarding the organization of the KiPG process within CZSK. In anticipation of the establishment and formalization of the implementation regulation, the OB&E bureau supported the introduction of the new (digital) operational process surrounding qualification. Simplified organizational chart of Training Royal Netherlands Navy.

Page 35 35 Directorate of Personnel and Organization Education Affairs Bureau (OWZ) The OWZ bureau has contributed to the operationalization of KiPG by supporting the development of various products such as qualification profiles for CZSK, qualification needs, and Training & Individual Training (O&iT) proposals. OWZ supported the Caribbean Training Center (OCC) in establishing the guidance structure and qualifications within the O&iT domain. In this context, OWZ qualified local instructors and training personnel in the West according to the curriculum of the Defense Expertise Center for Training Science (ECOD). School for Maritime Training and Operational Management Education (SMVBO) Commander: Lt. Commander (kltz) S.

[SECTION BREAK]

Feenstra Intake This year, 310 EMMV students enrolled, of whom 255 successfully completed the training. The 'soft landing' introduced in 2022 has been further developed to prevent dropouts and create a gradual buildup of mental and physical components. The EMMV is connected to Project PsyCap, as part of the Personnel Logistics Service Center (DCPL). PsyCap has been introduced in all 'purple' initial training programs. It focuses on the feedback loop to selection, the bridging function between DCPL and the training world, and broad advisory services (framework, student, observation, training & advice), where the training centers investigate the causes of training dropouts to determine which (existing) interventions can be implemented based on the research results. At the EMMV, exit interviews are conducted with students who drop out or choose to leave with Honorable Discharge.

[SECTION BREAK]

Intake 3 marked the start of training for the conscript soldiers at CZSK. In this regard, CZSK was the first Operational Support Command (OPCO) to choose to integrate the conscript soldiers with the regular soldiers in the EMMV. Interim evaluations have proven this to be successful for both the framework and the conscript soldiers themselves. This approach was received as an effective formula by the other OPCOs, even in a study with recommendations by the Inspector General of the Armed Forces (IGK).

text:
Page 40  
Directorate of Personnel and Organization  
To support the boarding process for incoming military personnel and to better prepare candidates for CZSK in general and the EMMV in particular, the Intake department has been closely involved in the development of the boarding app from Appical. It provides future military personnel with insight into what to expect during the Pre-Training and the initial EMMV training, as well as information about the specific service branches and units within the Fleet. 2023 was also the year that the EMMV provided tailored training for the horizontally recruited personnel of CSS Den Helder, with 6 military personnel in intake 2 and 3 in intake 3. A five-week EMMV program was offered as a pilot for this purpose. In order to gain better insight into the reasons for dropout during the Initial Training, a Fieldlab was established and research was conducted. Initially, the intention was to consider only the EMMV, but soon the follow-up training at the vocational schools and even the Practical Company Introduction (PBI) period on board were included in monitoring the students. Since several studies were already taking place, the Head of Training KM (HOKM) internally instructed to consolidate the information from all studies, including the Fieldlab at the EMMV, and to have it further developed by the Bureau Steering, Control and Coordination Training KM (SBC-OKM). The Fieldlab was thus dissolved.

[SECTION BREAK]

Flow Through  
In 2023, a total of 1300 students were trained in the various courses that fall under the Flow Through department. Unlike previous years, the marines from the corporal training also participated for the first time this year in the Management Training Course 1 (LMV1) at the SMVBO. Unfortunately, the department also faced a growing personnel shortage, which, combined with the increased demand for LMV1s from the marines, resulted in fewer other courses being offered. Part of the LMV1 until 2023 was the practical instructor.

[SECTION BREAK]

After consultation with the ECOD, this mandate was withdrawn. To continue meeting the requirements of the ECOD, the course had to change too much, which proved undesirable. The LMV1 still met the guidelines for Practical Instructor, which was implemented within the LMV1.

The Defense Diving School is designated as a Joint Organizational Component (JOD) with CZSK as the Single Service Manager (SSM). The JOD DDS houses both a Joint Knowledge and Expertise Center (K&EC) and a Joint Training and Education Center (O&TC). The following three domains are designated for the DDS: (1) working under pressure (diving), (2) Maritime Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) and the clearance of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) underwater, and (3) maritime search. The raison d'être of the DDS is thus the training of military divers. To fulfill this task, it comprises four formal training units and the 'informal' training unit T-squadron. This last training unit is hierarchically placed within the Netherlands Maritime Special Operations Forces (NLMARSOF) but provides training that fully complies with the training policy of OKM and reports educationally to the DDS. In June 2023, the new management team established a DDS Annual Plan with specific objectives to bring focus and priorities alongside all the training that the school provides. The main objectives for 2023 and 2024 are:  
- Ongoing attention and efforts for a socially safe working environment.

[SECTION BREAK]

- Development of the underwater CMD (Conventional Munition Disposal) training, which better prepares diving teams for DDG and Mine Service for their mine countermeasure tasks.

[SECTION BREAK]

- Pressure on the realization of projects Thetis and Uhlenbeck. The Uhlenbeck and Thetis projects are the two priority projects of the DDS aimed at achieving part of the necessary improvement of the available infrastructure for the DDS (assembly rooms, work deck with cranes, rubber boat shed, and training space with decompression tank and storage space). In 2019, the formal reorganization process for the restructuring of the DDG and DDS began, after which the evaluation of the reorganization was initiated and largely executed in 2023.

[SECTION BREAK]

In addition to the above specific matters, the DDS provided all regular diving, diving leader, and diving medical training for all military clients. The DDS provided this.

Flaman EMSD From August 31: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) ing.

[SECTION BREAK]

M. Huizenga EMSD The motto of the Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) is: ‘We train maritime technicians’. The KMTO provides vocational and functional education for the personnel of the Technical Service (TD), but also for the (technical) personnel of other services and Defense components. In addition, the school makes an important contribution to the upgrading and training of crews of operational units, both above and below water. For training and upgrading purposes, the KMTO has representative practical resources and simulators. Students The future sailors and non-commissioned officers of the TD at the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) start their careers at the KMTO to follow technical (vocational) education. This qualifies them for their first operational posting as a sailor or corporal of the TD. In 2023, 32 sailors started with the First Vocational Training (EVO) and 36 with the First Adjustment Module (EAM) of the Advanced Vocational Training (VVO). In addition, 24 non-commissioned officers, who have already gained operational experience as sailors, began their technical mbo4 training in Service and Maintenance, in collaboration with NCOI Opleidingen. Besides the ‘regular’ entrants, there are also VeVa (Safety and Craftsmanship) students and Marine Technician students. The KMTO collaborates with ROCs spread throughout the country, which provide the VeVa training with the specialization in Mechatronics levels 2 and 3. The VeVa students follow their vocational education at the ROCs and receive their Practical Training (BPV) at the KMTO during their education.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 44 44 Directorate of Personnel and Organization Additionally, the KMTO participates in a civil-military cooperation framework, the Maritime Capacity Alliance (MCA), which includes civil training institutions and vocational maritime schools. In this collaboration, a civil-military training program was initiated in 2022, titled Maritime Officer All Ships Marine Technician. Students from various maritime schools are enrolled in this four-year level-4 program, with the students completing the last two years of this training as military personnel. In September 2023, the second class started with 36 students at the maritime schools, and the students undertook internships at the KMTO. The number of new students is nearly double compared to the first class in 2022. It is expected that the number of applications for subsequent academic years will increase.

Various employees participate at different points in their careers in various technical vocational and/or functional training programs, both in groups and individually, ranging from one-day to long-term (functional) training.

Developments and Innovation A number of Learning & Development staff and the commander of the KMTO attended the international conference Learning 2023 in the autumn of 2023. During this dynamic conference, they were informed about the latest (international) developments in the field of learning and development. CCO training and assistants  

On January 9, 22 trainees (16 Dutch, 4 Belgian, and 2 German) started the Basic Warfare Course (BWC). For 12 trainees, this was the first step in a one-year training trajectory (Operational Service (OD) learning line for officers). This resulted in 10 trainees (7 Dutch, 1 Belgian, and 2 German) obtaining the CCO qualification on December 21. Concurrently with the BWC, the assistant training started with 1 ALVO trainee (from the Netherlands) and 6 ACCO trainees (4 Dutch and 2 Belgian). This year, for the first time, the Maritime Situational Awareness Coordinator (MSAC) training was officially conducted. Upon completion of this training, the successful candidate can serve as an assistant command center officer on an Ocean-Going Patrol Vessel (OPV) or Large Grey Unit. The training serves as an intermediate step towards obtaining the full ALVO/ACCO qualification. The first session was ultimately successfully completed by 4 trainees (3 Dutch and 1 Belgian). However, the Netherlands organized the International Teachers’ Conference in Amsterdam in September 2023, which was attended by instructors from eight different countries, where many ideas were exchanged regarding submarine training and command execution. Education Department Command Control and Information Management (C2IM) In several EVOs and VVOs, colleagues from the communications service have been trained to work on board with the latest equipment and doctrines in the field of maritime military communications. The ICT lessons for the EVO and VVO have been revised and improved. The ICT hours from the VVO have been combined and expanded into a full module. This module will be provided following the VVO. Training for the Horizontally Entering Network Manager and the Management Operational Information Provision (OIV) Networks training is complete, and the first sessions are scheduled. New batch of marines during the final exercise FINEX.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 50 50 Directorate of Personnel and Organization In 2023, the hardware for cyber demonstration purposes was deployed multiple times, allowing VVO students to actively participate in various cybersecurity scenarios. Through these practical applications, the students gained valuable experiences and enhanced their understanding of cybersecurity. After several years, two Information & Communication Control Manager (ICCM) courses were conducted in 2023 at NLBEOPS. Both sessions included an international group with diverse backgrounds.

[SECTION BREAK]

The trained non-commissioned officers are prepared during the ICCM training to be self-sufficient under all circumstances and to lead the communications service, informing and advising the command center about the status of connections and equipment. The Communications Officer (VO)/Information Management Officer (IMO) specialization at the beginning of the year successfully delivered several communications officers.

Through (guest) lectures and site visits, students gain as much insight as possible into what awaits them on board and expand their network with helpful departments that can assist them with advice and support. The lessons also focus on deepening their knowledge so that they can make sound decisions on board for the benefit of Command, Control & Information Management. Education Department Defense Sailing School (DVS) 2023 was an intensive year in which many different training programs were renewed or completely revamped. Most training programs were conducted according to the training calendar, and we notice that the DVS is increasingly being recognized by new ships (Combat Support Ship crew), as well as for ship exercises (on the Ship Handling Simulator or Poolster). The Poolster underwent extensive restorative maintenance, which resolved the larger leaks. This reduces the amount of water that needs to be pumped out for the permanent crew.

[SECTION BREAK]

Many training programs have been revised, including the VVO and NATO training, and the DVS has continued to digitize the sailing license 2. The new course, High Speed Navigation (HSN), developed by the Navigation Office together with the Surface Assault and Training Group (SATG), will be conducted for the first time in January 2024. Associated with this is the NavSim (a navigation simulator with VR). This has already been used in Fast Raiding Interception and Special Forces Craft (FRISC) training and will also be used during the first HSN course.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 51 51 Directorate of Personnel and Organization For the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) department, a lot has changed. Starting from July 2023, the theoretical exams will be conducted by the CBR at the CBR location. The practical exams can still be done at the Royal Netherlands Naval Institute (KIM) because the in-house trainer has been approved by the CBR. The DVS is increasingly being recognized as an expert center. As a result, the DVS is involved in new construction projects such as the ASWF, amphibious vessels, and the Amphibious Transport Ship (ATS). Navy Academy (NAC)  
Director: KTZ L. Desanghere (Belgian Navy)  
The Navy Academy was established on May 16, 2022, as a result of a reorganization of the Belgian Navy. In total, five schools (including the former Eugermin and the Catering School) have been merged into the Navy Academy. The various areas of expertise have been renamed to Expert Areas (EAs), with the EA Naval Mine Warfare (Campus Ostend) and the EA Catering (Campus Bruges) being the most important for the Netherlands. Ultimately, the Navy Academy will fully relocate to Ostend. As a result, the Director NAC is responsible for all training that takes place within the Belgian Navy. The position is comparable to the Head of Training of the Royal Netherlands Navy. Expert Area Naval Mine Warfare (NMW)  
This year, in addition to the international courses Principal Warfare Course and Staff Officers Course, there were also the binational courses such as the (Assistant) Mine Warfare Officer Training on the agenda. These courses filled the majority of the training capacity, alongside smaller courses for, among others, the REMUS, Mine Field Planning, and the user training for MCM Expert. In addition to providing training, this year also included support for the international exercise Dynamic Move, organized by Allied Maritime Command (MARCOM). The Navy Academy facilitated this exercise, with the EA NMW providing support by supplying a Boss, game controllers, and supporting personnel. The exercise was also held abroad, and this year the Gaming System was taken up and temporarily relocated to La Spezia (Italy). Due to the unique nature of the Gaming System, it was still seen as a valuable simulator for training and educating (international) staffs and personnel. Teams from NATO partners also made use of the Gaming System.

text: Page 53 53 Directorate of Personnel and Organization The Expert Area NMW provided not only training but also support to the Mine Countermeasures Vessels Operational Sea Training (MOST) that prepares ships for operations. Expert Area Catering This EA initiated four First Vocational Training (EVO) courses and two Advanced Vocational Training (VVO) courses in Logistics Service Provisioning (LDV) this year. These are the most prominent training courses offered in the context of operational requirements. In addition to these courses, the EA once again provided five functional training courses for ship bakers (one of which was on an operational platform). Furthermore, within the training spectrum, eight (mainly) customized functional training courses for bottlers (Bottelier Operational/Budget Management Nutrition/Automated Inventory Management Ship Stock and Automated Financial Management Ship Stock) and two laundry training courses were conducted. A special request came in from colleagues in the West in consultation with Zr.Ms.

Page 54  
Directorate of Personnel and Organization P&O. Due to personnel shortages within the Matrozen LDV (Sailors LDV) at the location, sailors from other sub-service groups are filling two positions within the LDV (after the reassignment of LDV personnel). P&O requested the Navy Academy/Expert Area Catering in Bruges to develop a customized solution for this. EA Catering developed this tailored training program, which led to the customized training for Assistant Defense Catering Staff (West). This can, if necessary, be added to the training calendar of EA Catering. Two sailors from other sub-service groups successfully and enthusiastically completed the three-week customized training.

[SECTION BREAK]

The competencies learned only pertain to the basic tasks within the LDV, meaning that the involved personnel cannot be deployed fully independently on all tasks, and good supervision is certainly needed in the initial period. This should be taken into account when assigning tasks.

[SECTION BREAK]

Given that the newly assigned personnel will not complete the full training to become a sailor LDV (EVO LDV), no Competence Certificate (BC) code will be issued for this process. The customized program was a temporary solution. Should the filling percentage of sailors LDV improve in the future and P&O resume the regular placement of LDV personnel, this customized program will be terminated. Thus, EA Catering has addressed the need to prepare personnel from outside LDV for task execution at the location in the West.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Marine Training Center (MOC)  
Commander: Lieutenant Colonel (ltkolmarns) S.M. Mastenbroek  
In 2023, the MOC further developed and documented its vision towards 2028. The MOC remains now and in the future a reliable training partner to sustain and enhance the operational readiness of the Marine Corps. The Corps values – Connectedness, Strength, and Commitment – form the basis for training students for the current professional context. A robust internal operation with modern and sufficient educational resources ensures an inspiring, functional, and professional learning and working environment.

Page 55  
Directorate of Personnel and Organization  
In 2023, approximately 320 trainees were expected to appear at the starting line of the initial training for Marines. This was not realized. Ultimately, about 120 qualified new Marines were delivered to the operational units. This was sufficient in relation to a healthy inflow, throughflow, and outflow (IDU) within the Marine Corps. Within the Career Training department, there remained sufficient new recruits from the Practical Officer Training for Marines (POTOM) in 2023, which was a point of concern. This concern is receiving the appropriate attention and is developing positively towards 2024.

[SECTION BREAK]

The training for non-commissioned officers of the Marines, which now starts once a year, was reasonably filled and provided (just) enough new recruits. Here too, for a healthy IDU, there remains a significant need for a well-filled non-commissioned officer training program. The Functional Training department once again ensured sufficient new specialists were trained both domestically and abroad in 2023.

[SECTION BREAK]

This includes, among others, shooting instructors, Mountain Leaders, reconnaissance operators, specialists in communications, and specialists in Military Operations in Extreme Conditions (MOX) domain. Marines are training for operations in mountainous areas in Bardufoss (Norway).

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 56  
Directorate of Personnel and Organization  

In 2023, the Force Design Marine Corps took shape increasingly. The MOC made a significant contribution through participation in the working group "development of Training & Education" and the working group "leadership." The Education Development Bureau within the Quality Assurance, Innovation, and Knowledge Management (KIK) department will play a prominent role in this in the coming years. The Physical Training and Sports department made a substantial contribution and provided support to all training programs through its specialists, in addition to training new sports instructors. This is done in an extremely professional manner, ensuring that the right physical stimuli were provided to trainees in 2023. The staff of the Learning and Innovation Studio (LIS) once again made positive strides in the further development of the Electronic Learning Environment Marines (ELO-MARNS) in 2023. Additionally, progressive new educational tools were acquired from external innovation budgets for the benefit of the MOC. The Fieldlab Bureau also made positive steps in the further professionalization of monitoring trainees; measuring is knowing, and the resulting data contributes to better training and trainees.

An example of this is the positive and professional interaction between the MOC and the British Commando Training Centre Royal Marines. Knowledge sharing regarding leadership was a prominent theme in this collaboration.

Furthermore, the MOC tapped into excellent new training and exercise locations both domestically and abroad. The MOC also made a significant personnel contribution to various ceremonial activities in 2023, such as Prinsjesdag and the wreath-laying ceremony at Oostplein in Rotterdam. Additionally, the MOC appropriately acknowledged the traditional arrivals of 'fresh' marines and officers.

[SECTION BREAK]

Despite its fragile instructor capacity, the MOC successfully conducted a large number of training programs, courses, and skills in 2023. In total, approximately 600 trainees participated in these activities. To implement Integrated Risk Management (IRM) and to have more control over execution, the Commanders Intent, risks, and focus for the execution year have been explicitly added to the plan. Additionally, the office has been expanded with 1 IRM position (scale 12) as part of the measures from DN22. Progress is reported every quarter through the regular Business Reports (BR). The establishment takes place through the Readiness Consultation (GSO), a dynamic process in which all stakeholders must flexibly respond to rapidly changing environmental factors that affect both the GSP and the various sub-plans. In addition, the Programming section provides accountability for the realization of the readiness assignment of CZSK in 3 trials per year. In 2023, the readiness report for the fleet was fully executed in BI-VEST, and preparations were made for the migration to BI-VEST for the Marine units. The Readiness Consultation (GSO) was utilized more to identify and untangle "knots" in the readiness of the Major Surface Units, which sometimes led to painful solutions being presented for decision-making to the AR in the autumn. Demand and Supply Management (VAM) Progress has been made in the area of demand and supply. A widely supported VAM presentation has been created for newcomers within the VAM process. Additionally, better coordination is taking place at VAM-1 level, and Defense personnel acting at VAM-2 level are increasingly finding common ground. This is partly due to the complementing of the Assortment Manager List/Demand Manager List. Financially, there are fewer concerns within VAM; however, the VAM process now needs to be optimized and applied to meet the needs of the armed forces.

Investments Bureau Investments (INV) CZSK is responsible for the planning and realization of bandwidth projects as well as for the replacement of maritime C-systems. For both categories, INV has a budget from the Defense Lifecycle Plan (DLP). Bandwidth projects start with a detailed project card (PK), in which a senior user indicates a need including the business justification. The INV Bureau appreciates the PK and subsequently includes the need in the bandwidth (BB) or not.

For the Information Provision (IV) Management Office (IVB), 2023 was the first year after the COVID-19 period. In particular, hybrid working (location and time-independent working) gained a visible presence in 2023. Multiple VTC setups were established at all CZSK locations, further professionalizing remote work with tools such as MS Teams. Additionally, the fiber optic renewal at Nieuwe Haven was actively pursued, with 90% of all buildings connected to the new fiber optic rings, including redundancy and connections. In 2023, an investigation was conducted on how and where Dutch TV channels could be received at the barracks in the Caribbean region. In collaboration with an external company, the BVIV department conducted a site survey at the barracks in Curaçao and Aruba. The Marine Days were also held in conjunction with Sail Den Helder. The BVIV department set up the Wi-Fi network that supported these events. By providing internet via Wi-Fi, many volunteers and exhibitors were able to utilize the internet. This enabled card payments and information to be offered through QR codes. An important milestone in 2023 was the replacement of fixed telephony with Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) telephony. As a result, the MULAN network is now also used for telephony. The conversion meant that all fixed phone numbers received a new number.

This year, work continued on inventorying the Business Internet lines to gain better insight into local IT at CZSK. Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) training in the West In June, MTC once again organized and conducted a two-week SOP training independently in Curaçao as part of relieving the operational units. Six organic sections from the operational units were addressed during this two-week period. text:
De Zeven Provinciën set sail for the Baltic Sea, where the ship and its crew, as part of SNMG1, protected the NATO summit in Vilnius against potential aerial threats. Notably, this operation featured the highest level of integration with NATO's air defense organization.

[SECTION BREAK]

On the return journey, the crew visited Aarhus. During the summer leave, a saltwater leak caused significant damage. Thanks to the quick and adequate response from DMI and chain partners, this damage was sufficiently repaired in a very short time so that the sailing program could continue. On September 20, the ship again set sail, this time as the flagship of COMNLMARFOR (Commander (cdr) J.M. Morang) for a longer national squadron voyage. Part of this squadron voyage included the exercises Joint Warrior and Frisian Flag, torpedo launches, and tests with counter-drone systems. During this voyage, Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën functioned for several periods as part of the UK Carrier Strike Group (UK CSG) around the aircraft carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth. During the journey, the ship made port visits to Bergen, Portsmouth, and Glasgow. After this, the frigate, also operating under the UK CSG, joined the exercise Neptune Strike, returning to Den Helder on November 10. At the end of November, the ship set sail again to support the practical part of NATO specialization (the training for navigation officers). During this period, it made a port visit to Le Havre. Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën returned to Den Helder on December 1.

Holland transported King Willem-Alexander, Queen Máxima, and Princess Amalia of Aruba to Curaçao. After the visit from the royal family, the final part of the training was completed, after which Zr.Ms. Holland began its deployment in the Caribbean region. This deployment was not conducted in isolation and was carried out with a shipboard helicopter and a boarding team from the United States Coast Guard. On November 3, OPV-W was informed that it had to set sail with Zr.Ms. Holland to Cyprus in the context of this Operation Mistral. Preparations for the operation began in Den Helder on November 8, and on November 17, Zr.Ms. Holland sailed to the Mediterranean Sea. During this journey, the crew completed the PDT, including a practice evacuation in Great Britain. On November 28, the ship reached the port city of Limassol in Cyprus. In the first week of December, the crew trained in cooperation with the marines, the FRISC’s, and the NH90 around Cyprus in preparation for the evacuation operation. The units successfully conducted the Full Dress Rehearsal together and were ready to carry out an evacuation in the lower spectrum of violence. Fortunately, this NEO ultimately proved unnecessary, and the operational deployment was limited to exercises with Italian, British, and American units and reconnaissance flights with the helicopter.

The unit was able to rescue the Taipan thanks to the outstanding cooperation between Hr.Ms. Tromp, the marine team, and the onboard helicopter. A non-commissioned officer from the Marines received the Cross of Merit twice on this day: once for his courageous actions during the UN mission United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) in Cambodia in 1993 and once for his brave and decisive actions in 2008 during the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) mission in Afghanistan. A special deployment of the Marine Corps involved the evacuation operation in Sudan in April. Shortly after the Marine Spearhead Task Unit (MSTU) was alerted to participate in a French exercise in New Caledonia, the security situation in Khartoum deteriorated. The fighting between the government army and militias intensified to such an extent that the evacuation of compatriots became necessary. The MSTU was tasked with conducting the evacuation together with units from the Royal Netherlands Air Force, personnel from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Brigade Speciale Beveiligingsopdrachten (KMAR). On-site in Khartoum, these units worked closely with their British counterparts from 40 Commando Royal Marines. The excellent cooperation led to successful and safe evacuation flights, during which over 300 nationals and compatriots were evacuated from Sudan.

In May, the Commandant of the USMC, General Dave Berger, visited and the Chief of the Marine Corps (CKM) briefed him on the Force Design of the Marine Corps. In September, there were visits from the Commandant Marine Corps Systems Command, Brigadier General David C. Walsh, and Deputy Commandant General Royal Marines, Brigadier Neil Sutherland. At the end of November, CKM hosted the visit of the Commandant of the Philippine Marine Corps, Major General Arturo Rojas, and the Commandant of the 1st Brigade of the Indonesian Marines, Brigadier General Umar Farouq. CKM also attended several international symposia in 2023.

An important milestone is that the Marine Corps has had a dedicated CKM since October 11, 2023, for the first time since 2005. Non-combatant Evacuation Operation (NEO) Sudan In April, 1MCG prepared for an activation exercise in New Caledonia. Shortly before the start, on April 18, the news came that the situation in Sudan had deteriorated to such an extent that a Non-combatant Evacuation Operation (NEO) was necessary to evacuate Dutch citizens from the area.

[Directie Operaties (p.36) — narrative]
The following day, 1MCG flew together with the Brigade Special Security Assignments (BSB) of the Military Police to Jordan, from where the operation was directed. Here, the unit became acquainted with the Rapid Consular Support Team (SCOT) of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (BuZa) and awaited the green light for departure to Sudan. In the evening of April 22, news arrived that partner countries near Khartoum had taken control of an airport, allowing the operation to commence.

text:
Page 110 110 Operations Directorate Two aircraft from the Royal Netherlands Air Force flew from Jordan to Sudan. The first aircraft was filled with 60 personnel, consisting of the advance party of marines, the SCOT, and the BSB. The second contained only six marines and was intended to, if possible, maximize the evacuation capacity.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Sudanese army did not grant permission for the first aircraft to land due to the overcrowding of the airport by foreign military personnel. The second aircraft arrived later and was allowed to land. Despite the very limited crew, the first evacuation flight could take place within an hour, transporting several dozen civilians. After this, the first aircraft was also able to land, and a total of seven more evacuation flights followed.

[SECTION BREAK]

When the British took over the airport from the Germans and the Netherlands would no longer conduct flights, the leadership, in consultation with the British, decided to leave four marines at the airport from April 26 to April 29. They worked together with the Royal Marines in Sudan during the Non-combatant Evacuation Operation.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 111 111 Directorate of Operations Marine Commandos remained available to provide assistance in 'complicated cases': Dutch nationals with an expired passport or families where only part had a Dutch passport. The remaining marines operated independently on-site but remained in contact with the SCOT, which continued to operate from Jordan and was responsible for screening evacuees. As a result, the evacuation of dozens of Dutch citizens was made possible. In total, at least 160 Dutch nationals were evacuated from Sudan, more than 85 of whom were transported by the Air Force's aircraft. Other Dutch nationals were able to fly on flights from other European countries. On the Dutch flights, approximately 130 evacuees from 18 other nationalities were also taken.

Functional Training June and July were focused on functional training for both 1MCG and 2MCG, namely the Sierra Team Commanders Course (STCC) and the Designated Marksman Course (DMC).

text:
Both courses began in the Netherlands, with the continuation taking place in Otterburn (UK).

[SECTION BREAK]

During the STCC, the corporals from the Raiding Squadrons learned to lead a Sierra team (S-team), focusing on the handling of group weapons, and learned to operate as an S-Team. In the first week, the teams received training in the use of all weapon systems: FN MAG, .50 QCB, and 60mm mortars. In the second week, the teams prepared for the final phase in Otterburn by practicing equipment camouflage and going through scenarios with blank ammunition. In Otterburn, the S-teams underwent Live Fire Training. A new element was the S-team competition, where the S-teams competed against each other with challenges in estimating distances, shooting, positioning, and gun drills, with the best-performing team receiving the trophy. To conclude the training, the units practiced providing fire support under the direction of the Troop Commander (TC). The Designated Marksman Course emphasized precision skills. During the training, participants learned to deal with ballistics, wind influences, breathing techniques, and aiming devices. They practiced identifying targets, taking positions, and shooting quickly and accurately with the HK417. During the first phase in the Netherlands, the shooters practiced their basic skills by firing at paper targets, first at 100 meters and ultimately at 600 meters. They then trained in shooting at moving targets and delivering fire in dynamic situations. In Otterburn, participants were able to train under varying weather conditions and

text:
Black Esox From September 25 to October 1, NLMARSOF organized the international maritime anti-terror exercise Black Esox. With challenging scenarios at sea and on land, it provided partner countries extensive opportunities to sharpen their maritime anti-terror tactics and strengthen ties with each other. Collaboration took place with Finnish, German, Danish, and Swedish units, among others. Autumn Waves From September 18 to September 30, C-squadron NLMARSOF participated with teams, staff, and dedicated vessels from SATG in the exercise Autumn Waves, which took place at various locations in Denmark. During the exercise, the unit undertook various Full Mission Profiles, focusing on executing maritime scenarios in a contested environment. The training provided valuable experience in remotely commanding a unit with limited communication capabilities. Jetpack Training Throughout the year, operators from NLMARSOF were trained to operate with a jetpack. The jetpack enables NLMARSOF to overcome heights more quickly and unexpectedly, thereby conducting boarding operations. It serves as an additional tool in the NLMARSOF's toolbox. During the implementation of the jetpack, intensive collaboration took place with research institutes, the business community, and legal authorities. In the coming years, NLMARSOF will further investigate how to best integrate the jetpack into the unit.

Black Esox From September 25 to October 1, NLMARSOF organized the international maritime anti-terror exercise Black Esox. With challenging scenarios at sea and on land, it provided partner countries extensive opportunities to sharpen their maritime anti-terror tactics and strengthen ties with each other. Collaboration took place with Finnish, German, Danish, and Swedish units, among others. Autumn Waves From September 18 to September 30, C-squadron NLMARSOF participated with teams, staff, and dedicated vessels from SATG in the exercise Autumn Waves, which took place at various locations in Denmark. During the exercise, the unit undertook various Full Mission Profiles, focusing on executing maritime scenarios in a contested environment. The training provided valuable experience in remotely commanding a unit with limited communication capabilities. Jetpack Training Throughout the year, operators from NLMARSOF were trained to operate with a jetpack. The jetpack enables NLMARSOF to overcome heights more quickly and unexpectedly, thereby conducting boarding operations. It serves as an additional tool in the NLMARSOF's toolbox. During the implementation of the jetpack, intensive collaboration took place with research institutes, the business community, and legal authorities. In the coming years, NLMARSOF will further investigate how to best integrate the jetpack into the unit.

text:
After the JAT, LCTU-1 supported various Landing Craft (LC) training as well as initial training and exercises. A team from LCTU-1 also contributed to the training of Ukrainian soldiers under the name Operation Interforge. After the summer, the unit supported the World Port Days in addition to its regular support and standby duties. Second Landing Craft Task Unit (LCTU-2) LCTU-2 has been the primary supporting unit for both LC and initial Marine training in 2023. A year after the large-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, a request was made to train Ukrainian soldiers, with LCTU-2 supporting the first rotation in the United Kingdom. Additionally, a structural LCTU training program has been included in the OJP, which LCTU-2 has completed for the first time in preparation for the OG position in 2024. Training, exercises, and deployment In the first half of 2023, LCTU-2 supported two complete LC-3 training courses alongside regular support for the basic Marine training courses. In the second quarter, the LC-1 and LC-2 training also began, with LCTU-2 playing a crucial role in supporting these. An important task was assigned to the first team of men from LCTU-2, who supported the first rotation of Operation Interforge in the United Kingdom. A successful amphibious training was also conducted together with 21RSQN, and LCTU-2 contributed to the Marine Days. After the summer leave, LCTU-2 began the LCTU training program in preparation for the OG position in 2024.

The reconnaissance team of the unit participated, as last year, in the exercise Coptic Whisper organized by 47 Commando Royal Marines (47CDO RM) in Cyprus. The program proved successful, and the unit has been prepared to begin the OG year. This program will continue next year.

Prior to that, on July 19, the keel laying took place of the second Dutch mine countermeasure vessel Scheveningen at the shipyard in Giurgiu (Romania). This was done through a ceremony in which a coin was welded into the keel. Captain (ktz) B. Roetering, former commander of the Mine Service, performed this act. The Scheveningen is the fourth ship in a series of a total of twelve mine countermeasure vessels for the Belgian and Dutch navies that will be delivered between 2025 and 2030, including the unmanned systems for the MCM toolbox. Heersema The Mine Countermeasure Module Group (MMG) conducted many Operational Tests & Evaluations (OT&E) throughout 2023 to extensively test the future MCM toolboxes.

Page 122 122 Operations Directorate. This was done from the civil ship Geosea, which has been leased for this specific task. The new MCM toolboxes will consist of unmanned systems to enhance the safety of personnel. By using these unmanned systems, personnel can conduct mine countermeasures according to the stand-off principle, remaining outside the mine danger area. In the first part of 2023, the personnel of the MMG underwent extensive training regarding the new MCM toolboxes. These training sessions were interspersed with periods at sea to test the acquired knowledge and the new MCM toolboxes during OT&E. In the meantime, the MMG conducted Beneficial Cooperation in the North Sea, during which several naval mines and aerial bombs were neutralized. This, however, created a vacancy for the position of Subject-Matter Expert Naval Mine Warfare (SME NMW). As the Ministry of Defence has shifted its focus to the primary task (defense of the NATO treaty area), this has significant implications for how the Ministry and thus also CZSK fulfill their tasks. The support request to MWC has changed drastically and increased in volume. MWC is contributing to the CZSK implementation of the new NATO Force Model, in which the force pool concept for all tasks is abandoned in favor of dedicated forces for specific regional deployment areas. MWC also contributes to the national Strategic Military Development (SKMO) and the derived plans for national defense, such as those for Integrated Air & Missile Defence. CZSK had to refocus on naval warfare, which necessitated painful choices regarding the capabilities that had previously been prioritized. Thus, the

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 129 129 Directorate Operations further development of an exo-atmospheric missile defense was sidelined, as the development capacity was necessary for regular war tasks. The Force Design efforts within the framework of the project Mastering the Littoral were primarily focused on a more specific region. Strategy and Advice began concept development for maritime operations, with the ultimate goal of delivering a Future Maritime Operating Concept (FMOC) in the course of 2024, which will serve as the framework for the functional concepts of CZSK. The many planned 'blue' material projects had to simultaneously reach a needs assessment, increasing the pressure on MWC to focus on Concepts of Operations (CONOPS) for this, based on explicit functional concepts. This required a significant effort but was valuable for the entire organization. In this context, there was also a reevaluation of the age-old anti-submarine warfare (ASW) discipline. During the period of focus on 'wars of choice,' there was little room for this war task, resulting in CZSK having only one operational ship that dealt with this part-time. As a consequence, the various capabilities that are strictly necessary to adequately fulfill this task became increasingly unavailable, leading to a lack of integrated capacity for some time.

[SECTION BREAK]

After MWC had requested attention for this undesirable situation for several years, a so-called palace session was convened with C-ZSK in 2023.

Thanks to the Maritime Battle Lab (MBL) and Maritime IT (MarIT), the data from the executed scenarios were further analyzed after FS23, from which various valuable lessons could be drawn. From September 4 to 29, the exercise Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping augmented by Maritime Unmanned Systems (REPMUS) 2023 took place in Troja (Portugal), followed by Dynamic Messenger (DM) 2023. The combination of both exercises aims to achieve Command & Control (C2) and standardization between Maritime Unmanned Systems (MUS) and other (manned) NATO units, as well as to test the Experimental Tactic (EXTAC) 885 (mine countermeasures). CZSK participated from various components, albeit in a smaller capacity than in 2022. From October 2 to 10, the MWC, under the supervision of the Joint Nucleus Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS), conducted a CD&E test aboard Zr.Ms. De Zeven Provinciën to test the usability of the currently available C-UAS resources in a maritime setting. The goal was to find a temporary solution to the threat posed by small Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) against surface ships. Given the operational threat, the reporting resonated extensively within the operational organization.

Van Amstel simultaneously acted as the torpedo recovery unit. The last successful launch of an MK46 torpedo by a frigate (FF) took place in 2017. Therefore, conducting this Lightweight Torpedo (LWT) Firing Exercise as part of TFX 23-3 aimed to enhance personnel capability, practice the supply and preparation of torpedoes, verify the proper functioning of the weapon and Ships Torpedo Weapon System (STWS), and investigate whether the SEMA exercise target is suitable for firing exercises with LWTs. BNS Louise-Marie successfully deployed its SEMA, allowing Zr.Ms. Van Amstel to fire successfully. Unfortunately, only three of the five planned LWT launches were executed, and there was insufficient time available for a firing run of the LOMA due to material issues and high sea conditions. On May 1, the former Chief of Hydrography, Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck, received the Prince Albert I Medal for Hydrography from Prince Albert II of Monaco, in recognition of his international efforts between 2014 and 2022. On World Hydrography Day (June 21), he received the British Alexander Dalrymple Award from Rear Admiral Rhett Hatcher, National Hydrographer of the United Kingdom.

[SECTION BREAK]

On May 4, the Hydrographic Service joined the Hydrographic Commission on Antarctica (HCA), upon the advice of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. This allows the Service to contribute to promoting safe navigation in the vulnerable waters around Antarctica.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 134 134 Directorate Operations Offer Development The International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) is developing new standards for the delivery of nautical datasets, based on S-100, the Universal Hydrographic Data Model. The Service actively contributes to this. The IHO Council, in which the Chief of Hydrography represents the Kingdom of the Netherlands, evaluates the S-100 Roadmap annually. The International Centre for ENCs (IC-ENC) has accepted the Dutch S-100 test datasets as the first set in which the S-100 data layers are combined and available for a single area. They are now freely available to everyone, allowing the industry to further develop and test its navigation systems.

[SECTION BREAK]

In 2023, an employee of the Hydrographic Service was appointed as vice-chairman of the Steering Group of the IC-ENC. Demand Development The demand for Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs) increased again, for both the North Sea and the Caribbean Sea. The decline in revenue from paper products aligns with the international trend of reducing paper charts. In 2023, the Hydrographic Service reached an agreement with the United Kingdom Hydrographic Office (UKHO) that the digital publication for tide predictions and current information NLTides, based on a similar British product, may be published online for free. Other nautical publications are already online or will follow soon. The sales of third-party navigation products under license increased significantly, as a major license holder has resumed using the official chart images as the basis for its own products. This is excellent news for safe navigation, as recreational and commercial shipping use a more uniform representation of the environment.

[SECTION BREAK]

Another notable development is that the reuse of open source data via online view services doubled.

The Hydrographic Service, like any other relevant government organization, conducted an impact analysis for the coordinating Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations (BZK). The Hydrographic Service does not need to release new datasets. Within the United Nations, a Working Group on Marine Geographic Information (WG-MGI) operates under the United Nations Committee of Experts on Global Geographic Information Management (UN-GGIM). The Hydrographic Service is part of this group, aiming to improve the supply and use of Marine Spatial Data Infrastructures (MSDI) worldwide, thereby enhancing the care for seas and oceans. This aligns with international initiatives such as the UN Sustainable Development Goal 14 (SDG14) Life below Water, the UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (UNESCO-IOC) Decade of Ocean Science 2020-2030, and the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO)/Nippon Foundation Seabed 2030 project. An employee of the Service gave a presentation at the UN headquarters on the importance of MSDI. Opening of the exhibition 'On the Map'.

Kool EMSD The year 2023 was marked for the Defense Diving Group (DDG) by intensive (inter)national deployments, operational enhancement, and a structural reorganization, given the geopolitical developments. Through participation in complex exercises and operations, the DDG further developed its diving capabilities and strengthened its role within the Royal Netherlands Navy in general and the Mine Service in particular. Operational Deployments and Exercises In 2023, the DDG conducted a wide range of specialized diving and mine countermeasures exercises, both domestically and abroad.

[SECTION BREAK]

The unit operated in challenging conditions and further optimized its expertise in military diving operations with a focus on human-machine teaming. Heliox Trials – A crucial testing phase for deep diving operations with heliox mixtures, aimed at expanding operational depth limits. With the further establishment of the heliox tables, safety has been further improved.

[SECTION BREAK]

Italian Mine Exercise (ITA MINEX) – A large-scale international mine countermeasures exercise in which the DDG, in cooperation with NATO partners, detected and neutralized underwater explosives in the Mediterranean Sea. Salvage and Explosive Ordnance Disposal (SALVEX) 23 – A salvage exercise in cooperation with Spanish naval divers from Cartagena focused on wreck diving and salvage operations, during which complex underwater works were carried out to support maritime operations. Sandy Coast 23 – A multidisciplinary deployment that combined underwater explosive clearance with amphibious operations, coastal defense tasks, and seabed security. Dive Exercise (DIVEX) CARIB – A deployment in the Caribbean where tactical diving operations were conducted under tropical conditions, focusing on underwater search actions and the recovery of a sunken pontoon. SNMCMG1 – Various diving teams aboard the minehunters were deployed in the rapidly deployable fleet of Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 1. The focus was on operations in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. In addition to international exercises, the DDG also increased its visibility and readiness in the Netherlands. Through flag displays with the diving vessels and various deployments in the context of judicial assistance, the operational presence in domestic waters was emphasized, and cooperation with civil authorities was strengthened.

text: Page 139 139 Operations Directorate Reorganization and Structural Improvements An important organizational milestone in 2023 was the restructuring of the Defense Diving Group and the Defense Diving School (DDS). Previously, both units fell under one command; they now operate under their respective responsible directorates, namely the Operations Directorate and the Personnel and Organization Directorate, where the training units are part of the Royal Netherlands Navy Training (Opleidingen Koninklijke Marine). This reorganization allows the Defense Diving Group to fully focus on operational tasks, deployability, and strategic development, such as the integration of the new mine countermeasures concept into their operational methods, while the Defense Diving School can better ensure training, certification, and knowledge development within the military diving domain. This clear separation of responsibilities has increased both operational effectiveness and the quality of diving training. J.F. Hodes To maintain the equipment of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) in the highest possible state of readiness, in a world where peace and security are no longer taken for granted, the Directorate of Material Maintenance (DMI) formulated a new vision in 2023. In the vision 'Together Strong DMI towards 2035', three pillars are emphasized: higher material readiness, strengthening knowledge, skills, and behavior, and investing in a modern and sustainable infrastructure and tooling. Due to tightness in the labor market and significant aging, an initiative has been started to investigate the extent to which intensive collaboration with market parties can contribute to ensuring the necessary maintenance capacity. Together with the large population of civilian employees and partners, this should lead to the establishment of Maintenance Valley Den Helder. To keep DMI attractive as an employer, plans have been made to further grow into an even more modern, technologically advanced company that also aligns with the changing needs of partners. In this context, DMI employees are increasingly expected to have an affinity for data management, data analysis, and the DMI organizational chart.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 142 142 Directorate of Material Maintenance cooperation with civilian parties The DMI (Directorate of Material Maintenance) gathers insight into the knowledge and skills required in these areas, in order to subsequently provide for its employees. A modern and sustainable environment helps to achieve the goals of the DMI and to remain a professional collaborative partner for the industry. With this in mind, an initial assessment has also been made to review the real estate portfolio.

[SECTION BREAK]

With modern central logistical support and office and workspaces, the DMI is better prepared for the maintenance of the new (weapon) systems. The premise for Maintenance Valley Den Helder, which is that joint production is localized in Den Helder, is something the DMI aims to facilitate with the expansion of the ship lift complex, the dock capacity, and the necessary infrastructure for this.
