Maintenance Group Large Grey  
In 2023, the Maintenance Group Large Grey strengthened collaboration with the industry by outsourcing periods of Designated Maintenance and support for the construction of the CSS externally. The department was also expanded this year with a shore support team. At the beginning of 2023, Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt returned from Vlissingen, where the ship had undergone its Mid-Life Update MLU/BO3. The work was far from complete, and the company Damen, along with its subcontractors, had to finish the work in Den Helder. It became clear that the security measures, which required every subcontractor to be registered, significantly delayed the activities, pushing back the delivery date.

[SECTION BREAK]

In October, DMI completed the maintenance on Zr.Ms. Johan de Witt, and under the leadership of Sea Training Command, it was brought up to the status of 'ready to sail'. At the end of 2023, the major replacement of four propulsion transformers of Zr.Ms.

[SECTION BREAK]

Karel Doorman took place. This was a significant task, requiring the ship to be alongside for an extended period. The replacement was necessary because there was a risk that, following the failure of the first transformer, the other three would also fail. During this time, the crankshaft of diesel generator 5 was also replaced, a task that had been cleared earlier and went smoothly this time as well. Good communication between the maintenance group, the ship's crew, and the industry was a clear success factor. The repair was carried out on time and completed just before Christmas. Finally, in 2023, a three-phase plan was initiated and started to bring Zr.Ms. Rotterdam into operational reserve, maintain it, and then take it out again. The ship went alongside at the beginning of 2023, allowing the crew to transfer to Zr.Ms.

In November 2023, the Transport section received a new vacuum truck. After twenty-three years, the section bid farewell to the previous Mercedes/Kos combination, which was replaced by a similar partnership. The specialists from Transport were closely involved in the composition of the new vehicle. This is equipped with the latest technological developments and features a comfortable study area in the cabin, where employees can study during long working hours.

Page 147 147 The Directorate of Material Maintenance was expanded with the weekly running training. This is still very well attended. Marine Swimming Pool Den Helder 2023 was a wonderful swimming year for the Marine Swimming Pool Den Helder. Various target groups from the navy and other military branches found this swimming pool very accessible. In addition, there were also external organizations that closely collaborated with the navy and frequently appeared in our current operations.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the beginning of the year, the first swimming clinic was organized. This was provided by Personal Swimming, and much knowledge and expertise was shared with Defense personnel. 43 Defense employees participated in the clinic. Following the swimming clinic, a week later the Swim-Run took place, in which 20 to 30 people participated. In week 25, after a long time, the Swim Four Days was organized again. Between 20 and 30 swimmers took part in this event. Afterward, an evaluation of the event took place, and a script was developed.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the end of June, a swimming competition was held in honor of the 50-year cooperation between the British and Dutch marines, in which a swimming team from the Marine competed against the Royal Marines. The event was a success, and these findings were also documented in a script that can be used as a guide for future swimming competitions. In week 28, the Run-Swim-Run was on the agenda, an event organized in collaboration with the gym of Marine Barracks Erfprins. The team from the Marine Swimming Pool was responsible for the swimming part, while Marine Barracks Erfprins was responsible for the running parts. At the beginning of October, the second swimming clinic was scheduled. During this clinic, video analysis was used, from which various exercises and improvements in skills emerged that were practiced in the swimming pool. This clinic was well attended by the first group, but the turnout for the second group was somewhat poor this time.

[SECTION BREAK]

In October and November, the organization of the Marine Swimming Pool provided the annual Swimming Rescue for Swimming Pools (ZRZ) license renewals. Through these renewals, the swimming instructors remain qualified, ensuring safety in and around the swimming pool.

General  
The new construction plans for the revitalization of the barracks have been encapsulated under the auspices of Defense Real Estate Management (DVM) in a 'functional Program of Requirements' (fPvE). The intention is for DVM to commission this fPvE in the first quarter of 2024 to the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf, which will then prepare a Project Initiation Document (PID) for the new construction at the MEA.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Jordaan team of the Amsterdam-Amstelland police unit left the MEA in the spring after their team building on the Lijnbaasgracht was completed. Given the shifted schedule for the demolition of building 12, a request has come from the police for the Amstelland-East team (Diemen) to make use of this during the renovation period of their team building. In principle, approval has been granted; the intention is for the team to arrive at the MEA in early 2024. A lease agreement will be concluded with the RVB for this purpose. From late April 2022 to mid-March 2023, a wing of the barracks building was used for crisis emergency shelter for approximately 250 asylum seekers and status holders, under the management of the Central Agency for the Reception of Asylum Seekers (COA). After the departure of the COA, the inventory and infrastructure of the barracks building had to be largely replaced and renovated.

[SECTION BREAK]

Events and Activities  
In 2023, approximately 28,000 visitors utilized the Event Center Amsterdam (ECA), the MEA organized around 50 boat tours, and various helicopter landings were carried out by the Defense Helicopter Command (DHC) and Police. This year, several noteworthy events were on the calendar. In April, the MEA supported the state visit of President Emmanuel Macron of France, during which Prime Minister Mark Rutte and President Macron commenced a boat tour from the MEA. The salute for the state visit was given from Kattenburg and was answered by the French frigate FS Normandie from the IJ.

In June, a ministerial meeting took place at the MEA where the defense ministers from the ten participating countries of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) gathered. Also in June, the Establishment organized a well-attended Veterans Day at the request of the municipality of Amsterdam. The MEA provided accommodation for British Royal Marines from late June to early July for their participation in Dutch Gauntlet, the sports competitions in the context of 50 years of UK/NL Amphibious Force. In September, the MEA acted as host for the start and finish, logistics, and swimmer event surrounding the Amsterdam City Swim, where approximately 2,500 swimmers swam through the canals in the fight against the disease ALS. In October, the Northern V-CHOD Conference took place at the MEA, where the PCDS received about 25 northern colleagues. In November, the MEA hosted the Conflict and Crisis Management Event of the Amsterdam Police, where among the approximately 250 participants, defense security partners were also present, and a police and trauma helicopter was part of an extensive static show by the Police, Fire Brigade, and Defense. In December, the state visit of the President of South Korea was supported, once again with a ceremonial salute from Kattenburg. FS Normandie fired salute shots during President Macron's visit to Amsterdam.

Page 154 154 Directorate of Material Maintenance Product Group Energy Distribution Company (EDB) Head: Drs. Ing. R.J.L.

[SECTION BREAK]

Put The Energy Distribution Company (EDB) has been the energy supplier and network manager for the Defense locations in Den Helder since 1957. Electricity is generated at its own power plant, the Combined Heat and Power Plant (KWS). The heat released from this process provides approximately half of the buildings at the Nieuwe Haven with heating.

[SECTION BREAK]

The Energy Distribution Company manages contracts and invoice control for electricity, gas, and water across the Defense sector. It also addresses demand forecasting and reports on consumption figures to provide advice on reducing energy use. This year, the EDB connected the battery testing center to the heating network. This is another step towards the ultimate goal of connecting the larger buildings on the Nieuwe Haven site to the heating network and subsequently linking it to a sustainable (geothermal) source. This will make the heating to the buildings sustainable all at once. First electric truck of the Navy.

After the event, the ship sailed to Drimmelen for its annual maintenance. This year, this was particularly challenging due to the replacement of the main engine and the galley. In November, the annual Tall Ships Races Conference took place. During this event, Urania was surprised with the awarding of the Greatest Loyalty Award. This award recognizes the dedication and long-term involvement of the ship with the mission of Sail Training International. Some facts about the year 2023 Last year, Urania embarked 212 people for training and multi-day trips. During these periods, the ship made a total of 98 sailing days. In Enkhuizen, a total of 165 relations became acquainted with the Royal Netherlands Navy over 16 sailing days.

[Directie Materiële Instandh (p.20) — narrative]
In terms of media, the focus was on Instagram; 88 posts were made on this platform, effectively reaching the target audience. Outside of this platform, media attention was also generated in other ways by the ship this year. Firstly, an intern from DOSCO sailed for a week with the vlog "On Course with Zr.Ms. Urania" to showcase the training activities. This vlog consists of eight episodes and can be viewed on YouTube. International media attention was generated during Oostende voor Anker and during the Tall Ships Races. Nationally, the following media outlets covered the ship: Eurosport during the Ocean Race, NH Nieuws with a report during Sail Den Helder, De Telegraaf, and the Noord-Hollands Dagblad during the opening of the Tall Ships Races.

[Directie Materiële Instandh (p.20) — narrative]
In 2023, Zr.Ms. Urania covered a total of 7,713 nautical miles.

Marine Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen Commander of military crew: Lieutenant (ltz2oc) T.D.

[SECTION BREAK]

Brouwer Master: M. de Wij The Marine Training Vessel (MOV) Van Kinsbergen is used for nautical practical training. The ship is specially built and equipped for this purpose. It accommodates 16 trainees.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 160 160 Directorate of Material Maintenance Navigation and Training Bridge The Van Kinsbergen has, in addition to the regular navigation bridge, a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for practicing all navigation procedures and safe mooring and unmooring. Deployment The Van Kinsbergen sails approximately 200 days per year. The main user is the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. The vessel serves as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, including team building and character development.

[SECTION BREAK]

Besides the KIM, the Netherlands-Belgium Operational School (NL-BEOPS) is also a major user.

[SECTION BREAK]

Students at NLBEOPS receive practical sailing training for the qualifications of Non-Commissioned Officers for minehunters, hydrographic survey vessels, and submarines. Civil Maritime Schools The civil maritime school on Terschelling, the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB), also makes good use of the Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Within the agreement, the MIWB has the vessel available for a number of weeks for training purposes. Second-year Maritime Officer students undertake short practical voyages on this ship. During their stay on board, navigation is particularly practiced. Additionally, the MIWB uses the ship for Advanced Fire Fighting training, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. Instructors from the MIWB provide lessons for the adelborsten of the KIM in Den Helder.

Page 162 162 Directorate of Material Maintenance oldest officer, a skipper with navigation authority, a chief technical service, and a cook. The civilians and military personnel are interchangeable. Sea Service Practicum 1 (ZPR1) For the first sailing period of 2023, the MOV Van Kinsbergen was deployed for the KIM for the so-called ZPR1 (Sea Service Practicum 1). This lays the foundation for safe (visual) navigation of a ship. This is the first sailing period of the cadets on board the Van Kinsbergen. This trip lasts 4 weeks and was conducted with the Sea Service class of 22. This period ran from January 26 to February 22. MIWB The Van Kinsbergen sailed from March 5 to March 10 and from March 20 to March 24 for the MIWB. During this time, two-day trips were made with the students, allowing them to become acquainted with working and sleeping on board a ship. The Van Kinsbergen sailed between the ports of Harlingen and Den Helder, and various exercises took place during the trip. Sea Watch Standard K (ZWST-K) Van Kinsbergen sailed from March 27 to April 6 for the Defense Sailing School (DVS) for the ZWST-K course.

[SECTION BREAK]

On the Monday of departure, it was decided to shelter for the night at Terschelling due to waves of 3.5m. The next day, the sea was calmer, and the Van Kinsbergen set course towards the Kiel Canal to then enter the Baltic Sea. The ship made a short trip through these waters before spending the weekend in Copenhagen. Various exercises were held to train the students and prepare them for their Practical Business Introduction (PBI) on the fleet. MIWB From April 11 to April 14, the Van Kinsbergen was at West-Terschelling in service of the MIWB for the Advanced Fire Fighting (AFF) training, during which realistic emergency scenarios were practiced on board.

[SECTION BREAK]

The ship returned to its home port of Den Helder on Friday evening.

ZPR2 During the sailing period for the KIM, from May 4 to June 1, the cadets became acquainted with their second sailing period at sea, during which radar was introduced. With port visits in Copenhagen, this was a fun and educational week for the sea service.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 163 163 Directorate of Material Maintenance ZPR4 The ZPR4, from June 26 to July 26, was the final sailing practice week for the Lieutenant Commanders (ltz) 3 and midshipmen (sgt adelborsten) before they go on PBI. During the ZPR4, the participants determine their own Weekly Practice Program (WPP) with various exercises and routes.

[SECTION BREAK]

Only the ports are determined by the crew. This practical training is an opportunity for the participant to demonstrate their capabilities, while the crew and instructors take a step back and only intervene when necessary. This trip consists of more sailing days per class than the participant has been accustomed to until then, to give them even more time and to experience the joy of sailing.

[SECTION BREAK]

In Oslo, there was a visit to the embassy where a briefing followed about the various interests in Scandinavia. Furthermore, during the various port visits, participants had the chance to climb or view glaciers. In some cases, it was necessary to leave the ports earlier due to bad weather conditions. The Van Kinsbergen performed well, and only the midshipmen and deckhands had some difficulty with the waves encountered. Major Maintenance From September 1 to November 10, major maintenance took place at Damen Shipyard Den Helder. Among other things, the entire underwater hull and the hull were repainted, the call 2 home internet system was installed, and the annual Zr.Ms. Van Amstel fired the 76mm cannon.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 164 164 Directorate of Material Maintenance checks completed. As a result, the ship has been declared seaworthy again and can operate for another year. Terneu Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of the CZSK and tasks from the Defense Readiness Directive (AGDEF), and states: ‘CZMCARIB provides peace and security in the Caribbean.’ This single sentence articulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at a strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of Defense by CZMCARIB in the Caribbean region: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. Promoting and maintaining the international rule of law and stability. Supporting civil authorities.

[SECTION BREAK]

Page 168 168 Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Vision In September, CZMCARIB redefined its mission in line with its main task, mission, and environmental factors, and articulated it more clearly. Previously, this was: "CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean." The new vision states: "CZMCARIB, as a reliable security partner, protects the Caribbean part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and contributes to stability in the Caribbean with adaptive military (continuation) capability and a robust information position." The vision emphasizes the adaptive military capability of CZMCARIB, which is crucial for responding quickly and effectively to threats and hostilities, thereby maintaining the integrity and interests of the Caribbean part of the Kingdom in the region. This formulation also underscores the importance of a robust information position, which is of critical significance in executing the second main task of CZMCARIB. A strong information position enables the organization to respond effectively to threats such as drug trafficking, but is also important in promoting international cooperation. Finally, the importance of partnerships and the necessity of Zr.Ms.

Page 169 The Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean emphasizes cooperation with national and international security organizations in the region, which is crucial for fulfilling the third main task. Retrospective 2023 The Royal House visited the Caribbean in early February, including visits to Defense units. In Aruba, the Royal family boarded the station ship Zr.Ms. Holland.

[SECTION BREAK]

Together with a mixed group from the Royal Marechaussee (KMAR), Curaçao military (CURMIL), and Aruban military (ARUMIL), as well as the Coast Guard, the ship sailed towards Curaçao. During the voyage, the Royal family also became acquainted with the FRISC’s.

[SECTION BREAK]

In March, Defense welcomed 33 new Caribbean military personnel, including the first woman in this unit. The training has been accessible to women since last year, and this milestone marked a new step in diversity within Defense. Minister of Defense Kajsa Ollongren made a working visit to Defense in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom in early May. During this visit, she attended the hurricane disaster relief exercise in Sint Maarten, organized by the Marines. The Parera naval base organized an open day in Curaçao on June 13 after ten years. The Marine Barracks Savaneta in Aruba also opened its doors during the annual open day.

[SECTION BREAK]

CARMIL To improve territorial defense on the islands, 200 Caribbean Military personnel (CARMIL) are developing into a fully-fledged light infantry unit. CARMIL is currently a collective term for the Curaçao and Aruban Militia, as the official names are. In the future, they will provide contributions in the form of light infantry support, humanitarian assistance, ceremonial tasks, and the guarding and securing of vital objects. They work closely with Dutch military personnel. The term 'militia' refers to the old situation with conscripts and is no longer relevant. Within the ongoing Project Professionalization CARMIL, various conditions for the new situation are being developed together with the countries of Curaçao and Aruba, and they are now referred to as 'military personnel.' CZMCARIB is responsible for their training, readiness, and deployment as the regional commander.

Page 172 172 Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean by C-ZMCARIB from October to December 2023 did not rely on a station ship. The SSCG once again did not have access to the NH90 this year, but could fall back on the collaboration established in 2014 with the American USCG helicopter squadron Helicopter Interdiction Tactical Squadron (HITRON). For the Commander Task Group (CTG) 4.4 periods, the SSCG had access to an MH-65 from HITRON. In addition to the regular cooperation with the Dash-8 of the Caribbean Coast Guard, the SSCG had access this year to air support from the Dutch MQ-9 of 306 Squadron of the Royal Netherlands Air Force. Counter-drugs The SSCG patrolled during its period of presence both for KWCARIB and for CTG 4.4, with various successful seizures. Despite the shortened presence of the SSCG, in collaboration with international units in 2023, CTG 4.4 and KWCARIB seized approximately 4,616 kg and 8,348 kg of contraband from the trade market, respectively. These international operations were carried out by the ship in cooperation with various countries such as the United States, France, Colombia, and the United Kingdom.

Page 173 Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Hurricane Relief 2023 was an above-average warm year due to the influence of El Niño and the warm seawater in the North Atlantic Ocean. This resulted in above-average high temperatures starting in May. The warm ocean water also contributed to an above-average active hurricane season with 20 tropical storms and 7 hurricanes, of which 3 were of the severe category.

[SECTION BREAK]

In 2023, CZMCARIB did not provide hurricane relief.

[SECTION BREAK]

However, the preparatory activities for the hurricane season were successfully carried out. This included exercises such as Communication Information Systems Sint Maarten, Saba, Sint Eustatius (CIS SSS), Patrol Exercise (PATROLEX), Hurricane Relief Exercise (HUREX), and Windward Express on the Windward Islands Sint Maarten, Sint Eustatius, and Saba. During the exercise, the MHKC worked intensively with local authorities and aid organizations to ensure that cooperation during the hurricane season runs smoothly and everyone knows what is expected of them. Land units CZMCARIB and visiting units In 2023, the land units of CZMCARIB conducted various exercises and readiness activities in preparation for primary task 1 and the hurricane season. The most important ones are the annual exercises Caribbean Urban Warrior in the United States and the apprehension of smugglers.

[SECTION BREAK]

In total, this resulted in 311 activities in the region.

Finally, a lot of time and energy has been invested in improving cooperation between Dutch units and units of the Caribbean military (CARMIL). This is necessary to bring CARMIL to the desired level within a reasonable timeframe, as described in the ambition document.

text:
The Search Team of the Company in the West (CidW) and the Detachment Sint Maarten provided assistance four times in the context of searches of prisoners, residences, properties, and vehicles. During these operations, the team found, among other things, phones, money, drugs, and documents that were used by the Korps Politie Curaçao (KPC) and Korps Politie Sint Maarten (KPSM) in ongoing investigations. The Explosive Ordnance Disposal Service (EODD) was active four times in Curaçao and Aruba to destroy ammunition, fireworks, and explosive materials. In April, soft military assistance was provided in Aruba in the search for a missing person. In Curaçao, the CidW contributed in the form of static observation to support local authorities in the investigation of illegal drug smuggling. In Bonaire, the MQ-9 provided assistance in the form of observation, supporting the IND. The CURMIL supported the KPC in Curaçao three times with traffic guidance, in connection with the visit of the Royal Family, carnival, and the harvest festival. During the passage of two weather systems in October, namely Hurricane Tammy near Sint Maarten and the passage of a depression near Curaçao, CZMCARIB provided assistance in the form of emergency aid and support to local police in maintaining public order. In December, CURMIL supported the Korps Politie Curaçao by setting up checkpoints and conducting joint traffic controls aimed at intercepting firearms.

Raiding Section (RS) Since the summer leave in August, there has been a significant personnel change. The first permanent element of the RS has been partially replaced by new personnel. With the start of the team in August, the first shooting exercises took place, and the Anaconda drivers obtained their driving licenses.

This was the main priority for the unit. This week has become a regular recurring training in the Integral Annual Plan (IJP). During the Barracuda Warrior 2023 (BAW23) exercise, the team trained at level 2 with the Marine Squadron Caribbean (MSC). Additionally, the team transitioned to the Caribbean Urban Warrior 2023 (CUW23) exercise at Camp Lejeune (USA). During this exercise, the team trained in Military Operations in Urban Terrain (MOUT). The unique training location and opportunities that Camp Lejeune offers provide the team with experience in Three Block War. This adds value to the training level and junior leadership of the unit. This year, the team also prepared for the hurricane season and participated in the Hurricane Relief Exercise (HUREX) and Windward Express (WWE). Further agreements were made with the MSC and local partners in Sint Maarten regarding cooperation in the event of a possible hurricane passage. Appreciation In consultation with the MHKC, the RS and the FRISC team participated in four major exercises that are conducted annually by, among others, the MSC, including Barracuda Warrior, Caribbean Urban Warrior, HUREX, and Windward Express, with the last two exercises taking place in the vicinity of the Leeward Islands. In addition to exercises, the unit also followed a number of annually recurring standard training courses, including the Military Tracker Course and the Baton Training. Additionally, there were training sessions that the detachment utilized but that do not yet recur annually, including a Combat Life Saver (CLS) retention week, a boarding training, and the Anaconda retraining. Given that the island of Sint Maarten is not very suitable as a training area for infantry operations, it is important that the team can relocate to the Windward Islands. It must be taken into account that the team is on standby for six months of the year for the hurricane season, which limits training outside the hurricane area. For this reason, active searches are being conducted for interesting training areas in the immediate vicinity. This is essential to maintain the motivation and training level of the team, which also fosters enthusiasm among newly assigned personnel. Furthermore, the permanent element now also has the task of organizing and sustaining the material maintenance of the unit, a role that was previously supported from the Netherlands. The reorganization into a fixed entity has ensured that the tasks of the team have become more challenging.

Venezuela Given the unstable situation in Venezuela, the Coast Guard also monitored developments in that country in 2023. Midway through 2023, borders between Venezuela and the Leeward Islands were reopened. Initially, this concerned the maritime borders for the transport of goods such as food. The reopening of the borders did not lead to significant changes in the environmental picture, and the Coast Guard was able to adequately manage the traffic flows and thereby ensure border security. Undocumented Individuals In 2023, the Coast Guard saw an increase in the number of undocumented individuals attempting to enter the islands illegally. In 2022, there were a total of 170 undocumented individuals who made the journey. In 2023, this number rose to 196. text:
Berkhout The Mission Statement of the Defense Security and Protection Organization is: ‘We ensure the physical security of the interests of the Defense components, day and night. The core values associated with this are cooperation, professionalism, reliability, communication, and responsibility.’ Access Control (AC) The DBBO carries out access control based on the Access Regulation A/007 of the Defense Security Policy (DBB). Daily checks are conducted on behalf of the garrison commanders. The access controls also include inspections. Access controls are carried out in cooperation with colleagues from the Curaçao and Aruba military (CURMIL and ARUMIL). Patrol, Intervention, and First Response Tasks The patrol, intervention, and First Response tasks that the DBBO carries out together with colleagues from ARUMIL and CURMIL are tasks that are performed every day throughout the year. The specifics arising from these tasks are shared with the garrison leadership to promote security awareness among everyone.

[SECTION BREAK]

Training, Certification, and Education The regular Integrated Professional Skills Training (IBT) applies to the DBBO as well as to ARUMIL and CURMIL. In blocks of 6 weeks, personnel are kept competent and capable by the IBT trainers according to the standards of the National Act. Additionally, the IBT trainer supports the Security and Protection (B&B) training of CURMIL and ARUMIL.

[SECTION BREAK]

Personnel In mid-2023, the DBBO commenced security operations at Coast Guard Support Point (KWSP) Hato and MSK Savaneta. At Hato, the organization carries this out in cooperation with an employee from Securitas (for Coast Guard (KW) tasks). At MSK Savaneta, colleagues from ARUMIL provide support. In addition to these additions to the DBBO personnel, a number of regular personnel changes took place.

Stunnenberg MBA Royal Netherlands Naval Institute (KIM) Commandant: Captain (ktz) W.L. van Zanten On January 8, the cadets and staff returned to the Royal Netherlands Naval Institute and began their lessons and activities for the new year. On Thursday, January 11, the traditional New Year's reception was held, hosted by the commandant of KIM and the dean of the Faculty of Military Sciences. The New Year's reception took place in 't Zaaltje of the Corps of Cadets. Annually, the cadets receive an invitation to the Wiener Ball. On February 11, this could take place for the 53rd edition after the coronavirus pandemic, where three couples from the Corps of Cadets participated. In the weekends leading up to the ball, mandatory participation in the rehearsals took place. In mid-April, a week of vocational education was scheduled, the so-called BO week. During this week, the mandatory KIM cross for the cadets took place, the boxing gala, and for the first time, a symposium on the Sugar Festival. This year's BO week concluded with the Dies Natalis, themed 'Challenges at Sea'.

[SECTION BREAK]

Sub-lieutenant (sbn) A. van de Sande gave a lecture on 'Experiences as C-SNMG1 and how KIM training and functions have prepared for this', and Lieutenant (ltz2) (TD) A.H. Koppes shared his experiences about his sailing race, the challenges, and how that relates to the training. In the second weekend of May, the annual competitions were held. The various promotion years then compete for honor and see this as preparation for the annual cadet and midshipman competitions.

After nearly a year of intensive training, the marines were 'welcomed' by their parents, the Commander of the Marine Corps (CKM), and the Commander of the Netherlands Defence Academy (C-NLDA) at the beginning of July. This part of the training has prepared the candidates for their first role as Troop Commander (TC) in operational marine units. The first role is essentially a hands-on position. The Practical Training for Officer of Marines (POTOM) reflects this by dedicating most of the training time to practical situations, focusing on the knowledge, skills, and attitudinal aspects that the candidate immediately needs in the role of a warrior (in accordance with the Training Vision of the Royal Institute for the Navy 2017-2030, established by C-KIM, dated April 7, 2017).

Coast Guard Netherlands Director: Captain (ktz) N.I.J. Kuipers EMSD The global security situation has drawn significant attention in 2023 to Dutch interests in the North Sea, the primary operational area of the Coast Guard. The awareness of the vulnerability of vital infrastructure at sea was underscored in 2023 by the presence of Russian research vessels in the North Sea. Although the Coast Guard does not yet have a formal task in this aspect of Maritime Security, it contributed to situational awareness at sea, an important condition for adequate protection of vital Dutch interests. The Maritime Information Node (MIK) provided an increasing contribution from its information position to the security picture for Dutch shipping and to the enforcement of sanctions against the Russian Federation. The ‘Bulletin maritime sanctions Russia’ has proven to be of great added value for the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, ports, Customs, and the Inspectorate for the Environment and Transport (ILT). The MIK is an example of successful cooperation as it occurs within the Coast Guard organization with various services and partners. The analytical function of the Coast Guard will be further developed in the coming years. In terms of service delivery, the Coast Guard has carried out its tasks in the North Sea as assigned.

In addition to the own Coast Guard units, the Royal Netherlands Rescue Society (KNRM) and a salvage company played an important role in getting the crew off the vessel in a timely manner. The Coast Guard deployed sailing and flying units and personnel for this incident for several days, who, in cooperation with our partners, contributed to a manageable situation without significant consequences for the environment. As is customary in major incidents, an extensive chain evaluation took place, alongside the investigation by the Dutch Safety Board (OVV). The new aircraft and helicopters that the Coast Guard received at the end of 2022 also proved to be of added value in this incident in the execution of Coast Guard tasks. Coast Guard vessel evacuates crew from burning Fremantle Highway.

Page 201 201 Appendices The availability of enforcement vessels at sea was lower than required for effective task execution. In consultation with the enforcement services and the Rijksrederij, the Coast Guard was able to deploy the emergency tug Guardian to fill some gaps in the sailing schedule. On the advice of the State Advocate, the planned assignment of ship crews from the Rijksrederij could not proceed, which meant that the patrol vessels Visarend and Zeearend were not deployable outside of the planned services.

The additional sailing capacity for enforcement promised in 2023 is an absolute requirement to make a step towards 24/7 execution of this primary task at sea. This will have a positive effect on the operations of the Coast Guard. The preliminary award of the contract for the new construction has already taken place. Its delivery is scheduled for 2026. At the beginning of 2023, the Coast Guard did not implement the new incident management application, Guardion Coastguard, as planned.

The project replaced this component with a solution that is integrated into Guardion Coastguard, developed by JIVC Maritime IT. The Coast Guard reviewed its organization and mapped out the necessary personnel capacity that aligns with the assignments and ambitions of the clients from 2025. The required personnel capacity has been summarized in the Council for the Coast Guard in the so-called imbalance note. This also includes other necessary capacities, such as investments in personnel and ships to carry out 24/7 enforcement tasks and investments in personnel and systems for the execution of tasks in the field of Maritime Security, Enforcement, and Services. The Council definitively approved the resolution of this imbalance in June 2023 and allocated the necessary financial resources for this purpose. This allows the reorganization process to begin.

text:
A cargo vessel in ballast arrived in a port to enter a shipyard under the guidance of a pilot. The pilot and Master agreed on a manoeuvring plan. The two tugs in attendance were to accept two mooring lines each, from the bow and stern central chock of the vessel respectively. The two lines were supposed to be passed to each attending tug together as one. At the arriving vessel’s stern, this was done quickly.

[SECTION BREAK]

At the bow, only one line was given to the attending tug forward. This line was attached to the tug’s towing hook and, unknown to the tug Master, it was made fast on the arriving vessel. While waiting for the second mooring line, the tug passed dangerously close to the port bow of the vessel. The two personnel in the tug’s towing area had to move around to avoid the risks posed by the line that had been secured. The forward tug then manoeuvred to take the second mooring line, which was now suspended from the bow of the vessel. As the tug manoeuvred, the line already secured came under strain, again coming dangerously close to the two seafarers on the stern of the tug.

[SECTION BREAK]

One of them ducked, and the mooring line made a glancing blow on his helmet, knocking it off his head. The deck hand next to him was struck in the chest by the line under tension and seriously injured. The stretched line then pulled the tug towards the vessel and caused the tug to contact the vessel. The uninjured seafarer released the line using the emergency release device on the hook.

[SECTION BREAK]

He also reported the events to the Master at the controls. The tug Master immediately reported the situation to the pilot and the pilot station and requested an ambulance. The victim was quickly transported to the dock, and medical teams were mobilised. The victim was in a serious condition and was taken to the hospital by the paramedics without delay. Despite all efforts the victim succumbed to his injuries.

text:
The investigation found, among other things, that the enclosed forecastle deck of the arriving vessel made it difficult for the crew on the fo’c’sle deck to establish effective communication or eye contact with the crew on the stern of the tug. The investigation also found that the tug company should establish procedures for situations where the mooring lines cannot be given at the same time, including precautions to be taken by the tug personnel.

[SECTION BREAK]

Line handling operations are very common but inherently hazardous for tug crews. Thorough failsafe procedures, crew compliance with the procedures and excellent communication are the touchstones for crew safety. There is no substitute for visual observation from one vessel to the other to inform the situational awareness of all involved.

chapter_title: 202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
section_titles: 202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
text:
Expectation bias + weak BRM = two groundings A fully laden bulk carrier was upbound in a tidal river under favourable tidal conditions and with a tug escort. During the initial leg of the transit, pilot A noted that the ship, loaded to 11.7 m draft fore and aft, was difficult to handle and required substantial, early rudder to control its swings. The channel had a dredged depth of 12.2 m which left only 0.5 under keel clearance (UKC) before considering squat. Pilot B boarded the vessel to relieve pilot A. The outgoing pilot advised him that the vessel needed substantial rudder to steer and recommended early initiation and counter rudder for turns. Pilot B found the vessel challenging to manage, noting that it frequently tended to, in his words, ‘dive to port’. He began intentionally manoeuvring the vessel outside the starboard side of the channel, expecting that the flood current north of the next bridge would push the ship toward the port side, where numerous piers protruded close to the channel boundaries. Actual environmental data later revealed that the real-time tide level was less than half of what had been predicted, meaning the actual current pushing the vessel to port, back toward the channel, was likely much weaker than the pilot anticipated. As the vessel passed under the bridge its centreline drifted about 42 metres outside the channel to starboard.

[SECTION BREAK]

Despite issuing some port rudder commands to correct the course, pilot B also compensated with starboard rudder orders to prevent what he expected to be a sharp port swing. Two and a half minutes later, the vessel’s bow was now some 88 metres outside the channel to starboard when, suddenly, its speed dropped (position 6 below). The crew felt a jerk and heard a rumble; the vessel had touched bottom. The Master pointed out that they were out of the channel. The pilot used a series of aggressive engine and rudder manoeuvres and assistance from the escort tug pushing on the starboard bow to free the vessel and resume moving forward. This ‘refloating’ took about six minutes.

chapter_title: 202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
section_titles: 202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
text:
Once back underway, the pilot continued navigating roughly parallel to the dredged channel, keeping the bulk carrier about 75 metres to starboard of the channel limit. As the ship accelerated, the Master repeatedly voiced concerns regarding their position, but the pilot reassured him that they were returning to the channel and that everything would be fine. About 8 minutes after coming free from the first grounding, the Master pointed out a red channel buoy nearly dead ahead on the starboard bow; they were running directly into shallow water.

[SECTION BREAK]

At about 6.5 knots, vibrations were heard and felt throughout the ship and the Master told the pilot that the ship needed to come to port. The pilot responded yes, but he was ‘running out of room’. Moments later, the crew heard air rushing from the bilge tank vents as the bottom shell plating ruptured on underwater shoals. Some two minutes later the vessel came to a complete stop, hard aground and listing to starboard due to the flooding of multiple ballast and fuel tanks. The vessel remained aground for three days before being refloated.

chapter_title: 202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
section_titles: 202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive
202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive (Lessons learned)
202628 BRM under pilotage takes a dive (Lessons learned)
text:
The official report found, among other things, that the pilot might have suffered ‘Expectation bias’, when a person responds in a way that is consistent with what they expect rather than what is actually occurring. He expected the vessel would be pushed to port by the current, and he also expected the vessel to ’dive to port’. He overcompensated and manoeuvred the vessel further outside the channel to starboard. After the first grounding, he continued to manoeuvre the vessel well to starboard of the channel even after the Master warned the pilot that the vessel was in danger, until the vessel grounded again.

[SECTION BREAK]

Pilots are human and can make mistakes. In this case the current pushing the vessel to port was not nearly as strong as predicted, and navigating outside the dredged channel to starboard only aggravated the hydrodynamic interactions. With only 0.5m of UKC before considering squat, the vessel was probably ’diving to port’ due to the stern experiencing bank suction. This phenomenon intensifies with the vessel’s speed, and was aggravated by conning the vessel to starboard of the channel. Strong BRM with a pilot on board is often a challenge, but this is the tool crew must use to avoid single point failure (ie the pilot making all decisions without challenge). Bridge officers, even Masters, are often hesitant to intervene with a local area expert at the con.

[SECTION BREAK]

When a pilot and bridge team clearly and openly share necessary information, both before and throughout a manoeuvre, they establish a shared mental model that increases collective situational awareness. Unexpected actions or deviations from the plan should be discussed between the crew and pilot to ensure a mutual understanding of the situation and prevent unrecoverable errors.

text: Although the escort tug was equipped with azimuth drives, it does not appear, from the report, that the tug was used as an active aid for steering but simply as a ‘Plan B’ in case of an emergency. In many ports, eg Halifax (Canada), a tethered tug aft is often employed by pilots in the indirect towing manner as an active aid to steering, or even as a brake to reduce speed over ground (SOG) while the pilot increases engine RPM to increase rudder response.

chapter_title: 202629 Collision in fog in a TSS
section_titles: 202629 Collision in fog in a TSS
202629 Collision in fog in a TSS
202629 Collision in fog in a TSS
text:
A loaded bulk carrier, Vessel A, was underway in a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) in fog, making about 7.6 kts. Visibility was about 350 m, so the Master had put in place a heightened bridge watch regime. The Master had the con, assisted by two other navigation officers, and there was a helmsperson at the wheel. Despite these precautions, the bridge team of vessel A were not aware that they were being overtaken by vessel B, behind them. Vessel B’s radar return was intermittent, and Vessel A had not plotted it as a radar target. Vessel B was not emitting an AIS signal. Neither vessel was sounding the one long blast every two minutes required in restricted visibility by the collision regulations.

[SECTION BREAK]

Vessel B was overtaking vessel A at full ahead, making about 11.8 kts. The bridge of vessel B was manned by a OOW and a lookout, with the helm on autopilot. The OOW of vessel B was aware of vessel A, but had not informed the Master of the reduced visibility. Vessel Traffic Services (VTS) contacted vessel A to instruct them to go to anchorage or drifting as visibility in the TSS was too low and traffic was now suspended. A few minutes later, when the Master saw that the opposite traffic lane was free, he ordered slow ahead on the engine and port helm to cross the lane to comply with the suspension order.

[SECTION BREAK]

The VTS agreed with this alteration, but the VTS operator was also ignorant of the exact position of vessel B, since there was no AIS transmission and the vessel’s radar return was intermittent.

section_titles: 202629 Collision in fog in a TSS
202629 Collision in fog in a TSS (Lessons learned)
text:
The OOW on vessel B became concerned about the developing close quarters situation and called vessel A on the VHF. Vessel A responded but there was no follow-up conversation. Within seconds the two vessels were in sight of one another. The Master of vessel A, now realising that vessel B was close behind, ordered hard to starboard to avoid a collision. On vessel B, the OOW put the helm hard to port, but a collision was now inevitable, and they struck vessel A on its port side. Damage was important on both vessels.

[SECTION BREAK]

AIS is an important watchkeeping tool but not foolproof. Overreliance on AIS targets on your radar can damage your situational awareness. ARPA and AIS are complementary systems, and in restricted visibility all contacts – whether AISequipped or not – must be tracked on radar. Speed in restricted visibility must reflect the stopping capability relative to visible range.

text: Finger trap/Stop Work Nap During planned maintenance, an engine crew member was attempting to close an under-piston inspection hatch cover on the main engine. Nearby crew saw him struggling and asked if he needed help, but he waved away their offer and continued to work alone. Although proper personal protective equipment was used, the heavy cover (28.5 kg) slipped and fell onto the victim’s hand. First aid was applied immediately, with follow-up medical treatment and monitoring, and the victim ultimately recovered.

section_titles: 202630 Stop work authority not started (Lessons learned)
text:
The company investigation found, among others, that the hazard posed by the heavy inspection cover was not identified in the risk assessment or toolbox talk. The requirement for two-person lifting was not specified. Lack of warning signage near the cover contributed to unsafe practices.

[SECTION BREAK]

Heavy covers always should be dismantled and mounted by two persons, regardless of whether crewmembers are using a chain block or not. Ideally, there should be two long studs mounted at the top position of every cover to keep it in position during dismantling/mounting. Work permits and toolbox talks should reinforce safe lifting techniques and roles to prevent solo handling. Stop Work Authority should be exercised by all crew if perceived unsafe actions are observed. Supervisory presence is crucial during potentially hazardous tasks.

text:
A tanker was preparing for departure at night, with light winds and two tugs alongside to help leave the berth. The Master and pilot had exchanged information on the manoeuvre, including the placement and use of the tugs. The plan was to use two tugs: one with a line forward near the bow and one with a line aft. The pilot expected the current to be running at about 1.9 knots from stern to bow. Given this, the plan was to have both tugs pull the vessel off the pier together, but with the aft tug pulling faster than the forward tug to open up the stern and have the current help push them off. Once the tugs had pulled the tanker far enough off the pier to allow a safe departure the tugs would be released.

[SECTION BREAK]

In his notebook and on the mooring plan diagram of the Master/pilot exchange form, the pilot wrote down the placement and names of each of the two tugs. As was his practice, he also wrote down the names and placement of each tug on a ‘radio card’, (reference card), which he would have with him on the bridge wing for quick reference. Tug DD was at the bow, with tug DC at the stern. It was discovered in the subsequent investigation that he had transposed the name of the two tugs on the radio card.

[SECTION BREAK]

At 0400, the pilot directed both tugs to push on the starboard side of the ship to hold it against the pier while the mooring lines were let go forward and aft. When all mooring lines were on deck, the pilot, using the tug’s names, ordered tug DD to pull dead slow away, followed by half away, and then ‘three-quarters away’ (meaning pull at 75% power away from the pier). He ordered tug DC to pull ‘minimum away’ (meaning to pull at minimum power away from the pier).

text: About the same time, in anticipation of the ebb current, the pilot ordered the tanker’s main propulsion to dead slow astern. As the vessel came off the berth, the pilot ordered tug DC to stop. Seconds later, the pilot radioed DD and asked the operator to be on a 90° angle to the tanker with the tug line. The operator responded that he was ‘pretty darn close’. The pilot replied, ‘You are at a 45 [degree angle] and you should be forward of the line’. Seconds afterward, the Master announced to the pilot that the ‘aft is too close’. The pilot ordered the main propulsion of the vessel stopped. The pilot then ordered tug DD to pull ‘full away’ and ordered the rudder hard to port.

Seconds later the vessel contacted the northeastern corner of the pier.

text:
The pilot asked the Master if the rudder was hard to port, which the Master confirmed. The pilot then ordered the tanker’s propulsion to dead slow ahead and asked tug DC if they were stopped. The tug operator confirmed he was. The Master asked the pilot, ‘What is going on?’ At this point, the pilot thought there had to be a miscommunication with the tugboats, but as the vessel was now coming away from the berth the tugs were released. Damage to the port side of the vessel was important while the berth was also somewhat damaged. The official investigation found, among other things, that the pilot had transposed the names of the tugs on his ‘radio card’. As such, orders intended for the tug aft were given to the tug on the bow and vice versa. The result was the bow being rapidly pulled away from the pier, causing the stern of the ship to move toward the pier in a 1.9-knot quartering current. This was contrary to the plan to pull the vessel’s stern off the pier quicker than the bow.

[SECTION BREAK]

Every member of the bridge team should have the same mental model of the manoeuvre so that an inconsistency can be detected early enough to avoid negative consequences. While the manoeuvre was understood by all, the vessel’s officers did not detect the pilot’s error in tug orders. This may have been due to the use of tug names as opposed to tug position (fore and aft) or number (tug 1, tug 2, usually from forward). Using tug names for vessel manoeuvres introduces a weak link in a multi-person operation. Everyone on the assisted vessel’s bridge must remember what tug, by its name, is where to have a correct mental model of the developing situation.

text: Fatal phosphine gas poisoning during underway fumigation A bulk carrier had been loaded with a cargo of cassava chips. Before departure, shore-based fumigators placed aluminium phosphide tablets on top of the cargo in each hold. The hatches were closed and the crew sealed the hatch coamings with tape before departure. The fumigation personnel provided a written handover to the Chief Officer, but apparently did not explain the risks associated with the fumigation to the crew.
text_with_context:
Source: mars_202632.html  ·  Chapter: 202632 Fumigation disaster

[202632 Fumigation disaster — incident_report]
Fatal phosphine gas poisoning during underway fumigation A bulk carrier had been loaded with a cargo of cassava chips. Before departure, shore-based fumigators placed aluminium phosphide tablets on top of the cargo in each hold. The hatches were closed and the crew sealed the hatch coamings with tape before departure. The fumigation personnel provided a written handover to the Chief Officer, but apparently did not explain the risks associated with the fumigation to the crew.

text:
Roughly 36 hours after departure, with the wind astern and the vessel’s speed slightly exceeding wind speed, gas escaping through the hatch and access covers began accumulating on the forward deck instead of dispersing. The accommodation air conditioning was running in recirculation mode, putting the accommodation under negative pressure. Several weathertight doors could not fully close, so contaminated air was drawn into the accommodation and recirculated through every space served by the system. The crew were unaware of these conditions.

[SECTION BREAK]

Watchkeepers in the wheelhouse, which had the highest air-change rate, fell ill first, suffering from chest tightness, nausea, vomiting, breathlessness and fatigue. Crew and even the Master initially attributed this to food poisoning or Covid-19. Repeated negative antigen tests reinforced the food-poisoning theory.

[SECTION BREAK]

As symptoms spread through the crew over several hours, no one connected the symptoms to the fumigant gas. At one point, the Master felt ill too. He asked the Chief Mate to relieve him on the bridge as he felt too weak to continue the bridge watch. When the Chief Engineer visited the Master in his cabin sometime later, he found him vomiting severely and his clothes soaked in sweat. The Chief Engineer telephoned the company’s Marine Superintendent to report that 17 crew members, including the Master, were experiencing persistent vomiting and limb weakness. The Chief Engineer and another crew stopped the vessel and anchored, awaiting search and rescue (SAR) resources. By the time the rescue services arrived at the vessel, about 12 hours after the Master had started to feel unwell, he had passed away. In all, thirteen of the 21 crew died from illness. Forensic findings confirmed toxic pulmonary oedema consistent with phosphine poisoning.

[SECTION BREAK]

The investigation subsequently found, among other things, that the vessel’s crew were not familiar with the IMO’s Recommendations on the Safe Use of Pesticides on Board Ships. Also, the vessel was not equipped with phosphine gas detection equipment, nor did the crew conduct safety inspections or concentration monitoring of phosphine gas after departure.

text:
Underway fumigation with aluminium phosphide is inherently hazardous. Vessels undertaking it must carry phosphine gas detection equipment, and gas concentrations should be checked regularly throughout the voyage – not just at loading.

[SECTION BREAK]

Recirculation-mode air conditioning can pull contaminated outside air into an entire accommodation block if door and hatch seals are imperfect. The weathertight integrity of accommodation doors deserves the same attention as hatch covers. Wind direction and relative vessel speed affect whether fumigant gas escaping from holds disperses or accumulates near the accommodation. Route and speed planning after fumigation should account for this.

text: Symptoms of phosphine poisoning (nausea, vomiting, chest tightness, breathlessness) overlap with seasickness, food poisoning and viral illness. Fumigation contractors and ships’ officers should ensure the crew receive a clear safety briefing on the specific risks of the fumigant used – not just paperwork sign-off – and that warning signs are posted at treated holds. When carrying fumigated cargo, the vessel’s company should have dedicated safety management procedures for fumigation, including risk assessment, equipment provision and shore support, rather than treating it as a routine cargo operation.

text:
As edited from MAIB (UK) report 7/2018 A bulk carrier was overtaking an oil tanker in a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) at night, in good visibility. The bulk carrier, moving at over 16 knots, had already passed several slower vessels that evening and was closing on the tanker from astern. A third vessel was also ahead, and was also passing the tanker.

[SECTION BREAK]

The bulker’s bridge team – Master, OOW, and a lookout who had briefly left the bridge – had focused on each overtaking situation individually rather than maintaining long-range radar and ECDIS scanning. As the range to the tanker closed to under a mile, the bulk carrier’s Master became concerned about the tightening CPA. He asked the OOW to call the tanker on VHF to establish intentions.

[202633 Collision in a TSS — incident_report]

The bulk carrier, moving at over 16 knots, had already passed several slower vessels that evening and was closing on the tanker from astern. A third vessel was also ahead, and was also passing the tanker.

[202633 Collision in a TSS — incident_report]
The bulker’s bridge team – Master, OOW, and a lookout who had briefly left the bridge – had focused on each overtaking situation individually rather than maintaining long-range radar and ECDIS scanning. As the range to the tanker closed to under a mile, the bulk carrier’s Master became concerned about the tightening CPA. He asked the OOW to call the tanker on VHF to establish intentions.

text:
The resulting conversation, conducted in English by non-native speakers, was ambiguous and each bridge team came away with opposite understandings.

[SECTION BREAK]

The tanker’s Master believed the agreement was that they would ease slightly to port while the bulk carrier passed them to starboard. The bulk carrier’s OOW, relaying the conversation in his own language to his Master (who had not listened to the call directly), reported the opposite: that the tanker did not want to be passed to starboard. Acting on this second-hand understanding, the bulk carrier’s Master ordered a gradual series of small helm movements to port, now intending to pass down the tanker’s port side. No sound signals were made, and the manoeuvre was carried out incrementally; it went unnoticed by the tanker’s bridge team. Meanwhile, the tanker’s Master – who had been on the bridge continuously for over 14 hours and was probably fatigued – was preoccupied with a separate crossing vessel on their port bow and a narrowing turn in the TSS ahead. Believing the bulk carrier would pass safely to starboard, he ordered hard-to-port to begin a full round turn to increase his sea room with the crossing vessel. Unfortunately, a visual check astern and a sound signal were not made before the turn began. Only when the tanker’s lookout spotted the bulk carrier close on the port quarter did the bridge team realised the danger. Both vessels attempted last-minute avoiding action, but with neither team understanding the other’s intentions, a collision ensued. Both vessels sustained significant structural damage but there were no injuries or pollution.

[SECTION BREAK]

VHF is not a substitute for compliance with the Collision Regulations.

[SECTION BREAK]

It should only be used, if at all, early enough to allow a resolved, unambiguous plan to be established – not as a late-stage fix for a closing CPA. If the officer with the con delegates a VHF exchange to another, they should listen to it directly rather than relying on a second-hand summary, particularly where a language relay is also involved. Unambiguous course alterations should be made decisively, not through a gradual series of small helm orders. Before any large alteration of course, always check for traffic in the direction you are about to swing into – including astern. The Collision Regulations require long-range scanning, not just short-range collision avoidance. This would in this case have allowed earlier, larger, and less ambiguous action.

The Collision Regulations require long-range scanning, not just short-range collision avoidance. This would in this case have allowed earlier, larger, and less ambiguous action.

[202634 Twisted ship — incident_report]
A six-hold panamax bulk carrier had loaded a full cargo of iron ore, but crew were unable to close three ...

text:
... of the forward hatch covers. Each hold had two hinged hatch-panels forward and two hinged panels aft. The hatch covers were of the standard McGregor type hydraulically operated sliding panels. As the hatch covers were being closed the leading rollers tended to skew off the guiding trackway in the hatch coaming, unable to roll further. The hatchway was no longer a rectangle but had become a parallelogram, whereas the hatch panels remained undistorted.

[SECTION BREAK]

It was suspected that the vessel had slightly ‘twisted’. This was established by taking freeboard measurements at various points on both sides of the vessel. The readings clearly confirmed the torsional twist of the vessel. Diagonal measurements of the hatch coamings also confirmed twisting of the vessel. The three aft holds were re-opened and an inspection of the cargo stow showed that iron ore in these three holds was slightly to starboard of centreline, whereas the cargo in the forward three holds was slightly to port of centreline. Bulldozers were used to level the cargo in each hold and diagonal measurements were periodically taken to ascertain if levelling the cargo was having the desired results. Finally, the torsion of the vessel was corrected, and the hatch covers were successfully closed.

[SECTION BREAK]

The vessel had broader than normal hatch squares, being a combination bulk/container type, thus more susceptible to torsional forces. Even a slightly uneven distribution of heavy cargo was sufficient to twist the vessel so that some hatches could not be closed. Manuals usually mention maximum trim and heel conditions but a note on the need for proper cargo trimming/ballasting the vessel to avoid coaming deflections during loading is equally useful. When making the loading/discharge plan, consider the potential need to close hatch covers at any time, for example if it rains. Continuous proper distribution of heavy cargo is a good practice to avoid nefarious twisting effects.

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: Responding To A SECURITE Message About A SAR Area
text: On hearing a SECURITE broadcast asking vessels to keep clear of a search-and-rescue area, note the position and extent of the area, plot it on the chart, and adjust the passage plan to stay well clear, typically at least two nautical miles unless the message states otherwise. Reduce speed, post an extra lookout, and if the new track will pass close regardless, call the station that issued the SECURITE to confirm safe passage: "MRCC, MRCC, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING CONFIRMATION SAFE TO PASS TWO MILES SOUTH OF THE REPORTED SAR AREA, OVER."

section_titles: Diverting Course After A SECURITE Hazard Warning
text: On receiving a SECURITE warning about a hazard in your planned route, such as a drifting container, plot the hazard's reported position on the chart, calculate a safe passing distance of at least two nautical miles, plan the new course, and inform the crew before altering course. No special proword is needed to acknowledge a SECURITE broadcast unless a direct reply is required; the appropriate response is usually simply to act on the information and to log it.

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: Repeating A MAYDAY Call After No Response
text: If no acknowledgement is heard, repeat the full MAYDAY call unchanged after about four minutes: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, SEA OTTER, MAYDAY SEA OTTER, POSITION FIFE ZERO DECIMAL WUN TOO NORTH, ZERO ZERO WUN DECIMAL FOWER FIFE WEST, TAKING ON WATER, FOWER PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." This four-minute repeat interval is a different step from the roughly fifteen-second wait between sending a DSC distress alert and starting the voice MAYDAY that follows it — the two numbers cover different parts of the sequence and should not be confused with each other. If there is still no answer after several repeated attempts, some DSC sets automatically retransmit the DSC distress alert; the operator should also try switching to Channel 70 briefly to confirm the DSC alert itself was sent, then return to Channel 16 to keep repeating the voice MAYDAY.

text: When the MRCC (Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre) asks for a repeat of essential facts, respond promptly and slowly, digit by digit for anything numerical, and do not paraphrase: "THIS IS SEA OTTER, MY POSITION IS FIFE ZERO DEGREES WUN TOO DECIMAL FIFE MINUTES NORTH, ZERO ZERO WUN DEGREES FOWER FIFE DECIMAL TREE MINUTES WEST, PERSONS ON BOARD FIFE INCLUDING WUN INJURED, OVER."

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: Responding To A Request For Continuous Situation Updates
text:
When an MRCC requests continuous updates at defined intervals, acknowledge and follow a fixed schedule, for example every fifteen minutes on the working channel, and use a consistent structure each time: "MRCC, THIS IS SEA OTTER, UPDATE, POSITION FIFE ZERO DECIMAL WUN TOO NORTH ZERO ZERO WUN DECIMAL FOWER FIFE WEST, CONDITION NO CHANGE, NEXT UPDATE IN WUN FIFE MINUTES, OVER." If conditions worsen between scheduled updates, call immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

A Full Escalation Sequence: Safety To Urgency To Medical Distress

A single developing situation can move through all three safety levels in sequence, and each stage needs its own correctly formatted call. First, a SECURITE warning is sent when a hazard is merely sighted: "SECURITE, SECURITE, SECURITE, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, HEAVY WEATHER DEVELOPING IN AREA, OUT." If the engine then fails and the vessel begins drifting seriously, this escalates to an urgency call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TOTAL LOSS OF PROPULSION, DRIFTING TOWARDS ROCKS, REQUESTING TOW, OVER." If a crew member is then injured and needs medical guidance, this becomes a PAN PAN MEDICO call, still using the PAN PAN urgency signal but specifically requesting medical advice rather than a general tow: "PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, PAN PAN MEDICO, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, REQUESTING MEDICAL ADVICE FOR A CREW MEMBER WITH A SUSPECTED FRACTURE, OVER." If the vessel then genuinely starts taking on water and lives are in immediate danger, this escalates a final time to a full MAYDAY: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, TAKING ON WATER, FOUR PERSONS ON BOARD, REQUIRE IMMEDIATE ASSISTANCE, OVER." The key discipline is to always use the signal that matches the actual current severity of the situation, escalating (or de-escalating, once resolved) as conditions change, rather than jumping straight to MAYDAY for a situation that is not yet grave and imminent, or staying at a lower level once it genuinely becomes one.

When Not To Escalate Straight To MAYDAY

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: Responding To A Request For Continuous Situation Updates
text: A vessel that is simply not under command, disabled, or requesting routine assistance is not automatically a MAYDAY situation; only grave and imminent danger to life justifies MAYDAY. For a vessel not under command but in no immediate danger, the correct call is a routine or, at most, a PAN PAN urgency call describing the situation and requesting assistance, not a distress call: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, SILENT WAVE, NOT UNDER COMMAND, DRIFTING, NO IMMEDIATE DANGER, REQUESTING A TOW, OVER." Sending an unwarranted MAYDAY diverts search-and-rescue resources from genuine emergencies and can result in the escalation being downgraded or disregarded by responding stations.

chapter_title: Securite, Mayday Repetition And Safety Escalation Sequences
section_titles: De-Escalating Once A Situation Is Resolved
text: Once the original danger has passed, whichever level was declared should be formally cancelled so other stations stop diverting attention or resources to it. For a resolved urgency situation: "ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, PAN PAN CANCEL, ASSISTANCE NO LONGER REQUIRED, OUT." For a resolved distress situation, the same pattern is used with MAYDAY: "ALL STATIONS, THIS IS OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, OCEAN VOYAGER, MAYDAY CANCEL, VESSEL SAFE, NO FURTHER ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OUT."

text:
[Part A - General | Rule 1: Application]
These rules apply anywhere you're operating on open water, plus any connected water a seagoing vessel could reach. A local authority can add stricter local rules for a harbour, river, or lake, but those can't contradict these rules — only tighten them.
Examples:
  1. Own-ship transits from open sea into a harbour approach: the same COLREG rules keep applying, plus whatever local traffic rules the port authority has layered on top.

text:
[Part A - General | Rule 2: Responsibility / good seamanship]
Following the letter of these rules doesn't excuse bad judgement. If ordinary prudent seamanship — or the specific circumstances — called for something extra, you're still on the hook for not doing it. And if departing from the rules is the only way to avoid an immediate danger, you're allowed to.
Examples:
  1. Own-ship technically has right of way, but a nearby vessel is clearly not maneuvering predictably (erratic heading changes, no response to hails) — Rule 2 expects own-ship to increase caution beyond the bare minimum the geometry alone would require.

text:
[Part A - General | Rule 3: Key definitions]
A few terms recur constantly in situation reports and need precise meaning: 'power-driven vessel' = under engine; 'sailing vessel' = under sail with engine off; 'underway' = not anchored, moored, or aground; 'vessels in sight of one another' = each can actually be seen, not just detected on radar/AIS; 'restricted visibility' = fog, heavy rain, or anything similarly reducing sight.
Examples:
  1. A contact is detected at 8000 m by AIS but visibility is 400 m due to fog — the two vessels are NOT 'in sight of one another' yet, even though own-ship has full positional data on the contact.

text:
[Section I - Any Visibility | Rule 5: Look-out]
Keep watching and listening at all times, using every tool available (radar, AIS, binoculars, hydrophone) — not just one sensor. The goal is a full, current picture of the situation and whether risk of collision exists.
Examples:
  1. Own-ship's AIS shows no nearby contacts, but a small unlit vessel without AIS could still be present — Rule 5 means own-ship can't treat 'AIS is empty' as equivalent to 'area is clear'.

text:
[Section I - Any Visibility | Rule 6: Safe speed]
Your speed has to let you stop or maneuver in time given the conditions — visibility, traffic density, your own stopping distance and turning ability, sea state, and (if you have radar) its range-scale limitations and how well it's actually detecting small or distant contacts right now.
Examples:
  1. Own-ship is doing 15 kt in an area with six other AIS contacts inside a 3 km radius and visibility dropping to 1500 m — even with no single contact yet showing high risk, Rule 6 argues for reducing speed given the traffic density and shrinking visibility together.

text:
[Section I - Any Visibility | Rule 7: Determining risk of collision]
Use everything available to work out whether risk of collision exists, and if there's any doubt, treat it as if the risk exists. A steady compass bearing on an approaching contact (the bearing barely changing) is the classic sign — even if the range is still opening slowly. Don't draw conclusions from a thin radar picture; a couple of scattered returns aren't enough to decide there's no risk.
Examples:
  1. Contact bearing holds at 047 +/- 1 deg over three successive readings while range closes from 4000 m to 3200 m — bearing isn't changing, so risk of collision should be treated as real even though 3200 m still feels comfortable.

text:
[Section I - Any Visibility | Rule 8: Action to avoid collision]
Whatever you do, do it early, do it decisively, and make it big enough that another vessel watching visually or on radar can actually tell you've done something — a string of tiny course nudges is worse than one clear turn. If there's sea room, a course change alone is often better than a speed change alone. Check that your action actually opens a safe gap, not just a technically-different number. And if you need thinking time, it's fine to slow down or stop to buy it.
Examples:
  1. Own-ship nudges course by 3 deg, waits, nudges another 4 deg, waits again — this pattern is exactly what Rule 8(b) warns against; a single clear 25-30 deg alteration would be far more readable to the other vessel and far more effective.

text:
[Section I - Any Visibility | Rule 9: Narrow channels]
Inside a narrow channel or fairway, keep to the outer edge on your own starboard side if it's safe to do so — don't hug the centre or the wrong side. Small craft and sailing vessels must not get in the way of a large vessel that can only safely navigate within the channel. Don't cross a channel if it would force a channel-bound vessel to react to you. Overtaking inside a channel needs a whistle-signal exchange first. And avoid anchoring in the channel altogether if you can help it.
Examples:
  1. A 12 m sailing yacht wants to cross a dredged channel while a 200 m bulk carrier is transiting it and physically cannot leave the channel to avoid the yacht — the yacht must wait, regardless of who'd normally have right of way in open water.

[Rule 9 - Narrow channels — rule]
[Section I - Any Visibility | Rule 9: Narrow channels]
Inside a narrow channel or fairway, keep to the outer edge on your own starboard side if it's safe to do so — don't hug the centre or the wrong side. Small craft and sailing vessels must not get in the way of a large vessel that can only safely navigate within the channel. Don't cross a channel if it would force a channel-bound vessel to react to you. Overtaking inside a channel needs a whistle-signal exchange first. And avoid anchoring in the channel altogether if you can help it.
Examples:
  1. A 12 m sailing yacht wants to cross a dredged channel while a 200 m bulk carrier is transiting it and physically cannot leave the channel to avoid the yacht — the yacht must wait, regardless of who'd normally have right of way in open water.

text:
[Section I - Any Visibility | Rule 10: Traffic separation schemes]
Inside a traffic separation scheme, go with the flow of that lane, stay clear of the separation zone/line as much as possible, and join or leave at a shallow angle near the ends of the lane rather than cutting across. If you must cross the whole scheme, cross as close to a right angle as you can, as quickly as possible — don't loiter in it.
Examples:
  1. Own-ship needs to cross a TSS to reach a berth on the far side — instead of angling diagonally across (spending more time inside the lanes than necessary), own-ship should turn onto a heading close to 90 deg from the lane's general traffic direction for the crossing itself.

text:
[Section II - In Sight | Rule 12: Sailing vessels meeting]
Between two sailing vessels: if the wind is on different sides for each, the one with wind on the port side keeps clear. If the wind is on the same side for both, whichever is upwind keeps clear of the one downwind. If you can't tell which side the wind is on for the other vessel, assume you're the one who has to keep clear.
Examples:
  1. Two sailboats converging, own-ship on a port tack (wind over the port side), the other on a starboard tack — own-ship is the one required to keep clear, regardless of which vessel reaches the crossing point first.

text:
[Section II - In Sight | Rule 13: Overtaking]
This one overrides every other steering rule in this section: whoever is overtaking must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken, full stop, no matter what category either vessel normally falls into. You're overtaking if you're coming up on someone from more than 22.5 deg abaft their beam — close enough that at night you'd only see their sternlight, not either sidelight. If it's genuinely unclear whether you're overtaking or crossing, assume overtaking. And once you're the overtaking vessel, you stay the overtaking vessel — a later bearing shift doesn't hand the obligation back.
Examples:
  1. Own-ship, doing 9 kt, is closing on a slower fishing vessel doing 4 kt dead ahead, from a position well behind its beam — even though fishing vessels normally rank above power-driven vessels in the general hierarchy, own-ship as the overtaking vessel still must keep clear here, not the other way around.
